0.title: The Word That Outlasts the Kings
0.overview:
The message. Second Kings tells how God’s people lost everything, and why. For three centuries the LORD showed them mercy after mercy and warned them “by every prophet and every seer” (17:13), “but they would not listen” (17:14). So the northern kingdom fell to Assyria, and then Judah to Babylon; the temple was burned and the king of David’s line was led away. Yet every word God spoke, of mercy or of judgment, came true. And because he had promised David “to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (8:19), the book ends not in the ashes but with David’s heir alive at a king’s table in Babylon: the promise not yet fulfilled, and not cancelled.

Background: the writer. Kings was one book in the Hebrew Bible, so 2 Kings begins in the middle of the story, soon after the death of Ahab. The author is not named. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, said that Jeremiah wrote it, and its last chapters reappear almost word for word in Jeremiah 52; but the book was finished after Jehoiachin’s release from prison, about 561 BC (25:27), so if Jeremiah had a hand in it, someone else completed it. The writer drew on records he names, the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel and of Judah (1:18; 8:23). Many scholars see Kings as the end of one long history from Deuteronomy onward, edited in stages up to the exile. This commentary agrees that it took its final shape in the exile, from older and trustworthy sources, and reads it as true history told from the prophets’ point of view.

When and where. The book runs from about 850 BC to about 561 BC. Two small kingdoms share the land: Israel in the north, ruled from Samaria, and Judah in the south, ruled by David’s line from Jerusalem. First the Arameans of Damascus (Syria in the ESV) press on Israel; then the empires come. Assyria carries off Galilee (15:29) and captures Samaria in 722 BC. In 701 BC Sennacherib overruns Judah; his own annals boast that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, but never claim that he took the city. Babylon replaces Assyria. Nebuchadnezzar takes King Jehoiachin and ten thousand captives in 597 BC, and burns Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC (587 on some reckonings). Ration lists from his palace list rations for Jehoiachin, king of Judah.

The kind of writing. This is narrative history, but history with a verdict. Each reign is framed the same way: when the king began, how long he reigned, and whether he did right or evil in the sight of the LORD. Judah’s kings are measured against David; Israel’s are almost all said to have kept “the sins of Jeroboam” (10:31), his golden calves. (See Kings of Israel and Judah, and on the dates, the introduction to 1 Kings.) Watch for the phrase “according to the word of the LORD” (4:44): again and again a prophecy is spoken and later fulfilled, once three centuries later, when Josiah does at Bethel what a prophet had foretold by name (1 Kings 13:2; 2 Kings 23:15–16).

How the book makes its case. First comes the prophet [1–8]. Elijah is taken up by a whirlwind (chapter 2), and Elisha, given a double portion of his spirit, fills these chapters with mercies: a widow’s oil, a dead boy given back to his mother, twenty loaves feeding a hundred men, the Syrian general Naaman washed clean in the Jordan, and a frightened servant shown that “those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (6:16). Then the north runs down [9–17]. Jehu wipes out Ahab’s house and the worship of Baal but keeps the calves; in Judah, Athaliah nearly destroys David’s line, and one child is hidden in the temple and saved (chapter 11). After a last prosperity under Jeroboam II, foretold by Jonah (14:25), murdered kings follow in quick succession, until Samaria falls and the writer stops to preach: “this occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God” (17:7). Then Judah stands alone [18–25]. Hezekiah “trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel” (18:5), and, as Isaiah promised, Jerusalem is spared in a single night (chapter 19). His son Manasseh undoes it all and fills the city with innocent blood (chapter 21). Josiah hears the rediscovered Book of the Law and leads the greatest reform in Judah’s history, yet “still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great wrath” (23:26). Within twenty-three years of his death Jerusalem lies in ruins. Four quiet verses about Jehoiachin’s release (25:27–30) are placed last, on purpose.

Two hard questions. Readers stumble over the youths mauled by bears (2:23–24) and Jehu’s bloodshed (chapters 9–10). The jeering crowd came out of Bethel, the town of the golden calf, and told the new prophet to “go up” as his master had; Elisha pronounced a curse the covenant had already named (Leviticus 26:22), and left the outcome to God. It gives no licence to curse anyone: when James and John wanted fire from heaven, Jesus “turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55). Jehu was commissioned to end Ahab’s house, and God commended it (10:30); yet a century later he said through Hosea, “I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel” (Hosea 1:4). Being used by God is not being approved in every act. The second question is Josiah’s book (22:8). Many scholars hold that it was Deuteronomy, newly written and “found” to support his reform. But it was recognised at once as the law of Moses, and Josiah tore his clothes “because our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book” (22:13), which fits an old book neglected through Manasseh’s long reign. This commentary’s view is that Moses wrote Deuteronomy in substance, and that 2 Kings records a law recovered, not composed.

Where it leads: to Christ. Second Kings leads to Christ first by the need it exposes. Even the best kings could not save their people. Josiah turned to the LORD “with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might” (23:25), and the judgment still came. The people needed a king who could bear that wrath himself, and Jesus did. It leads also by promise. For David’s sake the line survives Athaliah’s massacre and Babylon’s prison, and Matthew’s genealogy runs through Jehoiachin, whom he calls Jechoniah, “after the deportation to Babylon” (Matthew 1:12), to Jesus, to whom “the Lord God will give … the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). And it leads by pattern: Elisha’s ministry of mercy is a sketch of Christ’s. Jesus himself pointed to Naaman (Luke 4:27). Not far from Shunem he gave a widow back her son, and the crowd cried, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” (Luke 7:16). He fed five thousand from “five barley loaves”, with baskets left over (John 6:9, 13). Elisha’s name means “God saves”; Jesus was so named because “he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

For us. Second Kings warns that a church can keep its religion running smoothly while its Bible lies lost in the building. It shows that God’s patience is long but not endless, and that his word never fails. It shows what to do with a threat: Hezekiah took the letter and “spread it before the LORD” (19:14). And it teaches us to put our final hope in no leader, however good, but in the Son of David, in whom “all the promises of God find their Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The lamp that flickered in Babylon was never put out. He is the King who will not fail.

1.title: Ahaziah and the God of Ekron
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel.<sup>2</sup>Now Ahaziah fell through the lattice in his upper chamber in Samaria, and lay sick; so he sent messengers, telling them, "Go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this sickness."<sup>3</sup>But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, "Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say to them, 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?<sup>4</sup>Now therefore thus says the LORD, You shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" So Elijah went.<sup>5</sup>The messengers returned to the king, and he said to them, "Why have you returned?"<sup>6</sup>And they said to him, "There came a man to meet us, and said to us, 'Go back to the king who sent you, and say to him, Thus says the LORD, Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'"<sup>7</sup>He said to them, "What kind of man was he who came to meet you and told you these things?"<sup>8</sup>They answered him, "He wore a garment of hair, with a belt of leather about his waist." And he said, "It is Elijah the Tishbite."<sup>9</sup>Then the king sent to him a captain of fifty men with his fifty. He went up to Elijah, who was sitting on the top of a hill, and said to him, "O man of God, the king says, 'Come down.'"<sup>10</sup>But Elijah answered the captain of fifty, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty.<sup>11</sup>Again the king sent to him another captain of fifty men with his fifty. And he answered and said to him, "O man of God, this is the king's order, 'Come down quickly!'"<sup>12</sup>But Elijah answered them, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty.<sup>13</sup>Again the king sent the captain of a third fifty with his fifty. And the third captain of fifty went up and came and fell on his knees before Elijah and entreated him, "O man of God, please let my life, and the life of these fifty servants of yours, be precious in your sight.<sup>14</sup>Behold, fire came down from heaven and consumed the two former captains of fifty men with their fifties, but now let my life be precious in your sight."<sup>15</sup>Then the angel of the LORD said to Elijah, "Go down with him; do not be afraid of him." So he arose and went down with him to the king<sup>16</sup>and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron—is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word?—therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'"<sup>17</sup>So he died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. Jehoram became king in his place in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son.<sup>18</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Ahaziah that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
1.overview:
Where we are. Second Kings opens in the middle of the story, because Kings was once one book (see the introduction). Ahab has just died in battle, as Micaiah foretold (1 Kings 22), and his son Ahaziah, who served Baal as his father and mother had, sits on Israel’s throne in Samaria. Elijah is near the end of his ministry.

The message. There is a God in Israel, and he will not be ignored. A frightened king sends past the living God to ask a Philistine idol whether he will live, and God’s word reaches him first: on the road, on the hilltop and at last at his bedside. That word cannot be arrested or outrun. It judges those who give it orders and spares those who come to it on their knees.

Why it was said. The first readers had lost land, temple and king because Israel had done what Ahaziah did, looking everywhere for help except to the LORD (see the introduction); the word that judged them was still the word they could trust.

How the chapter makes its case. Moab breaks away and the king falls through the lattice of his upper room; he sends to Baal-zebub of Ekron, but Elijah meets the messengers with the LORD’s question and sentence, and the king knows him by his clothes (vv. 1–8). Two captains climb the hill with fifty men each to order the man of God down, and fire from heaven consumes them; a third comes on his knees, asks for mercy, and lives (vv. 9–15). Elijah goes down and tells the king the same word to his face, the king dies “according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken”, and his brother Jehoram reigns (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by the character of God it reveals, and by pattern. The king’s question was answered in full when God himself came into Israel: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Elijah’s clothes reappear on John the Baptist, the forerunner of that coming (Matthew 3:4; 11:14). And when James and John wanted to call down fire as Elijah had, Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55), because he had come to save and would bear the judgment himself. The third captain’s way, asking rather than ordering, is the way every sinner comes to Christ, and he turns none away (John 6:37).

For us. Few people deny God; many consult him last. When fear comes, where does your first enquiry go? In Christ the God of Israel is your Father, and you may bring him that fear before anyone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Is There No God in Israel?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The question that runs through the chapter is asked here first: is there no God in Israel? As soon as Ahab dies, Moab rebels (v. 1), and his son Ahaziah falls through the lattice of his upper room and lies injured. What he does next reveals his heart: he sends to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Philistine Ekron, whether he will recover (v. 2). The angel of the LORD sends Elijah to meet the messengers on the road with the LORD’s question and his sentence: the king will not rise from his bed (vv. 3–4). The messengers turn back and repeat it word for word, and Ahaziah knows the prophet from his clothes alone (vv. 5–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The question asked three times (vv. 3, 6, 16) is not "why are you consulting an idol?" but is it because there is no God in Israel. It assumes the thing the king has managed to forget.
verseByVerse.examples: Elijah's clothes become a kind of uniform, recognised by a king who had never met him, and worn again eight centuries later (see the note on v. 8).

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel. Now Ahaziah fell through the lattice in his upper chamber in Samaria, and lay sick; so he sent messengers, telling them, "Go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this sickness." But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, "Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say to them, 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Now therefore thus says the LORD, You shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" So Elijah went. The messengers returned to the king, and he said to them, "Why have you returned?" And they said to him, "There came a man to meet us, and said to us, 'Go back to the king who sent you, and say to him, Thus says the LORD, Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" He said to them, "What kind of man was he who came to meet you and told you these things?" They answered him, "He wore a garment of hair, with a belt of leather about his waist." And he said, "It is Elijah the Tishbite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab’s son, injured and afraid, sends past the living God to ask a Philistine idol whether he will live, and God answers first, with a question and a death sentence. His sin is not only consulting an idol but forgetting that there is a God in Israel at all.

Moab rebelled against Israel. Moab, east of the Dead Sea, had been paying Israel an enormous tribute, a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams (3:4). The moment Ahab is buried, it stops; the writer returns to it in chapter 3. We happen to have the other side: Mesha king of Moab set up a stone, the Moabite Stone, recording that Omri had humbled Moab for many days and that he had triumphed over Omri’s son (probably meaning one of his line). Two accounts of one rebellion, from opposite ends.

Fell through the lattice. A lattice was a wooden screen across an upper window, cut in a pattern to let the air through and keep out the sun and the neighbours. He leaned on it and it gave way. So the reign of Ahab’s son effectively ends: not in battle or by plague, but leaning on decorative woodwork in the palace his father built.

Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. The errand is worse than the fall. Ekron was a Philistine city about forty miles away, in a country Israel had been fighting for three centuries. He does not ask for victory or rain, only whether I shall recover: frightened about his own body, he sends past every prophet in his own kingdom to a foreign shrine. Baal-zebub is named in this chapter and nowhere else in the Old Testament, but the name lasted. Eight hundred years later, when the Pharisees wanted the worst thing they could say about Jesus, they said he cast out demons “by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Matthew 12:24; Mark 3:22). A local Philistine god ends up, under a name very close to his, as a title for Satan.

Is it because there is no God in Israel? God’s question (v. 3) is not the one we would have asked. We would ask what a Philistine god could do for him. God asks something more wounding, which assumes what the king has forgotten: there is a God in Israel, who brought the nation out of Egypt, gave them the land, and still has prophets living in it. Ahaziah has not concluded that God is unavailable. He has simply not thought of him.

The bed to which you have gone up. A grim play on words: you went up to that bed; you will not come down from it. Within a few verses the king will be sending soldiers up a hill to order Elijah to come down.

Why have you returned? The messengers are back far too soon; they cannot have been to Ekron. They repeat the message word for word, question and all. Whoever he was, they did not think of arguing.

He wore a garment of hair. They do not know his name; they describe his clothes, and the king names him at once. That is the measure of what Elijah had been to that family. Ahaziah had never met him, so far as we are told, but his father had hunted him through every kingdom in the region and called him “my enemy” (1 Kings 18:10; 21:20), and the son knows him from a description of what he wears.

A uniform for John the Baptist. Keep the description, because it becomes a uniform. Eight centuries later a man came out of the wilderness by the Jordan wearing “a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist” (Matthew 3:4), and told a king to his face what God thought of his marriage. Malachi had closed the prophets with the promise, “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes” (Malachi 4:5), and Jesus said of John, “if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14).

The forgetting runs one way. The surprise of the gospel is that we forgot God, but he did not forget us. He sent his word down the road to a king who had not asked for it, and at last sent his Son into a world that had stopped thinking of him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him” (John 1:10). He came anyway.

Forgetting is the commonest unbelief. We picture unbelief as a conclusion reached after weighing the arguments. Ahaziah never got that far: the moment he was frightened he went looking for a god, only not the one who was there. That is how faith usually fades in a comfortable society: not argued away but crowded out by schedules, screens and a hundred nearer voices, until God is not so much denied as unmentioned, and in trouble we reach for whatever is closest. So the question is aimed less at the sceptic than at the distracted, which is most of us.

In practice. Seeing a doctor is not sending to Ekron; the sin here is asking a rival god for the verdict on one’s life. But the question still searches a believer who is frightened about his body: whom do I ask first, and whose word do I trust about my future? A child of God can bring that fear to his Father before anyone else, call for the elders of the church when the illness is serious (James 5:14), and take every other help, the doctor’s included, as coming from his hand.

Uncertain wording. Baal-zebub means lord of the flies, but what the name meant to those who used it is not certain. It may have been a real title, for a god thought to send or drive away the flies that spread disease, which would suit a sick man’s enquiry. Many scholars think it more likely that Israel mockingly altered Baal-zebul, Baal the prince, a title known from Canaanite texts, into lord of the flies; the New Testament form Beelzebul seems to preserve the older title.
verseByVerse.note: Baal-zebub means “lord of the flies,” probably a mocking twist of Baal-zebul, “Baal the prince.” Ekron was a Philistine city.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — If I Am a Man of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king answers God’s word with soldiers, and the hill shows two ways of approaching God side by side. A captain with fifty men climbs to where Elijah sits and, in the king’s name, orders the man of God to come down (v. 9). Elijah answers with a condition, not a curse: if I am a man of God, let fire fall; and it does (v. 10). A second captain brings the same order, made more urgent, and meets the same end (vv. 11–12). The third comes on his knees, calls his men Elijah’s servants and asks for their lives (vv. 13–14). The angel of the LORD tells Elijah not to fear, and he goes down with him (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: What is being attempted on that hill is the arrest of the word of God, and Elijah's answer puts the office itself to the test: if I am what he called me, let heaven say so.
verseByVerse.examples: The third captain is the reason the chapter is not simply terrible: he comes up on his knees and asks, and every one of his men walks back down.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent to him a captain of fifty men with his fifty. He went up to Elijah, who was sitting on the top of a hill, and said to him, "O man of God, the king says, 'Come down.'" But Elijah answered the captain of fifty, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty. Again the king sent to him another captain of fifty men with his fifty. And he answered and said to him, "O man of God, this is the king's order, 'Come down quickly!'" But Elijah answered them, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty. Again the king sent the captain of a third fifty with his fifty. And the third captain of fifty went up and came and fell on his knees before Elijah and entreated him, "O man of God, please let my life, and the life of these fifty servants of yours, be precious in your sight. Behold, fire came down from heaven and consumed the two former captains of fifty men with their fifties, but now let my life be precious in your sight." Then the angel of the LORD said to Elijah, "Go down with him; do not be afraid of him." So he arose and went down with him to the king
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king tries to arrest the word of God with soldiers, and God judges the two captains who order his prophet about, while sparing the one who comes on his knees to ask for mercy. The passage is not about a prophet with a temper but about two ways of coming to God.

A captain of fifty men with his fifty. This is not a messenger but an arrest party: fifty armed men sent up a hill to bring in a prophet who has just delivered a word from the LORD, as the state had once shut Micaiah in a cell for the same offence (1 Kings 22:26–27). The captain’s sentence is a small masterpiece of insolence. He uses the title, O man of God, and in the same breath overrides it: the king says. He acknowledges the office and gives it orders.

If I am a man of God. Everything turns on if. Elijah does not curse them. He takes the title the captain has just used and puts it to the test before fifty witnesses: if that is what I am, let heaven say so. It is Carmel again in a new place (1 Kings 18:36–38). There the fire settled who God is; here it settles whose man this is, and the answer comes from the same sky.

Come down quickly! The king has just lost fifty-one men, and he sends fifty-one more with the word quickly added. He knows what happened on the hill, and all he changes is the urgency. That shows what kind of man he is.

Fell on his knees before Elijah. The third man has the same commission, the same fifty soldiers and the same hill, and he has watched a hundred and two men die on it. He goes up anyway, and at the top he does not deliver the order at all. He kneels, calls himself and his men your servants, and asks; and every one of them walks back down alive. The chapter distinguishes with great precision between men on an identical errand: two came to give orders to God’s prophet, and one came to ask him for mercy.

Do not be afraid of him. God finds it necessary to tell the man who has twice called fire out of heaven that he need not fear a junior officer. The reader has seen this before: Elijah faced four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and then ran from a messenger (1 Kings 19:2–3). Spiritual authority plainly does not come with steady nerves attached. God does not rebuke him for it; he tells him it is safe, and he goes.

But he turned and rebuked them. The New Testament settles what a Christian may do with this passage. When a Samaritan village would not receive Jesus, James and John asked, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” “But he turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:54–55). They had the precedent exactly right and had missed the change of era entirely. The fire on that hill fell on soldiers sent to silence a prophet, under a covenant with a nation, before the Son of God came into the world; and the two disciples who wanted to repeat it were standing beside the one man who could have done it and had come to do the opposite. No Christian may use this chapter to wish fire on those who oppose him. Every sinner who comes to Jesus as the third captain came, asking rather than ordering, finds his life precious in his sight: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Was it fair to burn soldiers who were only obeying orders? These men were not bystanders: they came armed to seize the LORD’s prophet for a king already under God’s sentence, and their captains spoke for that king with open contempt. Elijah threw no fire; he left the verdict to God, and God gave it. The judgment was severe, as judgment in Scripture is, but it was also limited: the captain who came humbly was spared at once, with all his men. And the judgment did not have the last word. Jesus would not repeat it, and in the end he bore the judgment of sinners himself, praying for the men who came against him (Luke 23:34; 1 Peter 2:24).

Textual note. Some manuscripts of Luke 9:54 add “as Elijah did”, which is certainly what the disciples had in mind. Some later manuscripts of Luke 9:55 also add Jesus’ words, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of, familiar from the King James Version; most modern translations put both additions in a footnote.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — According to the Word of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word that could not be arrested is spoken a third time, now to the king’s face, and it comes true. Elijah, who would not come down at a king’s order, goes down freely at God’s, and in the sickroom repeats the question and the sentence without softening either (v. 16). Ahaziah dies “according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken”, the refrain of the whole book. Having no son, he is succeeded by his brother Jehoram, while another Jehoram rules in Judah (v. 17), and the writer closes the record of a two-year reign remembered for a question it never answered (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet who would not come down when fifty soldiers required it walks down freely when God says go.
verseByVerse.examples: From here two kings named Jehoram reign at once, one in each kingdom; the note on vv. 17-18 sorts them out.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron—is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word?—therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.'" So he died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. Jehoram became king in his place in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son. Now the rest of the acts of Ahaziah that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah tells the dying king God’s word to his face, and it comes true exactly; the throne passes to his brother Jehoram. The word that could not be arrested on the hill cannot be escaped in the sickroom.

Thus says the LORD. The third time, Elijah says it in the man’s own room, standing over a dying king who has twice tried to have him arrested: exactly what he said on the road, with no bedside softening and no gloating. The third telling adds to inquire of his word. That is what had been available all along: not an oracle from a shrine, but the word of the LORD, which had been coming into that palace for two generations and had never once been wrong.

A quiet mercy. The king could have died without seeing him. God sends the prophet into the room, so that Ahaziah is told the truth to the last by a living man standing in front of him.

According to the word of the LORD. This is the refrain of these books (see the introduction), and here it closes a reign of two years that began by walking “in the way of his father and in the way of his mother” (1 Kings 22:52).

Two kings called Jehoram. Ahaziah has no son, so the throne of Israel passes to his brother Jehoram (also called Joram), another son of Ahab and Jezebel. At the same time the throne of Judah is held, or shortly will be, by a different Jehoram, the son of Jehoshaphat. And they are family. Jehoshaphat made a marriage alliance with Ahab (2 Chronicles 18:1), and his son married Ahab’s daughter Athaliah (8:18), so the two Jehorams are brothers-in-law. That is why they will campaign together; why Judah’s next king will be visiting when Jehu comes for the house of Ahab, and will die with them; and why Athaliah will then be in a position to try to destroy the royal family of David (chapters 9 and 11).

The rest of the acts of Ahaziah. The file is closed on a two-year reign, and what remains is a question asked three times to a court that never answered it. There was a God in Israel, with a prophet on a hill within reach of the palace, and the king sent forty miles the other way to ask a Philistine god whether he would get better.

The God who came near. The question was finally answered not by a prophet on a hill but by God himself coming into Israel. The Word that reached Ahaziah through Elijah “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), walked into sickrooms himself, and told a frightened father, “Do not fear, only believe” (Mark 5:36). No one now needs to send to Ekron. We have been told whom to ask.

Why do the reign lengths and dates not seem to add up? Israel and Judah counted reigns differently at different times: one counted the year a king came to the throne as his first year, the other did not; and sons often reigned alongside their fathers as co-regents, with the overlapping years counted to both. When these practices are allowed for, the dates largely fit together, as Edwin Thiele argued in detail, and match Assyrian records at key points (see Kings of Israel and Judah). This chapter shows the method at work: verse 17 dates Jehoram of Israel’s accession to the second year of Jehoram of Judah, while 3:1 dates it to the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat, which fits if Jehoshaphat had already made his son co-regent, as 8:16 also suggests.

1.theology:
The question, three times (vv. 3, 6, 16). The question takes for granted that there is a God in Israel. The king has not denied him, only forgotten him. That is the ordinary form the sin takes, then and now: we do not abandon God, we ask everyone else first.

The uniform (v. 8). Malachi promised Elijah before the day of the LORD, and when John the Baptist appeared at the Jordan in the same clothes, the crowds could read the sign.

If I am a man of God (v. 10). Elijah does not curse. He takes the title the captain used, man of God, and asks God to show whether it is true. Carmel settled who God is; this settles whose man this is.

The third captain (v. 13). Identical orders, identical fifty men, identical hill, and he kneels and asks, and they all live. What sets him apart is not his rank or his orders but his humility.

And Luke 9:54. James and John proposed to do this to a Samaritan village and were rebuked for it: they remembered the precedent correctly and missed that with Jesus the day of mercy had come. Every sinner who comes to Jesus as the third captain came, asking rather than ordering, finds his life precious in his sight (John 6:37).
1.examples:
Then: A king lay in the bed he could not get out of and sent runners forty miles past every prophet in his own country to ask a Philistine shrine whether he was going to live.

Now: Two things. First, the question fits us exactly as it stands. When the scan result is pending, or you cannot sleep for what you are frightened of, where does the first enquiry go? Very few people are tempted to abandon God. A great many consult him fourth. Yet the God who asks is there no God in Israel? is the one who has already made us his own in Christ, and his Spirit in us cries Abba! Father! (Romans 8:15), so the first enquiry is a child's right, not a test to pass. Second, the third captain, the most encouraging man on the hill. He was not braver than the other two and not on a better errand. He came up asking instead of ordering, and that was the whole of it.

keyVerse.quote: Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?
keyVerse.note: The question is asked three times (vv. 3, 6, 16) and carries the whole chapter. It accuses the king not of denying God but of forgetting him, and it assumes what he has forgotten: there is a God in Israel, who speaks, and whose word comes true. That same God has since come to us in his Son, so that no one need send to Ekron for an answer.

1.reflection:
Ahaziah did not deny God; he simply did not think of him when he was afraid (vv. 2–3). Where do you turn first when the news is bad or the future frightening? What nearer voices crowd God out of your life?

Two captains came to give orders to the man of God, and the third came on his knees to ask (vv. 9–14). What is the difference between those two ways of approaching God, and which is closer to the way you pray?

When James and John wanted to call down fire as Elijah did, Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55). Why? What does this teach us about how Christians should treat people who reject or oppose the gospel?

Ahaziah died “according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken” (v. 17). How does the certainty of God’s word both warn us and comfort us?

2.title: Elijah Taken Up; Elisha Succeeds Him
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven by a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were on their way from Gilgal.<sup>2</sup>And Elijah said to Elisha, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me as far as Bethel." But Elisha said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they went down to Bethel.<sup>3</sup>And the sons of the prophets who were in Bethel came out to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he said, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet."<sup>4</sup>Elijah said to him, "Elisha, please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to Jericho." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they came to Jericho.<sup>5</sup>The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho drew near to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he answered, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet."<sup>6</sup>Then Elijah said to him, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to the Jordan." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So the two of them went on.<sup>7</sup>Fifty men of the sons of the prophets also went and stood at some distance from them, as they both were standing by the Jordan.<sup>8</sup>Then Elijah took his cloak and rolled it up and struck the water, and the water was parted to the one side and to the other, till the two of them could go over on dry ground.<sup>9</sup>When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, "Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you." And Elisha said, "Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me."<sup>10</sup>And he said, "You have asked a hard thing; yet, if you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you, but if you do not see me, it shall not be so."<sup>11</sup>And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.<sup>12</sup>And Elisha saw it and he cried, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!" And he saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two pieces.<sup>13</sup>And he took up the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and went back and stood on the bank of the Jordan.<sup>14</sup>Then he took the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and struck the water, saying, "Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" And when he had struck the water, the water was parted to the one side and to the other, and Elisha went over.<sup>15</sup>Now when the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho saw him opposite them, they said, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." And they came to meet him and bowed to the ground before him.<sup>16</sup>And they said to him, "Behold now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. It may be that the Spirit of the LORD has caught him up and cast him upon some mountain or into some valley." And he said, "You shall not send."<sup>17</sup>But when they urged him till he was ashamed, he said, "Send." They sent therefore fifty men. And for three days they sought him but did not find him.<sup>18</sup>And they came back to him while he was staying at Jericho, and he said to them, "Did I not say to you, 'Do not go'?"<sup>19</sup>Now the men of the city said to Elisha, "Behold, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord sees, but the water is bad, and the land is unfruitful."<sup>20</sup>He said, "Bring me a new bowl, and put salt in it." So they brought it to him.<sup>21</sup>Then he went to the spring of water and threw salt in it and said, "Thus says the LORD, I have healed this water; from now on neither death nor miscarriage shall come from it."<sup>22</sup>So the water has been healed to this day, according to the word that Elisha spoke.<sup>23</sup>He went up from there to Bethel, and while he was going up on the way, some small boys came out of the city and jeered at him, saying, "Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!"<sup>24</sup>And he turned around, and when he saw them, he cursed them in the name of the LORD. And two she-bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of the boys.<sup>25</sup>From there he went on to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.
2.overview:
Where we are. Ahaziah has died by the word Elijah spoke (chapter 1), and his brother Jehoram reigns in Samaria. Elijah’s work is done. The writer tells us in his first sentence that the LORD is about to take him up, so that our attention is on the last miles he walks with Elisha, and on whether the prophetic word will outlive the prophet.

The message. The prophet goes, but the God of the prophet stays. Elijah is taken to heaven without dying, and Elisha inherits his office and his spirit. In Elisha’s first acts the same God parts the same river, heals a cursed spring and defends his word against those who mock it. God’s work never depended on one man, however great.

Why it was said. The first readers had watched their prophets die and their kings fail (see the introduction); God’s word, the chapter tells them, is not buried with his servants.

How the chapter makes its case. Elijah walks from Gilgal to the Jordan, Israel’s entry into the land run backwards; three times he offers Elisha an honourable exit, three times Elisha refuses, and the river opens before them (vv. 1–8). Elisha asks for the firstborn’s double portion of Elijah’s spirit, sees his master parted from him by chariots of fire and taken up by a whirlwind, takes up the cloak and asks, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” The river opens again (vv. 9–14). The prophets search three days before accepting that Elijah is gone (vv. 15–18). He heals Jericho’s deadly spring with a word (vv. 19–22); at Bethel, the town of the golden calf, a crowd that jeers at the new prophet falls under the covenant’s curse (vv. 23–24); and he goes on to Carmel and Samaria (v. 25).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by pattern, one Luke seems to echo: Jesus too was taken up while his friends looked on, promising power when the Spirit came (Acts 1:8–9). But the pattern is surpassed. Elijah could not give the Spirit: “You have asked a hard thing.” The ascended Christ received the Spirit from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:33). Elisha healed one cursed spring; “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). And the mockery that brought judgment on the road to Bethel was poured on Christ at the cross, where he prayed for those who mocked him.

For us. When a beloved leader dies or a church’s great days seem past, the question is not where Elijah is but where the God of Elijah is, and Christ’s people know the answer: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — I Will Not Leave You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithfulness is tested before the gift is given. The writer tells us at once that the LORD is about to take Elijah up (v. 1), so the passage is about how two men walk the last miles. From Gilgal to Bethel to Jericho to the Jordan, Israel’s entry into the land in reverse, Elijah three times offers Elisha the chance to stay behind, and three times Elisha swears he will not leave him (vv. 2, 4, 6). Twice the companies of prophets ask whether he knows what is coming, and twice he tells them to keep quiet (vv. 3, 5). Fifty of them watch from a distance as Elijah strikes the Jordan with his cloak and the two cross on dry ground (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Elijah walks out of the land the way Israel walked into it, and the water opens for him as it opened for Joshua and for Moses at the sea.
verseByVerse.examples: Keep quiet may be the truest thing Elisha says all day. Anyone who has walked the last week with someone they are about to lose knows why: the knowing is hard enough without hearing it said.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven by a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were on their way from Gilgal. And Elijah said to Elisha, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me as far as Bethel." But Elisha said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they went down to Bethel. And the sons of the prophets who were in Bethel came out to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he said, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet." Elijah said to him, "Elisha, please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to Jericho." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So they came to Jericho. The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho drew near to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that today the LORD will take away your master from over you?" And he answered, "Yes, I know it; keep quiet." Then Elijah said to him, "Please stay here, for the LORD has sent me to the Jordan." But he said, "As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So the two of them went on. Fifty men of the sons of the prophets also went and stood at some distance from them, as they both were standing by the Jordan. Then Elijah took his cloak and rolled it up and struck the water, and the water was parted to the one side and to the other, till the two of them could go over on dry ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing his master is about to be taken, Elisha refuses three times to leave him, and the Jordan opens before Elijah as it opened for Moses and for Joshua. The passage tests the faithfulness of the successor and sets the departing prophet in the line of Israel’s great deliverers.

When the LORD was about to take Elijah up. There is no suspense. We are told at the top what will happen, so that our attention is free for what the writer cares about: how two men walk the last few miles.

The route run backwards. Gilgal, then Bethel, then Jericho, then the Jordan. It reads like Israel’s entry into the land run backwards. The nation crossed the Jordan on dry ground while the water stood in a heap, camped at Gilgal and set up twelve stones there, and took Jericho. Many think this Gilgal is a different village in the hills, since the two men go down to Bethel from it; even so, Gilgal, Jericho and the Jordan in one journey cannot help recalling Joshua.

Please stay here… I will not leave you. The exchange happens three times. Elijah does not want to be rid of him; it is a test, gently put: you may stop here with honour; this next part is mine. Three times the younger man refuses in identical words, and the repetition is the point: not one impulsive decision, but a man declining the same honourable exit at every town on the road.

As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live. The oath recalls Ruth’s: “where you go I will go… May the LORD do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you” (Ruth 1:16–17). It is the language of someone attaching his whole future to another person’s and refusing to be released.

Today the LORD will take away your master. The sons of the prophets were companies of prophets living and learning together under a leader, here at Bethel and at Jericho; “sons” means members of the company, not children. They test him from the other side, and it is harder because it is done kindly. They come out with a piece of information they are sure he needs, put as a tactful question, and it is the one thing he does not want said aloud. Yes, I know it; keep quiet. He knows, and the knowing is hard enough.

Elijah took his cloak and rolled it up. He rolls up the cloak he once threw over a young man ploughing in a field (1 Kings 19:19), and strikes the river with it. The water parts “to the one side and to the other”, and the two cross on dry ground, the phrase the old accounts used. Moses stretched out his hand and the sea was divided (Exodus 14:21); Joshua’s priests stepped into the Jordan and the nation walked over on dry ground (Joshua 3:15–17). Now the water opens a third time, for one man leaving and one man watching, and Elijah has been set, quietly and unmistakably, in that line.

Stood at some distance. Fifty prophets follow all the way to the river and then stop, watching two figures at the water’s edge. It is the position a great many people take towards God: near enough to see, far enough to keep their footing.

Can faith be watched from a safe distance? Many thoughtful people stand where the fifty stood. They find Christianity interesting, admire its art and its hospitals, enjoy a carol service, and keep a respectful distance from the river. It feels like the balanced position. But C. S. Lewis observed, in his essay “Christian Apologetics”, that Christianity, if false, is of no importance, and if true, of infinite importance. “The only thing it cannot be is moderately important.” A claim that God has come and spoken cannot be held at the distance of a hobby, which is why Elisha would not stay behind. Yet the gospel does more than call spectators down to the water. Its whole story is of God refusing to keep his distance. The Son crossed the gap we kept, came down into the Jordan among sinners to be baptised (Matthew 3:13–15), and went on to the cross, so that people who had only watched from far off could be “brought near” (Ephesians 2:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — Where Is the LORD, the God of Elijah?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet is taken, but the God of the prophet remains. Offered a parting gift, Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, the share of a firstborn heir, and is told he will have it if he sees his master taken (vv. 9–10). Chariots and horses of fire part the two men, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven; Elisha sees it, cries out to his father, the true strength of Israel, and tears his clothes (vv. 11–12). Then he picks up the fallen cloak, strikes the Jordan and asks the question that matters: where is the LORD, the God of Elijah? The water parts, and the ministry has changed hands (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Elisha is not asking to be twice the prophet his master was. He is asking to inherit the office, not to outdo the man.
verseByVerse.examples: The question at the water is not "where is Elijah?" but where Elijah's God is, and that God is still standing on the bank.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, "Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you." And Elisha said, "Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me." And he said, "You have asked a hard thing; yet, if you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you, but if you do not see me, it shall not be so." And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. And Elisha saw it and he cried, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!" And he saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two pieces. And he took up the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and went back and stood on the bank of the Jordan. Then he took the cloak of Elijah that had fallen from him and struck the water, saying, "Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?" And when he had struck the water, the water was parted to the one side and to the other, and Elisha went over.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha asks to be Elijah’s heir, sees him taken up to heaven, and then, with his master’s cloak in his hands, shows that the power was never in the man or the cloak but in the God of Elijah, who is still there. The office passes, and the God who filled it does not change.

A double portion of your spirit. Not twice as much power. A double portion is a term from the law of inheritance: a father must give the firstborn “a double portion of all that he has” (Deuteronomy 21:17), two shares to the eldest and one to each of the others. So Elisha is asking to be the heir, the eldest son’s place in the house of the prophets with the responsibility that goes with it; three verses later he calls Elijah my father. It is the right request. Solomon at Gibeon, offered anything, asked for an understanding mind (1 Kings 3:9). Both asked for what the work required rather than what the man would enjoy.

You have asked a hard thing. Hard, because it is not Elijah’s to give. So he attaches a condition, and it is not obedience, effort or worthiness. It is sight: Elisha must see him taken. Keep that, because it is where this book is going. Four chapters on, Elisha will be surrounded by a Syrian army with a terrified servant beside him, and he will pray, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see”, and the young man will find the hills full of horses and chariots of fire (6:17). The gift Elisha is granted here is the gift he spends his ministry asking for others.

Chariots of fire and horses of fire. There is no farewell scene; they are in the middle of a conversation, and it simply stops. The chariot does not carry Elijah off. It separated the two of them, and he goes up by a whirlwind. The horses and chariots are not transport but escort, and their business in the verse is to part two friends who were still talking.

From the broom tree to the whirlwind. Put this beside a broom tree in the wilderness south of Beersheba, where this same man lay down and asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4). God refused that prayer. He fed him instead, gave him a mountain, a low whisper and a successor, and now takes him away without letting him die at all. Only Enoch had gone like that: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24). Two men in the whole Old Testament, and one of them had asked to die.

At the transfiguration. Nor is he finished. Nine hundred years later, on a high mountain, two men appear in glory talking with Jesus about the departure he is to accomplish at Jerusalem, and they are Moses and Elijah (Luke 9:30–31). Moses died, and God buried him where no one knows (Deuteronomy 34:6); Elijah never died at all. Both are there, which tells us that whether a believer dies or is taken alive matters less than we suppose.

My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! Elisha saw it: the condition is met, and the writer records it before the cry, so that we know the inheritance is secure before we hear the grief. Then the cry of a son, not of a colleague. The second line is a military term, and it is extraordinary. Chariotry was a nation’s strike force, the thing kings counted, boasted about and bankrupted themselves for; Ahab put two thousand chariots in the field at Qarqar. Elisha watches one man go up in a wind and says, there goes the army. He means it exactly: the defence of that country was never its cavalry but this. A king of Israel will say the same words over Elisha’s own deathbed (13:14), so the line opens and closes his ministry.

Tore them in two pieces. He tears his own garment in two and picks up his master’s. The last thing he owned as a farmer’s son lies on the ground, and he puts on the cloak.

Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah? Alone on the wrong side of a river with his departed master’s cloak and fifty colleagues watching, he asks the right question. Not “where is Elijah?”, which the fifty will spend three days searching for, but where Elijah’s God is. That is the whole doctrine of succession in one sentence, and every church that has buried a much-loved minister needs it. The cloak is cloth; it parted no water on its own and never will. What opened the Jordan that day was not a garment and not a great man but the God whose servant that man was, and that God did not go up in the whirlwind. The water parts, Elisha walks across, and the ministry has changed hands.

Elijah could not give the Spirit. The scene has a greater counterpart, and many readers hear this chapter behind Luke’s telling of it. Jesus too was taken up while his friends were looking on (Acts 1:9); he too promised power once he had gone (Acts 1:8); and the Spirit came, so that his work went on in their hands. The differences are the point. Elijah could not give the Spirit, and said so. The risen Christ received the Spirit from the Father and poured him out himself (Acts 2:33). Elijah left his cloak behind; Christ took our flesh with him and reigns in it. And Elisha had to ask where the God of Elijah was, but Christ’s people are not left asking, for he said, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

Will Elijah return, and are he and Enoch the two witnesses of Revelation 11? Malachi promised Elijah before the day of the LORD, and Jesus said John the Baptist was that Elijah (Matthew 11:14; 17:12). The two witnesses of Revelation 11 are best read as the witnessing church, pictured with Moses’ and Elijah’s powers; some faithful interpreters expect two individual prophets at the end, and the vision’s point stands either way. Did Elijah die? Scripture says he was taken. The letter from Elijah in 2 Chronicles 21:12 was most likely written before his departure, and John 3:13 means that no one has gone up to bring back heavenly knowledge as the Son has.
verseByVerse.note: A “double portion” was the inheritance of the firstborn son: Elisha asks to be Elijah’s heir.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — Salt in a New Bowl
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elisha’s first acts show what kind of ministry has begun: God’s word brings life to those who receive it and judgment on those who scorn it. The prophets at Jericho bow to him, yet press him until he lets them search three days for Elijah’s body, and they come back having found nothing (vv. 15–18). At the request of Jericho’s men he throws salt into their deadly spring and, by the word of the LORD, heals it at its source, lifting the death that had hung over the town (vv. 19–22). On the road to Bethel a crowd jeers at him to go up as his master had, and two bears maul forty-two of them (vv. 23–24). Then he goes to Carmel and on to Samaria (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The first public act of Elijah's successor is to heal, at its source, the water of the town that lay under Joshua's curse.
verseByVerse.examples: Faith does not always remove the instinct to go and check, and Elisha patiently lets the fifty spend three days finding out.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho saw him opposite them, they said, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." And they came to meet him and bowed to the ground before him. And they said to him, "Behold now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. It may be that the Spirit of the LORD has caught him up and cast him upon some mountain or into some valley." And he said, "You shall not send." But when they urged him till he was ashamed, he said, "Send." They sent therefore fifty men. And for three days they sought him but did not find him. And they came back to him while he was staying at Jericho, and he said to them, "Did I not say to you, 'Do not go'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets recognise Elisha as Elijah’s successor but cannot quite believe what they have seen, and he lets three days of fruitless searching teach them what his word could not.

The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha. They watched the river open for him and bowed. The succession is recognised by the men who stood at a distance, on the evidence of the one sign nobody could have staged. Then, in the next breath, they ask to send out a search party.

Fifty strong men. Consider what these men knew. They had been told that day that the LORD was taking his master; they had said it themselves, twice, in two towns; they had just watched the Jordan divide. And they propose a search of mountains and valleys for a body, on the theory that the Spirit picked him up and put him down somewhere inconvenient.

Cast him upon some mountain or into some valley. The idea was not new. Obadiah had feared exactly this in Elijah’s lifetime: “the Spirit of the LORD will carry you I know not where” (1 Kings 18:12). Elijah had a history of vanishing and reappearing, so the fifty reason from the past instead of from what they had just been told and seen.

Till he was ashamed. They kept on until it was easier to give in than to keep refusing, and he let them go. That is a very human piece of leadership, and it is not held against him. He had told them the truth once; he did not need to win the argument, and three days of searching would settle it better than three hours of insisting. When they return he does not gloat. One question closes the matter, and they now know something they would never have accepted on his authority alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the men of the city said to Elisha, "Behold, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord sees, but the water is bad, and the land is unfruitful." He said, "Bring me a new bowl, and put salt in it." So they brought it to him. Then he went to the spring of water and threw salt in it and said, "Thus says the LORD, I have healed this water; from now on neither death nor miscarriage shall come from it." So the water has been healed to this day, according to the word that Elisha spoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Jericho, the city under Joshua’s curse, Elisha heals the deadly spring at its source by the word of the LORD, and the death that had come from it is ended. The first public act of Elijah’s heir is to bring life where a curse had brought death.

The situation of this city is pleasant. This is Jericho. Over its ruins Joshua had said, “Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates” (Joshua 6:26). In Ahab’s reign Hiel of Bethel rebuilt it anyway, and buried his eldest son when the foundations went in and his youngest when the gates went up: the very last thing the reader is told before Elijah walks into the throne room and shuts the sky (1 Kings 16:34). Now the men of that town tell the new prophet that the site is lovely, the water kills, and nothing will grow.

A new bowl, and put salt in it. He goes to the spring, the source, not the pools where the water is drunk: whatever is wrong is dealt with where it starts. The salt is not a remedy. Salt kills ground rather than sweetening it, and a handful thrown into a spring is a sign and nothing more. The bowl is new because it has never been used for anything else. The whole procedure is designed so that nobody can credit the method instead of God: Thus says the LORD, I have healed this water.

Neither death nor miscarriage. Death and the loss of the unborn were what had been coming out of that spring, in the town where a builder had buried two sons under a curse. Set the two scenes side by side. In one, a man defies an old word of God and pays for it with his children. In the other, a new word of God is spoken over the same water, and the children live.

The water has been healed to this day. The spring at Jericho traditionally identified with this one, still called Elisha’s Spring, flows today.

The curse lifted. The healing of one spring is a small picture of what God was doing in the whole story. The curse on Jericho was just, and only God could lift it. In Christ he lifted the curse that lies on all of us, not by salt in a bowl but by bearing it: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). He healed at the source, the heart, and the Bible ends with a city of which it is said, “No longer will there be anything accursed” (Revelation 22:3).

Uncertain wording. The word the ESV translates unfruitful in verse 19 and miscarriage in verse 21 is the same Hebrew word, meaning causing bereavement, used elsewhere of losing young before birth (Exodus 23:26). It is not clear whether it refers to the land failing to bring its fruit to harvest, or to women and flocks losing their young, or to both. Either way the water was bringing death, and the word of the LORD ended it.

verseByVerse.quote: He went up from there to Bethel, and while he was going up on the way, some small boys came out of the city and jeered at him, saying, "Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!" And he turned around, and when he saw them, he cursed them in the name of the LORD. And two she-bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of the boys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A crowd from Bethel, the town of the golden calf, jeers at the new prophet to go up as his master had, and when Elisha pronounces the covenant curse in the LORD’s name, God sends judgment on them. This passage is used to embarrass Christians more than almost any other in the Old Testament, and it should be dealt with properly rather than hurried past. Three things need saying, and none of them makes it comfortable.

Go up, you baldhead! First, what they are saying. Go up is not a general insult. It is the chapter’s own word for what happened to Elijah: he went up by a whirlwind. A crowd from Bethel comes out onto the road and tells his successor to clear off after his master: go up, then, as he did. They are jeering at what God had done days before, and doing it to the man who had been given the office. And the crowd is large: forty-two of them are caught, a crowd coming out of a town gate, not three children playing in a lane.

Came out of the city. Second, where. Bethel is not a neutral town. It is where Jeroboam set up one of his two golden calves and built the rival sanctuary that every king of Israel since had maintained. The crowd that meets the LORD’s prophet at the gate of the calf-shrine town tells him to go away and die.

He cursed them in the name of the LORD. Third, what Elisha actually does. He does not attack them and does not call for bears. He pronounces a covenant curse, and the covenant itself names this exact penalty: “I will let loose the wild beasts against you, which shall bereave you of your children” (Leviticus 26:22). He calls down a penalty the covenant had already announced, and God decides whether to carry it out. The text says the bears tore them, which is mauling, not necessarily killing.

Still severe. It stays severe, and Scripture makes no apology for it. What is being defended on that road is not a prophet’s dignity or his hairline but the office, in the week it changed hands, at the gate of the town that had spent eighty years teaching Israel to worship a calf.

What should a Christian, or a sceptic, do with it? Three plain things. It is no licence for anyone to curse those who mock them: Christ forbade that (Luke 6:28; 9:55). It is a sign, given once at the start of a ministry, that God takes contempt for his word seriously, as the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira were at the start of the church (Acts 5:1–11). And it throws into relief what the Son of God did with mockery. Men stood under his cross and jeered at him to come down from it (Mark 15:29–32); “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23), and he prayed for them. The judgment that fell on the road to Bethel is the judgment he carried, so that mockers could become his children.

Uncertain wording. The ESV’s small boys translates words that cover a wide range of ages. The noun is used of Joseph at seventeen (Genesis 37:2), and Solomon early in his reign calls himself “a little child” (1 Kings 3:7). Small may push the age younger, or may simply mark them as juniors, and the picture is most likely of youths rather than infants or grown men. Why they call him baldhead is also unknown: he may have been naturally bald, or shaved as a mark of his calling, or the word may simply be the insult that came to hand.
verseByVerse.note: The baldness may have been natural or a prophet's shaved head; either way the jeer was aimed at his office.

verseByVerse.quote: From there he went on to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha goes to Carmel, scene of his master’s greatest day, and then settles in Samaria, the capital that had hunted Elijah.

He went on to Mount Carmel. Carmel is where his master stood against the prophets of Baal, and he goes there first; then down into Samaria, where his master’s enemies live.

Returned to Samaria. Elijah spent his life running towards that capital and away from it, hiding in ravines, foreign towns and caves in the far south. His successor walks into the city and stays. For the next fifty years the prophet of the LORD will be a fixture there, advising kings, healing generals, feeding the poor and outlasting three kings. The cloak has been picked up, and it is being worn differently.

2.theology:
The double portion (v. 9). Elisha asks for the heir's place in a family of prophets, and for the responsibility attached to it.

The condition is sight (v. 10). Elisha will receive what he asks only if he sees Elijah taken, and this book keeps returning to the gift of seeing what is really there (6:17).

What the verse does and does not say (v. 11). The chariot does not carry Elijah off; it separated the two of them, and he goes up by the whirlwind. And the man taken without dying is the man who had asked to die (1 Kgs. 19:4); God refused that prayer and gave him this instead. He is seen once more, beside Moses, talking with Jesus on the mountain (Luke 9:30-31).

The chariots of Israel (v. 12). Elisha watches one man go up in a wind and says, in effect, "there goes the army", and he means it.

Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah? (v. 14). This is the whole doctrine of succession in one line. The cloak is cloth; what opened the water was the God of the man, and that God did not go up in the whirlwind.

Jericho healed (vv. 19-22). Where defying an old word of God, Joshua’s curse, had cost a builder his sons, a new word spoken over the same water lets the children live.

The bears (vv. 23-24). The jeer was aimed at what God had done days before, from the calf-shrine town, and Elisha pronounced a covenant curse whose penalty the law itself names. It remains severe; the verse note sets out why, and what Christ did with mockery instead.
2.examples:
Then: Fifty men followed the two of them to the river, stood at a careful distance watching, near enough to see everything and far enough to keep their footing, and before long were organising a search party for a body.

Now: Three things. First, keep quiet. The lesson is for those who visit the grieving: they usually know already and do not need it said aloud, and it is often the kindest people who cannot help saying it. Second, the search party. Believing a thing and being able to stop looking for the body are two different accomplishments, and Elisha did not win the argument; he let them find out. Third, the question at the river. Every congregation that has buried a much-loved minister is tempted to ask "where is Elijah?" The question that opens the water is the other one, where the God of Elijah is, and Christ's people ask it knowing the answer: the Lord who went up has poured out his Spirit on them and is with them always (Acts 2:33; Matt. 28:20).

keyVerse.quote: Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?
keyVerse.note: Elisha’s question at the river is the hinge of the chapter. He does not ask where Elijah is, but where Elijah’s God is, and the parted water answers that he is still here. The work of God never rested on the man or his cloak, and the same truth holds for Christ’s people, who are promised not a cloak but the presence of their risen Lord by his Spirit.

2.reflection:
Three times Elisha refused an honourable exit (vv. 2, 4, 6), while fifty prophets watched from a distance (v. 7). Where are you tempted to keep a safe distance from Christ, interested but not committed?

Elisha asked for a double portion, the heir’s share, so that he could carry on his master’s work (v. 9). If you could ask God for one thing for the work he has given you, what would it be, and why?

At the river Elisha did not ask where Elijah was but “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” (v. 14). How does that help a church that has lost a much-loved leader, or a believer who has leaned on someone else’s faith? How does Christ’s promise in Matthew 28:20 answer it?

Jericho’s spring was healed and the mockers from Bethel were judged (vv. 19–24). What do these two scenes show about the word of God? How does the cross show both how serious it is to mock God and how great his mercy is to mockers?

3.title: Moab Rebels
3.text: <sup>1</sup>In the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twelve years.<sup>2</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, though not like his father and mother, for he put away the pillar of Baal that his father had made.<sup>3</sup>Nevertheless, he clung to the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from it.<sup>4</sup>Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder, and he had to deliver to the king of Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams.<sup>5</sup>But when Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.<sup>6</sup>So King Jehoram marched out of Samaria at that time and mustered all Israel.<sup>7</sup>And he went and sent word to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: "The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to battle against Moab?" And he said, "I will go. I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses."<sup>8</sup>Then he said, "By which way shall we march?" Jehoram answered, "By the way of the wilderness of Edom."<sup>9</sup>So the king of Israel went with the king of Judah and the king of Edom. And when they had made a circuitous march of seven days, there was no water for the army or for the animals that followed them.<sup>10</sup>Then the king of Israel said, "Alas! The LORD has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab."<sup>11</sup>And Jehoshaphat said, "Is there no prophet of the LORD here, through whom we may inquire of the LORD?" Then one of the king of Israel's servants answered, "Elisha the son of Shaphat is here, who poured water on the hands of Elijah."<sup>12</sup>And Jehoshaphat said, "The word of the LORD is with him." So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him.<sup>13</sup>And Elisha said to the king of Israel, "What have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father and to the prophets of your mother." But the king of Israel said to him, "No; it is the LORD who has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab."<sup>14</sup>And Elisha said, "As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not that I have regard for Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would neither look at you nor see you.<sup>15</sup>But now bring me a musician." And when the musician played, the hand of the LORD came upon him.<sup>16</sup>And he said, "Thus says the LORD, 'I will make this dry streambed full of pools.'<sup>17</sup>For thus says the LORD, 'You shall not see wind or rain, but that streambed shall be filled with water, so that you shall drink, you, your livestock, and your animals.'<sup>18</sup>This is a light thing in the sight of the LORD. He will also give the Moabites into your hand,<sup>19</sup>and you shall attack every fortified city and every choice city, and shall fell every good tree and stop up all springs of water and ruin every good piece of land with stones."<sup>20</sup>The next morning, about the time of offering the sacrifice, behold, water came from the direction of Edom, till the country was filled with water.<sup>21</sup>When all the Moabites heard that the kings had come up to fight against them, all who were able to put on armor, from the youngest to the oldest, were called out and were drawn up at the border.<sup>22</sup>And when they rose early in the morning and the sun shone on the water, the Moabites saw the water opposite them as red as blood.<sup>23</sup>And they said, "This is blood; the kings have surely fought together and struck one another down. Now then, Moab, to the spoil!"<sup>24</sup>But when they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose and struck the Moabites, till they fled before them. And they went forward, striking the Moabites as they went.<sup>25</sup>And they overthrew the cities, and on every good piece of land every man threw a stone until it was covered. They stopped every spring of water and felled all the good trees, till only its stones were left in Kir-hareseth, and the slingers surrounded and attacked it.<sup>26</sup>When the king of Moab saw that the battle was going against him, he took with him 700 swordsmen to break through, opposite the king of Edom, but they could not.<sup>27</sup>Then he took his oldest son who was to reign in his place and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. And there came great wrath against Israel. And they withdrew from him and returned to their own land.
3.overview:
Where we are. Ahab’s second son Jehoram now reigns in Israel (1:17), and Moab, which broke away when Ahab died (1:1), has to be dealt with. Elisha has just taken up Elijah’s office (chapter 2), and this is his first meeting with kings.

The message. God is not a last resort to be called on when our own plans run dry. Yet in mercy he answers even those who come late, for the sake of one who stands in his favour, giving water out of a clear sky and victory as “a light thing”. But a war begun without him ends in horror, and in nothing gained.

Why it was said. The exiles knew all about alliances made first and prayers made later, and about kings who reformed only as far as was safe (see the introduction). The chapter shows them both the mercy that had held them up so long and the emptiness of a faith kept for emergencies.

How the chapter makes its case. Jehoram removes Baal’s pillar but clings to Jeroboam’s calves; when Mesha of Moab stops his tribute, Jehoshaphat of Judah pledges himself again to a son of Ahab, and after seven days on a clever desert route the three kings have no water (vv. 1–12). Elisha will not answer Jehoram, but for Jehoshaphat’s sake, with a musician playing, he promises pools without wind or rain and victory besides, and at the hour of the morning sacrifice the water comes (vv. 13–20). The same water, red in the sunrise, lures Moab to defeat; Israel ruins the land, until Mesha burns his heir on the wall of Kir-hareseth, great wrath comes against Israel, and the armies go home with nothing (vv. 21–27).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by pattern and by contrast. An army drinks because of one man’s standing with God, “were it not that I have regard for Jehoshaphat” (v. 14): a faint shadow of the way sinners are received for the sake of God’s beloved Son. And Mesha’s son on the wall shows religion’s oldest transaction, a son given upward to buy a god’s favour. At the cross it runs the other way: God gave his own Son for people who were not asking, “while we were still sinners” (Romans 5:8).

For us. Ask where you have kept God for emergencies and trusted your own route until the wells ran dry, and what sin you are clinging to while you give up the ones everyone can see. Then come, even on day seven: the God who answered for Jehoshaphat’s sake hears for the sake of his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — I Am As You Are
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A half-hearted king and a good king who has not learned his lesson march into the desert without asking God. Jehoram puts away Baal’s pillar but clings to Jeroboam’s calves (vv. 1–3). When Mesha of Moab stops his huge tribute of lambs and wool, Jehoram asks Jehoshaphat of Judah to join him, and Jehoshaphat repeats word for word the pledge he once gave Ahab (vv. 4–7).
