They choose a clever route round through Edom, and after seven days there is no water for the men or the animals (vv. 8–9). Jehoram blames the LORD; Jehoshaphat, at last, asks for a prophet, and the three kings go down to Elisha, Elijah’s servant (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is word for word the pledge Jehoshaphat gave Ahab, and he was nearly killed for it and rebuked for it. He had learned about ships (1 Kgs. 22:49), but the lesson did not transfer to armies.
verseByVerse.examples: Elisha's only credential, as far as the army knows, is that he served Elijah.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twelve years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, though not like his father and mother, for he put away the pillar of Baal that his father had made. Nevertheless, he clung to the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from it. Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder, and he had to deliver to the king of Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams. But when Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel. So King Jehoram marched out of Samaria at that time and mustered all Israel. And he went and sent word to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: "The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to battle against Moab?" And he said, "I will go. I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses." Then he said, "By which way shall we march?" Jehoram answered, "By the way of the wilderness of Edom." So the king of Israel went with the king of Judah and the king of Edom. And when they had made a circuitous march of seven days, there was no water for the army or for the animals that followed them. Then the king of Israel said, "Alas! The LORD has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab." And Jehoshaphat said, "Is there no prophet of the LORD here, through whom we may inquire of the LORD?" Then one of the king of Israel's servants answered, "Elisha the son of Shaphat is here, who poured water on the hands of Elijah." And Jehoshaphat said, "The word of the LORD is with him." So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoram’s reform goes only as far as is safe, and when Moab rebels, he and the godly Jehoshaphat march into the desert on a plan of their own and are soon dying of thirst. Only then does anyone ask for the word of the LORD.

He put away the pillar of Baal. Here is a reform of the most instructive kind: genuine, and exactly as deep as it was convenient to go. Taking down the pillar was a real act; his father put it up and his mother is still alive. But Baal was humiliated in public on Carmel, his prophets are dead, and the country has watched fire fall from heaven. Removing that pillar was popular.

He clung to the sin of Jeroboam. What he keeps is the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and the writer chooses a strong verb: he clung to them. Those were state policy. They were installed to stop Israelites going south to worship in Jerusalem, and they held the northern kingdom together as a separate country. Give them up and the throne is in question.

Partial repentance. So he surrendered the sin that had become an embarrassment and held on to the one that was still paying. It is the ordinary arithmetic of partial repentance, and it happens in Christian lives constantly: the habit everybody can see goes first, and the one our life is built around is quietly kept. The way out is not to try harder at the visible sins but to bring that one into the light before a God who forgives it fully (1 John 1:9), and whose Spirit is given to put to death what we cling to (Romans 8:13).

A hundred thousand lambs. Mesha’s tribute was a hundred thousand lambs, probably every year, and the wool of a hundred thousand rams. That explains both why Moab stopped paying and why Israel could not let it go.

I am as you are. The reader has heard Jehoshaphat’s answer before: it is word for word what he said to Ahab (1 Kings 22:4). Recall what that pledge cost him. He went to a war he was never asked to fight, wore his royal robes while his ally went disguised, was chased by chariot captains who took him for the king of Israel, and cried out. On his way home a prophet met him and asked, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” (2 Chronicles 19:2).

He had learned something. What makes it worse is that he had. When Ahaziah proposed a joint shipping venture, “Jehoshaphat was not willing” (1 Kings 22:49). Chronicles tells how an earlier joint fleet with Ahaziah was wrecked at Ezion-geber (2 Chronicles 20:35–37), and Kings records the refusal that followed, so the two books record two stages of one story. He would not do it again, with ships. That is how most of us learn: not the principle, but one area of life at a time. We tie the lesson to the disaster that taught it, and the same mistake in a new form walks straight past us.

By which way shall we march? The plan is shrewd: instead of coming at Moab across the Arnon gorge, where they will be waiting, swing round the bottom of the Dead Sea and come up through Edom into their undefended flank. But after seven days in the desert, with three armies and their baggage animals, the wells are dry. The clever plan has put them somewhere they cannot survive, and nobody asked God about the route.

The LORD has called these three kings. The first time the LORD’s name is spoken in this campaign, it is an accusation. Jehoram has not consulted him or prayed to him, yet on day seven he knows exactly who is behind it. People who never speak to God are often remarkably confident about what he is doing.

Is there no prophet of the LORD here? Jehoshaphat asks in almost the words he used before Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:7). But then he asked before the battle; this time only after the march and the dry wells. He is a good king who does not forget God; he remembers him too late, and this chapter shows what it costs to be a day-seven believer.

Who poured water on the hands of Elijah. The officer describes Elisha not as the man who parted the Jordan or healed the spring, but as Elijah’s personal servant. Years before, a young farmer slaughtered his own pair of oxen, burned their yokes to cook them, fed his village and walked away to be somebody’s servant (1 Kings 19:21). That is what strangers in the army know him for. It is his only reference, and it is enough: three crowned heads walk out of the camp to a prophet’s tent, because the man with the water is the man with the word.

Uncertain wording. The word translated sheep breeder occurs elsewhere in the Bible only of Amos, who “was among the shepherds of Tekoa” (Amos 1:1). It probably means an owner or breeder of large flocks rather than a hired shepherd, and related words in neighbouring languages were used of officials in charge of herds. Either way, as a title for a king it marks how much of Moab’s wealth walked on four legs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — You Shall Not See Wind or Rain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word will not be used as a last resort, yet he answers in mercy for the sake of one who honours him. Elisha sends Jehoram back to his parents’ prophets, and says he would not even look at him except for Jehoshaphat (vv. 13–14). He calls for a musician, the hand of the LORD comes on him, and he promises that the dry streambed will fill with water though no one sees wind or rain; this is a light thing to the LORD, who will also give Moab into their hand and lay its land waste (vv. 15–19). The next morning, at the hour of the sacrifice, water flows from Edom and fills the land (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is water without weather. Elijah at Carmel watched the sky go black; this time the answer arrives from a storm nobody in the camp witnesses, and the army drinks a river without seeing a cloud.
verseByVerse.examples: What is killing three armies is a light thing: not small in itself, but small to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elisha said to the king of Israel, "What have I to do with you? Go to the prophets of your father and to the prophets of your mother." But the king of Israel said to him, "No; it is the LORD who has called these three kings to give them into the hand of Moab." And Elisha said, "As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not that I have regard for Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would neither look at you nor see you. But now bring me a musician." And when the musician played, the hand of the LORD came upon him. And he said, "Thus says the LORD, 'I will make this dry streambed full of pools.' For thus says the LORD, 'You shall not see wind or rain, but that streambed shall be filled with water, so that you shall drink, you, your livestock, and your animals.' This is a light thing in the sight of the LORD. He will also give the Moabites into your hand, and you shall attack every fortified city and every choice city, and shall fell every good tree and stop up all springs of water and ruin every good piece of land with stones." The next morning, about the time of offering the sacrifice, behold, water came from the direction of Edom, till the country was filled with water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha refuses to treat God as an emergency service for a king who ignores him, yet for Jehoshaphat’s sake God promises water without wind or rain, and victory besides, and sends it at the hour of the sacrifice.

What have I to do with you? A hard greeting for a man in trouble, and an entirely deserved one. The prophets of your father are the four hundred who sent Ahab to Ramoth-gilead; the prophets of your mother are Jezebel’s. You have prophets of your own, Elisha is saying, and you have never once come to me until the water ran out; go and ask them. The word of God is not a service to be called out when the arrangements we actually trust have failed.

God as the emergency number. Jehoram’s religion may be the commonest in the modern West. Plenty of people who never pray keep God in reserve, like the number for the emergency services: unused for years, but there if the water runs out. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison, warned against a God brought in only at the edges, as a stopgap where our knowledge or strength gives out, and wanted to speak of God at the centre of life, not only at its limits. The deeper trouble is that the things we really trust, the career, the plan, the clever route round the bottom of the Dead Sea, run our lives, and God is asked only to clean up after them. Yet here is the surprise. The God who will not be our servant on call is the one who actually came to serve: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). He refuses to be a convenience because he means to be something far better, a Father who is near on ordinary days as well as desperate ones.

As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand. Jehoram does not defend himself; he repeats that it is all God’s doing. Elisha answers with his master’s oath, word for word what Elijah swore to Obadiah in the famine (1 Kings 18:15), and then a sentence that should not be softened: you are getting an answer because of somebody else.

Were it not that I have regard for Jehoshaphat. That is more encouraging than it sounds. An army of thousands, most of whom had no more claim on God than their king, is about to drink because one man in the tent had a standing with God that the rest did not.

Heard for another’s sake. That is not a curiosity; it is the ground every one of us stands on. Nobody is heard on his own merits. The whole of the gospel is that the Father is pleased with his Son, and that those joined to Christ are received with the favour that belongs to him. Jehoshaphat could not transfer his standing to Jehoram, and the arrangement here is only a shadow of the real one; but its shape, mercy arriving because of whom you are standing beside, is exact.

Bring me a musician. He asks for music before he prophesies, and the writer records it without explaining it. Do not build a system on one verse. But it is not isolated: David’s playing settled Saul when the harmful spirit came (1 Samuel 16:23), and the temple musicians under David were men “who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals” (1 Chronicles 25:1). Elisha has just come out of a shouting match with a king who blames God for everything, and before he can listen he wants a musician.

You shall not see wind or rain. Somewhere south and east, up in the Edomite hills, it will rain on people who have no idea an army is dying in the valley below. The water will run down the dry wadi in the night and be standing in pools by dawn. Set that beside Carmel, where Elijah put his face between his knees and sent his servant to look seven times until a cloud the size of a hand rose from the sea (1 Kings 18:42–44). He watched his answer arrive; these men see no part of theirs. Most answered prayer is of the second kind. What saves you was set in motion days earlier, somewhere you have never been, by people you will never meet, and the first you know of it is that it is simply there in the morning.

This is a light thing in the sight of the LORD. The problem that has three kings on their knees is, in God’s sight, a light thing, mentioned in passing before the main business. He is not being dismissive but telling the truth about its size: what is at the limit of your strength is easy for him, and the God who is about to hand them a kingdom mentions the drinking water first only because that is what they came about.

Shall fell every good tree. Verse 19 orders every good tree felled, and Deuteronomy expressly forbids that in a siege: “you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them… Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you?” (Deuteronomy 20:19). Fruit trees take a generation to grow and feed people who had no part in the quarrel. The honest thing is to say that the tension is there. The best reading is that this is a particular sentence of judgment on Moab, announced by God and not devised by the army, rather than a repeal of the standing law for Israel’s ordinary wars; the two texts are doing different jobs. Like the conquest, it was a unique judgment, never a pattern or licence for how anyone fights today. But nobody should pretend the verse is comfortable, and the chapter’s ending suggests the writer did not think it was either.

About the time of offering the sacrifice. The writer times the miracle by the altar, most naturally the morning offering in Jerusalem, in the other kingdom, over the border. Elijah on Carmel had waited to pray until the hour of the evening offering (1 Kings 18:36). Twice now, the decisive moment in a northern crisis is dated by a clock in a temple these kings do not attend.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 16 says literally making this valley pits, pits. It can be read as God’s announcement of what he will do, as the ESV takes it (“I will make this dry streambed full of pools”), or as a command to the army to dig trenches to catch the water, as the King James Version took it (“Make this valley full of ditches”). Either way the water is God’s gift, coming without wind or rain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–27 — A Boy on the Wall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The victory God gave is real, but the campaign ends in horror and in nothing gained. Moab musters every man who can bear arms (v. 21). At sunrise the new water looks as red as blood, and the Moabites, sure the kings have destroyed one another, rush to plunder and are cut down (vv. 22–24). Israel ruins Moab’s cities, fields, springs and trees until only Kir-hareseth stands (v. 25). Mesha fails to break out through the Edomites, and then offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall (vv. 26–27). Great wrath comes against Israel, and the armies withdraw to their own land.
verseByVerse.theology: The water God sent to keep Israel alive is the same water that destroys Moab: in the night it is drink for one army, and at sunrise its red glare lures the other to its death.
verseByVerse.examples: The ending is left unexplained, deliberately. What the writer records is that a campaign which began with a pledge given before a prayer ended with a child burning on a city wall and three armies walking home with nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the Moabites heard that the kings had come up to fight against them, all who were able to put on armor, from the youngest to the oldest, were called out and were drawn up at the border. And when they rose early in the morning and the sun shone on the water, the Moabites saw the water opposite them as red as blood. And they said, "This is blood; the kings have surely fought together and struck one another down. Now then, Moab, to the spoil!" But when they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose and struck the Moabites, till they fled before them. And they went forward, striking the Moabites as they went. And they overthrew the cities, and on every good piece of land every man threw a stone until it was covered. They stopped every spring of water and felled all the good trees, till only its stones were left in Kir-hareseth, and the slingers surrounded and attacked it. When the king of Moab saw that the battle was going against him, he took with him 700 swordsmen to break through, opposite the king of Edom, but they could not. Then he took his oldest son who was to reign in his place and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. And there came great wrath against Israel. And they withdrew from him and returned to their own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The water that saved Israel lures Moab to defeat, but when Mesha burns his own heir on the wall of his last city, great wrath comes against Israel and the victorious armies go home with nothing.

From the youngest to the oldest. A general mobilisation, everyone who can carry a shield, drawn up along the frontier. They are ready and in position.

The sun shone on the water. Low morning sun, red sandstone country, and a valley full of standing water where yesterday there was nothing: the whole basin lights up the colour of blood. They read it exactly wrong, as people read evidence when they have already decided what they hope. Alliances of three kings come apart; obviously they have fought each other; obviously the field is full of unguarded baggage. So the army drawn up at the border breaks ranks and runs downhill after plunder, onto the swords of men it has just concluded are dead. God did not need a second miracle: the same water did both.

Every man threw a stone. Every man throwing one stone onto a field until the field is gone: a slow, deliberate, communal way to ruin farmland, and it takes an army to do it. Kir-hareseth, the one city left standing, was Moab’s great stronghold on a steep hill east of the Dead Sea, probably modern Kerak.

To break through, opposite the king of Edom. Mesha attacks the Edomite part of the line, the sensible choice: Edom is the junior partner, dragged along, with least reason to hold. Seven hundred men go at it, and the line does not break.

His oldest son who was to reign in his place. The last thing he has is his son, so he burns him on the city wall where the besieging army can watch. This is not a symbolic act: a boy who was to be king, burned as an offering in the open in front of thousands of men. The child had done nothing and had no say. His father is buying a god’s attention with him. A few interpreters have taken the boy to be the crown prince of Edom, captured in the breakout (Amos 2:1 condemns Moab for burning the bones of Edom’s king), but the natural reading is that Mesha burned his own heir. The god he appealed to was Chemosh, whom Mesha’s stone credits with his victories.

There came great wrath against Israel. The sentence has been argued over for centuries, because the text does not say whose wrath it was (see the box at the end of this note). What the writer does record is the outcome: the wrath came and the siege lifted, and he offers no explanation for a campaign in which God gave them water out of a clear sky and a kingdom into their hand.

Returned to their own land. They won every engagement and came away with nothing. Moab is not reconquered, the tribute never resumes, and Mesha’s own memorial stone, set up in Dibon, records his revolt against Israel as a victory.

A tally of sons. This book has begun to keep a tally that nobody in it is keeping. Hiel of Bethel laid Jericho’s foundations at the cost of his eldest son and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest, to finish a building (1 Kings 16:34). Naboth’s sons died with him so that a king could have a vegetable garden (2 Kings 9:26). Now a boy burns on a wall so that his father can hold a town. Three different religions, three different projects, and the price is always somebody’s children.

The transaction reversed. There is a resemblance here to the cross, and it runs the opposite way from how it first appears. Mesha gave up his firstborn to get something out of a god: pagan sacrifice is a payment offered upward to move a power that is not otherwise interested. The cross is not that transaction improved; it is that transaction reversed. Nobody gave God a son to buy his favour; God gave his own Son to people who were not asking: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). The offering came down, not up, not to purchase anything but to pay for everything, and no other has been needed since. Mesha’s son was burned to keep a wall standing, and walls fall eventually. The Son who was given is alive, and what he bought does not come down.

Where Christians differ: whose wrath came against Israel? Some take it to be God’s: the Hebrew word is most often used of his anger, and he may have been displeased with a campaign begun without him, or pushed to such an end. Others see the fury of the Moabites, roused by their king’s sacrifice, breaking on the besiegers, or a horror in Israel’s own ranks that broke their will to go on. Some scholars think the writer meant the wrath of Chemosh, but the text never says that Chemosh had power, and idols have none (1 Corinthians 8:4). This commentary’s view: most likely Israel’s horror and the Moabites’ fury together turned the battle, while God’s displeasure at a war pushed to such an end may lie behind them. The writer leaves it unexplained, and any reading should be held loosely; what is not in doubt is that every engagement was won and nothing was gained.
verseByVerse.note: The Moabite Stone, an inscription by King Mesha, tells of Moab’s revolt against Israel from Moab’s side.

3.theology:
The reform that costs nothing (vv. 2-3). The sin that had become an embarrassment goes; the one his throne rests on is kept.

Learning in departments (v. 7). Jehoshaphat had learned to refuse Israel’s kings at sea (1 Kgs. 22:49), yet joins one again on land. Most of us are careful about the precise disaster that taught us and let the identical mistake walk past in a different form.

For Jehoshaphat's sake (v. 14). An army drinks because of the standing one man in the tent has with God. It is only a shadow, but it is the shape of the ground every Christian stands on: the Father is pleased with his Son, and those who are joined to Christ are received with the favour that belongs to him.

Water without weather (v. 17). Elijah watched his answer come up out of the sea; these men see no part of theirs. Most answered prayer is of the second kind.

A light thing (v. 18). God is not making light of their thirst; he is telling the truth about its size. What is at the very limit of your strength is a small thing to him.

The trees (v. 19), honestly. Deuteronomy forbids felling fruit trees in a siege (Deut. 20:19-20), and the tension is real. The best reading is that this is a specific announced judgment on Moab, not a repeal of the standing law, but the verse is uncomfortable, and the chapter's ending suggests the writer knew it.

The wrath that is not identified (v. 27). The text does not say whose, and this commentary holds its preferred reading loosely (see the note on v. 27). What is not left open is the outcome: every engagement won, and nothing gained.

Sons, and which direction the offering runs (v. 27). Pagan sacrifice is a payment offered upward to move a power that is not otherwise interested. The cross is that transaction reversed: God gave his own Son to people who were not asking (Rom. 5:8).
3.examples:
Then: An army drew up along its own frontier, ready and in position, saw a valley of standing water turn red in the morning sun, decided the enemy had destroyed itself, broke ranks for the plunder, and ran downhill onto the swords of men it had just concluded were dead.

Now: Three things. First, Jehoshaphat, who is the most useful man in the chapter for ordinary Christians because he is genuinely good and genuinely caught. He never forgets God; here he remembers him too late, and the cost of being a day-seven believer is a seven-day march into a desert with no water at the end of it. Ask where you have been badly burned and carefully cautious ever since, and then whether you ever carried that caution into the other parts of your life; and if it did not, the God who still answered Jehoshaphat on day seven has not stopped answering. Second, Elisha as the army knew him: the man who poured water on Elijah’s hands, a servant. That was the whole of his reputation, and it was enough to bring three kings to his tent. Third, water without weather. If you are waiting on something and there is no cloud in the sky, notice that the men in this chapter never saw one either, and woke up beside a river.

keyVerse.quote: As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not that I have regard for Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would neither look at you nor see you.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds both halves of the chapter’s message. God will not be called on as a last resort by a king who ignores him, and Elisha says so to his face. Yet an army is saved for the sake of one man who stands in God’s favour, a faint shadow of the gospel, in which sinners are heard and welcomed for the sake of God’s beloved Son.

3.reflection:
Jehoram removed Baal’s pillar but “clung to the sin of Jeroboam” (v. 3). Why is it easier to give up the sins everyone can see than the one our life is built around? Is there one you are clinging to?

Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet only after seven days without water (v. 11), and Elisha told Jehoram to go to his own prophets (v. 13). Where do you treat God as an emergency service rather than the first one you consult?

The army was answered because Elisha had regard for Jehoshaphat (v. 14). How does this picture the way we are heard by God for the sake of Christ? How should that shape the confidence with which we pray?

God sent water though no one saw wind or rain (v. 17), while Mesha gave his son to buy his god’s favour (v. 27). How does the way God gives differ from the way people try to buy help from their gods? What does Romans 5:8 add?

4.title: The Widow's Oil and the Shunammite's Son
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the wife of one of the sons of the prophets cried to Elisha, "Your servant my husband is dead, and you know that your servant feared the LORD, but the creditor has come to take my two children to be his slaves."<sup>2</sup>And Elisha said to her, "What shall I do for you? Tell me; what have you in the house?" And she said, "Your servant has nothing in the house except a jar of oil."<sup>3</sup>Then he said, "Go outside, borrow vessels from all your neighbors, empty vessels and not too few.<sup>4</sup>Then go in and shut the door behind yourself and your sons and pour into all these vessels. And when one is full, set it aside."<sup>5</sup>So she went from him and shut the door behind herself and her sons. And as she poured they brought the vessels to her.<sup>6</sup>When the vessels were full, she said to her son, "Bring me another vessel." And he said to her, "There is not another." Then the oil stopped flowing.<sup>7</sup>She came and told the man of God, and he said, "Go, sell the oil and pay your debts, and you and your sons can live on the rest."<sup>8</sup>One day Elisha went on to Shunem, where a wealthy woman lived, who urged him to eat some food. So whenever he passed that way, he would turn in there to eat food.<sup>9</sup>And she said to her husband, "Behold now, I know that this is a holy man of God who is continually passing our way.<sup>10</sup>Let us make a small room on the roof with walls and put there for him a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp, so that whenever he comes to us, he can go in there."<sup>11</sup>One day he came there, and he turned into the chamber and rested there.<sup>12</sup>And he said to Gehazi his servant, "Call this Shunammite." When he had called her, she stood before him.<sup>13</sup>And he said to him, "Say now to her, 'See, you have taken all this trouble for us; what is to be done for you? Would you have a word spoken on your behalf to the king or to the commander of the army?'" She answered, "I dwell among my own people."<sup>14</sup>And he said, "What then is to be done for her?" Gehazi answered, "Well, she has no son, and her husband is old."<sup>15</sup>He said, "Call her." And when he had called her, she stood in the doorway.<sup>16</sup>And he said, "At this season, about this time next year, you shall embrace a son." And she said, "No, my lord, O man of God; do not lie to your servant."<sup>17</sup>But the woman conceived, and she bore a son about that time the following spring, as Elisha had said to her.<sup>18</sup>When the child had grown, he went out one day to his father among the reapers.<sup>19</sup>And he said to his father, "Oh, my head, my head!" The father said to his servant, "Carry him to his mother."<sup>20</sup>And when he had lifted him and brought him to his mother, the child sat on her lap till noon, and then he died.<sup>21</sup>And she went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God and shut the door behind him and went out.<sup>22</sup>Then she called to her husband and said, "Send me one of the servants and one of the donkeys, that I may quickly go to the man of God and come back again."<sup>23</sup>And he said, "Why will you go to him today? It is neither new moon nor Sabbath." She said, "All is well."<sup>24</sup>Then she saddled the donkey, and she said to her servant, "Urge the animal on; do not slacken the pace for me unless I tell you."<sup>25</sup>So she set out and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her coming, he said to Gehazi his servant, "Look, there is the Shunammite.<sup>26</sup>Run at once to meet her and say to her, 'Is all well with you? Is all well with your husband? Is all well with the child?'" And she answered, "All is well."<sup>27</sup>And when she came to the mountain to the man of God, she caught hold of his feet. And Gehazi came to push her away. But the man of God said, "Leave her alone, for she is in bitter distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me."<sup>28</sup>Then she said, "Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say, 'Do not deceive me?'"<sup>29</sup>He said to Gehazi, "Tie up your garment and take my staff in your hand and go. If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not reply. And lay my staff on the face of the child."<sup>30</sup>Then the mother of the child said, "As the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So he arose and followed her.<sup>31</sup>Gehazi went on ahead and laid the staff on the face of the child, but there was no sound or sign of life. Therefore he returned to meet him and told him, "The child has not awakened."<sup>32</sup>When Elisha came into the house, he saw the child lying dead on his bed.<sup>33</sup>So he went in and shut the door behind the two of them and prayed to the LORD.<sup>34</sup>Then he went up and lay on the child, putting his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. And as he stretched himself upon him, the flesh of the child became warm.<sup>35</sup>Then he got up again and walked once back and forth in the house, and went up and stretched himself upon him. The child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.<sup>36</sup>Then he summoned Gehazi and said, "Call this Shunammite." So he called her. And when she came to him, he said, "Pick up your son."<sup>37</sup>She came and fell at his feet, bowing to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.<sup>38</sup>And Elisha came again to Gilgal when there was a famine in the land. And as the sons of the prophets were sitting before him, he said to his servant, "Set on the large pot, and boil stew for the sons of the prophets."<sup>39</sup>One of them went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine and gathered from it his lap full of wild gourds, and came and cut them up into the pot of stew, not knowing what they were.<sup>40</sup>And they poured out some for the men to eat. But while they were eating of the stew, they cried out, "O man of God, there is death in the pot!" And they could not eat it.<sup>41</sup>He said, "Then bring flour." And he threw it into the pot and said, "Pour some out for the men, that they may eat." And there was no harm in the pot.<sup>42</sup>A man came from Baal-shalishah, bringing the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain in his sack. And Elisha said, "Give to the men, that they may eat."<sup>43</sup>But his servant said, "How can I set this before a hundred men?" So he repeated, "Give them to the men, that they may eat, for thus says the LORD, 'They shall eat and have some left.'"<sup>44</sup>So he set it before them. And they ate and had some left, according to the word of the LORD.
4.overview:
Where we are. Elisha has inherited Elijah’s spirit (chapter 2) and has just given water and victory to three kings in the wilderness of Edom (chapter 3). Now the scene shrinks from armies to households, and the double portion is spent on ordinary people in trouble.

The message. The LORD’s life-giving word reaches past the palace to the faithful few in an unfaithful land: a widow in debt, a childless wife, a grieving mother, a company of hungry students. Where Israel’s official religion had nothing to give, the God of Elisha fills what is empty, gives a son, raises the dead, takes death out of the pot and makes a little food enough, “according to the word of the LORD” (v. 44).

Why it was said. Under Ahab’s son the north still served Jeroboam’s calves, and those who feared the LORD were a poor minority (see the introduction). For them, and for exiles who later had nothing in the house, the chapter shows that God had not forgotten his remnant.

How the chapter makes its case. A prophet’s widow, about to lose her sons to a creditor, pours one jar of oil into every vessel she can borrow, pays the debt and lives on the rest (vv. 1–7). A wealthy woman of Shunem builds the prophet a room, asks nothing in return, and is promised the son she had stopped hoping for (vv. 8–17). The boy dies on her lap; she rides to Carmel, will not be put off with a servant and a staff, and Elisha, alone with the body, prays and stretches himself on the child until he lives (vv. 18–37). In a famine, poison in the stew is made harmless with a handful of flour, and twenty barley loaves feed a hundred men with some left over (vv. 38–44).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by pattern, and the Gospels draw it themselves. At Nain Jesus gave a widow’s only son back to his mother, and the crowd said that a great prophet had arisen (Luke 7:11–17); on a Galilean hillside barley loaves fed thousands, with baskets left over (John 6:9–14). The pattern is also surpassed: Elisha stretched himself twice on the dead, Jesus spoke one word; Elisha’s wonders were brief signs, and Christ is himself “the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25) and “the bread of life” (John 6:35).

For us. The God of this chapter notices a widow’s debt and a woman’s unspoken longing, and he usually begins with what is already in the house. Bring him your empty places honestly, as the Shunammite did, and be, for others, the neighbours with the jars.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Nothing in the House Except
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God meets the debt of a faithful household, and he begins with what is already in the house. The widow of one of the prophets tells Elisha that her God-fearing husband has died in debt and the creditor is coming for her two sons (v. 1). Elisha asks what she has: nothing but a jar of oil (v. 2). She borrows empty vessels from all her neighbours, shuts the door and pours, her sons bringing jar after jar, until there is not another vessel and the oil stops (vv. 3–6). The oil pays the debt in full and leaves enough for the family to live on (v. 7). The supply ran out only when the vessels did.
verseByVerse.theology: The thing she called nothing is the thing she is saved by. God asks for an inventory before he does anything, because he works with what is actually there rather than with what she wishes were there.
verseByVerse.examples: The oil stops at the last borrowed pot. God had not run out of oil; she had run out of pots.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the wife of one of the sons of the prophets cried to Elisha, "Your servant my husband is dead, and you know that your servant feared the LORD, but the creditor has come to take my two children to be his slaves." And Elisha said to her, "What shall I do for you? Tell me; what have you in the house?" And she said, "Your servant has nothing in the house except a jar of oil." Then he said, "Go outside, borrow vessels from all your neighbors, empty vessels and not too few. Then go in and shut the door behind yourself and your sons and pour into all these vessels. And when one is full, set it aside." So she went from him and shut the door behind herself and her sons. And as she poured they brought the vessels to her. When the vessels were full, she said to her son, "Bring me another vessel." And he said to her, "There is not another." Then the oil stopped flowing. She came and told the man of God, and he said, "Go, sell the oil and pay your debts, and you and your sons can live on the rest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God meets a faithful widow’s debt through the little she already has, filling every empty vessel she brings until the debt is paid and her sons are free. The oil stopped only when the vessels ran out.

The wife of one of the sons of the prophets. She is one of their own. Her husband belonged to the company of prophets, Elisha’s own men (see the note on 2:1–8); he has died and left debt, and she speaks on the assumption that Elisha will remember him.

The creditor has come. He is not a criminal. Debt-slavery was lawful in Israel: a debtor or his children could be taken, and the law regulated it rather than forbidding it. Service was limited, the seventh year brought release, and the Jubilee restored the land (Exodus 21:7; Leviticus 25:39–41). Nehemiah found the same thing in his day and was furious (Nehemiah 5:5). The creditor is within his rights, and the law’s protections are not reaching her in time.

You know that your servant feared the LORD. Her husband feared the LORD, and yet he died in debt, and his widow is losing her children. The Bible is unembarrassed about this: fearing God is no guarantee against poverty, and the families of faithful men have been poor in every century. That is no sign that God has forgotten them, as the rest of this scene shows.

What have you in the house? Elisha begins by asking what she has, as God habitually does. God asked Moses what was in his hand (Exodus 4:2), and Jesus asked his disciples how many loaves they had (Mark 6:38). He starts with what is actually there, not with what she wishes were there. She says she has nothing, and mentions the one jar only as an afterthought, because to her it does not count. It is about to be the means of her rescue.

Borrow vessels from all your neighbors, empty vessels and not too few. She has to knock on doors in a village where everybody knows her husband died owing money, and ask for empty pots with no reason that will not sound like madness. Faith is very rarely a private feeling; here it is a woman walking up a street carrying other people’s jars. Not too few is as close as the chapter comes to telling her the size of what is about to happen, and it leaves the number to her.

Shut the door. No crowd, no witnesses, nothing to see. Elijah’s great works were public: an altar on a mountain with a nation watching. A great deal of Elisha’s ministry happens behind a closed door in somebody’s house, and this is the first of it.

They brought the vessels to her. Picture the room: the boys running empty pots to their mother and carrying full ones away, while she pours from a flask that should have run dry after the first. The sons who were about to be taken are the workforce of their own rescue.

Then the oil stopped flowing. Not because the flask was empty, but because she ran out of pots. The supply was limited only by what she could receive, and that had been fixed out in the street, by how many doors she knocked on. Do not turn that into a formula about how much faith unlocks how much blessing, because the chapter does not say that and other chapters would contradict it. But let it stand as it is written: there were more pots in that village.

Pay your debts, and you and your sons can live on the rest. Paying comes first, and in full: the creditor is not struck down but paid what he is owed. Then God leaves her enough to live on, so that the same creditor is not back at the door a few months later.

A debt paid, not pretended away. This is the way of God’s mercy on the largest scale. Our debt to him was not overlooked; it was paid, when Christ cancelled “the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands… nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14). Those he sets free he does not leave to fall back into the creditor’s hands.

Should I expect God to pay my debts like this? Not by a flask that keeps pouring. What carries over is the pattern: God cares about the debts of widows and the futures of their children, he usually begins with what is already in the house, and his people are meant to be the neighbours with the jars (James 1:27). Pray, and take honest advice and the next ordinary step; and let the church be a place where no widow faces the creditor alone.

Where Christians differ: do miracles like this continue? Continuationists believe God still gives gifts of miracles and healing and may work wonders like Elisha’s today. Others hold that such wonders clustered in rare seasons when God was confirming his word: Moses, Elijah and Elisha, then Christ and his apostles. This commentary’s view: the sign-gifts ceased with the apostles, so no one today can work wonders at will; yet God is free to act as he pleases, and all agree that he still answers prayer and provides for his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — I Dwell Among My Own People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Generosity that asks nothing back is met with a gift the giver had not dared to ask for. A wealthy woman of Shunem feeds Elisha whenever he passes and, convinced that he is a holy man of God, builds and furnishes a room for him on the roof (vv. 8–10). Offered a word at court in return, she declines: she lives among her own people (vv. 11–13). Gehazi names what she lacks, a son, for her husband is old (vv. 14–15). Elisha promises one in the words once spoken to Sarah; she begs him not to raise her hopes falsely (v. 16), and the following spring she bears a son (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is given in words first spoken at Mamre about Sarah (Gen. 18:10). Elisha is not making up a promise of his own; he repeats one that God had made and kept before.
verseByVerse.examples: Her reply is the most human sentence in the chapter. It is not unbelief but a woman who has stopped permitting herself to hope in that particular place: it is what disappointment sounds like when it has been thorough.

verseByVerse.quote: One day Elisha went on to Shunem, where a wealthy woman lived, who urged him to eat some food. So whenever he passed that way, he would turn in there to eat food. And she said to her husband, "Behold now, I know that this is a holy man of God who is continually passing our way. Let us make a small room on the roof with walls and put there for him a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp, so that whenever he comes to us, he can go in there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wealthy woman recognises Elisha as a holy man of God and, with her husband, makes room for him in her home: generosity thought through, and freely given.

A wealthy woman. In Hebrew, a great woman, of standing and means. Shunem lay in the Jezreel valley, on the road Elisha travelled. Every initiative in this scene is hers: she notices him and presses him to eat until the meal becomes a standing arrangement.

A holy man of God who is continually passing our way. Nothing had happened to prompt it: he had performed no sign at her table and made no claim. She had watched a man eat in her house again and again over a long time, and drawn a conclusion. That is nearly always how a person’s godliness comes to be known, and it is a better method than the one most people use. She did not judge him by a platform, a reputation or an occasion when he was at his best.

A bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp. Somewhere to sleep, somewhere to eat, somewhere to sit, and light to see by: the entire requirement of a man who works with his mind, thought through item by item. She did not put up a shrine. She built him a room he could live in, on the flat roof, so that he could come and go without troubling the household. Hospitality of this kind is almost never spontaneous. It comes from thinking concretely about what another person needs, and then paying for it.

A room for the Lord’s servants. A greater prophet than Elisha had “nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58) and was housed by friends like Martha (Luke 10:38). He promised a prophet’s reward to whoever receives a prophet (Matthew 10:41), and counts what is done for the least of his people as done to him (Matthew 25:40). The spare room and the meal for a visiting missionary are never small things to him.
verseByVerse.note: Shunem lay in the Jezreel valley.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he came there, and he turned into the chamber and rested there. And he said to Gehazi his servant, "Call this Shunammite." When he had called her, she stood before him. And he said to him, "Say now to her, 'See, you have taken all this trouble for us; what is to be done for you? Would you have a word spoken on your behalf to the king or to the commander of the army?'" She answered, "I dwell among my own people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Offered a reward and a word at court, the Shunammite declines: she is content among her own people and wants nothing back.

He turned into the chamber and rested there. The gift is used as it was meant to be, quietly. And it is from that room, rested and grateful, that Elisha asks what can be done for her: kindness received makes him want to give something back.

Say now to her. She is standing in front of him, in her own house, and he speaks to her through Gehazi. Some of that is the ordinary formality of the age between a holy man and a woman of the household, and it is not presented as a fault. But keep it in view, because it puts one man permanently between Elisha and the people who come to him: the man who will try to push her off his master’s feet (v. 27), and who in the next chapter runs after a foreign general with a lie in his mouth and his master’s name on it. Controlling access to an important person does something to a man.

A word spoken on your behalf to the king. He offers what a wealthy woman might want: a word in the right ear at court or with the army. In a country where disputes and requisitions were settled by who knew whom, that was a substantial gift.

I dwell among my own people. It is a refusal of payment and a statement of contentment, the rarest answer anybody gives a powerful man. Remember it, because four chapters on she will be a refugee who has lost her land, standing before the king she declined to be introduced to (8:1–6).

The freedom of wanting nothing from the king. Few answers sound stranger to modern ears, in a culture of the next step: the better contact, the introduction that might open a door. Ambition is not wrong, but the restless kind turns every friendship into a ladder and never arrives, because there is always a king further up. This woman is not lacking energy; she has just built and furnished a room. She is simply not for sale, because she is not afraid of being overlooked. Her contentment is not low expectations but a heart already secure. The New Testament gives its ground in one sentence: “be content with what you have, for he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5). And in Christ we already have what no court could give: “access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18). People who have been brought into the King’s own presence can stop climbing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "What then is to be done for her?" Gehazi answered, "Well, she has no son, and her husband is old." He said, "Call her." And when he had called her, she stood in the doorway.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman who wanted nothing has one great unspoken longing, a son, and Gehazi names it.

She has no son, and her husband is old. She had told the truth as far as it went, and there was one thing she wanted so much that she had not mentioned it. There will be no son, and the room she built is on a house that will pass to somebody else’s family.

The one unmentioned thing. People who say they need nothing are often telling the truth about everything except one thing, and the reason it goes unmentioned is not modesty. Saying it aloud costs more than doing without.

She stood in the doorway. Half in and half out, which is exactly where a person stands when she suspects what is coming and is not sure she can bear it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "At this season, about this time next year, you shall embrace a son." And she said, "No, my lord, O man of God; do not lie to your servant." But the woman conceived, and she bore a son about that time the following spring, as Elisha had said to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha promises a son in the words God once spoke to Sarah, and though the woman cannot bear to hope again, God keeps his word.

About this time next year. The promise is not in Elisha’s own words. It is the sentence spoken at a tent door at Mamre: “I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son” (Genesis 18:10, 14). The woman inside that tent laughed, and was asked whether anything is too hard for the LORD.

Do not lie to your servant. This woman does not laugh. She says something sharper and sadder. It is neither unbelief nor rudeness. It is what a person says who has been disappointed so often in one particular place that she has decided to stop hoping there, and who hears a fresh promise about it as a cruelty rather than a kindness. Anyone who has longed for a child, a marriage, sobriety or a reconciliation long enough knows the feeling: do not start me off again.

He lets it stand. The man of God does not argue with her, rebuke her for weak faith or explain that God is able. He has said what he was given to say.

The woman conceived, and she bore a son. The promise is kept, recorded almost like a ledger entry, and the writer does not linger. He needs us to have the boy, and to know exactly how he was given, before the next paragraph takes him away.

Sons given against hope. Sarah’s Isaac, Hannah’s Samuel, Elizabeth’s John: again and again God gives a son where there was no hope, so that all know the child came from him. The line reaches its height when an angel tells a virgin she will bear a son, because “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). The boy at Shunem is a small mercy in that story; the Son given through Mary is the promise itself.

What it does not mean. Not that every childless couple who prays will be given a child. Many faithful believers carry that longing unanswered all their lives, and it is no sign of weak faith or of God’s displeasure. But God sees the longing no one mentions, and it is safe to bring it to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–37 — Did I Ask My Lord for a Son?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who gave the son gives him back from death, through a prophet who prays and lays himself on the dead. The boy collapses in the harvest field and dies on his mother’s lap at noon (vv. 18–20). She lays him on the prophet’s bed, tells no one, and rides hard to Carmel (vv. 21–25). At Elisha’s feet she pours out her grief: she never asked for a son (vv. 26–28). She will not leave without the prophet himself, and the staff Gehazi lays on the child’s face does nothing (vv. 29–31). Behind a shut door Elisha prays and stretches himself on the boy until he sneezes and opens his eyes (vv. 32–35), and the mother receives her son again (vv. 36–37).
verseByVerse.theology: The man of God says plainly that he does not know what is wrong (v. 27), and does not pretend otherwise for a moment.
verseByVerse.examples: She has been offered a staff and a servant, but she insists on the prophet himself, and she says so in the very words Elisha once used to Elijah (v. 30; 2:2).

verseByVerse.quote: When the child had grown, he went out one day to his father among the reapers. And he said to his father, "Oh, my head, my head!" The father said to his servant, "Carry him to his mother." And when he had lifted him and brought him to his mother, the child sat on her lap till noon, and then he died. And she went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God and shut the door behind him and went out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promised son dies in his mother’s arms, and she lays him on the prophet’s bed and goes for the man who promised him.

Oh, my head, my head! A boy old enough to walk out to the harvest field to be with the men, in the sun, and something goes wrong in his head.

Carry him to his mother. His father, in the middle of the harvest and with no idea that this is serious, sends him home with a servant. It is the ordinary reflex of an ordinary busy man, and it is not held against him.

The child sat on her lap till noon, and then he died. There is no medical detail and there are no last words. The writer gives the hours, the lap and one verb, and anyone who has sat like that does not need the rest filled in.

Laid him on the bed of the man of God. From here to the end of the scene this woman does not put a foot wrong. She lays him on the bed she bought, in the room she built, for the man who promised he would be born. Then she shuts the door and tells nobody. She is not in denial. She has taken the body to the place the promise came from, and she is going to fetch the man who made it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she called to her husband and said, "Send me one of the servants and one of the donkeys, that I may quickly go to the man of God and come back again." And he said, "Why will you go to him today? It is neither new moon nor Sabbath." She said, "All is well." Then she saddled the donkey, and she said to her servant, "Urge the animal on; do not slacken the pace for me unless I tell you." So she set out and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her coming, he said to Gehazi his servant, "Look, there is the Shunammite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Telling no one more than “All is well”, the mother rides hard to Carmel to find the man of God.

It is neither new moon nor Sabbath. Her husband’s question tells us in passing about the religion of ordinary people in the northern kingdom: they visited a prophet on the holy days, at the new moon and the Sabbath, as you might go to church. A visit on an ordinary working day needed explaining.

All is well. The word is shalom. His son is dead on a bed on his own roof, and she says all is well and rides out. It is not quite a lie. It is a woman who has decided that the conversation which would follow the truth is one she has no time for.

Urge the animal on. Carmel is a long ride across the plain, fifteen miles or more. Her instruction is: do not slow down on my account. She will be shaken half to pieces and she does not care.

To the man of God at Mount Carmel. The place matters. That ridge is where Elisha’s master Elijah stood alone against the prophets of Baal and called down fire (1 Kings 18), and it is where Elisha now keeps his base. The mother of a dead boy has come to the mountain where God answered.

verseByVerse.quote: Run at once to meet her and say to her, 'Is all well with you? Is all well with your husband? Is all well with the child?'" And she answered, "All is well." And when she came to the mountain to the man of God, she caught hold of his feet. And Gehazi came to push her away. But the man of God said, "Leave her alone, for she is in bitter distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me." Then she said, "Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say, 'Do not deceive me?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the prophet’s feet the mother pours out the grief she has hidden from everyone: she never asked for this son, and now he has been taken.

Is all well with the child? All is well, she says again, to Gehazi, and rides past him. She is not going to hand this over at the door.

Gehazi came to push her away. His instinct is protective and entirely wrong. It is the standing hazard of everybody who works close to a person others need: managing access, deciding who is in a fit state to be seen. Leave her alone should be written over the desk of every gatekeeper in every church.

The LORD has hidden it from me. The man who saw her coming from a distance does not know why she has come, and he says so aloud, in front of his servant and of her, without embarrassment and without inventing anything to cover it. Prophets in this book are not all-knowing and never claim to be; they know what they are told and nothing else. A man who will admit that God has not told him can be trusted when he says God has.

Did I ask my lord for a son? Did I not say, “Do not deceive me”? She asked for nothing; the child was a gift she never applied for. And she had said, in that doorway, in those words, that this was exactly what she was afraid of. That is the hardest version of this sorrow, and a great many people live in it: not the thing longed for and never given, but the thing never asked for, given anyway, and then taken back. She had protected herself carefully, God overruled the protection, and now the wound is exactly where she said it would be.

Grief brought to the right feet. Elisha does not rebuke her bluntness, and neither does God; the Psalms are full of such words. When Mary of Bethany fell at Jesus’ feet saying, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:32), he wept, and went to the tomb. Honest grief at his feet is not unbelief but faith that still knows where to go.

Answered with a living boy. The chapter does not answer her with an argument but with a living boy. Not every grieving reader is given that answer in this life; the question at the end of the note on vv. 36–37 speaks to them.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to Gehazi, "Tie up your garment and take my staff in your hand and go. If you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not reply. And lay my staff on the face of the child." Then the mother of the child said, "As the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you." So he arose and followed her. Gehazi went on ahead and laid the staff on the face of the child, but there was no sound or sign of life. Therefore he returned to meet him and told him, "The child has not awakened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mother will not settle for the prophet’s servant and staff, and she is right: the staff laid on the child does nothing.

Tie up your garment. Tuck up your robe so you can run, and greet nobody on the road: greetings in that world were long, and this is an instruction about speed.

As the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you. That is word for word what Elisha himself said to Elijah, three times, on the road from Gilgal to the Jordan (2:2, 4, 6). She may not have known it; the writer did, and the effect is that a woman from Shunem holds the prophet to the standard he set for himself. She will not be handed off to an assistant with a piece of equipment. If he comes, there is hope; if he sends, there is not.

Lay my staff on the face of the child. The staff does nothing, and the failure is in the chapter on purpose. Elisha’s staff is the nearest thing in these books to a relic, a holy object thought to carry power in itself. His own servant carries it, and laid on a dead child’s face it produces no sound and no movement. There is no power in the object or in the deputy. The mother was right.

No substitute for the living God. Every age is tempted to trust an object, a ritual or a minister in place of God himself. The church’s helpers point to Christ; they cannot stand in for him, and no one need settle for less than coming to him (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: When Elisha came into the house, he saw the child lying dead on his bed. So he went in and shut the door behind the two of them and prayed to the LORD. Then he went up and lay on the child, putting his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. And as he stretched himself upon him, the flesh of the child became warm. Then he got up again and walked once back and forth in the house, and went up and stretched himself upon him. The child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind a shut door Elisha prays and stretches himself on the dead boy, mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, hands to hands, until God gives the child back his life.

Prayed to the LORD. The door shuts on the prophet and the body, and the first thing he does is pray, though we are not given a word of it. Elijah’s prayer over the boy at Zarephath is recorded, and it is an accusation: “O LORD my God, have you brought calamity even upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by killing her son?” (1 Kings 17:20). Whatever a man says to God with a dead child on the bed behind him, this writer does not think it ours to overhear.

Putting his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. A living man lies along a dead one, matching himself to him part for part. Elijah had done something like it, stretching himself on the widow’s son three times (1 Kings 17:21). This is closer and more costly. It is more than a way of passing on warmth: he has to get down onto the bed of the dead, take that small body’s posture, put his living mouth where a dead mouth is and his open eyes on closed ones, and stay there. He cannot do it from the doorway, and he cannot do it with a staff.

Walked once back and forth in the house. Then he climbs onto the bed a second time. No inventor of stories would supply that detail: something has happened and it is not enough, and he can only keep on.

The child sneezed seven times. Then the boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes, the other detail nobody would have made up. It is the least dignified way imaginable for a resurrection to begin, and exactly what an eyewitness remembers.

Matched to us part for part. It is a picture, not a prophecy, but many Christians have seen in it the shape of what God did. “Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14). Not a word from a safe distance or an instrument sent ahead: the Son lay down alongside us, in our own flesh, matched to us part for part, and went as far down as we had gone, into death itself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he summoned Gehazi and said, "Call this Shunammite." So he called her. And when she came to him, he said, "Pick up your son." She came and fell at his feet, bowing to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha gives the boy back to his mother, a sign of the God who gives life, and a pointer to the one who would raise the dead by his own word.

Call this Shunammite… Pick up your son. “Call this Shunammite” are the words Elisha used when the promise was first given (v. 12). He does not carry the boy down or make a speech; he has her called and hands the child back in three words. The son she never asked for is given to her a second time.

Fell at his feet, bowing to the ground. She says not a word. She had spoken plenty on the mountain; here she gets down on the floor, and then she picks up her boy and walks out with him.

Zarephath and Nain. The scene has been played once before and will be once more. Elijah carried the widow’s boy down and said, “See, your son lives” (1 Kings 17:23). And at Nain a man stopped a funeral, spoke to a dead body, “and Jesus gave him to his mother” (Luke 7:15). When Hebrews lists what faith has done in the world it includes this line: “Women received back their dead by resurrection” (Hebrews 11:35), very probably with this chapter and 1 Kings 17 in mind.

The prophets asked; the Son commanded. Measure the three against each other; the difference is not in the men’s sincerity. Elijah stretched himself out three times and pleaded. Elisha prayed, lay on the body twice and paced the room in between. Jesus touched the bier and said, “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke 7:14), and death did as it was told.

Why did her son come back when mine did not? A bereaved parent cannot help asking, and this chapter must never be used to wound. These raisings were rare signs given at turning points, and every child raised in Scripture died again later. They were not a promise that faith brings every child home from the sickbed, and a parent whose child died has not failed a test this mother passed. What the signs point to is the one who said, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25), who wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35), and who will one day give back all his people, when “death shall be no more” (Revelation 21:4). Believers grieve, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13); and a grieving family needs the patient company of the church far more than explanations.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In famine the word of the LORD takes death out of the pot and makes a little food enough. At Gilgal one of the prophets shreds poisonous wild gourds into the company’s stew, and the cry goes up that there is death in the pot (vv. 38–40). Elisha throws in flour, and the stew is harmless (v. 41). Then a man brings the prophet twenty barley loaves of the firstfruits. Elisha has them set before a hundred men, and, as the LORD said, they eat and have some left (vv. 42–44). The God who heals what is poisoned also supplies what is lacking.
verseByVerse.theology: Flour cannot cure poison, any more than salt could heal the spring at Jericho (2:21). The sign is arranged so that nobody can give the credit to the method. The poison got into the common pot through a man who was trying to help, and the answer was not to throw out the pot.
verseByVerse.examples: The last three verses are a rehearsal for a hillside in Galilee: barley loaves, the poor man's grain; a servant objecting that the numbers do not work; a crowd fed; and food left over.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elisha came again to Gilgal when there was a famine in the land. And as the sons of the prophets were sitting before him, he said to his servant, "Set on the large pot, and boil stew for the sons of the prophets." One of them went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine and gathered from it his lap full of wild gourds, and came and cut them up into the pot of stew, not knowing what they were. And they poured out some for the men to eat. But while they were eating of the stew, they cried out, "O man of God, there is death in the pot!" And they could not eat it. He said, "Then bring flour." And he threw it into the pot and said, "Pour some out for the men, that they may eat." And there was no harm in the pot. A man came from Baal-shalishah, bringing the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain in his sack. And Elisha said, "Give to the men, that they may eat." But his servant said, "How can I set this before a hundred men?" So he repeated, "Give them to the men, that they may eat, for thus says the LORD, 'They shall eat and have some left.'" So he set it before them. And they ate and had some left, according to the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In famine the word of the LORD makes a poisoned pot harmless and makes twenty loaves feed a hundred men, with some left over.

Set on the large pot. A famine, a company of student prophets with nothing, and the head of the school telling his servant to put the big pot on. Whatever else Elisha is, he is running a household that has to be fed.

He found a wild vine… not knowing what they were. One of them goes out hungry to find something for the pot, comes back with a lapful of wild gourds (see the box below), and shreds the lot into the communal stew. No wickedness appears anywhere in this story. A well-meaning man tried to help, was ignorant, and poisoned the whole company’s dinner.

Then bring flour. Flour does not neutralise poison, any more than salt sweetens a spring. Elisha’s signs are arranged so that the material used could not possibly have done it: a handful of salt at Jericho (2:21), a handful of flour here, a stick thrown into the water two chapters on (6:6). And what he does not do is throw out the pot. The meal is not abandoned, and the man who spoiled it is not named or shamed. The stew that was death is served out and eaten.

Bread of the firstfruits. A small detail carries a good deal. Firstfruits belonged by law to the priests (Numbers 18:13), and this man carries his to a prophet instead, because the priesthood in the north belonged to Jeroboam’s system, men appointed to serve two golden calves. A believer in the north, in a famine, walks past the official religion and brings his offering to Elisha.

Give to the men, that they may eat. The loaves were a gift to the man of God personally, in a famine, and they are out of his hands in the same breath.

How can I set this before a hundred men? The servant’s arithmetic is correct: twenty small barley loaves among a hundred men is a mouthful each. Elisha does not argue. He repeats the instruction with the word of the LORD attached, and a detail that cannot be hedged: they shall eat and have some left. And it happened according to the word of the LORD, the phrase that runs through this whole book (see the introduction).

The same shape, a greater scale. Hold this beside a hillside in Galilee: a crowd with nothing to eat; a disciple who says, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little” (John 6:7); loaves that only John calls barley (John 6:9); everyone fed, and food left over. Elisha had twenty loaves for a hundred men; Jesus had five for five thousand, and twelve baskets of fragments were gathered. The people who ate had this chapter in their Scriptures, and straight afterwards they said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!” (John 6:14). They were right to call him a prophet, but the word was too small for him. Elisha handed on bread that ran out; Jesus said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

There is death in the pot! Take the cry out of the kitchen, because it names something that happens in churches. The poison came in not through an enemy but through a member of the household trying to contribute, who had picked something off a wild vine without knowing what it was. That is how most bad teaching enters a congregation. The answer is neither to throw out the pot nor to shame the man, but to bring what makes it wholesome again: the word of God rightly taught.

Uncertain wording. The word translated wild gourds occurs only here, though a related word describes the carved gourds in Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:18). The exact plant is not certain. Most identify it with the colocynth, a bitter desert gourd that looks like a small melon and is a violent purgative, dangerous in quantity; others suggest a wild cucumber. Either way, the men knew at the first mouthful that something was badly wrong.

4.theology:
What have you in the house? (vv. 2-6). God begins with what is actually there, and the jar she counted as nothing is what saves her. The oil stopped because she ran out of pots, not because God ran out of oil. That is no formula for getting more from God, but it should be left to say what it says.

Do not lie to your servant (v. 16). Her answer is not unbelief but self-protection, and Elisha does not rebuke her for it. He says what he was given to say and lets it stand.

The LORD has hidden it from me (v. 27). The willingness to say "God has not told me" is most of the reason you can trust a man when he says God has. In the same verse Gehazi is stopped in three words: leave her alone.

The staff fails (v. 31). There is no power in the staff or in the servant who carried it. The mother had refused both, using the very words of loyalty Elisha once spoke to Elijah (2:2), and she was right.

Three boys handed back. Elijah and Elisha pleaded and laboured over the body; Jesus touched a bier and spoke. The prophets asked. The Son commanded.

Twenty barley loaves (vv. 42-44). Twenty loaves to a hundred, with some left; five barley loaves to five thousand, with twelve baskets gathered. The crowd that ate in Galilee called Jesus the Prophet. They were right that he was a prophet, but he is far more than that.
4.examples:
Then: A woman whose son had died on her lap at midday carried him upstairs, laid him on the prophet's bed, shut the door, told everyone that all was well, and rode to Carmel without slowing down.

Now: Three things. First, do not lie to your servant. If there is a place where you have quietly decided to stop hoping, you will recognise her, and nobody in this chapter treats her as faithless for it. Second, Gehazi's hand out to push her away. Anyone who works near a person others need becomes a gatekeeper eventually; leave her alone belongs over that desk, and the church that serves a Lord who never turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37) has no business keeping the undignified at a distance. Third, the pot. Bad teaching usually comes into a church through a well-meaning member who did not know what he had picked up. The answer is to put the teaching right, without giving up on the church or shaming the man.

keyVerse.quote: So he set it before them. And they ate and had some left, according to the word of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s last words name what has been at work in all four scenes: not oil, a staff or flour, but the word of the LORD. It fills empty vessels, gives and restores a son, and makes a little food enough, and the phrase runs through the whole of Kings. It also prepares for the day when the Word made flesh would feed the hungry with barley loaves and have baskets left over.

4.reflection:
Elisha began by asking the widow, “What have you in the house?” (v. 2), and her one jar of oil became the means of her rescue. What small resources, gifts or opportunities do you tend to dismiss as nothing, and how might God use them? Who around you needs a neighbour with jars?

The Shunammite answered the offer of influence at court with “I dwell among my own people” (v. 13). Where do you feel the pull to climb, impress or secure the right connections? How does Christ’s promise “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5) set us free from it?

The grieving mother would not be handed off to Gehazi and his staff, and spoke to Elisha with raw honesty (vv. 27–30). What does her example teach about bringing grief and disappointment to God? Why is it important not to use this chapter to suggest that every sick or dying child will be restored?

Compare Elisha’s raising of the boy and feeding of the hundred with Jesus at Nain (Luke 7:11–17) and the feeding of the five thousand (John 6:1–14). What is the same, and what shows that Jesus is far greater than Elisha?

5.title: Naaman Healed
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master and in high favor, because by him the LORD had given victory to Syria. He was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.<sup>2</sup>Now the Syrians on one of their raids had carried off a little girl from the land of Israel, and she worked in the service of Naaman's wife.<sup>3</sup>She said to her mistress, "Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy."<sup>4</sup>So Naaman went in and told his lord, "Thus and so spoke the girl from the land of Israel."<sup>5</sup>And the king of Syria said, "Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel." So he went, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten changes of clothing.<sup>6</sup>And he brought the letter to the king of Israel, which read, "When this letter reaches you, know that I have sent to you Naaman my servant, that you may cure him of his leprosy."<sup>7</sup>And when the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, "Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends word to me to cure a man of his leprosy? Only consider, and see how he is seeking a quarrel with me."<sup>8</sup>But when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent to the king, saying, "Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come now to me, that he may know that there is a prophet in Israel."<sup>9</sup>So Naaman came with his horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha's house.<sup>10</sup>And Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, "Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall be restored, and you shall be clean."<sup>11</sup>But Naaman was angry and went away, saying, "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me and stand and call upon the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the place and cure the leper.<sup>12</sup>Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be clean?" So he turned and went away in a rage.<sup>13</sup>But his servants came near and said to him, "My father, it is a great word the prophet has spoken to you; will you not do it? Has he actually said to you, 'Wash, and be clean'?"<sup>14</sup>So he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.<sup>15</sup>Then he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and he came and stood before him.
