And he said, "Behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel; so accept now a present from your servant."<sup>16</sup>But he said, "As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none." And he urged him to take it, but he refused.<sup>17</sup>Then Naaman said, "If not, please let there be given to your servant two mule loads of earth, for from now on your servant will not offer burnt offering or sacrifice to any god but the LORD.<sup>18</sup>In this matter may the LORD pardon your servant: when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship there, leaning on my arm, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, when I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, the LORD pardon your servant in this matter."<sup>19</sup>He said to him, "Go in peace." But when Naaman had gone from him a short distance,<sup>20</sup>Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, "See, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not accepting from his hand what he brought. As the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him."<sup>21</sup>So Gehazi followed Naaman. And when Naaman saw someone running after him, he got down from the chariot to meet him and said, "Is all well?"<sup>22</sup>And he said, "All is well. My master has sent me to say, 'There have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim two young men of the sons of the prophets. Please give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothing.'"<sup>23</sup>And Naaman said, "Be pleased to accept two talents." And he urged him and tied up two talents of silver in two bags, with two changes of clothing, and laid them on two of his servants. And they carried them before Gehazi.<sup>24</sup>And when he came to the hill, he took them from their hand and put them in the house, and he sent the men away, and they departed.<sup>25</sup>He went in and stood before his master, and Elisha said to him, "Where have you been, Gehazi?" And he said, "Your servant went nowhere."<sup>26</sup>But he said to him, "Did not my heart go when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Was it a time to accept money and garments, olive orchards and vineyards, sheep and oxen, male servants and female servants?<sup>27</sup>Therefore the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your descendants forever." So he went out from his presence a leper, like snow.
5.overview:
Where we are. So far Elisha’s mercies have reached Israelites in their homes (chapter 4). Now they reach an enemy: the commander of the Syrian army that has been raiding Israel’s villages.

The message. God’s grace cannot be earned, bought or sold, and it reaches beyond Israel to the enemy and the outsider who will humble himself to receive it. Proud Naaman is cleansed only when he goes down into the Jordan as he was told, and goes home confessing that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Gehazi, who stood beside the prophet every day, tries to sell what God gave freely and takes Naaman’s leprosy instead.

Why it was said. Israel’s king had forgotten that there was a prophet in Israel, let alone a God (vv. 7–8; compare 1:3), and the nation prided itself on being God’s people while living like the nations (see the introduction). The chapter humbles that pride: the clearest confession of faith comes from a Syrian, and the judgment falls on an Israelite insider.

How the chapter makes its case. A great general is a leper, and a captive Israelite girl tells her mistress about the prophet in Samaria (vv. 1–3). Two kings turn it into diplomacy and a fortune, and the king of Israel despairs (vv. 4–7). Elisha sends for Naaman but will not come to the door; Naaman, enraged by a plain command to wash in the Jordan, is talked round by his servants, dips seven times and is clean (vv. 8–14). He confesses the LORD, Elisha refuses his gift, and Naaman asks for Israelite earth and for pardon in the house of Rimmon (vv. 15–19). Gehazi runs after him, lies for silver, lies again to his master, and goes out a leper (vv. 20–27).

Where it leads. Jesus drew the line from this chapter himself: “there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:27). It points to him by pattern and by the need it exposes. Christ touched lepers and made them clean (Mark 1:40–42), and opened God’s mercy to the nations. And Naaman’s cleansing, received freely, is the shape of the gospel: we are washed not by anything we pay or achieve, but by Christ, who went down into the Jordan among sinners, and then to the cross for them.

For us. Like Naaman, we would rather do some great thing, or pay, than simply receive. Get down off the chariot and be washed; then, like the captive girl, tell others where cleansing is found, and guard your heart against Gehazi’s sin of turning holy things into gain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — But He Was a Leper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s mercy begins with a great man’s need and a small girl’s word. Naaman is great, victorious by the LORD’s own hand, honoured, and a leper (v. 1). A captive Israelite girl serving his wife says the sentence the chapter turns on: if only her master were with the prophet in Samaria (vv. 2–3). The message climbs to the king of Syria, who sends a letter and a fortune to the king of Israel, assuming such favours are arranged between kings (vv. 4–6). The king of Israel tears his clothes. He knows that only God can kill and make alive, but he suspects a pretext for war and forgets the prophet in his own land (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's God was handing victories to Israel's enemy through a general who did not know his name, and one of that army's spoils was the child who would tell its commander where to be healed.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the address get lost on its way up. She said the prophet who is in Samaria; by the time the request reaches the top it is a state letter between kings with no prophet in it at all, and the king of Israel, who has a prophet a few streets away, can think of nothing but diplomacy. Power talks to power, and mislays the address a slave girl had exactly right.

verseByVerse.quote: Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master and in high favor, because by him the LORD had given victory to Syria. He was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. Now the Syrians on one of their raids had carried off a little girl from the land of Israel, and she worked in the service of Naaman's wife. She said to her mistress, "Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy." So Naaman went in and told his lord, "Thus and so spoke the girl from the land of Israel." And the king of Syria said, "Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel." So he went, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten changes of clothing. And he brought the letter to the king of Israel, which read, "When this letter reaches you, know that I have sent to you Naaman my servant, that you may cure him of his leprosy." And when the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, "Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends word to me to cure a man of his leprosy? Only consider, and see how he is seeking a quarrel with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naaman has everything the world admires except the one thing it cannot give, and God sends him the answer through a captive Israelite girl, while Israel’s own king forgets that there is a God in Israel who heals.

Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria. A great man, in high favour, a mighty man of valour: the sort of sentence a state funeral is built out of. And then, but he was a leper. Everybody’s life has a but in it somewhere, and most people’s is not visible from the outside; Naaman’s was on his skin. The Hebrew word covers a range of skin diseases, not only what we call leprosy, and plainly it had not put him out of society: he commands an army and stands before a king, which he could not have done in Israel, where such a man lived outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45–46). But it was there every morning, and no amount of favour touched it.

By him the LORD had given victory to Syria. The most startling clause in the chapter, mentioned on the way to something else. Not Rimmon, not Syrian arms: the God of Israel had handed victories to Israel’s enemy through a pagan general. He rules the nations, including the ones that trouble his people.

A little girl from the land of Israel. One of the things that army brought home from one of those raids was a child. Count what she has lost: home, country, parents, freedom, and even her name, which the writer never gives. She is now domestic staff in the house of the man whose army took her.

Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! She had every reason to say nothing, and some reason to be quietly glad about the disease. What she says instead, to her mistress, in the enemy’s house, is that there is a man in her country who could heal him. A slave, a child, a foreigner and a girl, four reasons in that world for her opinion to count for nothing, and she is the only person in the chapter who does any evangelism. Nobody asked her. She volunteered it, and she never appears again; the greatest thing that happened to that household happened because of her, and nobody is recorded as telling her how it turned out.

I will send a letter to the king of Israel. The message climbs the chain of command and loses the one thing that mattered. The girl said the prophet; the king writes to the king, because in his world such favours are arranged between kings. With the letter go ten talents of silver, something like seven hundred and fifty pounds in weight, six thousand shekels of gold and ten changes of clothing: a fortune on the road, to buy a cure.

Am I God, to kill and to make alive? The king of Israel is right about the theology and wrong about everything else. He is echoing Scripture, perhaps without knowing it: “I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39). What he cannot do is take the next step. There is a prophet in his kingdom who has raised a dead child and fed a hundred men, and everyone seems to know where he lives except the king, who is calculating how Syria means to use this for a war. It is the question of chapter 1 again: is there no God in Israel (1:3)? There is, and Israel’s own king has forgotten him.

What success cannot reach. Our culture is very good at the first half of Naaman’s verse: the record, the reputation, the life that reads well at a retirement dinner. It has no answer for the clause that follows. Leo Tolstoy’s story The Death of Ivan Ilyich tells of a successful, correct judge who knocks his side in a small fall while hanging curtains in his fine new house, and slowly realises, as the injury kills him, that a life built on being proper and approved has nothing to say to death. The Bible is more honest, and more hopeful. It agrees that every human story carries a but that no favour can reach: sin, and the death that comes with it. Then it adds a second that changes the whole sentence: “But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us” (Ephesians 2:4). Naaman’s cure did not come out of his record, and neither does ours.

In everyday life. Most of what God does through ordinary Christians is like the girl’s word: one sentence, said to somebody in your own house, and no way of finding out what became of it. Say it anyway.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” covers several skin diseases (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cleansing comes not by ceremony or payment but by humbly obeying God’s word. Elisha sends for Naaman so that he may know there is a prophet in Israel (v. 8), yet does not come out to him: a messenger tells him to wash in the Jordan seven times (vv. 9–10). Naaman is furious; he had pictured a ceremony, and Damascus has better rivers (vv. 11–12). His servants reason with him: he would have done some great thing, so why not this simple one (v. 13)? He goes down and dips seven times, as the man of God said, and his flesh becomes like a little child’s (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Naaman had the whole ceremony written before he arrived: the prophet emerges, stands, invokes the name, waves a hand over the spot. What offends him is that God does not follow his plan.
verseByVerse.examples: The Jordan is not medicine but the border, the river Israel crossed to come into the land. Naaman is being asked to go down into the water of the people he has spent his career raiding, and to come up out of it six times still a leper before anything happens at all.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent to the king, saying, "Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come now to me, that he may know that there is a prophet in Israel." So Naaman came with his horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha's house. And Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, "Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall be restored, and you shall be clean." But Naaman was angry and went away, saying, "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me and stand and call upon the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the place and cure the leper. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be clean?" So he turned and went away in a rage. But his servants came near and said to him, "My father, it is a great word the prophet has spoken to you; will you not do it? Has he actually said to you, 'Wash, and be clean'?" So he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naaman is cleansed not by ceremony, payment or the prophet’s touch, but by humbling himself to do the plain thing God’s word told him.

That he may know that there is a prophet in Israel. Elisha’s message to the king is the sentence the chapter exists for. Not that he may be cured, though he will be: what is at stake is whether a Syrian commander goes home knowing whose country he has been raiding.

With his horses and chariots… Elisha sent a messenger to him. Picture it from the street: chariots, cavalry, a general and a fortune in silver drawn up outside somebody’s front door. And Elisha does not come out. He sends a servant with a sentence: no interview, no laying on of hands. That is deliberate.

Behold, I thought. Naaman had it all planned: the prophet comes out, stands, calls on the name of his God, waves his hand over the place, and the cure follows. He had rehearsed the scene on the road from Damascus, and he got a messenger telling him to go and take a bath. He has not been refused; he has been promised a complete cure, free, on the spot. He is furious because it is being done the wrong way, without ceremony or deference, and with no part for him to play.

Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus. About the rivers he is simply correct. They run clear and cold off the mountains, and the Jordan south of Galilee is a slow, brown river between mud banks. That is the point: nothing in that water is good for skin. The Jordan is the border, the water Israel crossed into the land and the water that opened for Elijah and Elisha (2:8, 14). It matters for what it means, not for anything its water can do.

My father… will you not do it? His servants have nerve as well as logic: junior men addressing a raging general as my father, the word for a man you serve and also love. Their argument is a good one. If the prophet had asked something enormous, he would have done it without blinking; he has been asked something small, and the smallness is his only objection. This is the second time Naaman is rescued by people beneath him: a captive child told him where to go, and his servants get him into the water.

He went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan. The armour comes off in front of his men, and the commander of the army of Syria puts his head under the river of the people he has spent his career raiding, seven times. No gradual improvement is described. He goes under and comes up a leper, and again, and again: six times he has obeyed with nothing to show for it, with the men holding his clothes watching. That is where most people give up.

Like the flesh of a little child. The writer’s phrase for the healed skin echoes a little girl in verse 2: the same two Hebrew words, there in the feminine. His flesh came up like the flesh of the child who told him where to go. The writer leaves it there for anyone reading slowly.

But only Naaman the Syrian. At Nazareth Jesus told his neighbours that “there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:27), having just said the same of the widow of Zarephath (Luke 4:25–26). Israel had the promises, the law and the temple, and God healed the enemy commander. The congregation drove Jesus out and tried to throw him off a cliff for saying so. He read this chapter as a sign of the mercy he had come to bring to the nations, and then did in person what Elisha did at a distance: he touched a leper with his own hand, and the man was clean (Mark 1:40–42). When ten lepers were healed, the only one who came back to give thanks was a Samaritan (Luke 17:15–18), and Naaman’s ride back from the Jordan (v. 15) is the same journey.

A searching question. How much of our disappointment with God is disappointment that he did not do it the way we had pictured? Not that the prayer went unanswered, but that the answer came through an ordinary person, a long dull process, or advice from somebody junior, instead of the way we had staged it. Naaman’s story answers that with mercy: he was healed anyway.

Why is a free cure so offensive? Naaman’s anger is one of the most modern things in the Old Testament. Ask a high achiever for something heroic and he will rise to it; tell him there is nothing to achieve, only something to receive, and he feels insulted. The moralist wants to earn the cure by some great thing; the free spirit, like Naaman with his clear rivers, wants it on his own terms, through what he already admires. Both are ways of staying in charge of our own rescue, and the gospel offends them both by asking only that we go down and be washed. Yet notice where Naaman had to go. Centuries later the Son of God walked into this same river and asked to be baptised, though he had nothing to wash away (Matthew 3:13–15). He went down into the water of sinners first, standing in our place, so that what is left for us is the humble thing Naaman nearly refused: to get down off the chariot and receive.
verseByVerse.note: The Abana and Pharpar were the rivers of Damascus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Two Mule Loads of Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cleansed enemy becomes a worshipper, and grace refuses payment. Naaman returns and confesses that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel, and presses a gift on Elisha, who refuses it under oath (vv. 15–16). He asks for two mule loads of Israel’s earth, because he will sacrifice to no god but the LORD (v. 17). Then he raises, unasked, the one duty that troubles him: when his king bows in the house of Rimmon, leaning on his arm, he must bow too, and he asks the LORD’s pardon (v. 18). Elisha answers, Go in peace (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The gift is refused so that nobody can go home having bought it: a talent of silver would have turned the cure into something Naaman had paid a fair price for. Six verses later a man will sell it to him after all.
verseByVerse.examples: Naaman's theology is still half pagan (he thinks the God of Israel needs Israelite soil under the altar), while his devotion is entirely real. Elisha does not examine him on it. He sends a brand-new believer away in peace with a tender conscience and leaves God to do the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and he came and stood before him. And he said, "Behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel; so accept now a present from your servant." But he said, "As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none." And he urged him to take it, but he refused. Then Naaman said, "If not, please let there be given to your servant two mule loads of earth, for from now on your servant will not offer burnt offering or sacrifice to any god but the LORD. In this matter may the LORD pardon your servant: when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship there, leaning on my arm, and I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, when I bow myself in the house of Rimmon, the LORD pardon your servant in this matter." He said to him, "Go in peace." But when Naaman had gone from him a short distance,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cleansed general comes back to confess the LORD as the only God; Elisha refuses all payment so that grace stays free; and the new believer honestly names the one duty that troubles his conscience.

He returned to the man of God. He brings the whole column back, some twenty-five miles, to say one sentence to a man who would not come to the door for him.

There is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Not a compliment to a local deity but a denial of every god he has served, from the commander of a country whose state god is Rimmon. Elisha said he would know there is a prophet in Israel (v. 8); he has gone further, to the God of the prophet.

I will receive none. Elisha refuses flatly, under oath, and again when pressed. He has no objection to gifts as such; he lives on gifts from farmers (4:42). He refuses this one because of what it would make the healing into. If Naaman pays, he goes home with something he purchased, a rich foreigner and a useful holy man having settled on a price, and everything the chapter has been doing (the girl, the muddy river, the messenger at the door, the six fruitless dips) is undone at the last minute. Grace that can be paid for is not grace. God’s invitation has always been to come and buy “without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1). A few verses on, Gehazi will take a fee for it behind his master’s back.

Two mule loads of earth. A brand-new believer’s theology, and a strange mixture. The commitment is total: from now on, no sacrifice to any god but the LORD. The reasoning beneath it is still half pagan. He wants Israelite soil to take home because he assumes the God of Israel is attached to the ground of Israel, so that a proper altar in Damascus must stand on a patch of the right country. It is the territorial thinking of the age, the same instinct as the Syrian officers who decided that Israel’s God was a god of the hills and not of the valleys (1 Kings 20:23).

Room to grow. Elisha does not correct him. A man whose doctrine of God is plainly muddled is about to build an altar on imported dirt, and the prophet lets him go home with it. What is right in him is what matters most: he will sacrifice to nobody else. The rest will be sorted out, and not by an examination on the day of his conversion.

When I bow myself in the house of Rimmon. This is the difficult verse. Rimmon was the Syrian storm god, and Naaman’s office included being the arm the king leaned on in the temple; when the king went down, the man supporting him went down with him. It was a posture of state, and he could not resign the duty without resigning the office. Four things stand out. He raises it himself; nobody asked, and the first thing he does with his new faith is look ahead through his duties for the one that will not fit with it. He describes the act exactly, without softening it: the house of Rimmon is named three times in one verse. He asks pardon, not permission, which admits that the thing needs pardoning. And he is not asking to worship Rimmon; he has just renounced every other god, and is asking mercy in advance for a bodily posture in the course of a duty, because he knows how it looks and cannot see a way out.

Go in peace. The ordinary farewell, not a ruling that the compromise is fine (see the box below). Elisha sends a new believer home with a tender conscience, an honest question and God to work on him.

Naming the compromise. Here the passage is most useful. A man who names his one compromise aloud on the first day and asks God to pardon it is in a far better condition than a long-standing believer who has stopped noticing his. The danger is the compromise that has gone quiet. And the pardon Naaman asked for is the one God gives freely in Christ to everyone who confesses his sin (1 John 1:9), with the Spirit who keeps training a tender conscience.

Where Christians differ: was Naaman allowed to bow in Rimmon’s temple? Some interpreters, ancient and modern, read Go in peace as permission for an outward bow made purely as a civil duty, with no worship in the heart. Others hear only the ordinary farewell, which neither approves nor condemns but leaves a new believer’s conscience to God. This commentary’s view: Go in peace was not a ruling that compromise is fine; it sent a new believer home with the earth of Israel to worship the LORD alone (v. 17). Naaman asked pardon in advance because he knew the act was wrong, and the better reading is that he meant to bow only as the king’s attendant, not to the idol. Christians in public life may serve unbelieving rulers, but must not join in false worship (1 Corinthians 10:20–21).
verseByVerse.note: Naaman took Israelite soil home so that he could worship the LORD on it. Rimmon was a Syrian storm god.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The insider who tries to sell God’s free grace receives the leprosy the outsider left behind. Gehazi scorns this Naaman the Syrian and swears by the LORD to get something from him (v. 20). He runs after the chariot with an invented, plausible need, and Naaman gladly gives twice what he asks (vv. 21–23). Gehazi hides the silver and tells his master he went nowhere (vv. 24–25). Elisha saw it all, and names the estate Gehazi meant to build at the very moment grace was being shown to be free (v. 26). Naaman’s leprosy clings to him, and he goes out a leper, like snow (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Elisha's question in verse 26 names things Gehazi never touched, because he is describing not the theft but the plan: silver becomes land, land becomes flocks, and flocks become households. Elisha saw every step of the plan, and he saw the moment Gehazi chose for it.
verseByVerse.examples: Gehazi took Naaman's silver and got Naaman's leprosy. The chapter that opened with a captive girl who had nothing and gave away the best thing she knew closes with a servant who had everything and sold it.

verseByVerse.quote: Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, "See, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not accepting from his hand what he brought. As the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him." So Gehazi followed Naaman. And when Naaman saw someone running after him, he got down from the chariot to meet him and said, "Is all well?" And he said, "All is well. My master has sent me to say, 'There have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim two young men of the sons of the prophets. Please give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothing.'" And Naaman said, "Be pleased to accept two talents." And he urged him and tied up two talents of silver in two bags, with two changes of clothing, and laid them on two of his servants. And they carried them before Gehazi. And when he came to the hill, he took them from their hand and put them in the house, and he sent the men away, and they departed. He went in and stood before his master, and Elisha said to him, "Where have you been, Gehazi?" And he said, "Your servant went nowhere." But he said to him, "Did not my heart go when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Was it a time to accept money and garments, olive orchards and vineyards, sheep and oxen, male servants and female servants? Therefore the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your descendants forever." So he went out from his presence a leper, like snow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gehazi, who had lived beside the prophet, turns God’s free grace into money with a lie, and the leprosy Naaman left in the Jordan clings to him instead.

This Naaman the Syrian. Not the man just healed, not the convert who has confessed the God of Israel, but a foreigner who has got away with something. The contempt is plain. Then Gehazi swears as the LORD lives, his master’s oath (v. 16), in order to commit a fraud. He has stood next to holiness all this time and picked up the vocabulary and nothing else.

He got down from the chariot to meet him. A general climbs down to meet a household servant running up the road, a courtesy that shows what the Jordan has done to him. Is all well? he asks, and Gehazi says it is.

A talent of silver and two changes of clothing. The lie is well made. It is modest, one talent, not ten. It is plausible: the sons of the prophets are real and poor, and Elisha does feed them. It explains the change of mind without embarrassing his master, and it looks charitable. Fraud in religious work almost always looks like this: not a raid on the treasury but a small, credible, sympathetic need, invented by someone with enough inside knowledge to get the details right.

Be pleased to accept two talents. There is something painful in Naaman’s pleasure. He doubles the sum, presses it on Gehazi as he had pressed the gift on Elisha, ties up the bags and sends two of his own servants to carry them, because he thinks he is at last being allowed to give something back. At the hill Gehazi takes the bags, sends the men away and puts the silver in the house: the work of a man who has thought about how not to be caught.

Your servant went nowhere. He lies to the face of a man who all through this book has known things he was not told, with the silver in the next room. Did not my heart go means that Elisha was there in spirit and saw it all.

Olive orchards and vineyards, sheep and oxen, male servants and female servants. The list is longer than the crime. Gehazi took silver and clothing; Elisha names money and garments, and then orchards, vineyards, flocks, herds and servants. He is describing not the theft but the plan: an estate, with terraces and flocks and a household, and Gehazi living on it, retired from serving the man of God. Gehazi did not want two talents. He wanted a life, and the talents were the first instalment.

Was it a time? The question carries the whole rebuke. It is not whether it is ever right to accept money; Elisha lived on the gifts of the faithful. But at the very moment a Gentile soldier was being taught that the mercy of God is not for sale, the prophet’s servant sold it to him. Naaman will reach Damascus believing something slightly different about Israel’s God from what he believed on the riverbank, and it will be Gehazi’s doing.

The leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you. Not leprosy in general but his. The disease did not vanish when the Syrian came up out of the Jordan; it changed address. The writer’s last words are among the coldest in the book: a leper, like snow.

Sold for silver. Gehazi tried to sell the gift of God. Centuries later Judas, another man who had lived beside a great master, would sell the Giver himself for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), and Peter would tell Simon the magician, “you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money” (Acts 8:20). And the chapter’s strange exchange, one man’s leprosy moving onto another, finds its opposite in the gospel. Gehazi took Naaman’s disease as the punishment of his own sin. Christ, who had no sin, took ours on himself, freely: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Two servants. The chapter opens with a girl robbed of everything, in a foreign kitchen, giving away the one thing she had left, what she knew about her God. It closes with a man who had everything she lacked, his own country, his liberty and a place at the side of the greatest prophet of his generation, running down a road to turn it into silver. She was left with nothing and he went home a leper. The difference lay in their hearts, not their opportunities.

To your descendants forever: is that fair? The sentence is severe, and the clause about his descendants troubles modern readers. Two things can honestly be said. Households in that world stood or fell together, and a man building an estate for his sons out of stolen money is told that what they will actually inherit is the disease. And the writer does not tie it off neatly: in 8:4–5 Gehazi is found talking with the king of Israel about Elisha’s great works, which is not where a man excluded for leprosy would normally be. Kings does not always arrange its material in time order, and we are not told how to reconcile the two. It is better to say so than to invent something.

A word to the sick. This was a prophet’s particular judgment on a particular fraud, not a rule that sickness is punishment. Jesus refused that reading of a blind man’s suffering (John 9:2–3), and the law forbade Israel’s courts to put children to death for their fathers’ crimes (Deuteronomy 24:16).

5.theology:
The LORD had given victory to Syria (v. 1). Mentioned almost in passing, it says the God of Israel was handing victories to Israel's enemy, quite possibly including the raid that carried off the child who would tell that general where to be healed. He governs the armies of people who have never heard of him, and their spoils.

The address gets lost (vv. 3-7). A slave girl names the prophet exactly; kings turn it into diplomacy. It is chapter 1's question again: is there no God in Israel?

The script (v. 11). Naaman had planned in his head how the healing would go. He is not angry at being refused, for he is being healed for nothing. He is angry at being healed the wrong way, without ceremony and with no part for him to play. Much disappointment with God is of this kind: not that nothing came, but that it came through an ordinary person or a dull process instead of the way we had staged it.

Why the Jordan (v. 12). Nothing in that river is good for skin. It is Israel’s border, the water Israel crossed to enter the land.

Carried by juniors (vv. 3, 13). A captive child tells him where to go and his own staff get him into the water, opening with my father and an argument he cannot answer. The great man is carried the whole distance by people whose names are not recorded.

Like the flesh of a little child (v. 14). His flesh came up like the flesh of the little girl who told him where to go.

Nazareth (Luke 4:27). In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus pointed to Naaman and the widow of Zarephath as outsiders who received God’s mercy, and his home town tried to throw him off a cliff for it.

Refused, so that it cannot be bought (v. 16). Grace that can be paid for is not grace. Six verses later Elisha’s own servant takes payment for it after all.

Rimmon (vv. 17-19). A brand-new believer with half-pagan theology and an entirely real devotion raises his compromise himself and asks pardon rather than permission. Go in peace is a farewell, not a ruling that the compromise is acceptable. A compromise that still troubles you is less dangerous than one you have stopped noticing.

Was it a time? (v. 26). The charge is about timing: at the moment a Gentile was learning that God's mercy cannot be bought, the prophet's servant sold it to him.
5.examples:
Then: A girl taken in a raid, stripped of home, family, freedom and even her name, stood in the kitchen of the man whose army did it and told his wife where he could be healed, and never found out what came of it.

Now: Three things. First, the script in verse 11: how much of your disappointment with God is that the answer came the wrong way, through somebody junior, or a long dull process, or a plain instruction with no ceremony? Naaman was being healed for free while he raged. Second, Rimmon: name your compromise out loud and bring it to God, who pardons freely; the compromise to fear is the one that no longer troubles you. Third, the two servants: one had nothing and gave away the best thing she knew, the other had everything and sold it. The difference lay in their hearts, not in their opportunities.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel
keyVerse.note: This is what the whole chapter was for: Elisha sent for Naaman “that he may know” (v. 8), and here the enemy commander knows. The clearest confession of faith in the chapter comes from a Syrian outsider, cleansed by grace he could not buy, which is why Jesus used his story to show that God’s mercy was always meant for the nations (Luke 4:27).

5.reflection:
The captive girl had every reason to stay silent, yet her one sentence led to Naaman’s healing (vv. 2–3). Who is the “Naaman” in your own household or workplace, and what keeps you from speaking a simple word about where help is found?

Naaman was angry because God’s cure came in a plain and humbling way, not the way he had pictured (vv. 11–12). In what ways do we resist receiving God’s grace simply, and try to earn it or to have it on our own terms? How does Jesus going down into the Jordan for us (Matthew 3:13–15) answer that pride?

Naaman’s faith was real but his understanding was muddled, and he raised his own compromise honestly (vv. 17–18). How should a church welcome new believers whose understanding is still growing? Are there compromises in your life that have “gone quiet”?

Gehazi lived beside Elisha yet tried to profit from God’s free grace (vv. 20–27). What are the modern forms of treating spiritual things as a way to gain, and how can we guard our hearts against them?

6.title: The Borrowed Axe Head and the Siege of Samaria
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the sons of the prophets said to Elisha, "See, the place where we dwell under your charge is too small for us.<sup>2</sup>Let us go to the Jordan and each of us get there a log, and let us make a place for us to dwell there." And he answered, "Go."<sup>3</sup>Then one of them said, "Be pleased to go with your servants." And he answered, "I will go."<sup>4</sup>So he went with them. And when they came to the Jordan, they cut down trees.<sup>5</sup>But as one was felling a log, his axe head fell into the water, and he cried out, "Alas, my master! It was borrowed."<sup>6</sup>Then the man of God said, "Where did it fall?" When he showed him the place, he cut off a stick and threw it in there and made the iron float.<sup>7</sup>And he said, "Take it up." So he reached out his hand and took it.<sup>8</sup>Once when the king of Syria was warring against Israel, he took counsel with his servants, saying, "At such and such a place shall be my camp."<sup>9</sup>But the man of God sent word to the king of Israel, "Beware that you do not pass this place, for the Syrians are going down there."<sup>10</sup>And the king of Israel sent to the place about which the man of God told him. Thus he used to warn him, so that he saved himself there more than once or twice.<sup>11</sup>And the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled because of this thing, and he called his servants and said to them, "Will you not show me who of us is for the king of Israel?"<sup>12</sup>And one of his servants said, "None, my lord, O king; but Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom."<sup>13</sup>And he said, "Go and see where he is, that I may send and seize him." It was told him, "Behold, he is in Dothan."<sup>14</sup>So he sent there horses and chariots and a great army, and they came by night and surrounded the city.<sup>15</sup>When the servant of the man of God rose early in the morning and went out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was all around the city. And the servant said, "Alas, my master! What shall we do?"<sup>16</sup>He said, "Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them."<sup>17</sup>Then Elisha prayed and said, "O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see." So the LORD opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.<sup>18</sup>And when the Syrians came down against him, Elisha prayed to the LORD and said, "Please strike this people with blindness." So he struck them with blindness in accordance with the prayer of Elisha.<sup>19</sup>And Elisha said to them, "This is not the way, and this is not the city. Follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom you seek." And he led them to Samaria.<sup>20</sup>As soon as they entered Samaria, Elisha said, "O LORD, open the eyes of these men, that they may see." So the LORD opened their eyes and they saw, and behold, they were in the midst of Samaria.<sup>21</sup>As soon as the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, "My father, shall I strike them down? Shall I strike them down?"<sup>22</sup>He answered, "You shall not strike them down. Would you strike down those whom you have taken captive with your sword and with your bow? Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink and go to their master."<sup>23</sup>So he prepared for them a great feast, and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. And the Syrians did not come again on raids into the land of Israel.<sup>24</sup>Afterward Ben-hadad king of Syria mustered his entire army and went up and besieged Samaria.<sup>25</sup>And there was a great famine in Samaria, as they besieged it, until a donkey's head was sold for eighty shekels of silver, and the fourth part of a kab of dove's dung for five shekels of silver.<sup>26</sup>Now as the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried out to him, saying, "Help, my lord, O king!"<sup>27</sup>And he said, "If the LORD will not help you, how shall I help you? From the threshing floor, or from the winepress?"<sup>28</sup>And the king asked her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give your son, that we may eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.'<sup>29</sup>So we boiled my son and ate him. And on the next day I said to her, 'Give your son, that we may eat him.' But she has hidden her son."<sup>30</sup>When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes—now he was passing by on the wall—and the people looked, and behold, he had sackcloth beneath on his body—<sup>31</sup>and he said, "May God do so to me and more also, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat remains on his shoulders today."<sup>32</sup>Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. Now the king had dispatched a man from his presence, but before the messenger arrived Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see how this murderer has sent to take off my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and hold the door fast against him. Is not the sound of his master's feet behind him?"<sup>33</sup>And while he was still speaking with them, the messenger came down to him and said, "This trouble is from the LORD! Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"
6.overview:
Where we are. Naaman has gone home cleansed and Gehazi has gone out a leper (chapter 5). Elisha is still among the companies of prophets, but Syria’s raids go on, and by the end of the chapter its whole army has Israel’s capital under siege.

The message. The LORD sees and rules everything, from a borrowed axe head in a river to plans whispered in an enemy king’s bedroom, and those he protects are surrounded by more than surrounds them. Faith is not pretending the danger is not there; it is being given eyes to see the God who is. But where a people will not see, the covenant’s warnings come true, until even a king in sackcloth gives up waiting for the LORD.

Why it was said. Under Ahab’s son the north still served Jeroboam’s calves, though warned for generations (see the introduction). The chapter told them, and later exiles, that the God who guarded his prophet could guard them, and that the horrors of a siege were the covenant’s warnings coming to pass.

How the chapter makes its case. A student prophet loses a borrowed axe head in the Jordan, cries, “Alas, my master!”, and the iron floats (vv. 1–7). Elisha keeps warning Israel’s king of Syrian ambushes (vv. 8–12). An army surrounds Dothan by night; Elisha’s servant cries the same words, and is given eyes to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (vv. 13–17). The Syrians are struck blind, led into Samaria and fed, and the raids stop (vv. 18–23). Then Samaria is besieged, mothers eat their children, the king swears to behead Elisha, and the chapter ends in despair: “Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” (vv. 24–33).

Where it leads. The chapter points to Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. The God who opened a servant’s eyes came in person to give sight to the blind and to open his disciples’ eyes (Luke 24:31). The fiery host around Elisha stood ready again on the night Jesus was arrested, when he could have asked for more than twelve legions of angels and did not (Matthew 26:53), because he had come to die for his enemies, as Elisha fed his. And the covenant’s curse that fell on starving Samaria he bore himself: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

For us. When the count goes against you, ask God to open your eyes to what is really there. Bring him the lost axe heads as well as the armies, feed your enemy, and when waiting seems pointless, do not give up one sentence too soon (7:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Alas, My Master! It Was Borrowed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No trouble of God’s people is too small for him. The company of prophets has outgrown its quarters, a sign of God’s blessing, and asks to build by the Jordan; Elisha goes with them because they ask him (vv. 1–4). As one man fells a tree, the iron head of his axe flies into the river, and he cries out that it was borrowed (v. 5). Elisha asks where it fell, throws in a stick, and the iron floats (v. 6). Then he tells the man to take it up himself, and he reaches out and takes it (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Remember what Elijah believed about the size of this movement. I, even I only, am left, he said, twice, on Horeb (1 Kgs. 19:10, 14), and God answered with seven thousand. One generation later the problem is that the building is too small.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the least consequential miracle in either book, done for the least consequential person in it. No one is healed and no army is turned, yet the man who will stop an invasion goes down to the river about a lost tool.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the sons of the prophets said to Elisha, "See, the place where we dwell under your charge is too small for us. Let us go to the Jordan and each of us get there a log, and let us make a place for us to dwell there." And he answered, "Go." Then one of them said, "Be pleased to go with your servants." And he answered, "I will go." So he went with them. And when they came to the Jordan, they cut down trees. But as one was felling a log, his axe head fell into the water, and he cried out, "Alas, my master! It was borrowed." Then the man of God said, "Where did it fall?" When he showed him the place, he cut off a stick and threw it in there and made the iron float. And he said, "Take it up." So he reached out his hand and took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God cares about a poor man’s borrowed axe head as truly as about armies, and he makes the iron float.

The place where we dwell… is too small for us. A good problem to have. A generation earlier Elijah told God at Horeb that he was the only one left, and was answered with a number he could not check: seven thousand who had not bowed the knee to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Now his successor’s community of prophets has outgrown its building. Elijah never saw it, but the overcrowding is God’s answer to his despair.

Be pleased to go with your servants. They are cutting their own timber, and one of them asks the head of the school to come along, not to supervise but simply to be there. He goes.

Alas, my master! It was borrowed. The disaster is easy to smile at; it was not funny to him. Iron was expensive in that century, well beyond a student prophet living on donated barley, which is why he did not own the axe. He had borrowed it from somebody who trusted him, it is in the mud at the bottom of the Jordan, and he cannot replace it. It is the widow’s debt of chapter 4 on a small scale. Hold on to the cry, because it will be shouted again in this chapter by someone in an incomparably worse position (v. 15).

He cut off a stick and threw it in there and made the iron float. Elisha asks where; the man points at a patch of moving brown water; a stick goes in, and iron comes up. A stick does not float iron, any more than salt sweetens a spring (2:21) or flour draws poison out of a stew (4:41). The things Elisha uses are always chosen so that nobody can think the thing itself did it.

Take it up. Not “here you are”: the man has to put his own hand into the river and close it round what he lost. God’s help seldom leaves us with nothing to do.

Not one sparrow. This is the Father Jesus described, without whom not one sparrow falls and who numbers the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:29–30).

No trouble too small. There is a kind of piety that would be ashamed to trouble God with a lost axe head, that treats its own small troubles as beneath his notice and prays only about the large ones. This chapter puts the axe head first, before the army, and the same prophet attends to both.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–23 — Those Who Are With Us Are More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those whom God protects are surrounded by more than surrounds them. Elisha keeps telling Israel’s king where the Syrian camps will be, and Ben-hadad, suspecting a traitor, learns that the prophet hears even what he says in his bedroom (vv. 8–12). He sends a great army by night to seize Elisha at Dothan (vv. 13–14). At dawn the servant cries out in terror; Elisha prays not for rescue but for sight, and the young man sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (vv. 15–17). The Syrians are struck blind, led into Samaria and, at the prophet’s word, fed rather than killed, and the raids stop (vv. 18–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing on those hills changed; they were full of horses and chariots of fire the whole time. Elisha prays not for reinforcements but for eyes.
verseByVerse.examples: The campaign ends with a banquet, after which the raids stop (v. 23). A king who wanted to kill his captives feeds them instead, as Proverbs commands (Prov. 25:21), and it works.

verseByVerse.quote: Once when the king of Syria was warring against Israel, he took counsel with his servants, saying, "At such and such a place shall be my camp." But the man of God sent word to the king of Israel, "Beware that you do not pass this place, for the Syrians are going down there." And the king of Israel sent to the place about which the man of God told him. Thus he used to warn him, so that he saved himself there more than once or twice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again and again God, through Elisha, warns Israel’s faithless king where the Syrian ambushes lie, and so spares his people.

Thus he used to warn him. This was a standing practice, repeated often enough to be called a habit: more than once or twice, the king avoided the trap.

Who is being protected. This is Ahab’s son, who keeps Jeroboam’s golden calves and will shortly swear to have Elisha’s head off (v. 31). Yet God’s prophet supplies him with military intelligence. Most likely the protection was for Israel rather than its king: the men those ambushes would have killed were the LORD’s people, the flock he had wanted sent home in peace at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:17).

Kindness that calls to repentance. Every ambush avoided was undeserved mercy and an invitation to turn back. God still treats those who ignore him so: his kindness is “meant to lead you to repentance” (Romans 2:4), and it was shown in full when Christ died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled because of this thing, and he called his servants and said to them, "Will you not show me who of us is for the king of Israel?" And one of his servants said, "None, my lord, O king; but Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Syria looks for a traitor, but the truth is worse for him: Israel’s God hears even what is said in a bedroom.

Who of us is for the king of Israel? Ben-hadad’s first thought is a traitor in his own council, the natural suspicion of a king who knows how courts work. His servant’s answer is more alarming than a spy: there is no leak, because the prophet in Israel hears what no spy could.

The words that you speak in your bedroom. Not the plans announced in council, but the sentences said privately, at night, in the one room a king has to himself.

In everyday life. Take it out of the war for a moment. “Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether” (Psalm 139:4). What is said in the dark, in the last hour of the day, when the performance is over and there is nobody to impress, God hears. That is a terror or a comfort depending on one thing only: whether the one listening is for you. In Christ he is, and “if God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Go and see where he is, that I may send and seize him." It was told him, "Behold, he is in Dothan." So he sent there horses and chariots and a great army, and they came by night and surrounded the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king sends a great army by night to seize one unarmed prophet: a sensible plan in a world where God does not hear, which is not the real world.

Go and see where he is, that I may send and seize him. He has just been told that Elisha knows what he says in his bedroom, and his plan is a surprise raid. The joke and the lesson are the same: you cannot ambush a man who hears you planning the ambush. The king is a competent soldier making a sensible decision, and everyone can see the flaw except him.

Horses and chariots and a great army. All of it, moved by night, to take one unarmed man in a small town north of Samaria.
verseByVerse.note: Dothan lay about 10 miles north of Samaria.

verseByVerse.quote: When the servant of the man of God rose early in the morning and went out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was all around the city. And the servant said, "Alas, my master! What shall we do?" He said, "Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them." Then Elisha prayed and said, "O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see." So the LORD opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded by an army, Elisha asks not for rescue but for his servant to see, and God opens the young man’s eyes to the fiery host that was there all along.

Alas, my master! What shall we do? The cry again, word for word: ten verses ago over an axe head in a river, now over a ring of chariots at first light. The writer has put the two cries in one chapter on purpose. Our small disasters and our large ones produce the same sentence, and they are answered by the same God.

Those who are with us are more than those who are with them. As a count it looks simply false: there are two of them in that house and an army outside.

O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see. Not the prayer we would have prayed: not for deliverance, or for God to strike the enemy, but for sight. And nothing outside changes. The horses of fire were on that mountain while the servant counted Syrian chariots; the only thing that altered was one young man’s capacity to see what was in front of him.

Horses and chariots of fire. Elisha’s own inheritance turned on seeing: “If you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you” (2:10). He saw horses and chariots of fire part him from Elijah, and cried, “The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” (2:12), meaning that the country’s real defence was not its army. Now he asks the same gift of sight for a frightened servant. The horses and chariots of fire are God’s angels, the army of heaven (Psalm 68:17; compare Psalm 34:7). God still sends them “to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14), though we do not see them.

Is realism just counting the chariots? The servant’s view is what our age calls realistic: count what can be measured and plan accordingly. There is wisdom in that, and the Bible never asks anyone to pretend the Syrian army is not there. But if the visible count is the whole truth, sooner or later it goes against everyone: the scan result, the job cut, the ageing body, the last enemy. Much modern anxiety is simply the servant’s arithmetic done honestly. Elisha does not ask God to change the facts or give the young man a comforting feeling, but that he may see more of what is real. Faith is not a refusal to look but the gift of seeing further, and what it sees in the end is more than angels. “We do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him… namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:8–9). A person who has seen that can look at the chariots.

What it does not mean. Not that believers will always be spared harm: Elisha himself fell sick and died (13:14). God’s angels guard his people all the way to salvation, not from every trouble on the road, and nothing can separate them from his love (Romans 8:38–39).

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Syrians came down against him, Elisha prayed to the LORD and said, "Please strike this people with blindness." So he struck them with blindness in accordance with the prayer of Elisha. And Elisha said to them, "This is not the way, and this is not the city. Follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom you seek." And he led them to Samaria. As soon as they entered Samaria, Elisha said, "O LORD, open the eyes of these men, that they may see." So the LORD opened their eyes and they saw, and behold, they were in the midst of Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha prays the attackers blind, leads them into the middle of Samaria and prays their eyes open: the would-be captors become captives without a blow struck.

Please strike this people with blindness. Like the men at Lot’s door in Sodom (Genesis 19:11), they are struck with a blindness that still lets them walk, follow a voice and cover the road to Samaria (see the box below).

This is not the way, and this is not the city. It is a ruse, and it should be called one rather than defended too eagerly or condemned too heavily; the text passes no judgment on it. What can fairly be said is that his last words, I will bring you to the man whom you seek, are kept exactly. He walks in front of them the whole way and hands himself over in the middle of the enemy’s capital, which is a strange thing for a deceiver to do.

O LORD, open the eyes of these men, that they may see. The same prayer as verse 17, prayed for the other side. Twice in four verses Elisha asks God to let men see what is actually around them; both times it is a mercy, and both times it is terrifying to the men it happens to.

Uncertain wording. The word translated blindness is rare, used elsewhere only at Lot’s door (Genesis 19:11), and its exact sense is uncertain. Since the Syrians could still walk and follow Elisha, it probably means a dazzled confusion, an inability to recognise what was in front of them, rather than total loss of sight.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, "My father, shall I strike them down? Shall I strike them down?" He answered, "You shall not strike them down. Would you strike down those whom you have taken captive with your sword and with your bow? Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink and go to their master." So he prepared for them a great feast, and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. And the Syrians did not come again on raids into the land of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha forbids the king to kill the helpless prisoners and has them fed instead, and the kindness ends the raids.

My father, shall I strike them down? He asks twice, which shows how much he wants to. He calls the prophet my father, and before the chapter ends he will swear to cut this father’s head off.

With your sword and with your bow. Elisha’s answer is about ownership. These men were not taken with the king’s sword and bow; God handed them over, and a gift from God is not a trophy. A prophet pressed the same principle on Ahab, who spared Ben-hadad when God had appointed him to die (1 Kings 20:42). There it meant killing and here it means sparing; the question is what God has appointed.

He prepared for them a great feast. Told to give bread and water, the king lays on a banquet. A force that marched all night to kidnap a prophet dines in the enemy capital at the enemy king’s expense and walks home unharmed. And the Syrians did not come again on raids: the most effective military operation in the book of Kings was a dinner.

If your enemy is hungry. Proverbs had put it in writing: “If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink” (Proverbs 25:21), and Paul quotes it when he tells Christians how to treat people who mean them harm (Romans 12:20). The Lord said it in three words: love your enemies (Matthew 5:44). Here it is done, reluctantly, by a bad king under orders, and it works.

Twelve legions, and he did not ask. The same armies stood ready on another night and were not called. When men came with swords and clubs to seize Jesus, he said he could ask his Father and at once be given more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). He did not ask, because he had come to be taken, and to die for enemies (Romans 5:10). Elisha led his captors to a table and sent them home fed; Christ gave himself up to his, and enemies now sit at his table reconciled.

What it does not mean. Not that a nation may never defend itself: Scripture forbids personal revenge, not the state’s lawful use of force (Romans 13:4). Elisha forbids vengeance on the helpless.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–33 — A Woman on the Wall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When a people refuse God’s word, the covenant’s warnings come true, and despair turns on the messenger. Ben-hadad returns with his whole army and besieges Samaria, and famine makes refuse worth a fortune (vv. 24–25). A woman cries to the king on the wall, not for mercy but for justice in a bargain: she and a neighbour agreed to eat their sons, and the neighbour has hidden hers (vv. 26–29). The king tears his robes, showing sackcloth beneath, and swears to behead Elisha that very day (vv. 30–31). Elisha, sitting with the elders, has the door barred, and the messenger arrives with the words of a man who has given up waiting for the LORD (vv. 32–33).
verseByVerse.theology: What the king hears on that wall had been written down centuries before as a penalty for breaking the covenant (Lev. 26:29). It is not random horror but that warning taking effect, as the note on verses 28-29 shows.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what she is complaining about: not the eating of a child, but the breach of an agreement.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward Ben-hadad king of Syria mustered his entire army and went up and besieged Samaria. And there was a great famine in Samaria, as they besieged it, until a donkey's head was sold for eighty shekels of silver, and the fourth part of a kab of dove's dung for five shekels of silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The raids have stopped, but now Ben-hadad’s whole army besieges Samaria, and the famine makes refuse worth a fortune.

Afterward Ben-hadad king of Syria mustered his entire army. Do not read this as a contradiction of verse 23. The raids stopped: the border skirmishing, the ambush parties, the seizing of prophets. What comes now is a different thing, the entire army in a formal siege of the capital. Enemies are not always cured by kindness, and the Bible does not pretend otherwise.

A donkey’s head was sold for eighty shekels of silver. A donkey was unclean under the law and its head the least edible part, yet it fetches eighty shekels of silver; a quarter of a kab, roughly half a pint, of dove’s dung costs five. The writer lets the price list speak.

Uncertain wording. Dove’s dung may mean exactly that, bought in desperation as fuel or even food, or it may be a popular name for the small bulbs of a wild plant eaten only in hard times. We cannot be sure; either way, things nobody would normally touch were selling for a fortune.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried out to him, saying, "Help, my lord, O king!" And he said, "If the LORD will not help you, how shall I help you? From the threshing floor, or from the winepress?" And the king asked her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give your son, that we may eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.' So we boiled my son and ate him. And on the next day I said to her, 'Give your son, that we may eat him.' But she has hidden her son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The siege brings the covenant’s darkest curse to pass: mothers eat their children, and a woman’s only complaint is that the other mother has not kept the bargain.

If the LORD will not help you, how shall I help you? The king’s answer is bitter and half right. There is no grain on the threshing floor and no wine in the winepress. What he cannot see is that his own sentence names the only one who could help.

But she has hidden her son. The worst thing here is what she is complaining about. She is not asking for mercy or for the war to end; she kept her side of the bargain, the other woman has not, and she wants the king to enforce it. There is not one word of horror in her mouth about what she did to her own son. That is what starvation had done in Samaria, and it is a picture of what any sustained evil does to the people inside it. The sense of right and wrong goes first, while the sense of what is owed to me keeps working, so that the last thing left standing in a person is a grievance about being cheated.

Written in the covenant. All of this had been written down. Long before there was a Samaria, Moses set out the penalties for breaking the covenant: “You shall eat the flesh of your sons, and you shall eat the flesh of your daughters” (Leviticus 26:29). Deuteronomy describes it at appalling length, in “the siege and in the distress with which your enemy shall distress you in all your towns”, down to the most tender and refined woman secretly eating her own children (Deuteronomy 28:53–57). This is not a random horror from a brutal age but a term of the covenant taking effect, in a kingdom warned for generations. It would happen again in Jerusalem (Lamentations 4:10).

Why would God write such a curse into his covenant at all? Because the warning was meant to make it unnecessary. He told Israel in advance, plainly, where turning from him would end, and sent prophet after prophet so that it need not end there. And the curses did not have the last word. Carrying his cross, Jesus warned the women of Jerusalem of another siege to come (Luke 23:28–29), and then went outside the city to bear the curse himself: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes—now he was passing by on the wall—and the people looked, and behold, he had sackcloth beneath on his body— and he said, "May God do so to me and more also, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat remains on his shoulders today."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s hidden sackcloth shows real anguish, but not repentance: in the same breath he swears to kill the prophet who has told him the truth.

He had sackcloth beneath on his body. The robes come apart and the people see sackcloth worn against the skin, where nobody was meant to see it. His father Ahab put sackcloth on his flesh too, and God noticed it and deferred a judgment for it (1 Kings 21:27–29).

If the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat remains on his shoulders today. In consecutive sentences he shows sackcloth and swears to behead the prophet. His anguish is real and religious, and his fury is aimed at the one man who has kept him alive by telling him where the ambushes were. The sackcloth was real, and it was not repentance. It was grief wearing the costume of repentance, with nothing underneath it changed.

A test for repentance. The test is not how bad you feel but what you do next with the person who has been telling you the truth. Paul draws the same line: “godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Real repentance turns toward God’s word rather than against it, and the God who sent this king prophet after prophet still receives, in Christ, everyone who comes back that way.

verseByVerse.quote: Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. Now the king had dispatched a man from his presence, but before the messenger arrived Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see how this murderer has sent to take off my head? Look, when the messenger comes, shut the door and hold the door fast against him. Is not the sound of his master's feet behind him?" And while he was still speaking with them, the messenger came down to him and said, "This trouble is from the LORD! Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the king’s executioner comes for Elisha, the chapter ends with a man who has given up waiting for the LORD, one sentence before the LORD’s answer.

Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. Elisha knows what is coming before the man is at the door, as he knew what was said in a Syrian bedroom. And the leaders of the city are not in the palace but in the prophet’s house: in the worst of the siege, the elders have gone where the word of the LORD is spoken.

This murderer. Literally this son of a murderer, and the reader knows whose son he is. Ahab had Naboth killed for his vineyard only a few years before (1 Kings 21), and it has not been forgotten.

Shut the door and hold the door fast against him. Elisha trusts God and still bars the door. Faith in God’s protection has never ruled out sensible precautions, and he means to hold the executioner off until the king himself arrives. Is not the sound of his master’s feet behind him? The king sent an executioner and then came after him; whatever he means to do at that door, he cannot stay away from it.

Why should I wait for the LORD any longer? The most honest sentence in these two chapters, and the sentence of a man giving up. He has two things right: the trouble is from the LORD, and waiting is what has been asked. He is not denying that God is there; he has reached the end of what he can bear of waiting. Anyone who has prayed long about something that is getting worse knows the sentence, spoken not in a fit of unbelief but flatly, by an exhausted person, as a conclusion.

One sentence too soon. It is the last verse of the chapter, and the words that follow it in the very next breath are “Hear the word of the LORD: thus says the LORD, Tomorrow about this time” (7:1). He gave up one sentence too soon.

What it means to wait for the LORD. We hear “wait” as dead time, a delay to be put up with. In the Bible, to wait for the LORD is to hold on to what he has said before he has done it, and to refuse to look for rescue anywhere else. When God seems slow, the heart quietly turns to the market, the doctor or its own ability to fix things, and calls it being realistic. But “the LORD waits to be gracious to you” (Isaiah 30:18); the delay is not indifference. The proof is Christ. Israel waited centuries, and then, “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4). “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). So when a prayer has gone unanswered for years, tell God so, as bluntly as this man did, and then bring it to him again tomorrow rather than to the thing you were tempted to trust.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says that the messenger came down and spoke. But Elisha has just said that the king is close behind (v. 32), and in the next scene the king and his officer are plainly present (7:2), so many take the king to be the speaker; in Hebrew the words for messenger and king look very alike. Either way, the despair is the king’s, whether spoken by him or carried in his servant’s mouth.

6.theology:
Too small for us (v. 1). Elijah thought he was the only one left; a generation later the building will not hold the students. Nobody sees how things will turn while he is still in the middle of them.

God hears the bedroom (v. 12). Nothing said in private is hidden from him. Whether that is terror or comfort depends on whether the one listening is for you.

Eyes, not help (v. 17). Elisha does not ask God to change the situation but to let his servant see the help already standing in it. Nothing in the valley changed except one young man's capacity to see.

Captives as a gift (v. 22). Prisoners handed over by God are not trophies, and feeding them ends the raids. Yet verse 24 is a siege: kindness does not guarantee against every future enemy, and Scripture does not claim it does.

The clause coming due (vv. 28-29). God warned in the covenant itself where breaking it would end (Lev. 26:29), so that it need not end there. Here the warning takes effect. The woman's lack of horror shows what sustained evil does: it takes the moral sense first and leaves only a grievance about being cheated.

Sackcloth where it does not show (vv. 30-31). The king had been wearing it against his skin under the robes, as his father Ahab did, and his next sentence is an oath to take the prophet's head. The grief was real; it was not repentance. The test of that is never how bad a man feels, but what he does next with the person who has been telling him the truth.

One verse early (v. 33). Why should I wait for the LORD any longer? is not a denial that God is there; it grants that the trouble is from him and that waiting was the thing asked. It is an exhausted man announcing a conclusion. The next words on the page are hear the word of the LORD... tomorrow about this time (7:1).
6.examples:
Then: A young man walked out at first light, found the hills solid with the chariots of an army that had marched all night to take his master, and cried out in the words another man had used about an axe head.

Now: First, the axe head is placed before the army on purpose. If you have trouble too small to pray about, the thing you have broken that belongs to someone else, the sum you cannot quite cover, this chapter shows the same prophet attending to it as to the invasion. Second, the prayer at Dothan is not for rescue but for eyes. Before asking God to alter your circumstances, ask him to show you what is already standing in them. And when the harder command comes, to feed the enemy who came to take you, remember that you were first an enemy fed and reconciled by Christ (Rom. 5:10), and that his Spirit in you is the strength for it. Third, if you have prayed a long time while things got worse and are close to saying verse 33, remember that the king said it one verse before the deliverance. God does not despise the exhausted; keep waiting, and bring him the exhaustion too.

keyVerse.quote: Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.
keyVerse.note: Elisha speaks this with an army round the town and no soldier on his side that the eye can see. It is the chapter’s answer to both cries of “Alas, my master!”: God’s people are never as alone as they look. Its final ground is not angels but the God who is for us in Christ, so that nothing can separate us from his love (Romans 8:31, 38–39).

6.reflection:
The same cry, “Alas, my master!”, is raised over a lost axe head and over a surrounding army (vv. 5, 15). Do you find it easier to bring God your large troubles or your small ones? Why might it matter that he cares about both?

Elisha prayed, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see” (v. 17). What “chariots” are you counting at the moment, and what truths about God would you most need your eyes opened to? How does seeing Jesus “crowned with glory and honor” (Hebrews 2:9) change how we face what frightens us?

Elisha told the king to feed his helpless enemies rather than kill them, and the raids stopped (vv. 21–23). What would it look like for you to “give bread” to someone who has opposed or hurt you? How does Christ’s death for his enemies (Romans 5:10) shape our response?

The king wore sackcloth yet turned his anger on God’s messenger, and gave up waiting for the LORD one verse before the promise (vv. 30–33; 7:1). How can we tell the difference between real repentance and mere distress? What helps you keep waiting on God when nothing seems to change?

7.title: Four Lepers and the End of the Siege
7.text: <sup>1</sup>But Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD: thus says the LORD, Tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria."<sup>2</sup>Then the captain on whose hand the king leaned said to the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could this thing be?" But he said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it."<sup>3</sup>Now there were four men who were lepers at the entrance to the gate. And they said to one another, "Why are we sitting here until we die?<sup>4</sup>If we say, 'Let us enter the city,' the famine is in the city, and we shall die there. And if we sit here, we die also. So now come, let us go over to the camp of the Syrians. If they spare our lives we shall live, and if they kill us we shall but die."<sup>5</sup>So they arose at twilight to go to the camp of the Syrians. But when they came to the edge of the camp of the Syrians, behold, there was no one there.<sup>6</sup>For the Lord had made the army of the Syrians hear the sound of chariots and of horses, the sound of a great army, so that they said to one another, "Behold, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come against us."<sup>7</sup>So they fled away in the twilight and abandoned their tents, their horses, and their donkeys, leaving the camp as it was, and fled for their lives.<sup>8</sup>And when these lepers came to the edge of the camp, they went into a tent and ate and drank, and they carried off silver and gold and clothing and went and hid them.
