Then they came back and entered another tent and carried off things from it and went and hid them.<sup>9</sup>Then they said to one another, "We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come; let us go and tell the king's household."<sup>10</sup>So they came and called to the gatekeepers of the city and told them, "We came to the camp of the Syrians, and behold, there was no one to be seen or heard there, nothing but the horses tied and the donkeys tied and the tents as they were."<sup>11</sup>Then the gatekeepers called out, and it was told within the king's household.<sup>12</sup>And the king rose in the night and said to his servants, "I will tell you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we are hungry. Therefore they have gone out of the camp to hide themselves in the open country, thinking, 'When they come out of the city, we shall take them alive and get into the city.'"<sup>13</sup>And one of his servants said, "Let some men take five of the remaining horses, seeing that those who are left here will fare like the whole multitude of Israel who have already perished. Let us send and see."<sup>14</sup>So they took two horsemen, and the king sent them after the army of the Syrians, saying, "Go and see."<sup>15</sup>So they went after them as far as the Jordan, and behold, all the way was littered with garments and equipment that the Syrians had thrown away in their haste. And the messengers returned and told the king.<sup>16</sup>Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians. So a seah of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>Now the king had appointed the captain on whose hand he leaned to have charge of the gate. And the people trampled him in the gate, so that he died, as the man of God had said when the king came down to him.<sup>18</sup>For when the man of God had said to the king, "Two seahs of barley shall be sold for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel, about this time tomorrow in the gate of Samaria,"<sup>19</sup>the captain had answered the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could such a thing be?" And he had said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it."<sup>20</sup>And so it happened to him, for the people trampled him in the gate and he died.
7.overview:
Where we are. Samaria is under Syrian siege and starving. A donkey’s head sells for eighty shekels, a mother has eaten her son, and the king, blaming God, has sworn to behead Elisha and asked, “Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” (6:24–33). Chapter 7 begins in the next breath with the prophet’s answer.

The message. When his people have given up waiting, God answers with a word anyone can check, and keeps it to the letter. He saves the city alone, without a sword drawn in Israel, and the news is carried by outcasts who cannot keep it to themselves. The same word that feeds those who receive it condemns the man who scorns it: he sees it with his own eyes and does not eat.

Why it was said. The first readers knew siege, famine and the fall of a capital at first hand (see the introduction). The chapter tells them that God’s word does not fail, however impossible it sounds, and that the deadliest response to it is not weak faith but contempt.

How the chapter makes its case. Elisha names the price of flour and barley at the gate tomorrow, and the king’s aide sneers that not even windows in heaven could bring it about (vv. 1–2). Four lepers outside the gate find the Syrian camp empty, because the Lord made the army hear chariots that did not exist; they eat and hide plunder, and then stop: “We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news” (vv. 3–11). The king suspects an ambush, scouts find the road to the Jordan littered with abandoned gear, the flour sells at the named price, and the aide is trampled in the gate (vv. 12–20).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by pattern. The LORD won the victory alone, in the dark, while the city could do nothing; all that remained was to hear the news, go out and take what had been won. That is the shape of the gospel. On the cross Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). The two ends of the chapter are the two ways of meeting that report: the starving went out and ate, and the man who called it impossible saw it and had none.

For us. Christians are beggars fed by a victory they did not win, and to keep such news to ourselves is, in the lepers’ words, “not doing right”. When God’s answer comes, do not explain it away as the king did, and never treat a word God has spoken as too good to be true.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers despair with a promise anyone can check. The king has just sworn to kill Elisha and announced that he has finished waiting for the LORD (6:31–33). Elisha’s reply is not general comfort but a price list: by this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, fine flour and barley will sell at ordinary prices, in a city where a donkey’s head costs eighty shekels (v. 1). The officer on whose arm the king leans answers with a sneer about windows in heaven, and is told exactly what will happen to him: he will see the promise kept, and will not eat of it (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is deliberately checkable. Elisha does not say God will provide; he names a time, a place, two foods and a price for each, to a city where a donkey's head costs eighty shekels.
verseByVerse.examples: God's answer to despair is often concrete. He told a starving city what bread would cost tomorrow, and kept his word to the shekel.

verseByVerse.quote: But Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD: thus says the LORD, Tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria." Then the captain on whose hand the king leaned said to the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could this thing be?" But he said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To a king who has given up waiting for God, Elisha promises ordinary food prices at the city gate by this time tomorrow, and tells the officer who sneers that he will see it happen and eat none of it.

Hear the word of the LORD. The last words of chapter 6 were a man saying he had finished waiting for God (6:33). Elisha’s promise is the very next thing on the page.

Tomorrow about this time. Elisha does not say that God is good or that help is coming. He names a time, tomorrow about this hour; a place, the gate of Samaria; two foods; and a price for each. Anybody in the city with a shekel and a memory can hold it up against the facts, and if it fails, Elisha is finished.

A seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel. A seah was a dry measure of about seven litres. These are not giveaway prices but ordinary market prices. In a city where a donkey’s head sells for eighty shekels and mothers are eating their children (6:25–29), he promises that by tomorrow people will be doing the shopping at normal rates. Sometimes what God promises is not abundance. It is an ordinary day, back the way it should have been.

The captain on whose hand the king leaned. He is the king’s personal aide, literally the officer on whose arm the king leans, the duty Naaman performed for his own king in the temple of Rimmon (5:18). He is the closest man to the throne, and the first to speak.

If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven. His sneer is well made, and it is built out of Scripture. Windows in heaven is the language of the flood, when “the windows of the heavens were opened” (Genesis 7:11), and it is also the language of blessing: “put me to the test, says the LORD of hosts, if I will not open the windows of heaven for you” (Malachi 3:10). So he is saying: even if God did the biggest thing anybody has ever heard of, this could not happen. He does not deny that God exists or that he is powerful. He denies that a particular word, just spoken in his hearing, could possibly be true.

You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it. The reply is not a curse thrown at a heckler but a sentence measured to the offence. The man who said the promise could not be kept will be given the fullest possible proof that it was, and no share in it (see the note on vv. 12–20).
verseByVerse.note: A seah was about 7.7 quarts or 7.3 liters (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–11 — This Day Is a Day of Good News
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God wins the victory alone and hands the news to the men the city had shut out. Four lepers, living outside the gate as the law required, reason that surrender to the Syrians is their only chance of life (vv. 3–4). At dusk they find the camp empty: the Lord had made the Syrians hear the noise of a great army, and they had fled, leaving everything standing (vv. 5–7). The lepers eat, drink and hide plunder from two tents, and then stop. “We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news” (vv. 8–9). So they go back and shout it to the gatekeepers, and it reaches the palace (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The men the law had put outside the community are the ones who find the community's deliverance.
verseByVerse.examples: Four starving outcasts who have found more food than they can carry decide that eating it quietly while the city dies is not a thing they can do.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were four men who were lepers at the entrance to the gate. And they said to one another, "Why are we sitting here until we die? If we say, 'Let us enter the city,' the famine is in the city, and we shall die there. And if we sit here, we die also. So now come, let us go over to the camp of the Syrians. If they spare our lives we shall live, and if they kill us we shall but die." So they arose at twilight to go to the camp of the Syrians. But when they came to the edge of the camp of the Syrians, behold, there was no one there. For the Lord had made the army of the Syrians hear the sound of chariots and of horses, the sound of a great army, so that they said to one another, "Behold, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come against us." So they fled away in the twilight and abandoned their tents, their horses, and their donkeys, leaving the camp as it was, and fled for their lives. And when these lepers came to the edge of the camp, they went into a tent and ate and drank, and they carried off silver and gold and clothing and went and hid them. Then they came back and entered another tent and carried off things from it and went and hid them. Then they said to one another, "We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come; let us go and tell the king's household." So they came and called to the gatekeepers of the city and told them, "We came to the camp of the Syrians, and behold, there was no one to be seen or heard there, nothing but the horses tied and the donkeys tied and the tents as they were." Then the gatekeepers called out, and it was told within the king's household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four lepers with nothing left to lose walk into the enemy camp and find that God has already emptied it with a sound; after eating their fill, they realise that keeping such news to themselves is wrong. The men the city had shut out are the ones who find its deliverance and carry the news of it.

Four men who were lepers at the entrance to the gate. They are at the gate because that is where the law put them. A man with that condition “shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:46). In a city under siege, outside the camp means the strip of ground between the gate and the enemy.

Why are we sitting here until we die? Their reasoning is clear-eyed arithmetic. Of three options, two are certain death; the third might be death and might not. “If they kill us we shall but die”: that is the whole calculation, and there is not a scrap of heroism in it. They have simply run out of things that could be taken from them, and that is exactly why it is these four who go. Everybody behind the wall still had something to protect: a house, a position, a last handful of grain, a reason to sit tight one more night. Nobody inside walked out to look. The men with nothing left to lose are the ones who find out that the siege is over.

For the Lord had made the army of the Syrians hear. Your Bible prints Lord in verse 6 in ordinary letters rather than the capitals (LORD) used for God’s personal name, because the Hebrew word here is adonai, Master. Do not build much on it; but the title means the one who owns and rules all things, and what follows is God moving an entire army off a battlefield with a noise.

The sound of chariots and of horses. Count the chariots in these two chapters, for there are three sets, and only the first is made of wood and iron. In chapter 6 a servant walked out at dawn into a ring of real Syrian chariots and panicked; on the same hillside, invisible to him, stood horses and chariots of fire (6:15–17). And here a professional army hears chariots that do not exist at all, and runs. God gave them the noise of the very thing they most feared, and their own imaginations did the rest, even supplying a list of the foreign kings they assumed had been hired against them. The “kings of the Hittites” were the rulers of the small Hittite kingdoms that survived in northern Syria after the Hittite empire fell.

Leaving the camp as it was. Tents up, animals tethered: they did not pack up the camp, they ran out of it. Nobody in Israel drew a sword.

They went into a tent and ate and drank. The lepers do the entirely human thing first. Four starving men walk into a tent with food in it, eat, and then start burying treasure, and the writer does not scold them for it.

We are not doing right. Somewhere after the second tent one of them says it, one of the great sentences of the Old Testament. Nothing had changed outside them. The camp was still empty, the silver still theirs for the taking, and nobody in Samaria knew anything. What happened was that four men, in the middle of the best night of their lives, could not go on enjoying it.

Punishment will overtake us. The text is honest about the order of their reasons. Conscience comes first, then fear, and they are right to fear: a city that found out they had kept this to themselves would not have been gentle. Compassion for the starving is not actually mentioned.

This day is a day of good news. The Hebrew word means glad news, and it lies behind the Greek word the New Testament uses for the gospel. They shout it up to gatekeepers who are not allowed to let them in, and the gatekeepers pass it straight on; the message reaches the palace in two verses.

The gospel’s shape. The news itself has the gospel’s shape. Nobody in Samaria won this victory. The LORD routed the enemy alone, in the dark, while the city sat starving, and all that was left for anyone to do was to hear, go out and take what had been won. That is how the New Testament speaks of Christ’s work: on the cross he “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15), and the gospel is the report of a battle already over. The lepers did not have to empty the camp. They only had to say that it was empty.

Beggars telling beggars. One of the Old Testament’s clearest pictures of evangelism is four unclean men, shut out of the congregation, who have found more bread than they can eat while the city that shut them out is starving, and who cannot keep it to themselves. They are not experts with a strategy but beggars who found food, going back to tell other beggars where it is. And their motives were a mixture, yet God used them and the news got told. Nobody has to wait for a pure heart before opening their mouth.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” covers several skin diseases (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — You Shall See It With Your Own Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word comes true to the letter, both for those who receive it and for the one who scorned it. The king, woken with the news, decides it must be an ambush, until a servant persuades him to risk a few dying horses and look (vv. 12–14). The scouts follow a trail of abandoned gear to the Jordan, the people plunder the camp, and flour and barley sell at the very prices Elisha named, “according to the word of the LORD” (vv. 15–16). The officer who sneered, posted to the gate, is trampled there by the crowd, and the writer tells his end twice so that no reader can call it coincidence (vv. 17–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Everyone in this chapter is slow with the good news, the four men who had nothing least of all. The lepers delay only for the length of two tents; the gatekeepers pass it on at once; and the king, given verified good news in the middle of the night, sits up in bed and works out how it might be a trap.
verseByVerse.examples: The sentence on the captain is exact rather than merely severe: posted to the very gate the prophecy named, he saw the flour sold at the promised price and was trampled by the crowd before he could eat any.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king rose in the night and said to his servants, "I will tell you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we are hungry. Therefore they have gone out of the camp to hide themselves in the open country, thinking, 'When they come out of the city, we shall take them alive and get into the city.'" And one of his servants said, "Let some men take five of the remaining horses, seeing that those who are left here will fare like the whole multitude of Israel who have already perished. Let us send and see." So they took two horsemen, and the king sent them after the army of the Syrians, saying, "Go and see." So they went after them as far as the Jordan, and behold, all the way was littered with garments and equipment that the Syrians had thrown away in their haste. And the messengers returned and told the king. Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians. So a seah of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD. Now the king had appointed the captain on whose hand he leaned to have charge of the gate. And the people trampled him in the gate, so that he died, as the man of God had said when the king came down to him. For when the man of God had said to the king, "Two seahs of barley shall be sold for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel, about this time tomorrow in the gate of Samaria," the captain had answered the man of God, "If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could such a thing be?" And he had said, "You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it." And so it happened to him, for the people trampled him in the gate and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king explains the good news away as a trap until a servant persuades him to look; then the food comes exactly as God said, and the officer who scorned the word sees it and is trampled before he can eat.

I will tell you what the Syrians have done to us. Handed the best news in a generation, the king at once explains it away. The theory is not stupid; a feigned retreat was a standard tactic. But this is the man who that same day swore to behead the prophet and announced that he had finished waiting for God (6:31–33), and now, given the fulfilment in the night, he works out how it must be a trap. A settled expectation of the worst does not lift when the good arrives. It simply sets about explaining the good away.

Let some men take five of the remaining horses. Again it is a servant who talks sense to a king, with an argument as bleak as the lepers’: these horses will die with the rest of us, so there is nothing to lose by risking them.

All the way was littered with garments and equipment. The scouts follow some twenty-five miles of discarded gear. Men throw away cloaks and armour when they believe something is right behind them, and the road to the Jordan is the record of a terror with no army behind it. It is the most complete rout in the book, and nobody in Israel was there for any of it.

A seah of fine flour was sold for a shekel. Verse 16 repeats the prophecy word for word as a price report: the same foods, the same rates, the same gate, one day later, “according to the word of the LORD”.

To have charge of the gate. Of all the postings in the city, the officer is given the gate. Whatever the king intended, crowd control most likely, the man who said the thing could not happen is standing on the exact spot where it happens, holding back a starving population that has just heard there is food outside.

And so it happened to him. The writer sets out the whole exchange a second time, question and answer, and states the outcome again, because he does not intend a single reader to finish the chapter thinking it was a coincidence.

The people trampled him in the gate. It matters exactly what the man died for, because it is easy to make him a warning about doubt in general, and he is not that. He was not condemned for finding a promise hard to believe; half the people in this book find promises hard to believe, and Elisha’s own servant panicked at Dothan without being trampled. He stood next to a prophet who had just spoken a specific word from God, and sneered at it. Even so there was a hard mercy in his sentence: he was told in advance, in plain words, what would happen, and he had a day in which to repent.

Saved by the people it shut out. Set the two ends of the chapter side by side. The man closest to the throne heard the promise first and treated it as absurd. Four men the law had put outside the gate, with no standing, no health and no prospects, found the deliverance and could not keep quiet about it. The city was saved by the people it had excluded, because four starving men decided in the night that a day of good news is not a thing you eat by yourself.

Why is cynicism so attractive? The king’s reaction feels very modern. Cynicism has become a mark of sophistication: assume the motive is selfish, the offer a trap, the good news spin. Oscar Wilde had one of his characters define a cynic as a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing, and it fits a city living by a price list for donkeys’ heads. There are reasons for it; people who have been fooled do not want to be fooled again. But cynicism is not wisdom. It is a way of never being disappointed, bought at the cost of never being glad, and it takes no courage to expect the worst. The gospel meets it on its own ground. When the women came back from the empty tomb, “these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them” (Luke 24:11). Then the risen Christ stood among them and showed them his hands and his feet (Luke 24:36–40), and the good news did what the cynic says good news never does. It turned out to be true.

7.theology:
The shape of the promise (v. 1). God binds himself to a word anyone can check, and what he promises is ordinary: not abundance but a normal day, back the way it should have been.

Windows in heaven (v. 2). The officer does not deny God's power in the abstract, only that this particular word could be true, and his sentence fits the offence: he is given the fullest possible proof, and no share in the food.

Outside the camp (vv. 3-4). The city is saved by the men it had shut out, because they were the only people with nothing left to protect.

Three sets of chariots. There were real Syrian ones that terrified a servant (6:15); fiery ones standing on the same hill that he could not see (6:17); and these, which do not exist at all (7:6). Nobody in Israel drew a sword.

A day of good news (v. 9). The lepers' reasons were mixed, conscience and fear together, and God used the mixture. Nobody has to wait for a pure heart before opening their mouth.

Explaining the good away (v. 12). A settled expectation of the worst does not lift when good news arrives; it sets about explaining the good news away.

Told twice (vv. 17-20). The writer tells his end twice so that nobody takes it for coincidence. He was not condemned for finding a promise hard to believe, as Elisha's own servant did at Dothan. He sneered at a word he had just heard God speak, and was told a day in advance what it would cost.
7.examples:
Then: Four men who were not allowed inside the gate sat in the strip of ground between a starving city and a besieging army, worked out that every option except one ended in certain death, and walked toward the enemy at dusk because they had nothing left that anybody could take.

Now: First, verse 9 is a missionary verse, and what makes it useful is its honesty about the lepers. They had eaten and buried treasure before conscience caught up with them. Mixed motives did not disqualify them and will not disqualify you: you go not as one who has earned the news but as a beggar who was fed by a victory Christ won alone, and his Spirit gives the words (Acts 1:8). Second, the king in the night. If you have prayed a long time and are braced for disappointment, notice how easily a man in this chapter turns an answer to prayer into evidence of a trap. Third, God does not forget the people on the edges. If you feel shut outside the gate, notice whom he chose to carry the news.

keyVerse.quote: Then they said to one another, “We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come; let us go and tell the king’s household.”
keyVerse.note: Four outcasts sitting on more food than they can eat, while the city that shut them out starves, realise that silence would be a wrong. The word for good news lies behind the New Testament word for the gospel, and the verse has become a charter for every beggar who has found bread and goes to tell other beggars where it is. Their motives were mixed, and God used them anyway.

7.reflection:
Elisha’s promise named a time, a place and a price (v. 1), and the king’s aide scoffed that not even windows in heaven could make it happen (v. 2). What is the difference between struggling to believe a promise and scorning it? Where are you tempted to treat God’s word as too good to be true?

The four lepers had nothing left to protect, and that is why they were the ones who walked out and found the deliverance (vv. 3–5). How can having nothing left to lose become an advantage in coming to Christ? What do people around you still feel they must protect?

“We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news” (v. 9). The lepers ate first and their motives were mixed, yet God used them. What keeps you quiet about the gospel, and how does this verse speak to it?

Woken with verified good news, the king worked out how it might be a trap (v. 12). Why is cynicism so easy, and how did the risen Jesus answer the disciples who thought the women’s report “an idle tale” (Luke 24:11, 36–43)?

8.title: The Shunammite's Land and Hazael
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had restored to life, "Arise, and depart with your household, and sojourn wherever you can, for the LORD has called for a famine, and it will come upon the land for seven years."<sup>2</sup>So the woman arose and did according to the word of the man of God. She went with her household and sojourned in the land of the Philistines seven years.<sup>3</sup>And at the end of the seven years, when the woman returned from the land of the Philistines, she went to appeal to the king for her house and her land.<sup>4</sup>Now the king was talking with Gehazi the servant of the man of God, saying, "Tell me all the great things that Elisha has done."<sup>5</sup>And while he was telling the king how Elisha had restored the dead to life, behold, the woman whose son he had restored to life appealed to the king for her house and her land. And Gehazi said, "My lord, O king, here is the woman, and here is her son whom Elisha restored to life."<sup>6</sup>And when the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed an official for her, saying, "Restore all that was hers, together with all the produce of the fields from the day that she left the land until now."<sup>7</sup>Now Elisha came to Damascus. Ben-hadad the king of Syria was sick. And when it was told him, "The man of God has come here,"<sup>8</sup>the king said to Hazael, "Take a present with you and go to meet the man of God, and inquire of the LORD through him, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'"<sup>9</sup>So Hazael went to meet him, and took a present with him, all kinds of goods of Damascus, forty camels' loads. When he came and stood before him, he said, "Your son Ben-hadad king of Syria has sent me to you, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'"<sup>10</sup>And Elisha said to him, "Go, say to him, 'You shall certainly recover,' but the LORD has shown me that he shall certainly die."<sup>11</sup>And he fixed his gaze and stared at him, until he was embarrassed. And the man of God wept.<sup>12</sup>And Hazael said, "Why does my lord weep?" He answered, "Because I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel. You will set on fire their fortresses, and you will kill their young men with the sword and dash in pieces their little ones and rip open their pregnant women."<sup>13</sup>And Hazael said, "What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?" Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you are to be king over Syria."<sup>14</sup>Then he departed from Elisha and came to his master, who said to him, "What did Elisha say to you?" And he answered, "He told me that you would certainly recover."<sup>15</sup>But the next day he took the bed cloth and dipped it in water and spread it over his face, till he died. And Hazael became king in his place.<sup>16</sup>In the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, when Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>17</sup>He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.<sup>18</sup>And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>19</sup>Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.<sup>20</sup>In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own.<sup>21</sup>Then Joram passed over to Zair with all his chariots and rose by night, and he and his chariot commanders struck the Edomites who had surrounded him, but his army fled home.<sup>22</sup>So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time.<sup>23</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>24</sup>So Joram slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.<sup>25</sup>In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah the son of Jehoram, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>26</sup>Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah; she was a granddaughter of Omri king of Israel.<sup>27</sup>He also walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for he was son-in-law to the house of Ahab.<sup>28</sup>He went with Joram the son of Ahab to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, and the Syrians wounded Joram.<sup>29</sup>And King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.
8.overview:
Where we are. The siege of Samaria has been lifted by a word (chapter 7). Chapter 8 closes the long run of Elisha’s stories and turns toward judgment. It reaches back to the woman of Shunem, takes Elisha to Damascus, and crosses to Judah, where the house of Ahab has married into the house of David.

The message. God rules the small things and the great. He times a widow’s appeal to the minute. He raises up Hazael as the rod of his judgment on Israel, and his prophet weeps over it. And when David’s own line goes the way of Ahab, he keeps the lamp burning for David’s sake alone. His promises do not rest on the worthiness of those who inherit them.

Why it was said. The first readers had lost their land and their king (see the introduction). A woman given back her house after years abroad, and a lamp kept alight through the worst of David’s sons, told them God had not finished with them.

How the chapter makes its case. The Shunammite, back after seven years away at Elisha’s word, appeals for her property just as Gehazi is telling the king how her son was raised, and everything is restored (vv. 1–6). In Damascus Elisha tells Hazael that his sick master will die, weeps over the cruelty Hazael will bring on Israel, and hears him protest that he is a mere dog; the next day Hazael smothers his master (vv. 7–15). In Judah, Jehoram, married to Ahab’s daughter, walks in Ahab’s ways, yet the LORD will not destroy Judah, for David’s sake (vv. 16–19). Edom and Libnah break away (vv. 20–24), and Ahaziah, Athaliah’s son, goes down to visit his wounded uncle at Jezreel, where judgment is waiting (vv. 25–29).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by promise. God kept “a lamp” for David “and to his sons forever” (v. 19) through kings who deserved to lose it, down to one hidden baby (11:2), and in the end to the one who says, “I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16). It also shows God’s character as Christ reveals it: Elisha weeping over the judgment he foresaw is a small likeness of Jesus weeping over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44), who then bore the judgment of his people himself.

For us. God’s faithfulness to you does not rise and fall with your obedience this month; it rests on the Son of David, whose obedience stands where ours fails. Yet Hazael’s “I could never” warns us all, and Jehoram’s marriage shows how far one compromise can carry a family. And the God who timed a widow’s appeal to the minute is not careless with your affairs either.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Here Is the Woman, and Here Is Her Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God cares for his people through ordinary providence as well as through miracles. The woman of Shunem, whose son Elisha had raised (4:8–37), obeyed his warning of a seven-year famine and lived among the Philistines (vv. 1–2). Coming home, she finds her house and land in other hands and goes to the king to appeal (v. 3). She arrives at the very moment Gehazi is telling the king how Elisha raised her son, so her case is made before she opens her mouth (vv. 4–5). The king restores everything, adds seven years of harvests, and sends an officer to see it done (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Go back to chapter 4 and remember what she turned down. Offered a word spoken on her behalf to the king, she answered I dwell among my own people (4:13). Years later she needs precisely that introduction, and God arranges a better one: a servant is already telling her story to the king when she opens the door.
verseByVerse.examples: God's care for her ran through seven years of exile and an ordinary court of law. Not every rescue is a miracle; some come as a fair hearing and an officer sent to see it done.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had restored to life, "Arise, and depart with your household, and sojourn wherever you can, for the LORD has called for a famine, and it will come upon the land for seven years." So the woman arose and did according to the word of the man of God. She went with her household and sojourned in the land of the Philistines seven years. And at the end of the seven years, when the woman returned from the land of the Philistines, she went to appeal to the king for her house and her land. Now the king was talking with Gehazi the servant of the man of God, saying, "Tell me all the great things that Elisha has done." And while he was telling the king how Elisha had restored the dead to life, behold, the woman whose son he had restored to life appealed to the king for her house and her land. And Gehazi said, "My lord, O king, here is the woman, and here is her son whom Elisha restored to life." And when the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed an official for her, saying, "Restore all that was hers, together with all the produce of the fields from the day that she left the land until now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman who obeyed God’s warning and left her home for seven years comes back to find it gone, and God so orders events that her story is being told to the king as she walks in, and she receives everything back with interest.

Now Elisha had said to the woman. The words had said show the writer reaching back. This is not the next thing that happened after the siege lifted; Kings is not always laid out in the order events occurred.

The LORD has called for a famine. God calls for it as a man calls a servant: seven years of failed harvests across a region are not just weather. She is not spared the famine, since she has to leave her home for seven years, but she is warned in good time, and being told is itself a mercy the rest of the country does not get.

She went with her household and sojourned in the land of the Philistines. She obeys at once and completely, which by now is what we expect of her. Think what it costs a woman of standing in Shunem to take her household out of the land God gave her family and live seven years among the old enemy, because a prophet told her to.

She went to appeal to the king for her house and her land. In seven years the house has been occupied or the land taken over, perhaps by the crown itself, and she has to go to court to get it back: a widow, apparently, since her elderly husband is not mentioned again, with no one to speak for her.

Tell me all the great things that Elisha has done. The king wants the Elisha stories, all of them, and has sent for the man who was there.

While he was telling the king. The timing is exact: not merely the same day, but the middle of Gehazi’s sentence. She has come about a property claim, with no idea that the one man in the kingdom who can confirm her story is standing at the king’s elbow, and the door opens on the one moment in seven years when her case has already been made for her.

Here is the woman, and here is her son. Put this beside chapter 4. Elisha had offered her exactly this, a word spoken on her behalf to the king, and she said no: “I dwell among my own people” (4:13). Years later she needs the introduction she turned down, and gets a better one: somebody is already telling the king her story as the best thing he knows, and she and the living evidence walk in on the sentence. She had declined a friend at court, and God had one waiting in the room.

Restore all that was hers. She gets it all back, and then something nobody asked for: seven years of harvests, counted from the day she left. The king assigns an official to put her in possession. Not every rescue is a miracle; this one is a thorough, administrative, entirely unmiraculous piece of justice.

For the first readers. Kings was finished for Israelites who had themselves been driven out of the land and were waiting to go home (25:27–30). A woman who left the land at the word of the LORD, lived for years among foreigners, and came back to have her house and fields restored by the king’s order is a story they would have read with particular attention. Probably that is one reason it is told here: it is a small picture of the God who brings his people back and gives back what was theirs.

How could Gehazi, a leper, be talking with the king? This is a real difficulty. Gehazi was struck with leprosy in chapter 5 and went out from Elisha’s presence “a leper, like snow” (5:27), and a leper did not sit making conversation with the king of Israel. The first verse of this chapter has already told us we are looking backwards, so the episode may belong to an earlier time; or the rule may not have been enforced at the northern court, which kept golden calves and a Baal temple and was not scrupulous about the law of Moses. The text does not say, and it is better to leave it open than to invent an answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — The Man of God Wept
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God carries out his purposes among the nations, and his prophet grieves over what they will cost. The king of Syria is sick and sends Hazael with a lavish gift to ask Elisha whether he will recover (vv. 7–9). Elisha answers that the illness will not kill him, but that he will certainly die (v. 10). Then he stares at Hazael until the man is ashamed, and weeps, because he has been shown the cruelty Hazael will bring on Israel (vv. 11–12). Hazael protests that he is a nobody; told that he will be king, he reports half the message and smothers his master the next day (vv. 13–15). The commission given to Elijah at Horeb is fulfilled (1 Kings 19:15).
verseByVerse.theology: The two halves of verse 10 are both true. The illness is not going to kill Ben-hadad; someone else is, and he is standing in the room holding the message.
verseByVerse.examples: Knowing what is coming does not make God's prophet cold about it: he stands in a room in Damascus crying about children who have not been born yet.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Elisha came to Damascus. Ben-hadad the king of Syria was sick. And when it was told him, "The man of God has come here," the king said to Hazael, "Take a present with you and go to meet the man of God, and inquire of the LORD through him, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'" So Hazael went to meet him, and took a present with him, all kinds of goods of Damascus, forty camels' loads. When he came and stood before him, he said, "Your son Ben-hadad king of Syria has sent me to you, saying, 'Shall I recover from this sickness?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of the nation that has been besieging Samaria sends to Israel’s prophet to ask whether he will recover, with a king’s gift, taking it for granted that the God of Israel answers through this man.

Now Elisha came to Damascus. The prophet of Israel walks into the enemy capital, and its king asks to consult him. That may be Naaman’s doing, indirectly. The commander of that army went home clean (chapter 5), and years later the throne of Syria assumes that the God of Israel answers through Elisha.

Shall I recover from this sickness? It is the question King Ahaziah of Israel asked in the first chapter of this book, almost word for word (1:2). The king of Israel sent to a Philistine shrine and was told he would die. The king of Syria sends to the prophet of Israel.

Take a present with you. It was the custom to bring a gift when consulting a prophet: Saul’s servant thought of it at once (1 Samuel 9:7–8), and Jeroboam’s wife came with loaves and honey (1 Kings 14:3). Naaman had brought silver, gold and clothing, and Elisha would not take any of it (5:5, 16). Forty camel-loads is a king’s gift, probably meant to secure a favourable answer, and the king of Syria calls himself “your son” to an Israelite prophet. The answer, as verse 10 shows, is not for sale.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elisha said to him, "Go, say to him, 'You shall certainly recover,' but the LORD has shown me that he shall certainly die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha’s answer is not an instruction to lie: the sickness will not kill Ben-hadad, but he will certainly die, because the man carrying the question is going to kill him.

You shall certainly recover. Both halves are true. Elisha is not composing a deception. He hands a man a message and watches what he does with it: Hazael will deliver the first half and act on the second.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read the first half as a negative, “You shall certainly not recover” (see the note on this verse). Either way the second half stands: the LORD has shown Elisha that Ben-hadad will die.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “You shall certainly not recover.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he fixed his gaze and stared at him, until he was embarrassed. And the man of God wept. And Hazael said, "Why does my lord weep?" He answered, "Because I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel. You will set on fire their fortresses, and you will kill their young men with the sword and dash in pieces their little ones and rip open their pregnant women."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha stares at Hazael until the man is ashamed, and then weeps, because God has shown him the atrocities this man will inflict on Israel; knowing the future does not make God’s prophet cold.

He fixed his gaze and stared at him. Nothing happens except a look. The prophet goes on staring past the point where either man could pretend it was accidental, until the Syrian cannot stand it. And then he starts to cry.

I know the evil that you will do. He names it in four clauses, with nothing softened. None of it is exaggeration. Amos will indict Damascus by name for exactly this kind of campaign, “because they have threshed Gilead with threshing sledges of iron” (Amos 1:3–5), and this book records the results: Hazael cutting Israel down until Jehoahaz had fifty horsemen left (10:32–33; 13:7). God had told Elijah that Hazael’s sword would be his judgment on an Israel that had gone after Baal (1 Kings 19:15–17).

And the man of God wept. This answers something people genuinely worry about. If God knows the future, does he watch it coldly, like a play he has already seen? Here is a man let in on it, and the effect of foreknowledge on him is tears. Knowing in advance did not make it smaller; even a just judgment is no pleasure to God (Ezekiel 33:11).

Another Prophet wept over a city. The tears point beyond Elisha. Some nine centuries later another Prophet came down the Mount of Olives, saw Jerusalem and wept over it, foretelling the day its enemies would tear it down, “you and your children within you” (Luke 19:41–44). He wept over a judgment he foresaw, and then went to bear the judgment of his people himself. The God who knows the end from the beginning is no cold spectator: in Christ he has wept over his enemies and died for them.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hazael said, "What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?" Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you are to be king over Syria."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hazael recoils at the idea that a nobody like him could do such things, and within a day he has begun: the man who says “I could never” has simply not yet met his opportunity.

What is your servant, who is but a dog? Hazael’s answer has been read two ways, as false modesty and as genuine revulsion, and the second is more likely and more frightening. He calls himself a dog, a nobody without the standing to do anything on that scale, and he means it. The idea was so far outside his picture of himself that he could make no sense of it. He murders his master the following day.

The LORD has shown me that you are to be king over Syria. Elisha’s reply supplies exactly one piece of information Hazael did not have: that the throne was going to be his. God has him say it, knowing what Hazael will do with it. Hazael was not made a murderer by being told. He was shown what he was, and what he did with it, he chose. God rules even such deeds for his purposes without being the author of the sin.

An outside witness. An Assyrian inscription of Shalmaneser III, from about 841 BC, describes the event from outside: it calls Hazael the son of a nobody who seized the throne.

“I could never.” That is the thing to carry out of this chapter. Almost nobody who does a terrible thing was, the week before, a person who thought he might. Between “What is your servant, who is but a dog” and a wet cloth held over a sick man’s face there is one night, one opportunity, and one new piece of information. Our safety is not in our own character but in the God who keeps us and whose Spirit in us resists what we would otherwise become. So we pray “lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), and mean it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he departed from Elisha and came to his master, who said to him, "What did Elisha say to you?" And he answered, "He told me that you would certainly recover." But the next day he took the bed cloth and dipped it in water and spread it over his face, till he died. And Hazael became king in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hazael tells his master only the half of the answer that suits him and smothers him the next day, and so God’s old commission to Elijah is fulfilled through a murderer’s own choice.

He told me that you would certainly recover. Hazael reports half a sentence, accurately, and the half he leaves out is the half about dying. It is the most effective kind of lie, because every word of it is true.

He took the bed cloth and dipped it in water. A heavy cloth, soaked so that it clings, laid over the face of a sick man. The writer gives it one flat sentence with no adjectives, which is worse than any amount of horror.

And Hazael became king in his place. With that, an instruction given on Mount Horeb is finally carried out. God told Elijah, in the whisper after the wind and the earthquake and the fire, “Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. And when you arrive, you shall anoint Hazael to be king over Syria” (1 Kings 19:15). Elijah never went. A generation later his successor walks into Damascus and the thing is done, not by anointing but by telling a man the truth about himself. The command outlived the man who received it: Elijah was told to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha (1 Kings 19:15–16), and Jehu is still to come (chapter 9).

Uncertain wording. The word translated bed cloth occurs only here; it was some thick cloth or coverlet, but exactly what is not known. The Hebrew also does not name who spread it. A few think it was meant to cool a fever and the death was natural, but Elisha’s tears and Hazael’s sudden reign point to Hazael, as the ESV takes it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–29 — For the Daughter of Ahab Was His Wife
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the house of David takes on the ways of Ahab’s house, God keeps it alive for David’s sake alone. Jehoram of Judah, married to Ahab’s daughter, walks in the ways of Israel’s kings, yet the LORD will not destroy Judah, because he promised David a lamp for ever (vv. 16–19). In his reign Edom and Libnah break away (vv. 20–24). His son Ahaziah, whose mother is Athaliah, reigns one year in the same ways (vv. 25–27), fights beside his uncle Joram of Israel at Ramoth-gilead, and goes down to visit him, wounded, at Jezreel (vv. 28–29). Without knowing it, both kings are gathering at the place where God’s sentence on Ahab’s house has been waiting.
verseByVerse.theology: That marriage was recorded in one neutral sentence (2 Chron. 18:1). Here is what it cost, stated as a reason: the house of David began behaving like the house of Ahab because a daughter of Ahab was in it.
verseByVerse.examples: The lamp is the only reason there is still a Judah to ruin. It is kept burning even under a man who married Ahab's daughter: Judah survives on a promise God made to David, who is long dead.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, when Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, began to reign. He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done, for the daughter of Ahab was his wife. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoram of Judah, married to Ahab’s daughter, brings the ways of Ahab’s house into the house of David, and Judah survives only because God promised David a lamp that would not go out.

Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, began to reign. The account crosses to Judah, where the wickedness of Ahab’s house now reaches the house of David. The odd phrase “when Jehoshaphat was king of Judah” probably means that Jehoram began to reign alongside his father before Jehoshaphat died (a few ancient copies leave the phrase out), which is how these books can date the same years by both kings.

For the daughter of Ahab was his wife. Verse 18 gives the cause, the price of a decision made many chapters ago. In 1 Kings 22 a good king of Judah went north on a friendly visit to Ahab, and Chronicles supplies the detail: “he made a marriage alliance with Ahab” (2 Chronicles 18:1). Jehoshaphat’s son married Ahab’s daughter, and everybody would have called it statesmanship. Chronicles also records what Kings leaves out: when Jehoram came to the throne “he killed all his brothers with the sword” (2 Chronicles 21:4). The method of Ahab’s house had arrived in Jerusalem within one generation.

A lamp to him and to his sons forever. The lamp is a descendant of David still reigning in Jerusalem, and the reader has met it twice before. When the kingdom was torn from Solomon, God kept one tribe for his son, “that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem” (1 Kings 11:36). When Abijam’s heart was not whole, the lamp was the reason his line survived: “for David’s sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem” (1 Kings 15:4). And here it is again, under a man who married Ahab’s daughter and killed his brothers. The picture is deliberately small. It is not a fire or a beacon but an oil lamp, the clay dish with a wick that a household kept burning through the night so that the house was never wholly dark. It does not light up much. It only refuses to go out.

For the sake of David his servant. Not for Jehoram’s sake, and not because Judah is better than Israel, which it is not; it is “for the sake of David his servant, since he promised”. The nation is being carried by an oath sworn to a man dead more than a century, about descendants unborn when it was sworn. God’s promises do not depend on the quality of the people who inherit them.

The lamp burns low. It will burn very low under Athaliah, who is about to try to wipe out the whole royal line, until it is down to one baby hidden in a bedroom in the temple (11:1–3). It goes into exile and comes back. And at the end of the Bible the one who was promised says of himself, “I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16). God keeps faith with his people now for the same kind of reason: for the sake of the Son of David, whose obedience stands where theirs fails.

What it does not mean. God’s patience with Judah was not approval of Jehoram, who was judged in his own lifetime (see the note on vv. 20–24). The promise kept the line alive; it never shielded a wicked king from his sin’s consequences.
verseByVerse.note: Joram is another spelling of Jehoram (ESV note). Confusingly, the king of Israel and the king of Judah both bore this name at the same time.

verseByVerse.quote: In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own. Then Joram passed over to Zair with all his chariots and rose by night, and he and his chariot commanders struck the Edomites who had surrounded him, but his army fled home. So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time. Now the rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? So Joram slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under Jehoram Judah starts to come apart: Edom throws off its yoke for good, and even Libnah, a town of Judah itself, breaks away.

In his days Edom revolted from the rule of Judah. Edom had been subject to Judah since David conquered it (2 Samuel 8:14); in Jehoshaphat’s day “there was no king in Edom; a deputy was king” (1 Kings 22:47), and Edom held the road south to the Red Sea port at Elath. Now it sets up its own king. Isaac had foreseen the day when Esau’s descendants would “break his yoke from your neck” (Genesis 27:40).

He and his chariot commanders struck the Edomites. He breaks out of an encirclement by night and loses the war: his army runs home, and Edom is gone “to this day”.

Then Libnah revolted at the same time. Libnah is not a foreign vassal but a town in Judah’s own lowlands. The kingdom is coming apart at the edges and in the middle. Chronicles gives the reason for both revolts: “because he had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers” (2 Chronicles 21:10).

So Joram slept with his fathers. Kings closes the reign with its usual formula (vv. 23–24). Chronicles tells how it actually ended: a letter of judgment from Elijah, a raid by Philistines and Arabs that carried off his household and all his sons except the youngest, and a slow, painful disease of the bowels. “He departed with no one’s regret. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings” (2 Chronicles 21:12–20). Eight years on the throne, and nobody mourned him.

Uncertain wording. Zair (v. 21) is otherwise unknown. It was probably on the road south into Edom, and some think the name is a copying slip for Seir, Edom’s own hill country. The battle is told in a few compressed words and its course is hard to follow, but its result is not.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah the son of Jehoram, king of Judah, began to reign. Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah; she was a granddaughter of Omri king of Israel. He also walked in the way of the house of Ahab and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as the house of Ahab had done, for he was son-in-law to the house of Ahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaziah’s one-year reign is summed up by his mother’s name: Athaliah, Ahab’s daughter, has brought the house of Ahab to the throne of Judah.

His mother’s name was Athaliah. The notice introducing a king of Judah usually names his mother, and this time the name matters more than any other in the book. Athaliah is Ahab’s daughter (v. 18), quite possibly Jezebel’s too, and so Omri’s granddaughter (v. 26). The King James Version says “daughter of Omri” in verse 26, because the Hebrew word for daughter is regularly used of a female descendant. Her husband is dead and her son will reign one year. Keep her in view. When that year is over she will try to wipe out the royal line (11:1), and the lamp of verse 19 will come down to a single infant.

He also walked in the way of the house of Ahab. Chronicles names his teachers: “his mother was his counselor in doing wickedly”, and after his father’s death the men of Ahab’s house “were his counselors, to his undoing” (2 Chronicles 22:3–4). A king of twenty-two, advised by his mother and her family, ruled Judah as though it were a province of Samaria.

For he was son-in-law to the house of Ahab. Verse 27 gives the same explanation for the son as verse 18 gave for the father, in case anyone thought the first was incidental.

Twenty-two or forty-two? Ahaziah is twenty-two here and forty-two in 2 Chronicles 22:2. Forty-two is impossible, since his father died at forty (8:17), so the Chronicles figure was very probably miscopied in transmission; some ancient translations of Chronicles have a lower figure.

verseByVerse.quote: He went with Joram the son of Ahab to make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, and the Syrians wounded Joram. And King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaziah fights beside his uncle Joram at Ramoth-gilead and then visits him, wounded, at Jezreel, so that without knowing it both kings are gathered where God’s sentence on Ahab’s house has been waiting.

To make war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. Ramoth-gilead is the town Ahab went to war for on the strength of four hundred prophets and a lying spirit, and where a random arrow found the join in his armour (1 Kings 22). Now his son fights at the same place, against the man Elisha wept over, with a king of Judah beside him, as Ahab had.

The wounds that the Syrians had given him at Ramah. Ramah here is a short form of Ramoth-gilead, not the Ramah north of Jerusalem. The wound matters to the story: it is why Joram is lying in Jezreel, away from his army, when one of his own commanders is anointed in the camp (9:1–15).

Ahaziah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel. The writer has deliberately gathered everyone in one place. The king of Israel is lying wounded in Jezreel. The king of Judah, his nephew, has come to visit him and is in the same house. The queen mother of the north, Jezebel, is in that town. And Ahab’s daughter is sitting in Jerusalem waiting for news.

Why Jezreel matters. Jezreel is where Naboth had a vineyard. It is the ground on which Elijah told Ahab that dogs would lick his blood where they had licked Naboth’s, and that the dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of that same town (1 Kings 21:19, 23). Ahab humbled himself, and the sentence was deferred, not cancelled: “in his son’s days I will bring the disaster upon his house” (1 Kings 21:29). Everyone it was to fall on is now in Jezreel or a day’s ride from it, and Jehu, the last name on the list God gave Elijah at Horeb, is an officer in the army at Ramoth-gilead.

Deferred, not cancelled. God’s delays are mercies, room to repent (2 Peter 3:9), but not a change of mind. The only safe place when his sentence falls is the one he has provided in Christ.

8.theology:
The timing (vv. 4-5). The word in the king’s ear that she declined out of contentment (4:13), God supplied out of kindness, at the exact minute it was needed.

Foreknowledge and tears (vv. 11-12). Does knowing the future make God cold about it? His prophet is let in on decades of atrocity and weeps over children not yet conceived.

I could never (v. 13). What is your servant, who is but a dog? is most likely genuine, and that is what makes it frightening. Almost nobody who does a terrible thing was, the week before, a man who thought he might. Between that sentence and the wet cloth over his master’s face there is one night, one opportunity, and one new piece of information. God gave him the information; what he did with it, he chose.

A commission outliving the man (v. 15). God's word to Elijah on Horeb (1 Kgs. 19:15) is carried out a generation later by his successor. God's purposes do not depend on one servant's lifetime.

Whom you marry (v. 18). A marriage alliance that everyone called statesmanship brought the house of Ahab's ways into the house of David within a generation.

The lamp (v. 19). The lamp is David’s royal line: a small light that refuses to go out, kept for the sake of David and not of the man on the throne. God's promises are not maintained by the quality of the people who inherit them.
8.examples:
Then: A woman came home after seven years in enemy country to find strangers on her land, walked up the steps of a palace to beg for it back, and opened the door on the one minute in seven years when the king was being told her own son's story by the one man who could confirm it.

Now: First, her introduction. She had turned down a word in the king's ear because she wanted nothing and owed nothing, and years later got a better version of it than the one she refused. A contented person who turns down a favour is not left without God’s provision. Second, Hazael. The sentence to be afraid of in your own mouth is "I could never", because the man who said it meant it, and did it the following day. Your safety is not in your own character but in the God who keeps you and whose Spirit in you resists what you would otherwise become; so pray lead us not into temptation (Matt. 6:13) and mean it. Third, the lamp. If you are measuring whether God will keep faith with you by the state of your own obedience this month, notice that in verse 19 the lamp was kept for David’s sake, not the king’s. God keeps faith with you for the sake of the Son of David, whose obedience stands where yours fails.

keyVerse.quote: Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of a murdered king and a son of David behaving like Ahab, this verse explains why Judah is still standing. The reason is not the king or the people but an oath sworn to David long before. It is the thread that runs through the rest of the book, through Athaliah’s massacre and Babylon’s prison, to the Son of David who is the lamp that never goes out.

8.reflection:
The woman of Shunem had turned down a word to the king (4:13), and years later walked in at the very moment her story was being told to him (vv. 4–6). Where have you seen God’s care in the timing of ordinary events? How does this help you trust him with what you cannot arrange?

Elisha wept over the evil Hazael would do, even though it would be God’s judgment on Israel (vv. 11–12). What does that show about how God regards the suffering he foresees? How does Jesus weeping over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44) take it further?

“What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?” (v. 13). Why is “I could never” such a dangerous thing to say? How does praying “lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13) guard us?

Judah survived a wicked king “for the sake of David his servant” (v. 19). How does that encourage a believer whose faithfulness has been poor? What is the difference between resting on God’s promise and presuming on it?

9.title: Jehu Anointed; Joram and Jezebel Fall
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, "Tie up your garments, and take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead.<sup>2</sup>And when you arrive, look there for Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. And go in and have him rise from among his fellows, and lead him to an inner chamber.<sup>3</sup>Then take the flask of oil and pour it on his head and say, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.' Then open the door and flee; do not linger."<sup>4</sup>So the young man, the servant of the prophet, went to Ramoth-gilead.<sup>5</sup>And when he came, behold, the commanders of the army were in council. And he said, "I have a word for you, O commander." And Jehu said, "To which of us all?" And he said, "To you, O commander."<sup>6</sup>So he arose and went into the house. And the young man poured the oil on his head, saying to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, I anoint you king over the people of the LORD, over Israel.<sup>7</sup>And you shall strike down the house of Ahab your master, so that I may avenge on Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD.<sup>8</sup>For the whole house of Ahab shall perish, and I will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel.<sup>9</sup>And I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah.<sup>10</sup>And the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the territory of Jezreel, and none shall bury her." Then he opened the door and fled.<sup>11</sup>When Jehu came out to the servants of his master, they said to him, "Is all well? Why did this mad fellow come to you?" And he said to them, "You know the fellow and his talk."<sup>12</sup>And they said, "That is not true; tell us now." And he said, "Thus and so he spoke to me, saying, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.'"<sup>13</sup>Then in haste every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, "Jehu is king."<sup>14</sup>Thus Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi conspired against Joram. (Now Joram with all Israel had been on guard at Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Syria,<sup>15</sup>but King Joram had returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him, when he fought with Hazael king of Syria.) So Jehu said, "If this is your decision, then let no one slip out of the city to go and tell the news in Jezreel."<sup>16</sup>Then Jehu mounted his chariot and went to Jezreel, for Joram lay there. And Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to visit Joram.<sup>17</sup>Now the watchman was standing on the tower in Jezreel, and he saw the company of Jehu as he came and said, "I see a company." And Joram said, "Take a horseman and send to meet them, and let him say, 'Is it peace?'"<sup>18</sup>So a man on horseback went to meet him and said, "Thus says the king, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu said, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me." And the watchman reported, saying, "The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back."<sup>19</sup>Then he sent out a second horseman, who came to them and said, "Thus the king has said, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu answered, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me."<sup>20</sup>Again the watchman reported, "He reached them, but he is not coming back. And the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously."<sup>21</sup>Joram said, "Make ready." And they made ready his chariot. Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his chariot, and went to meet Jehu, and met him at the property of Naboth the Jezreelite.<sup>22</sup>And when Joram saw Jehu, he said, "Is it peace, Jehu?" He answered, "What peace can there be, so long as the whorings and the sorceries of your mother Jezebel are so many?"<sup>23</sup>Then Joram reined about and fled, saying to Ahaziah, "Treachery, O Ahaziah!"<sup>24</sup>And Jehu drew his bow with his full strength, and shot Joram between the shoulders, so that the arrow pierced his heart, and he sank in his chariot.<sup>25</sup>Jehu said to Bidkar his aide, "Take him up and throw him on the plot of ground belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite. For remember, when you and I rode side by side behind Ahab his father, how the LORD made this pronouncement against him:<sup>26</sup>'As surely as I saw yesterday the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons—declares the LORD—I will repay you on this plot of ground.' Now therefore take him up and throw him on the plot of ground, in accordance with the word of the LORD."<sup>27</sup>When Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled in the direction of Beth-haggan. And Jehu pursued him and said, "Shoot him also." And they shot him in the chariot at the ascent of Gur, which is by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo and died there.<sup>28</sup>His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem, and buried him in his tomb with his fathers in the city of David.<sup>29</sup>In the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab, Ahaziah began to reign over Judah.<sup>30</sup>When Jehu came to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. And she painted her eyes and adorned her head and looked out of the window.<sup>31</sup>And as Jehu entered the gate, she said, "Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?"<sup>32</sup>And he lifted up his face to the window and said, "Who is on my side? Who?" Two or three eunuchs looked out at him.<sup>33</sup>He said, "Throw her down." So they threw her down. And some of her blood spattered on the wall and on the horses, and they trampled on her.<sup>34</sup>Then he went in and ate and drank. And he said, "See now to this cursed woman and bury her, for she is a king's daughter."<sup>35</sup>But when they went to bury her, they found no more of her than the skull and the feet and the palms of her hands.<sup>36</sup>When they came back and told him, he said, "This is the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Elijah the Tishbite: 'In the territory of Jezreel the dogs shall eat the flesh of Jezebel,<sup>37</sup>and the corpse of Jezebel shall be as dung on the face of the field in the territory of Jezreel, so that no one can say, This is Jezebel.'"
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 ended with everyone in place: Joram of Israel lying wounded at Jezreel, Ahaziah of Judah visiting him, Jezebel in the same town, and the army holding Ramoth-gilead. The last commission God gave Elijah at Horeb, to anoint Jehu, is still unfulfilled, and the sentence on Ahab’s house, pronounced in Naboth’s vineyard (1 Kings 21:19–24), has waited for years.

The message. God’s word of judgment, however long delayed, falls exactly where and as he said. He has not forgotten the blood of Naboth or of his prophets: Ahab’s son dies on the field Ahab stole, and Jezebel as Elijah foretold. There is no peace while idolatry reigns. Yet the man God uses is not thereby approved: Jehu carries out God’s word with ruthless efficiency and little reverence.

Why it was said. The first readers had watched oppressors seem to go unpunished (see the introduction). The chapter assures them that God keeps the account and that his word does not fail, and shows that being used by God is not the same as being right with him.

How the chapter makes its case. Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu in secret, with God’s commission to strike down Ahab’s house (vv. 1–10), and the officers proclaim him king at once (vv. 11–13). Jehu drives to Jezreel (vv. 14–20). The kings meet him at Naboth’s property; Jehu answers that there can be no peace while Jezebel’s idolatry goes on, and Joram is shot and thrown onto Naboth’s plot, “in accordance with the word of the LORD”, and Ahaziah dies at Megiddo (vv. 21–29). Jezebel taunts Jehu from a window, is thrown down by her own eunuchs, and the dogs leave nothing to bury: “This is the word of the LORD” (vv. 30–37).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes. “Is it peace?” is asked five times, and no answer given in Jezreel brings peace. Jehu could end a dynasty, but he could not make anyone right with God, and a century later God would punish his own house “for the blood of Jezreel” (Hosea 1:4). True peace comes another way: “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1), who made “peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). Naboth’s blood cried out for justice and received it here; the blood of Jesus “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).

For us. If you are waiting on God over a great wrong that no one has answered for, the wait will end. But beware Jehu’s way of serving God, efficient and scornful; and the chapter gives no private Christian a licence for violence. The only safe place when judgment comes is under the blood that speaks a better word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Open the Door and Flee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his word through obscure servants and flawed instruments. Elisha does not go himself but sends an unnamed young prophet with a flask of oil and orders to run as soon as it is done (vv. 1–3). The young man finds Jehu in a council of commanders, takes him aside, anoints him king over the people of the LORD, and gives him God’s commission: strike down the house of Ahab and avenge the blood of the prophets Jezebel killed, as Elijah had foretold (vv. 4–10). Then he flees. Jehu’s fellow officers call the prophet a madman, but when they hear what he said, they spread their cloaks on the steps, sound the trumpet and proclaim Jehu king (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's great turning points are often carried by people whose names nobody records.
verseByVerse.examples: Jehu's first public act as God's anointed is to laugh at God's messenger with the men who despise him, with the oil still wet in his hair.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, "Tie up your garments, and take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead. And when you arrive, look there for Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. And go in and have him rise from among his fellows, and lead him to an inner chamber. Then take the flask of oil and pour it on his head and say, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.' Then open the door and flee; do not linger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu in secret and then run, carrying out the last of the commissions God gave Elijah at Horeb.

Then Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets. Elisha does not go. The last commission on the list God gave Elijah at Horeb (Hazael over Syria, Jehu over Israel, Elisha in Elijah’s place; 1 Kings 19:15–16) is the most dangerous errand in the kingdom, and the prophet hands it to a student and stays home.

Tie up your garments. Hitch up your robe so that you can run. It is the instruction Elisha gave Gehazi on the road to the Shunammite’s house (4:29), and it means the same thing here. This is not a ceremony but a raid.

Look there for Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. This Jehoshaphat is not the king of Judah; Jehu’s father and grandfather are otherwise unknown, and he is usually called simply “the son of Nimshi” (1 Kings 19:16; 2 Kings 9:20). He is one of the commanders of the army holding Ramoth-gilead against Syria (8:28). The young man is to take him into an inner room: the anointing is to be private, and what happens next is left to Jehu.

Then open the door and flee; do not linger. Consider the errand: walk into a room of senior officers in the field, pick one out by name, get him alone, pour oil on his head and tell him he is king, which is treason, and then run without stopping to see what happens.

verseByVerse.quote: So the young man, the servant of the prophet, went to Ramoth-gilead. And when he came, behold, the commanders of the army were in council. And he said, "I have a word for you, O commander." And Jehu said, "To which of us all?" And he said, "To you, O commander." So he arose and went into the house. And the young man poured the oil on his head, saying to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, I anoint you king over the people of the LORD, over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young prophet singles Jehu out from his fellow commanders and anoints him king, not over a prize to be seized, but over “the people of the LORD”.
