The young man, the servant of the prophet. We are never told his name. He is one of the students from the overcrowded house by the Jordan (6:1), and he does it. God’s great turning points are often carried by people whose names nobody records.

To which of us all? He announces himself to a room of ranking officers; Jehu asks which of them he means; and the young man says: you.

I anoint you king over the people of the LORD. His words go beyond the short sentence Elisha gave him (v. 3), and the rest of the message (vv. 7–10) is spoken in God’s own first person. The added phrase matters: Israel, for all its calves and Baal altars, is still “the people of the LORD”. Jehu is not handed a kingdom to do with as he likes. He is given God’s people, to rule under God.

Another Anointed. Every anointed king in Israel was a sign of the Anointed One to come, the Messiah, and the contrast is instructive. Jehu was anointed to bring judgment by the sword. When Jesus opened his ministry he read, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18). He too will judge, but he came first to bear judgment, not to deal it out.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall strike down the house of Ahab your master, so that I may avenge on Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD. For the whole house of Ahab shall perish, and I will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel. And I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah. And the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the territory of Jezreel, and none shall bury her." Then he opened the door and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu’s commission is not politics but justice: God will avenge on Jezebel the blood of his prophets and end Ahab’s house exactly as Elijah had said.

So that I may avenge on Jezebel the blood of my servants the prophets. The reason for the commission is blood. The reader was told of it long ago, almost in passing: “when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD”, Obadiah hid a hundred of them in caves and fed them (1 Kings 18:4). The rest were killed, uncounted, and for decades nothing was done about it.

God kept the account. This is what delayed judgment looks like from the inside: years in which nothing appears to happen, and then a young man with a flask of oil. The martyrs in Revelation still cry, “how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:10), and the answer is the same: God keeps the account. Yet the blood of the prophets is not the Bible’s last word on innocent blood. The blood of Christ “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24): it pleads not for vengeance but for mercy, and wins it for all who flee to him.

For the whole house of Ahab shall perish. Every clause of verses 8–10 is taken from what Elijah said in a vineyard a dozen years or more before: every male cut off, the house made like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, the dogs eating Jezebel at Jezreel (1 Kings 21:21–24). Nothing has been added and nothing softened. The sentence has simply been waiting.

Then he opened the door and fled. The young man runs, exactly as instructed.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated bond or free (v. 8; also 1 Kings 14:10; 21:21) is an old idiom, literally something like “shut up and left”, and its exact sense is uncertain. It may mean slave and free, under age and of age, or simply everyone. On any reading the point is the same: no male of Ahab’s house is to be left.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jehu came out to the servants of his master, they said to him, "Is all well? Why did this mad fellow come to you?" And he said to them, "You know the fellow and his talk." And they said, "That is not true; tell us now." And he said, "Thus and so he spoke to me, saying, 'Thus says the LORD, I anoint you king over Israel.'" Then in haste every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, "Jehu is king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu’s fellow officers dismiss the prophet as a madman, and Jehu joins their scorn; but the moment they hear his message they throw down their cloaks and make him king.

Why did this mad fellow come to you? The word means a madman, a lunatic. That is what army officers thought of prophets, and it was not an unusual view: Hosea records the nation saying exactly this, “The prophet is a fool; the man of the spirit is mad” (Hosea 9:7).

You know the fellow and his talk. Jehu joins in: you know what they are like. With the oil still running down his hair from a word of God he has just accepted, his first public act is to laugh at the messenger with the men who despise him. This man will carry out God’s judgment with total efficiency, quoting the Scriptures as he does it, and the writer has shown us, in the second sentence Jehu speaks, what he is. A man can do God’s work accurately and hold God in contempt.

That is not true; tell us now. The officers will not accept the brush-off; the Hebrew is blunt, something like “A lie! Tell us.” They have seen the oil and the running young man, and guess that this concerns them all.

Then in haste. The speed is the point. Cloaks come off and go down on the bare steps, a trumpet sounds, and the army has a new king in moments. Spreading garments for a man to walk on was an act of homage to a king; the crowd on the road into Jerusalem would do the same for Jesus (Matthew 21:8). Omri’s house has held power for more than forty years, and one flask of oil and one sentence end it, because the army had long been ready and nobody had said so.

Does Jehu’s anointing license rebellion by believers? No. God himself appointed Jehu through his prophet, as he had foretold (1 Kings 19:16). It was a unique act of judgment, not a pattern. Christians are to honour rulers (Romans 13:1–7), and private persons may not take up the sword to overthrow them. Nor does being used by God mean being approved in every act: God later said he would punish Jehu’s house “for the blood of Jezreel” (Hosea 1:4; see the introduction and 10:30–31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–29 — At the Property of Naboth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s sentence on Ahab’s house falls on the very ground where Ahab’s crime was committed. Jehu seals the town and drives to Jezreel, where Joram lies wounded and Ahaziah of Judah is visiting (vv. 14–16). Two riders sent to ask “Is it peace?” are made to fall in behind him, and the watchman knows him by his furious driving (vv. 17–20). The kings drive out and meet him at Naboth’s property. Jehu answers that there can be no peace while Jezebel’s idolatry and sorcery go on, shoots Joram through the heart, and has the body thrown onto Naboth’s plot, as the LORD had said (vv. 21–26). Ahaziah flees, is shot, and dies at Megiddo (vv. 27–29).
verseByVerse.theology: Is it peace? is asked five times in this chapter (vv. 17, 18, 19, 22, 31). The Hebrew word is shalom: not only the absence of war but wholeness, being right with God. Verse 22 answers all five: there is no peace while the idolatry and sorcery Jezebel brought in still go on.
verseByVerse.examples: Of all the ground outside Jezreel, the meeting happens on the field Ahab stole. Nobody planned it; God's justice found its own way back to the place of the crime.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi conspired against Joram. (Now Joram with all Israel had been on guard at Ramoth-gilead against Hazael king of Syria, but King Joram had returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that the Syrians had given him, when he fought with Hazael king of Syria.) So Jehu said, "If this is your decision, then let no one slip out of the city to go and tell the news in Jezreel." Then Jehu mounted his chariot and went to Jezreel, for Joram lay there. And Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to visit Joram.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu turns his anointing into a coup at once, sealing the town so that no warning reaches Jezreel, where both kings lie unaware.

Thus Jehu conspired against Joram. The word is the one used for the palace plots of these books (1 Kings 15:27; 16:9). The bracket that follows (vv. 14–15) tells the reader why the moment was right: the army was in the field at Ramoth-gilead, and the king was away from it, wounded, in Jezreel (8:28–29).

Let no one slip out of the city. The first order of the new reign is a news blackout: seal the town; nobody rides out. Jehu is a professional, and everything he does from here is fast, correct and effective. Notice that early, because efficiency is almost all that can be said for him.

Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to visit Joram. Both kings are in one town, one wounded in bed, the other on a family visit. The writer set that up at the end of the last chapter, and now it matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the watchman was standing on the tower in Jezreel, and he saw the company of Jehu as he came and said, "I see a company." And Joram said, "Take a horseman and send to meet them, and let him say, 'Is it peace?'" So a man on horseback went to meet him and said, "Thus says the king, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu said, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me." And the watchman reported, saying, "The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back." Then he sent out a second horseman, who came to them and said, "Thus the king has said, 'Is it peace?'" And Jehu answered, "What do you have to do with peace? Turn around and ride behind me." Again the watchman reported, "He reached them, but he is not coming back. And the driving is like the driving of Jehu the son of Nimshi, for he drives furiously."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From his tower the watchman sees rider after rider swallowed up, and at last knows the leader by his furious driving; Jezreel learns nothing until it is too late.

I see a company. The scene works entirely by what a man on a tower can and cannot see. He sees a dust cloud. A rider goes out and is swallowed, then a second. Then, as the column draws near, he recognises not a face or a standard but a style of driving.

Turn around and ride behind me. Each rider is offered a choice with no real choice in it: fall in behind the new king. Both do. Neither goes back, so the king in Jezreel learns nothing except that his messengers are not returning.

He drives furiously. Jehu drove in a way that could be known at a distance. The word for furiously comes from the same root as mad fellow in verse 11: the officers called the prophet mad, and their new king drives like a madman.

Is it peace? The question is asked five times in this chapter: in the king’s order, twice by messengers, by the king himself, and at the end by Jezebel (vv. 17–19, 22, 31). The answer never changes (see the note on vv. 21–24).

verseByVerse.quote: Joram said, "Make ready." And they made ready his chariot. Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each in his chariot, and went to meet Jehu, and met him at the property of Naboth the Jezreelite. And when Joram saw Jehu, he said, "Is it peace, Jehu?" He answered, "What peace can there be, so long as the whorings and the sorceries of your mother Jezebel are so many?" Then Joram reined about and fled, saying to Ahaziah, "Treachery, O Ahaziah!" And Jehu drew his bow with his full strength, and shot Joram between the shoulders, so that the arrow pierced his heart, and he sank in his chariot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Naboth’s field Joram asks whether Jehu comes in peace and is told that there can be no peace while Jezebel’s idolatry goes on; then Jehu’s arrow finds him, as God’s sentence had said.

At the property of Naboth the Jezreelite. Of all the ground outside the town, the two kings meet their killer on the plot a farmer refused to sell, because it was the inheritance of his fathers and not his to give away. Ahab wanted it for a vegetable garden. His wife had the owner and his sons killed by a properly conducted legal procedure with two sworn witnesses, and Elijah met Ahab standing among the vines and pronounced God’s sentence (1 Kings 21). Nobody in either chariot chose that field. The writer simply records where the horses stopped.

What peace can there be? Joram is asking a diplomatic question: are you loyal, is this a friendly approach? Jehu answers a larger one. There is no peace to be had, because of idolatry that has gone on for more than thirty years and never been dealt with. Whorings is the prophets’ word for idolatry, unfaithfulness to the LORD like a wife’s to her husband (Hosea 2); sorceries are the occult practices that came in with Baal. It is what Isaiah says twice over: “There is no peace,” says my God, “for the wicked” (Isaiah 57:21; 48:22). Peace is not a mood or a ceasefire. It is being right with God, and where that is missing, any quiet is only a pause before judgment.

Treachery, O Ahaziah! Joram understands at last and shouts a warning to his nephew. The word (mirmah) means deceit, a strange word in the mouth of Jezebel’s son: deceit, forged letters and false witnesses were how his mother took Naboth’s life (1 Kings 21:8–13), beside this very field.

Jehu drew his bow with his full strength. At Ramoth-gilead a Syrian soldier “drew his bow at random” (literally in his innocence, aiming at nobody in particular), and the arrow found the one gap in the armour of the one man on the field who was in disguise (1 Kings 22:34). Here a man draws his bow with his full strength, at a named target, at close range, and puts the arrow between the shoulders. One arrow aimed at nothing and one aimed exactly, and both went precisely where God had said. He can work through what looks like chance or through deliberate skill.

Making peace by the blood of his cross. The question asked five times in Jezreel is finally answered somewhere else. Jehu could end a dynasty, but he could not make anyone right with God, and his own house would end in blood too. The peace Joram asked about is the peace the gospel announces: “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). It was not won by an arrow drawn at full strength against the guilty. It was made “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20), when the judgment that falls on Joram here fell instead on the one who had done nothing to deserve it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehu said to Bidkar his aide, "Take him up and throw him on the plot of ground belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite. For remember, when you and I rode side by side behind Ahab his father, how the LORD made this pronouncement against him: 'As surely as I saw yesterday the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons—declares the LORD—I will repay you on this plot of ground.' Now therefore take him up and throw him on the plot of ground, in accordance with the word of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu has Joram’s body thrown onto Naboth’s plot because he was there the day Elijah pronounced the sentence, and now he carries it out to the letter.

When you and I rode side by side behind Ahab his father. Jehu was there. He was a junior officer in the escort the day Ahab drove down to take possession of the vineyard, close enough behind the royal chariot to hear Elijah step out of the vines and pass sentence on the king. So was Bidkar, who is still riding beside him. Two young men heard it, and one of them is now its instrument and can still quote it.

The blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons. His version contains what the account in 1 Kings 21 did not: the children. They must have died, since with an heir alive the land would have stayed in the family. Here, years later, in a soldier’s memory of what a prophet said, they are named. And God speaks of it “as surely as I saw yesterday”: he does not forget.

In accordance with the word of the LORD. Jehu does not leave the body where it fell. He has it thrown onto Naboth’s plot, so that the sentence is carried out to the letter, “on this plot of ground”. Ahab humbled himself when he first heard it, and God put off the disaster on his house to his son’s days (1 Kings 21:27–29). This is the son.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled in the direction of Beth-haggan. And Jehu pursued him and said, "Shoot him also." And they shot him in the chariot at the ascent of Gur, which is by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo and died there. His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem, and buried him in his tomb with his fathers in the city of David. In the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab, Ahaziah began to reign over Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaziah of Judah, there only on a family visit, is caught in the judgment on Ahab’s house because he had walked in its ways.

He fled in the direction of Beth-haggan. Beth-haggan is probably En-gannim, modern Jenin, on the road south. He was hit on the climb near Ibleam, a few miles on, and got as far as Megiddo before he died. His servants brought the body home by chariot (v. 28).

Shoot him also. There is nothing in Jehu’s commission about the king of Judah. Ahaziah had come down to Jezreel to see his uncle, his mother’s brother, and is caught up in a judgment on another family. Yet Chronicles, looking at the same event from God’s side, says that his downfall “was ordained by God” through that visit (2 Chronicles 22:7): he had walked in the ways of Ahab’s house, and he fell with it. And he is in that chariot because two generations earlier a good king of Judah made a marriage alliance with Ahab and thought it was peace.

Buried him in his tomb with his fathers. He is given a proper burial in the royal tombs, which Joram of Israel is not. Chronicles supplies the reason: “They buried him, for they said, ‘He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart’” (2 Chronicles 22:9). Jehoshaphat’s alliance put his grandson in that chariot; Jehoshaphat’s reputation got his body into the family tomb. His two legacies met over one body, and what we choose echoes in our grandchildren’s lives.

How do Kings and Chronicles fit together? Chronicles says Ahaziah was caught hiding in Samaria and brought to Jehu (2 Chronicles 22:9); here he is shot near Ibleam and dies at Megiddo. Both accounts are compressed. One common way of fitting them together is that, wounded, he reached Samaria and hid, was found and brought to Jehu, and died at Megiddo; Chronicles may also use Samaria for the northern kingdom as a whole. The details cannot be fitted together with certainty, but nothing essential is in doubt. The “eleventh year” of verse 29 and the “twelfth” of 8:25 differ because there were two ways of counting a king’s first year.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–37 — This Is the Word of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment comes to Jezebel late, but exactly as Elijah said. She paints her eyes, dresses her hair and meets Jehu from an upper window with a taunt: is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master? (vv. 30–31). Jehu calls up to her household, and two or three eunuchs throw her down to be trampled (vv. 32–33). He goes in to eat, and only then sends to bury her as a king’s daughter; but the dogs have left nothing except her skull, her feet and the palms of her hands. Jehu recognises the word of the LORD spoken by Elijah: no one will be able to say, This is Jezebel (vv. 34–37).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment came to Jezebel late but exactly, in the very place Elijah had named. She meets it with her courage intact, and courage on its own saves no one.
verseByVerse.examples: She had run that palace for three decades, kept eight hundred and fifty prophets at her table and had men killed by letter, and in the end her own household threw her out.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jehu came to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. And she painted her eyes and adorned her head and looked out of the window. And as Jehu entered the gate, she said, "Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?" And he lifted up his face to the window and said, "Who is on my side? Who?" Two or three eunuchs looked out at him. He said, "Throw her down." So they threw her down. And some of her blood spattered on the wall and on the horses, and they trampled on her. Then he went in and ate and drank. And he said, "See now to this cursed woman and bury her, for she is a king's daughter." But when they went to bury her, they found no more of her than the skull and the feet and the palms of her hands. When they came back and told him, he said, "This is the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Elijah the Tishbite: 'In the territory of Jezreel the dogs shall eat the flesh of Jezebel, and the corpse of Jezebel shall be as dung on the face of the field in the territory of Jezreel, so that no one can say, This is Jezebel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jezebel meets her end with defiance, her own servants throw her down, and the dogs leave so little that no one can say, “This is Jezebel”: God’s word through Elijah is fulfilled to the letter.

She painted her eyes and adorned her head. Verse 30 is usually preached as vanity, and it is almost certainly not. Her son is dead on Naboth’s field, his killer is driving into the town, and she knows she will not survive. She is a king’s daughter of Sidon (1 Kings 16:31) and has been queen of this country for more than thirty years, and she will meet him as one. It is not seduction; a woman of her age with an army at the gate is not trying to charm a usurper. It is defiance, and it is the last decision she gets to make.

What must be said of her. Say it plainly: she did more harm than anyone else in the northern kingdom’s history. She had prophets killed as policy and a man and his sons murdered through the courts for a field, and she was never once frightened. Courage is only ever as good as what it is spent on, and on its own it saves no one.

Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master? She asks the question a fifth time, and it is not a question at all. Every soldier in that courtyard knew the name. Zimri commanded half the chariots, killed his king while he lay drinking, took the throne, and lasted seven days before the army made someone else king and he burned the palace down over his own head (1 Kings 16:9–18). She is telling Jehu, in one word, in front of his men, that she has seen a usurper before, and that he will last a week. She is the only person in the chapter who is not afraid of him, and she is standing at a window with nothing left.

Who is on my side? Who? He does not answer her. He looks past her into the room and asks the staff, and two or three faces appear at the window beside hers. These men had served her for decades and knew her better than anyone alive. A stranger rode into the courtyard, called up one question, and they took hold of her and put her out of the window. That is what thirty years of rule by fear actually buys: obedience while there is something to be afraid of, and nothing at all the moment there is something worse in the courtyard. Nobody in that room loved her.

Then he went in and ate and drank. The queen of Israel is lying in the street under the horses, and Jehu sits down to eat. Only afterwards does it occur to him that there is a body outside, and notice the reason he gives for burying her. It is not decency and certainly not pity: she is a king’s daughter, and a Sidonian princess left in a gateway is a diplomatic problem.

This is the word of the LORD. The prophecy was given in a vineyard by Elijah, who has since been taken up to heaven, and it is quoted here by a soldier standing over a skull. Look at the last clause, for it is the point of the whole horrible scene: “so that no one can say, This is Jezebel.” The name had terrified a kingdom for two generations. And when they go out to do the one thing that fixes a name to a person, putting a body in a grave, there is not enough left to fix it to.

The name in Revelation. Yet the name survived, so completely that nine centuries later the risen Christ, writing to the church at Thyatira, could use it as the one word that told them what was wrong: “you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants” (Revelation 2:20). He did not have to explain it. The woman was erased from the face of a field, and the name outlived her by nine hundred years as a warning. Neither is the name she had worked to make for herself. The same Lord still judges what corrupts his people, and still gives “time to repent” (Revelation 2:21).

What it does not mean. The writer records Jehu’s callousness; he does not commend it. The judgment and the word were God’s, but God later held Jehu’s house to account (Hosea 1:4). God’s justice is never a licence for our cruelty.

9.theology:
A delayed judgment, seen from inside (v. 7). The prophets Jezebel killed went uncounted and unavenged for decades. That is what waiting for God's judgment looks like from the ground: a very long time in which nothing appears to happen, and then a young man with a flask of oil. The martyrs in Revelation still ask, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? (Revelation 6:10), and the answer is the same: God keeps the account. Yet Naboth’s blood is not the Bible’s last word on innocent blood. The blood of Christ speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). Naboth’s blood cried for justice and received it at Jezreel; Christ’s blood pleads for mercy, and wins it for all who flee to him.

This mad fellow (v. 11). A man can carry out God's word with complete accuracy and despise it at the same time, and the writer shows us that about Jehu before he shows us anything else.

Is it peace? (vv. 17-31). Joram means "are you loyal?"; Jehu answers the larger question. Peace is not a mood or a ceasefire but being right with God, and where that is missing any quiet is only a pause before judgment.

The two arrows. The arrow that killed Ahab was aimed at nobody (1 Kgs. 22:34), and the arrow that kills Joram is aimed exactly. Both went where God had said. He can work through what looks like chance or through deliberate skill.

Jehu was there (vv. 25-26). He rode in the escort the day Elijah met Ahab in Naboth’s vineyard, and he can repeat the prophecy word for word a dozen years or more later. God's sentence waited all that time, yet he speaks of Naboth's blood as surely as I saw yesterday.

Collateral (vv. 27-28). The king of Judah dies on a family visit, inside a judgment on somebody else's house, because two generations earlier good King Jehoshaphat made a marriage alliance with Ahab and called it peace. Yet he is buried in the royal tombs because he was the grandson of a man who sought the LORD. Jehoshaphat's two legacies, a foolish alliance and a godly name, met over one body, and what we choose echoes in our grandchildren's lives.

What fear buys (vv. 32-33). Her own eunuchs threw her out of the window when a stranger in the courtyard asked one question. Thirty years of rule by fear purchases obedience while there is something to be afraid of and nothing at all the moment something worse rides into the yard.

So that no one can say, This is Jezebel (v. 37). When they went to fix her name to a grave there was not enough left to fix it to. Yet the name survived so completely that the risen Christ could use it without explaining it. She was erased from a field and remembered for nine centuries as a warning, and neither was the name she had worked to make for herself.
9.examples:
Then: A watchman on a tower saw a dust cloud, then a rider go out and not come back, then a second rider go out and not come back, and then recognised the man at the head of the column, before he could make out a face or a standard, purely by the way he drove.

Now: First, the long wait. The blood this judgment avenges was shed a generation earlier, and for decades nothing appeared to be happening about it. If you are waiting on God over something genuinely wicked that nobody has answered for, this chapter shows what such a wait is like, and that it ends. Second, Jehu in verse 11, laughing at the messenger with the oil still in his hair. It is possible to carry out a commission from God accurately, quoting the Scriptures throughout, and hold the whole thing in contempt; what keeps a servant from that is not efficiency but a heart the Spirit keeps soft toward the God who called him. Third, what Jezebel's household did. She had three decades of obedience from those men and not one of them was loyal to her; the morning something more frightening arrived in the courtyard, they were at the window before he had finished asking.

keyVerse.quote: And when Joram saw Jehu, he said, “Is it peace, Jehu?” He answered, “What peace can there be, so long as the whorings and the sorceries of your mother Jezebel are so many?”
keyVerse.note: The question that runs through the chapter is asked here a fourth time and answered for them all. Joram means a diplomatic peace, but Jehu answers the deeper question: there can be no peace while a people’s idolatry goes unjudged. The verse exposes a need that no coup could meet, and that is met only by the one who made peace with God by the blood of his cross.

9.reflection:
The prophets Jezebel killed went unavenged for decades before God acted (v. 7). How does this chapter help someone who is waiting for justice that seems never to come? How does the cry of Revelation 6:10 speak to it?

Jehu laughed at God’s messenger with the oil still on his head (v. 11), yet carried out God’s word to the letter. What is the difference between being used by God and being right with him? What does Hosea 1:4 add to the picture?

“What peace can there be, so long as the whorings and the sorceries of your mother Jezebel are so many?” (v. 22). Why can there be no real peace while sin is left undealt with? How does Christ make peace (Romans 5:1; Colossians 1:20)?

Jezebel met her death with courage, and her own servants threw her down (vv. 30–33). What does her end teach about courage spent on the wrong things, and about ruling others by fear?

10.title: Jehu's Purge
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the rulers of the city, to the elders, and to the guardians of the sons of Ahab, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Now then, as soon as this letter comes to you, seeing your master's sons are with you, and there are with you chariots and horses, fortified cities also, and weapons,<sup>3</sup>select the best and fittest of your master's sons and set him on his father's throne and fight for your master's house."<sup>4</sup>But they were exceedingly afraid and said, "Behold, the two kings could not stand before him. How then can we stand?"<sup>5</sup>So he who was over the palace, and he who was over the city, together with the elders and the guardians, sent to Jehu, saying, "We are your servants, and we will do all that you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever is good in your eyes."<sup>6</sup>Then he wrote to them a second letter, saying, "If you are on my side, and if you are ready to obey me, take the heads of your master's sons and come to me at Jezreel tomorrow at this time." Now the king's sons, seventy persons, were with the great men of the city, who were bringing them up.<sup>7</sup>And as soon as the letter came to them, they took the king's sons and slaughtered them, seventy persons, and put their heads in baskets and sent them to him at Jezreel.<sup>8</sup>When the messenger came and told him, "They have brought the heads of the king's sons," he said, "Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until the morning."<sup>9</sup>Then in the morning, when he went out, he stood and said to all the people, "You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him, but who struck down all these?<sup>10</sup>Know then that there shall fall to the earth nothing of the word of the LORD, which the LORD spoke concerning the house of Ahab, for the LORD has done what he said by his servant Elijah."<sup>11</sup>So Jehu struck down all who remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, all his great men and his close friends and his priests, until he left him none remaining.<sup>12</sup>Then he set out and went to Samaria. On the way, when he was at Beth-eked of the Shepherds,<sup>13</sup>Jehu met the relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah, and he said, "Who are you?" And they answered, "We are the relatives of Ahaziah, and we came down to visit the royal princes and the sons of the queen mother."<sup>14</sup>He said, "Take them alive." And they took them alive and slaughtered them at the pit of Beth-eked, forty-two persons, and he spared none of them.<sup>15</sup>And when he departed from there, he met Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him. And he greeted him and said to him, "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" And Jehonadab answered, "It is." Jehu said, "If it is, give me your hand." So he gave him his hand. And Jehu took him up with him into the chariot.<sup>16</sup>And he said, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD." So he had him ride in his chariot.<sup>17</sup>And when he came to Samaria, he struck down all who remained to Ahab in Samaria, till he had wiped them out, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke to Elijah.<sup>18</sup>Then Jehu assembled all the people and said to them, "Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much.<sup>19</sup>Now therefore call to me all the prophets of Baal, all his worshipers and all his priests. Let none be missing, for I have a great sacrifice to offer to Baal. Whoever is missing shall not live." But Jehu did it with cunning in order to destroy the worshipers of Baal.<sup>20</sup>And Jehu ordered, "Sanctify a solemn assembly for Baal." So they proclaimed it.<sup>21</sup>And Jehu sent throughout all Israel, and all the worshipers of Baal came, so that there was not a man left who did not come. And they entered the house of Baal, and the house of Baal was filled from one end to the other.<sup>22</sup>He said to him who was in charge of the wardrobe, "Bring out the vestments for all the worshipers of Baal." So he brought out the vestments for them.<sup>23</sup>Then Jehu went into the house of Baal with Jehonadab the son of Rechab, and he said to the worshipers of Baal, "Search, and see that there is no servant of the LORD here among you, but only the worshipers of Baal."<sup>24</sup>Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Now Jehu had stationed eighty men outside and said, "The man who allows any of those whom I give into your hands to escape shall forfeit his life."<sup>25</sup>So as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guard and to the officers, "Go in and strike them down; let not a man escape." So when they put them to the sword, the guard and the officers cast them out and went into the inner room of the house of Baal,<sup>26</sup>and they brought out the pillar that was in the house of Baal and burned it.<sup>27</sup>And they demolished the pillar of Baal, and demolished the house of Baal, and made it a latrine to this day.<sup>28</sup>Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel.<sup>29</sup>But Jehu did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin—that is, the golden calves that were in Bethel and in Dan.<sup>30</sup>And the LORD said to Jehu, "Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab according to all that was in my heart, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel."<sup>31</sup>But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin.<sup>32</sup>In those days the LORD began to cut off parts of Israel. Hazael defeated them throughout the territory of Israel:<sup>33</sup>from the Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the Valley of the Arnon, that is, Gilead and Bashan.<sup>34</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehu and all that he did, and all his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>35</sup>So Jehu slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria. And Jehoahaz his son reigned in his place.<sup>36</sup>The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 ended with Joram dead on Naboth’s field, Ahaziah of Judah dead and Jezebel thrown from her window. Jehu holds Jezreel, but seventy sons of Ahab are still alive in Samaria, and Baal still has his temple in the capital.

The message. God keeps his word to the letter: the house of Ahab falls exactly as he said through Elijah, and the state religion of Baal is ended in a day. Yet the man who carries it out is commended for the deed, held answerable for the manner, and stops short of the one sin that props up his own throne. Zeal against other people’s idols is not the same as a heart given wholly to God.

Why it was said. Readers who had lost everything (see the introduction) needed to know that God’s judgments are sure. They also needed to know why even a king who destroyed Baal had not saved the north: Jehu kept Jeroboam’s golden calves, the very sin the writer later names as the cause of Israel’s fall (17:21–23).

How the chapter makes its case. Jehu dares Samaria’s leaders to fight, and they surrender (vv. 1–5); he makes them kill Ahab’s seventy sons, heaps the heads at Jezreel’s gate and preaches over them (vv. 6–11). He kills forty-two princes of Judah on the road (vv. 12–14) and takes Jehonadab along to “see my zeal for the LORD” (vv. 15–17). By a staged festival he traps every worshipper of Baal in one temple and destroys them (vv. 18–28). Then comes the “but”: he keeps the golden calves; God rewards his obedience yet finds him not wholehearted, and Hazael begins to cut Israel down (vv. 29–36).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes. Jehu could pull down Baal’s temple, but he could not change Israel’s heart or his own; zeal that served his throne left the calves standing, and a century later God punished his house “for the blood of Jezreel” (Hosea 1:4). Israel needed a King whose zeal for God’s house would consume himself rather than others (John 2:17), and who could say, “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8). That King is Jesus, who by his Spirit pulls down the idols we would quietly keep.

For us. Be honest about which sins you attack loudly and which you keep because they hold something up. Being right about a cause never licenses the methods, and God keeps both accounts. Bring the idol you would rather not touch to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Who Struck Down All These?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s sentence on Ahab’s house is carried out to the letter, but in a manner that is Jehu’s own. His first letter dares the leaders of Samaria to crown one of Ahab’s seventy sons and fight, and they surrender at once (vv. 1–5). His second makes them kill the princes and send the heads, which he heaps at the gate of Jezreel before telling the crowd that God’s word through Elijah has been fulfilled (vv. 6–11). Then he kills forty-two relatives of Judah’s king met on the road (vv. 12–14), and takes Jehonadab the Rechabite into his chariot to watch his zeal as the purge reaches Samaria (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: He never touches the seventy. He makes the great men of Samaria do it, which makes the leading families guilty with him and unable to oppose him, and then asks the crowd at the gate who could possibly have done such a thing.
verseByVerse.examples: The deed was commanded; the manner was his own. It is possible to do what God has said in a way God never asked for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the rulers of the city, to the elders, and to the guardians of the sons of Ahab, saying, "Now then, as soon as this letter comes to you, seeing your master's sons are with you, and there are with you chariots and horses, fortified cities also, and weapons, select the best and fittest of your master's sons and set him on his father's throne and fight for your master's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu dares the leaders of Samaria to crown one of Ahab’s sons and fight him, confident that none of them will.

Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. Seventy sons probably means the whole royal clan, sons and grandsons together, raised by the great families of the capital, as was the custom. The arrangement tied the leading families to the royal house. It also put every prince in somebody else’s house on the day the dynasty fell.

So Jehu wrote letters. Read the first letter as what it is: a dare from a man certain it will not be taken. He lists their strengths for them, chariots and horses, fortified cities also, and weapons, as though helpfully, and invites them to crown a candidate and come and fight.

As soon as this letter comes to you. Jezebel called him Zimri and gave him a week (9:31). This is his answer: he means to find out at once whether anyone in Samaria has the nerve, and to settle it before it becomes a war.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were exceedingly afraid and said, "Behold, the two kings could not stand before him. How then can we stand?" So he who was over the palace, and he who was over the city, together with the elders and the guardians, sent to Jehu, saying, "We are your servants, and we will do all that you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever is good in your eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samaria’s rulers count the odds and surrender without a fight, promising in advance to do whatever Jehu says.

The two kings could not stand before him. If Joram and Ahaziah, with their chariots and guards, could not stand, the guardians of the princes will not. The four parties who send the reply, the steward of the palace, the governor of the city, the elders and the guardians, are the whole government of the capital.

Do whatever is good in your eyes. Note the sentence they end on. In writing, they have agreed beforehand to whatever he asks next.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he wrote to them a second letter, saying, "If you are on my side, and if you are ready to obey me, take the heads of your master's sons and come to me at Jezreel tomorrow at this time." Now the king's sons, seventy persons, were with the great men of the city, who were bringing them up. And as soon as the letter came to them, they took the king's sons and slaughtered them, seventy persons, and put their heads in baskets and sent them to him at Jezreel. When the messenger came and told him, "They have brought the heads of the king's sons," he said, "Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until the morning."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu’s second letter makes the nobles of Samaria kill Ahab’s seventy sons with their own hands, and he displays the heads at the gate of Jezreel. Now the trap closes, and it is well made.

Take the heads of your master’s sons. He sends no soldiers and does not go himself. He requires the men who have been raising those boys in their own houses to kill them and bring the proof. The wording may be deliberately double: in Hebrew “heads” can also mean leaders, so the order could be read bring the chief men of your master’s sons, leaving Jehu free to say later that he never asked for a killing. The nobles took it literally, as he must have known they would.

Three things in one letter. He disposes of the royal line. He makes every leading family in the capital an accomplice, so that none of them can ever raise a rebellion in the name of the old house. And he keeps his own hands clean enough to make a speech about it in the morning.

Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate. The gate was not a back alley but the public square, where the elders sat, the courts met and business was done, and everyone entering or leaving passed through it. The heaps are left there overnight, so that the whole town walks into them in the morning.

verseByVerse.quote: Then in the morning, when he went out, he stood and said to all the people, "You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him, but who struck down all these? Know then that there shall fall to the earth nothing of the word of the LORD, which the LORD spoke concerning the house of Ahab, for the LORD has done what he said by his servant Elijah." So Jehu struck down all who remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, all his great men and his close friends and his priests, until he left him none remaining.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu acquits the crowd, asks who killed all these, and preaches God’s word over the heads: the word is true, but he uses it to cover his own hand.

You are innocent. Verses 9–10 are a staged speech. He acquits a crowd nobody has accused, frankly admits the one crime everybody already knows about, and then, standing before two heaps of heads that arrived on his own written orders, asks: but who struck down all these? The question cannot be answered in public, and it is meant not to be. The men who did it are the aristocracy of Samaria; they cannot come forward, and he has just told a whole town that somebody else did this.

The LORD has done what he said. Then he preaches, and every word is true. God did say the house of Ahab would be cut off, through Elijah, in Naboth’s vineyard, a dozen years or more before (1 Kings 21:21–24), and Jehu quotes a real prophet accurately. He is also using it to close down the only question anyone might have asked him.

The deed and the manner. The whole chapter turns on this distinction. The deed was commanded; the manner was not. Nothing God said through Elijah, or through the young prophet with the flask of oil (9:1–10), involved tricking the guardians of seventy children into doing it, stacking the evidence at a gate, or preaching God’s purposes over the top of it.

His great men and his close friends and his priests. These (v. 11) are not a dynasty but a social circle, and killing them is the ordinary business of a new regime removing everyone who might stay loyal to the old one. The commission has been finished, and the killing has not stopped.

A century later, Hosea. God does not let it pass. Through Hosea he names this town and this family: “in just a little while I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel” (Hosea 1:4). The God who ordered the judgment holds to account the man who carried it out (see the note on vv. 29–36).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he set out and went to Samaria. On the way, when he was at Beth-eked of the Shepherds, Jehu met the relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah, and he said, "Who are you?" And they answered, "We are the relatives of Ahaziah, and we came down to visit the royal princes and the sons of the queen mother." He said, "Take them alive." And they took them alive and slaughtered them at the pit of Beth-eked, forty-two persons, and he spared none of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the road Jehu meets forty-two princes of Judah, travellers who know nothing of what has happened, and has every one of them killed at a cistern.

The relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah. They are kin to Ahab’s house only through Ahaziah’s mother Athaliah (8:26), and they are not in rebellion. They do not even know what has happened: they are going north on a courtesy visit to relatives who are already dead, and they answer his question openly because they have no reason not to.

Take them alive. He has them taken alive, and then killed at the pit of Beth-eked, probably a cistern, the kind of place where bodies could be hidden. No word from God in Kings names these men. The writer records it without comment, in the same flat voice he uses for everything Jehu does, and lets the deeds pile up. Chronicles adds that Ahaziah’s downfall was ordained by God because he had bound himself to the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:7–8): God can bring judgment through a man’s excess without approving the excess.

Uncertain wording. The name Beth-eked of the Shepherds probably means something like “the shepherds’ binding house”, perhaps a place where sheep were tied for shearing. It lay on the road from Jezreel to Samaria, but its site is unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he departed from there, he met Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him. And he greeted him and said to him, "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" And Jehonadab answered, "It is." Jehu said, "If it is, give me your hand." So he gave him his hand. And Jehu took him up with him into the chariot. And he said, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD." So he had him ride in his chariot. And when he came to Samaria, he struck down all who remained to Ahab in Samaria, till he had wiped them out, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke to Elijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu enlists the respected Jehonadab and invites him to watch his zeal for the LORD, and in Samaria he finishes off Ahab’s house as God had said.

Jehonadab the son of Rechab. He was the ancestor of the Rechabites. About two and a half centuries later Jeremiah set jars of wine before his descendants in the temple, and they refused, because “Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us”; and God held up their obedience to a dead ancestor as a rebuke to a nation that would not obey the living God (Jeremiah 35:6–16). Their rule of life, no wine, no houses, no sown fields (Jeremiah 35:6–10), was probably a protest against the settled Canaanite ways that Baal worship stood for, so Jehonadab had reasons of his own to welcome a purge. Whether he understood what he was being enlisted for, the text does not say.

Is your heart true to my heart? Jehu asks for loyalty before anything else, and seals it with a handshake and a seat in the royal chariot. Jehonadab is a serious man, and Jehu wants him seen beside him.

Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD. The invitation gives the whole man away. Zeal that requires a passenger is performance with a witness in the seat. Jehu has collected the most respected religious figure in the district first, so that someone creditable can say afterwards what he saw. Nobody who is genuinely burning for the honour of God arranges an audience first.

According to the word of the LORD. The writer records the fulfilment plainly, as he always does. Both are true at once: God’s word to Elijah was fulfilled, and the manner was Jehu’s own. The chapter will not let go of either.

Zeal for your house will consume me. The Gospels show what zeal for the LORD looks like when it is real. When Jesus drove the traders out of the temple, “his disciples remembered that it was written, ‘Zeal for your house will consume me’” (John 2:17). Jehu’s zeal consumed other people and left him on a throne; Christ’s consumed himself and put him on a cross. He did not seek his own glory (John 8:50) and often told those he healed to tell no one. Jehu wanted a witness in his chariot; Christ went to the cross with his friends scattered.

The masters of suspicion arrived late. Many distrust religion for exactly what this chapter shows. The philosopher Paul Ricoeur called Marx, Nietzsche and Freud the masters of suspicion, because each taught us to ask what lies beneath a pious claim: class interest, the will to power, a wish. Jehu fits all three: his God-talk clears his road to the throne, silences the one awkward question at the gate, and needs a respected witness in the chariot. But notice who is doing the unmasking: the Bible itself, written by believers about their own king, seeing through him nearly three thousand years before the suspicious school had a name. And suspicion followed all the way down eats itself: if every claim is only a bid for power, so is that one. What breaks the circle is a King who had all power and spent it on being stripped: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). At the cross there is nothing left for suspicion to uncover: no throne gained, no witness arranged, only a man giving himself away.

How could God sentence a whole royal house, children included? Because he is the judge of all the earth, who alone has the right to give and take life (Deuteronomy 32:39). The sentence was neither sudden nor secret: it was announced to Ahab years before, delayed when he humbled himself (1 Kings 21:29), and it fell on a house that had led a nation into Baal worship and had killed Naboth’s sons for a field (9:26). It was God’s judgment in history on a dynasty, not his final verdict on each soul in it; at the last judgment each person answers for his own life (Ezekiel 18:20). Scripture neither hides how terrible it was nor blesses Jehu’s methods. No one may take it as licence for violence today, and the God who judged this house is the God who in Christ bore judgment himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–28 — A Great Sacrifice to Baal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The state religion of Baal ends in a single day, through a trap. Jehu announces that he will serve Baal far more than Ahab did, and the writer tells us at once that it is cunning (vv. 18–19). A festival is proclaimed with attendance on pain of death; every worshipper in the kingdom fills the temple, robes are issued, and the crowd is searched to be sure no servant of the LORD is inside (vv. 20–23). When the sacrifice is finished, eighty men go in (vv. 24–25). The pillar is burned, the temple becomes a latrine, and Baal is wiped out of Israel (vv. 26–28): a real deliverance, won by deceit and slaughter.
verseByVerse.theology: The care Jehu takes in verse 23 is real, and he should be given credit for it: he takes trouble to make sure none of the LORD's people are inside when the doors close. He is not indiscriminate. He is, the writer says plainly, acting with cunning, and the word is not a compliment.
verseByVerse.examples: The achievement is real too, which is why the writer states it flatly. The official Baal worship Jezebel imported, with its temple in the capital and its priests paid by the palace, was ended in a single day and the building became the public toilet. Nobody else in the history of that kingdom did anything of the kind.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jehu assembled all the people and said to them, "Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much. Now therefore call to me all the prophets of Baal, all his worshipers and all his priests. Let none be missing, for I have a great sacrifice to offer to Baal. Whoever is missing shall not live." But Jehu did it with cunning in order to destroy the worshipers of Baal. And Jehu ordered, "Sanctify a solemn assembly for Baal." So they proclaimed it. And Jehu sent throughout all Israel, and all the worshipers of Baal came, so that there was not a man left who did not come. And they entered the house of Baal, and the house of Baal was filled from one end to the other. He said to him who was in charge of the wardrobe, "Bring out the vestments for all the worshipers of Baal." So he brought out the vestments for them. Then Jehu went into the house of Baal with Jehonadab the son of Rechab, and he said to the worshipers of Baal, "Search, and see that there is no servant of the LORD here among you, but only the worshipers of Baal." Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Now Jehu had stationed eighty men outside and said, "The man who allows any of those whom I give into your hands to escape shall forfeit his life." So as soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guard and to the officers, "Go in and strike them down; let not a man escape." So when they put them to the sword, the guard and the officers cast them out and went into the inner room of the house of Baal, and they brought out the pillar that was in the house of Baal and burned it. And they demolished the pillar of Baal, and demolished the house of Baal, and made it a latrine to this day. Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By a staged festival Jehu gathers every worshipper of Baal in Israel into one temple and destroys them, ending the state religion of Baal in a single day.

Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much. Verse 18 is a lie, and the writer does not leave us to work it out. His word for what Jehu is doing, with cunning, is not neutral: it is the word for craftiness, for tripping somebody by the heel, from the same root as Jacob’s name (Genesis 27:36).

Whoever is missing shall not live. One clause guarantees a full house. Attendance is compulsory on pain of death, and the Baal community understands that the new king is a keener supporter than the old one and that absence will be noticed. Not a man left who did not come: that is the point of the operation. The temple Ahab built in Samaria (1 Kings 16:32) is packed from wall to wall with every Baal worshipper in the kingdom, gathered by their own eagerness.

Bring out the vestments. Robes for everyone look like the generosity of a devout new king. They also mean that when the moment comes every man in the building can be identified at a glance, and no one can escape by looking like a bystander.

See that there is no servant of the LORD here. The care in verse 23 is real and should be credited. Jehu takes public trouble to make certain that no worshipper of the LORD is inside when the doors close.

As soon as he had made an end of offering the burnt offering. There is something cold in the detail: he stands through the whole service, at a sacrifice he has ordered to a god he means to abolish, and gives the signal only when it is complete.

And made it a latrine to this day. The building Ahab put up in his capital for his wife’s god, with its altar and its pillar and its priests and prophets on the palace budget, was pulled down and the site turned into the public lavatory of Samaria, and so it remained when the account was written. What Baal’s worshippers called holy is made unclean for good.

Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel. Elijah killed the prophets of Baal at the brook Kishon (1 Kings 18:40), and the religion carried on with a temple in the capital. Jehoram put away one pillar and kept everything else (3:2). Jehu ended the state cult of Baal in the northern kingdom in a single day; it never again had a royal temple in Samaria, though Hosea shows Baal worship lingering among the people (Hosea 2:13). That is a real achievement, accomplished by lies, staging and mass killing, and the Bible credits it to him in seven words and then spends the next verse on what he would not touch.

Uncertain wording. “The inner room” (v. 25) translates a phrase that reads literally “the city of the house of Baal”. It probably means an inner, walled sanctuary or stronghold within the temple, where the pillar stood, but the exact sense is not known.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — But He Did Not Turn Aside
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reformer who destroyed Baal will not touch the calves that hold up his throne. Jehu keeps Jeroboam’s golden calves at Bethel and Dan (v. 29). God’s verdict is double: he commends what Jehu did and promises his sons four generations on the throne (v. 30), yet Jehu was not careful to walk in God’s law with all his heart (v. 31). At once the LORD begins to cut Israel down, and Hazael of Damascus takes everything east of the Jordan (vv. 32–33). Jehu dies after twenty-eight years (vv. 34–36), founder of the north’s longest dynasty, and not a wholehearted man.
verseByVerse.theology: Put verse 28 next to verse 29 and you have the whole man in two sentences. He wiped out the imported god it cost him nothing to destroy, and kept the golden calves that held up his own throne.
verseByVerse.examples: A man may be the instrument of a judgment, be rewarded for carrying it out, and still be answerable for how he did it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jehu did not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin—that is, the golden calves that were in Bethel and in Dan. And the LORD said to Jehu, "Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab according to all that was in my heart, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel." But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin. In those days the LORD began to cut off parts of Israel. Hazael defeated them throughout the territory of Israel: from the Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the Valley of the Arnon, that is, Gilead and Bashan. Now the rest of the acts of Jehu and all that he did, and all his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? So Jehu slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria. And Jehoahaz his son reigned in his place. The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehu destroyed Baal but kept the golden calves that held up his throne, so God rewarded his obedience with four generations of kings and answered his half-heartedness by letting Hazael begin to cut Israel down.

But Jehu did not turn aside. The word the whole chapter has been waiting for is but (v. 29). He destroyed the imported god and kept the home-grown one, and look at which was which. Baal was Jezebel’s religion, his predecessors’ project, a Sidonian import never popular outside the court and publicly humiliated on Carmel. Tearing it down cost him nothing and made him the champion of every Israelite who had resented the Phoenician queen.

The golden calves that were in Bethel and in Dan. These were something else. Jeroboam, the founder of the northern kingdom, set them up expressly to stop Israelites going south to worship in Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:26–30), and they were the reason the north existed as a separate country with its own throne. Touch those, and you are not a reformer; you are a man removing the reason for his own crown. So he was ferocious about the sin that belonged to somebody else’s regime, and left standing the one that was holding up his.

Because you have done well. God commends him, and not faintly: he has done well, done what is right in my eyes, done according to all that was in my heart. The reward is the longest dynasty the northern kingdom ever had: Jehu, Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam II and Zechariah, four generations of sons on the throne (fulfilled in 15:12), in a country where most dynasties ended in murder.

Jehu was not careful. Not careful, and not “with all his heart”. He had been meticulous about everything else: the letters, the vestments, the search of the temple, the eighty men on the door. He was capable of great care, and spent none of it here.

The LORD began to cut off parts of Israel. Elisha wept in Damascus because he had been shown what Hazael would do (8:12), and here it begins. The whole Transjordan goes: Gilead, Bashan, the land of Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh, all the way down to the Arnon, a great slice of the kingdom not won back until Jeroboam II (14:25). Gilead, Elijah’s home country (1 Kings 17:1), is the first part of Israel to be lost. Assyrian records fill in the wider picture: on the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (about 841 BC) Jehu, or his envoy, is shown bowing to the ground with tribute, and when Assyria stopped campaigning in the west a few years later, Israel was left to face Hazael alone.

Twenty-eight years. He died in peace, was buried in the capital, and got everything he was promised. He was the man who ended Baal in Israel and whom God commended; he was also the man who collected an audience for his zeal, killed forty-two travellers at a cistern, and kept two golden calves standing for twenty-eight years because they held up his throne. The book records both, and does not blend them into a single verdict.

Commended here, condemned in Hosea. A century later Hosea was told to name his first son Jezreel, “for in just a little while I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel” (Hosea 1:4). The same events are commended here and condemned there. That is not a contradiction, and Kings has shown the principle before: Baasha wiped out the house of Jeroboam, which God had sentenced, and God’s charge against him was that he walked in Jeroboam’s ways “and also because he destroyed it” (1 Kings 16:7). Being used by God to carry out a judgment is not the same as having his approval for every act done in carrying it out. God rewarded what was obedience in Jehu, and held him answerable for the baskets, the heaps at the gate, the friends and priests, the forty-two men at the cistern, and the speech.

A King with all his heart. Israel needed a king who would keep God’s law with his whole heart, and the psalm that Hebrews applies to Christ gives his voice: “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8; Hebrews 10:5–7). Jesus brought no hidden calves to his throne. And he receives those who have kept theirs, when they bring them to him.

In everyday life. The sins we are most willing to be fierce about are almost always the ones that cost us nothing to renounce and that our neighbours already dislike. The one to look for is the one that is holding something up: the arrangement, the income, the reputation, the relationship that would take the roof off if it went. And anyone who has been on the right side of a dispute should take Jehu to heart: being right about the cause does not license the conduct, and God keeps the two accounts separately.

Two readings of Hosea 1:4. Some interpreters take “the blood of Jezreel” to mean the bloodshed Jehu’s dynasty went on adding rather than the purge itself, but most read it as the purge. On either reading God holds Jehu’s house to account for Jezreel.
verseByVerse.note: Shalmaneser III’s Black Obelisk shows Jehu (or his envoy) bowing before the Assyrian king, about 841 BC; it is the only known picture of a king of Israel. Assyrian records also put Ahab at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC, and the twelve years between fit the reigns of Ahaziah and Joram once part-years are counted as Israel then counted them.

10.theology:
Verse 28 against verse 29. He destroyed Baal, an imported religion that cost him nothing to renounce, and kept the golden calves that held up his throne. The sin to look for in yourself is never the one your neighbours already dislike; it is the one that something in your life rests on.

True theology used as cover (vv. 9-10). He quotes a real prophet accurately to close down the one question anyone might ask him. God commanded the deed; the way it was done was Jehu’s own. The whole chapter turns on that distinction.

Commended and prosecuted (v. 30; Hos. 1:4). God rewards Jehu with four generations on the throne, and a century later promises to punish his house for the blood of Jezreel. Both are about the same events. The principle was stated earlier in these books: Baasha destroyed a house God had sentenced and was charged also because he destroyed it. Being used by God to carry out a judgment does not mean God approves every act done in carrying it out, and God keeps the two accounts separately.

Come and see my zeal (v. 16). He detours to collect the most respected religious figure in the district before doing the next thing. Zeal that needs someone watching is a performance. Nobody genuinely burning for the honour of God arranges a witness first.

Where the commission ended (vv. 11-14). The killing went on past the house of Ahab to his great men, friends and priests, a social circle rather than a dynasty, and then to forty-two travellers who did not know what had happened and answered his question openly. No word from God covers that, and the writer records it in the same flat voice and lets the deeds pile up.

The losses begin (vv. 32-33). Elisha wept in Damascus over what Hazael would do, and here it starts, beginning with Gilead, Elijah's own hill country.
10.examples:
Then: The great families of Samaria, who had been bringing up seventy royal children in their own houses, received a letter and sent the heads to Jezreel at once; and the man who wrote the letter stacked them in two piles at the town gate overnight and asked the crowd in the morning who could possibly have done it.

Now: First, verses 28 and 29 together. Ask which of your sins you are willing to be publicly severe about, and notice how reliably it turns out to be one that costs nothing to renounce. The one that needs attention is the one that is holding something up; bring that one into the light before the God who forgives it for Christ's sake, and whose Spirit can take the weight off it. Second, verse 16. If you find yourself wanting a particular person present while you do the right thing, stop there: come with me and see my zeal is not a sentence a zealous man needs to say. Third, the double verdict. Being right about the cause does not make every method right, and this chapter is as plain a case as Scripture gives of a man rewarded for what he did and judged for how he did it.

keyVerse.quote: But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin.
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of ruthless efficiency, this is God’s deepest verdict on Jehu: careful about everything except the one thing that mattered most. The calves he would not touch became the sin that brought the northern kingdom down (17:21–23). The verse exposes Israel’s need of a King who would keep God’s law with all his heart.

10.reflection:
Jehu’s speech at the gate was true in every word, and he used it to hide his own hand (vv. 9–10). How can true words about God be used to cover what we have done? Where are we tempted to do it?

“Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD” (v. 16). What is the difference between zeal for God and zeal to be seen? How does the zeal of Jesus (John 2:17) expose and heal ours?

Jehu destroyed Baal, which cost him nothing, but kept the calves that held up his throne (vv. 28–29). Which sins are easy for you to oppose, and which would cost you something to give up?

God commended Jehu (v. 30) and later punished his house for the blood of Jezreel (Hosea 1:4). What does this teach about being right in a cause but wrong in the way we pursue it?

11.title: Athaliah and the Hidden King
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family.<sup>2</sup>But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus they hid him from Athaliah, so that he was not put to death.<sup>3</sup>And he remained with her six years, hidden in the house of the LORD, while Athaliah reigned over the land.<sup>4</sup>But in the seventh year Jehoiada sent and brought the captains of the Carites and of the guards, and had them come to him in the house of the LORD. And he made a covenant with them and put them under oath in the house of the LORD, and he showed them the king's son.<sup>5</sup>And he commanded them, "This is the thing that you shall do: one third of you, those who come off duty on the Sabbath and guard the king's house<sup>6</sup>(another third being at the gate Sur and a third at the gate behind the guards) shall guard the palace.<sup>7</sup>And the two divisions of you, which come on duty in force on the Sabbath and guard the house of the LORD on behalf of the king,<sup>8</sup>shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever approaches the ranks is to be put to death. Be with the king when he goes out and when he comes in."<sup>9</sup>The captains did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, and came to Jehoiada the priest.<sup>10</sup>And the priest gave to the captains the spears and shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>And the guards stood, every man with his weapons in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house on behalf of the king.<sup>12</sup>Then he brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king and anointed him, and they clapped their hands and said, "Long live the king!"<sup>13</sup>When Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and of the people, she went into the house of the LORD to the people.<sup>14</sup>And when she looked, there was the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!"<sup>15</sup>Then Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains who were set over the army, "Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death with the sword anyone who follows her." For the priest said, "Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD."<sup>16</sup>So they laid hands on her; and she went through the horses' entrance to the king's house, and there she was put to death.<sup>17</sup>And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people.<sup>18</sup>Then all the people of the land went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest posted watchmen over the house of the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And he took the captains, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the gate of the guards to the king's house. And he took his seat on the throne of the kings.<sup>20</sup>So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword at the king's house.<sup>21</sup>Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign.
11.overview:
Where we are. While Jehu was purging the north (chapters 9–10), his men also killed Ahaziah of Judah (9:27). Ahaziah’s mother Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab, is left in Jerusalem, and the story turns south to the house of David.

The message. God keeps his promise to David even when every visible sign says it has failed. A murderous queen sets out to put out David’s lamp, and for six years it looks as though she has; but God has one child hidden in his own house, and at the right time the true king is crowned with the book of God’s law in his hands, and the people bind themselves to the LORD again. No one can destroy what God has sworn to keep.

Why it was said. The first readers had seen David’s heir led away to Babylon and could easily believe the line was finished (see the introduction). This chapter shows them that it had once come down to a single hidden child, and God had kept it.

How the chapter makes its case. Athaliah kills the royal family and seizes the throne, but Jehosheba steals away the infant Joash, who is hidden six years in the temple (vv. 1–3). In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest binds the guard by oath, uses the Sabbath change of duty and David’s own spears and shields, and crowns the boy, giving him the testimony (vv. 4–12). Athaliah cries “Treason!” and is put to death outside the temple; the covenant is renewed, Baal’s house in Jerusalem is torn down, and the seven-year-old takes the throne (vv. 13–21).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by pattern. Every promise of a coming King from David’s line hung that day on one hidden child (2 Samuel 7:16). Eight centuries later another child of the same line was carried away by night from a king who was killing children (Matthew 2:13–16), and grew up unnoticed in Nazareth. Joash would fail once his guardian died; the Son of David who came at last never failed, and “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

For us. When God seems silent and evil seems to hold the throne, he has not stopped keeping his promises; often he is at work quietly, through faithful, ordinary people. Do your part with courage and careful planning, as Jehosheba and Jehoiada did, and renew your belonging to the Lord who bound himself to you first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — She Destroyed All the Royal Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David’s line comes down to one hidden child, and God keeps it alive. When Athaliah, Ahab’s daughter, hears that her son Ahaziah is dead, she has the whole royal family killed, her own grandchildren, and takes the throne (v. 1). But Jehosheba, the dead king’s sister, goes into the slaughter and carries out the infant Joash with his nurse (v. 2). For six years the boy lives hidden in the house of the LORD, the one building the Baal-worshipping queen never enters, while Athaliah reigns and the promise to David seems to have failed (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the nearest the royal line of David ever came to being wiped out. Everything God had sworn, the throne, the promised offspring, the one who would crush the serpent's head, ran through the children in that room.
verseByVerse.examples: When the promise hung by a thread, God kept it hidden in the one place the enemy never looked.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family. But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus they hid him from Athaliah, so that he was not put to death. And he remained with her six years, hidden in the house of the LORD, while Athaliah reigned over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Athaliah murders her own grandchildren to seize David’s throne, but one baby is stolen from the slaughter and hidden six years in the temple, and the promise to David survives in him.

When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead. Her son had reigned one year and been shot in his chariot in the north (9:27). She was the queen mother, Ahab’s daughter (8:18) and very likely Jezebel’s, long established in Jerusalem. When the news came she did not mourn and she did not retire. She arose and destroyed all the royal family: her own grandchildren, in her own house. Every remaining heir of David she could find was put to death, and she took the throne.

What was at stake. God had sworn to David that his house and kingdom would be made sure forever and his throne established forever (2 Samuel 7:16). Every promise in Scripture about a coming king ran through those children, back to the word in Eden about the offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), forward to a birth in Bethlehem.
