Three chapters earlier the writer said that Judah still stood only because God had “promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (8:19). Here is Ahab’s daughter, methodically putting out the lamp. For six years no descendant of David sat on David’s throne; a woman who worshipped Baal ruled in Jerusalem, and as far as anyone in the city knew, the line was finished.

But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram. The whole of it turns on one woman. Jehosheba is Joram’s daughter and Ahaziah’s sister, so either Athaliah’s daughter or her stepdaughter. Chronicles adds the detail that changes everything: she was the wife of Jehoiada the priest (2 Chronicles 22:11). The royal house and the priesthood were joined in one marriage, which is why what happens next is possible at all.

Stole him away from among the king’s sons. She went into the room where it was happening, while it was happening, and took one out. And she took him and his nurse: a one-year-old hidden without a wet nurse would not have survived, and somebody, in the middle of a massacre, thought that through.

Hidden in the house of the LORD. Picture six years in the temple precincts: a boy from one to seven, living in rooms attached to the house of God, never seen by anyone who might mention it. A priest, his wife and a nurse knew, and none of them told. Notice why it worked. Athaliah worshipped Baal and had a temple of her own in Jerusalem (v. 18); she had no reason whatever to walk into the house of the LORD, and she did not. The one building in the capital she never entered was the building with the heir in it. On the throne sat a queen who had killed every child she could find; a few hundred yards away, the lamp promised to David was still burning, fed by a nurse.

How God keeps promises. Not usually the way we would keep them. There was no army, no angel, no thunderclap. There was a woman with enough nerve to walk into that room, a wet nurse who could be trusted, a priest with a spare bedroom, and six years of nobody saying anything.

Why is God so hard to see? For six years nothing happened. To anyone in Jerusalem watching, the line of David was finished and heaven said nothing. Many people today make the same argument on a larger scale: if God existed and wanted to be known, surely he would make himself plain; his silence looks like absence. It is a serious objection. But this chapter shows that silence and absence are not the same thing. God was doing the most important thing in the kingdom a few hundred yards from the throne, quietly on purpose, because an announcement would have got the child killed. Pascal argued that God gives enough light for those who want to see him and leaves enough shadow for those who would rather not. Isaiah put the two together in one breath: “Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior” (Isaiah 45:15). Hidden, and Saviour. When God at last came into the open, he came as a child again, grew up unnoticed in Nazareth, and the world still did not recognise him (John 1:10). The question is not only whether God can be seen, but whether we are looking where he hides.
verseByVerse.note: Athaliah was Ahab’s daughter, probably by Jezebel. Had she succeeded, David’s line would have ended.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–12 — The Spears and Shields That Had Been King David's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s time comes, the true king is shown, guarded and crowned. In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest brings the captains of the guard into the temple, binds them by oath, and only then shows them the king’s son (v. 4). He uses the Sabbath change of duty to fill the courts with armed men without raising suspicion, and arms them with King David’s own spears and shields (vv. 5–11). Then the boy is brought out, crowned, given the testimony, anointed and acclaimed: “Long live the king!” (v. 12). Patient faith and careful planning serve the promise together.
verseByVerse.theology: Jehoiada puts the men under oath and then shows them the child, so that every one of them risks his life having seen the reason for it with his own eyes.
verseByVerse.examples: Weapons dedicated to God in one generation are taken down to protect his promise in another.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the seventh year Jehoiada sent and brought the captains of the Carites and of the guards, and had them come to him in the house of the LORD. And he made a covenant with them and put them under oath in the house of the LORD, and he showed them the king's son. And he commanded them, "This is the thing that you shall do: one third of you, those who come off duty on the Sabbath and guard the king's house (another third being at the gate Sur and a third at the gate behind the guards) shall guard the palace. And the two divisions of you, which come on duty in force on the Sabbath and guard the house of the LORD on behalf of the king, shall surround the king, each with his weapons in his hand. And whoever approaches the ranks is to be put to death. Be with the king when he goes out and when he comes in." The captains did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded, and they each brought his men who were to go off duty on the Sabbath, with those who were to come on duty on the Sabbath, and came to Jehoiada the priest. And the priest gave to the captains the spears and shields that had been King David's, which were in the house of the LORD. And the guards stood, every man with his weapons in his hand, from the south side of the house to the north side of the house, around the altar and the house on behalf of the king. Then he brought out the king's son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. And they proclaimed him king and anointed him, and they clapped their hands and said, "Long live the king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After six years of waiting Jehoiada binds the guard by oath, fills the temple with armed men on the Sabbath, and crowns the hidden boy with both the crown and the book of God’s law.

But in the seventh year. Consider what those six years cost Jehoiada: the priest of the LORD in a nation ruled by a Baal-worshipping usurper, with the rightful king asleep down the corridor, waiting every day until the boy was old enough to be crowned in public and until he could judge the loyalty of the men he would need. When he does move, note the order of the meeting: oath first, then the child. He binds the captains, in the temple, and only then opens a door and shows them a seven-year-old.

Those who come off duty on the Sabbath. The detail is dull to read, and it is why the plan works. He picks the Sabbath because it is changeover day. The shift going off and the shift coming on are both in the temple at once, so twice the usual number of armed men can stand in those courts without anyone in Jerusalem thinking it odd.

Faith that plans. He is not relying on a miracle; he is using the guards’ duty roster. Some think planning is a failure of trust; this chapter quietly disagrees. A man who has waited six years for God to keep a promise spends the end of it working out shift patterns and gate assignments, and the promise is kept through the shift patterns.

The spears and shields that had been King David’s. These were trophies and ceremonial arms from David’s own campaigns (compare 2 Samuel 8:7, where he brings Hadadezer’s gold shields to Jerusalem), dedicated to God and hung in his house for well over a century. Nobody had expected to use them. Now David’s own spears come down off the wall to guard David’s last heir, in the house David wanted to build, to keep alive the promise David was given.

Put the crown on him and gave him the testimony. Two things are put on him, and the second matters as much as the first. The testimony is almost certainly a copy of God’s law, which Deuteronomy requires every king of Israel to write out, keep beside him, and “read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God” (Deuteronomy 17:19). Crown and book together are what make a king in Israel and not merely a ruler: authority in his hand, and over him God’s law, which he did not write and cannot change. Athaliah had the throne for six years and never had that: the whole difference between the house of David and the house of Ahab.

Long live the king! Then the sound: hands clapping, and men shouting long live the king at a seven-year-old who had spent six years in hiding.

Was Jehoiada right to overthrow Athaliah? Yes. She was a usurper who had murdered the royal family, and Jehoiada did not seize power for himself but restored the lawful king of David’s line, with the officers of the guard and the people of the land. It gives no licence to private believers today to take up the sword against a government (see the note on vv. 13–21).

Uncertain wording. The Carites (vv. 4, 19) were probably foreign mercenaries in the royal guard, like David’s Cherethites (2 Samuel 8:18), but the name is rare and their origin uncertain. The arrangement of the guard in vv. 5–7 is also hard to reconstruct: exactly which thirds stood where, and what “the gate Sur” was, are not known, though the plan is clear enough: both shifts together surround the king. “The testimony” is most naturally a written witness, God’s law or the covenant terms; a few scholars suggest a royal emblem instead, but most take it as the law.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The usurper falls, and the people bind themselves to the LORD again. Athaliah hears the noise, enters the temple, sees the crowned boy by the pillar and cries treason (vv. 13–14). Jehoiada has her taken out so that she is not killed in the house of the LORD, and she dies at the horses’ entrance of the palace (vv. 15–16). He makes a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD’s people, and between king and people (v. 17). The people tear down the house of Baal, and the seven-year-old king takes the throne while the city is quiet (vv. 18–21).
verseByVerse.theology: The usurper is the only person in the building with no right to cry treason, and she cries it loudest.
verseByVerse.examples: The reform goes further than a change of ruler: the people are bound to God first, and then king and people to one another.

verseByVerse.quote: When Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and of the people, she went into the house of the LORD to the people. And when she looked, there was the king standing by the pillar, according to the custom, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!" Then Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains who were set over the army, "Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death with the sword anyone who follows her." For the priest said, "Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD." So they laid hands on her; and she went through the horses' entrance to the king's house, and there she was put to death. And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD's people, and also between the king and the people. Then all the people of the land went to the house of Baal and tore it down; his altars and his images they broke in pieces, and they killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest posted watchmen over the house of the LORD. And he took the captains, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the LORD, marching through the gate of the guards to the king's house. And he took his seat on the throne of the kings. So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after Athaliah had been put to death with the sword at the king's house. Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Athaliah finds the true king crowned and cries treason, and is put to death outside the temple; then king and people bind themselves to the LORD, tear down Baal’s house, and the boy takes David’s throne.

She went into the house of the LORD to the people. For the first time in the six years she has ruled the city, she walks into the temple, drawn by a noise she cannot account for. She had counted the bodies six years ago, and she had been queen ever since on the strength of it. And there stands a living heir by the pillar, according to the custom, in the place where the kings of Judah stood, crowned, with the trumpets going and the whole city cheering.

Treason! Treason! The woman who murdered her own grandchildren to seize a throne that was never hers stands in the temple and accuses everybody else of treason. People who have taken something are often the loudest about theft, and they are not being cynical when they say it; they have held it long enough to feel robbed.

Let her not be put to death in the house of the LORD. In the middle of a coup the priest stops to give an instruction about where she may be killed. Nobody would have said a word had she been cut down where she stood; he has her walked out first, because the house of God is not a place for that, even for her. That is restraint of a rare kind. Jehu, in the north, killed a temple full of men and turned the building into a latrine (10:25–27). Jehoiada, in the south, will not have one guilty woman executed on holy ground. Both were doing God’s work; only one of them was careful.

Through the horses’ entrance. She dies at the horses’ entrance to the palace, as Jezebel died in a gateway in Jezreel, trampled by horses (9:31–33). The writer does not point out the likeness, and it may mean nothing; but the two women who brought Baal into two kingdoms both died in a gateway among horses.

That they should be the LORD’s people. Two covenants make the day more than a palace coup. The first is between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD’s people: the language of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 19:5–6), taken up again by a nation that had spent six years under a Baal-worshipping queen. We are yours. The second is between the king and the people, the seven-year-old bound to them and they to him. Judah has just seen what happens when a ruler answers to nothing, and the answer is an agreement in both directions before the boy has so much as sat on the throne.

What a covenant is. To modern ears “covenant” sounds like a contract: terms agreed, and kept while they suit both sides. A covenant is deeper: it binds you to a person even when it costs you. Judah renews here not a deal with God but belonging, and it began on God’s side. He bound himself first, to Abraham and to David, and kept his word through Athaliah’s six years when Judah kept nothing. Our instinct is to hold God on consumer terms, for as long as he delivers. The new covenant does not rest on that. On the night he was betrayed Jesus said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). He bore the cost of our unfaithfulness, so that God can say, “I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jeremiah 31:33), and never take it back. So come to the Lord’s Supper not to strike a bargain but to be reminded whose you are. See Covenant in the Theological Dictionary.

Went to the house of Baal and tore it down. Athaliah had built her father’s religion into Judah’s capital, with a temple, altars, images and a named priest. That is what one marriage alliance, made in friendship two generations earlier (8:18), had grown into. It comes down at once, torn apart not by the guard or by decree but by the people of the land, ordinary Judeans who had evidently been waiting a long time for permission. Within a few years Baal has been put out of both kingdoms: by a soldier in the north, by the people themselves in the south.

What it does not mean. The killing of Mattan the priest of Baal belonged to Israel as a nation governed by God’s own law (Deuteronomy 13:6–10). The church answers false religion with the word, not the sword, for “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Jehoash was seven years old. End on seven years old (v. 21), because the writer does. The whole weight of every promise God ever made about a king from David’s line, the throne established forever, the offspring of the woman, the one whose kingdom would have no end, rested that day on a boy who had spent six of his seven years hidden in the temple, out of sight of the city he was king of.

Twice the promise came down to one infant. Eight hundred years later another child of that line was carried out of reach of a king who was killing children, by parents who moved at night, and kept alive in obscurity until it was safe (Matthew 2:13–16). Twice the promise came down to one infant and a family willing to hide him, and both times those trying to put out the light did not know which room to look in.

What came later. One honest word more. This boy will do well for as long as Jehoiada lives; after the old priest dies he will listen to other men, and he will have Jehoiada’s own son stoned to death in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). The rescue in this chapter was real and God’s promise was kept, and the child who was saved grew into a man who needed saving from himself. That is not a flaw in the story. It is why the line had to keep going, until a Son of David came who would not fail.
verseByVerse.note: Jehoash is another spelling of Joash (ESV note).

11.theology:
What was at stake (v. 1). Every promise about David's throne, and about the offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent (Gen. 3:15), depended on the family of children Athaliah killed.

How the promise was actually kept (vv. 2-3). There was no army, no angel and no sign: only a woman with the nerve to walk into the room, a priest with a spare bedroom, and six years of silence. God usually keeps his word through ordinary means: somebody's courage and somebody else's competence.

The rota (vv. 5-9). Some believers treat planning as a failure of trust. Yet Jehoiada, who had waited six years for God to keep a promise, carefully planned the guards’ shifts and gate duties, and the promise was kept through that plan.

David's weapons (v. 10). Spoil from David's own wars, hanging unused in the house of the LORD for well over a century, was taken down to guard David's last heir. Nothing given to God is wasted, even when it seems forgotten.

Crown and testimony (v. 12). The testimony is God’s law. A king in Israel rules under a law he did not write and cannot change, and that is the whole difference between the house of David and the house of Ahab.

Not in the house of the LORD (v. 15). Jehu killed a temple full of men; Jehoiada will not have one guilty woman put to death on holy ground. Zeal for God can be careful as well as fierce.

Two covenants (v. 17). Judah has just seen what a ruler does who answers to no one. So the nation binds itself first to God, and then king and people bind themselves to one another.
11.examples:
Then: A woman walked into the room where her family's children were being killed, took one of them out, and remembered to take the wet nurse too; and then a priest, his wife, and a nurse kept a boy alive in a back bedroom of the temple for six years without one of them ever mentioning it.

Now: First, how the rescue was done. If you are waiting for God to keep a promise, notice that in one of the largest such moments in the Old Testament he used a brave aunt, a nurse, a spare room and a duty roster, and that from inside those six years it must have looked exactly like nothing happening. He has already kept the largest promise of all, in the Son of David who was also hidden as a child (Matt. 2:13), so you are not waiting on a God who forgets. Second, Jehoiada's planning: careful preparation is not a failure of faith but one of the ways faith works. Third, Athaliah's cry. Treason was shouted by the one person in the building with no right to the word, and she almost certainly meant it, because six years of possession is long enough to feel robbed of something you stole.

keyVerse.quote: And he remained with her six years, hidden in the house of the LORD, while Athaliah reigned over the land.
keyVerse.note: For six years the whole promise of a King from David’s line rested on one small boy in a back room of the temple, while a Baal-worshipping queen ruled outside. The verse shows how God often keeps his word: hidden, quiet and unhurried, but never failing. The same promise would later be carried in another hidden child, until it came to its fulfilment in Christ.

11.reflection:
For six years it seemed that David’s line was finished, yet God was keeping his promise in a back room of the temple (vv. 2–3). When has God seemed silent to you? How do this chapter and Isaiah 45:15 help in such times?

Jehosheba risked her life to rescue one child, and Jehoiada spent years planning, down to the duty roster of the guard (vv. 2, 4–8). How do courage, careful planning and trust in God belong together?

Joash received both the crown and the testimony, God’s law (v. 12). Why does every ruler, and every Christian, need to live under a word they did not write?

Jehoiada made a covenant “that they should be the LORD’s people” (v. 17). What is the difference between belonging to God by covenant and treating him as a contract, and how does the Lord’s Supper remind us of it (Luke 22:20)?

12.title: Joash Repairs the House of the LORD
12.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba.<sup>2</sup>And Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him.<sup>3</sup>Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away; the people continued to sacrifice and make offerings on the high places.<sup>4</sup>Jehoash said to the priests, "All the money of the holy things that is brought into the house of the LORD, the money for which each man is assessed—the money from the assessment of persons—and the money that a man's heart prompts him to bring into the house of the LORD,<sup>5</sup>let the priests take, each from his donor, and let them repair the house wherever any need of repairs is discovered."<sup>6</sup>But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash, the priests had made no repairs on the house.<sup>7</sup>Therefore King Jehoash summoned Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and said to them, "Why are you not repairing the house? Now therefore take no more money from your donors, but hand it over for the repair of the house."<sup>8</sup>So the priests agreed that they should take no more money from the people, and that they should not repair the house.<sup>9</sup>Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest and bored a hole in the lid of it and set it beside the altar on the right side as one entered the house of the LORD. And the priests who guarded the threshold put in it all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>And whenever they saw that there was much money in the chest, the king's secretary and the high priest came up and they bagged and counted the money that was found in the house of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>Then they would give the money that was weighed out into the hands of the workmen who had the oversight of the house of the LORD. And they paid it out to the carpenters and the builders who worked on the house of the LORD,<sup>12</sup>and to the masons and the stonecutters, as well as to buy timber and quarried stone for making repairs on the house of the LORD, and for any outlay for the repairs of the house.<sup>13</sup>But there were not made for the house of the LORD basins of silver, snuffers, bowls, trumpets, or any vessels of gold, or of silver, from the money that was brought into the house of the LORD,<sup>14</sup>for that was given to the workmen who were repairing the house of the LORD with it.<sup>15</sup>And they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money to pay out to the workmen, for they dealt honestly.<sup>16</sup>The money from the guilt offerings and the money from the sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests.<sup>17</sup>At that time Hazael king of Syria went up and fought against Gath and took it. But when Hazael set his face to go up against Jerusalem,<sup>18</sup>Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers, the kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts, and all the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king's house, and sent these to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem.<sup>19</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>20</sup>His servants arose and made a conspiracy and struck down Joash in the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla.<sup>21</sup>It was Jozacar the son of Shimeath and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, who struck him down, so that he died. And they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
12.overview:
Where we are. The boy hidden in the temple has been crowned, and Baal’s house in Jerusalem torn down (chapter 11). Now his reign is told, while in the north Jehu’s dynasty rules and Hazael of Damascus grows stronger (10:32–33).

The message. A life can be outwardly right for decades on borrowed convictions and still give way when the teacher is gone. Joash did right “because Jehoiada the priest instructed him” (v. 2). He repaired God’s house well, through wise and honest arrangements; but when danger came he stripped it to buy off an enemy without a word to God, and he died at his own servants’ hands. Faith has to become one’s own, resting on God himself.

Why it was said. Readers asking why even Judah’s good kings had not saved the nation (see the introduction) see here how shallow a reform can be, and how much depended on whether the king’s heart belonged to the LORD or only to his teacher.

How the chapter makes its case. Joash reigns forty years and does right under Jehoiada’s instruction, though the high places remain (vv. 1–3). His first plan for repairing the temple leaves the money with the priests, and by his twenty-third year nothing has been done (vv. 4–8). A chest beside the altar, opened by two officials together and paid straight to honest workmen, gets the building mended (vv. 9–16). When Hazael threatens Jerusalem, Joash sends him the temple’s sacred gifts and gold (vv. 17–18), and his own servants kill him (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes. A king raised in the temple and crowned with the law could not keep himself faithful; Chronicles adds that he had Jehoiada’s son Zechariah stoned in the temple court, and Jesus still named that blood (Matthew 23:35). Zechariah died crying, “May the LORD see and avenge!” (2 Chronicles 24:22); Jesus died praying for those who killed him (Luke 23:34). He is the King who needed no guardian to stay faithful, who raises God’s true temple (John 2:19–21), and whose priesthood is never ended by a death (Hebrews 7:24–25).

For us. Ask whether your faith rests on Christ himself or only on the people who taught you. Build honest, careful arrangements for money and trust in the church. And when trouble comes, bring it to God before you spend what was given to him to make it go away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Because Jehoiada the Priest Instructed Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king can do right for years on borrowed convictions. Jehoash reigns forty years and does what is right, and the writer gives the reason: because Jehoiada the priest instructed him (vv. 1–2). The high places remain (v. 3). His first plan for repairing the temple is sensible on paper: all the money comes to the priests, and they are to see the work done (vv. 4–5). In the twenty-third year of his reign nothing has been mended, so the king asks why, and the priests give up both the collection and the responsibility (vv. 6–8). Money that no one is answerable for simply disappears.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 2 governs the reign: he did right because somebody instructed him. Chronicles records what happened when that somebody was buried.
verseByVerse.examples: Good intentions without anyone answerable for them can leave a house unmended for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba. And Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him. Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away; the people continued to sacrifice and make offerings on the high places. Jehoash said to the priests, "All the money of the holy things that is brought into the house of the LORD, the money for which each man is assessed—the money from the assessment of persons—and the money that a man's heart prompts him to bring into the house of the LORD, let the priests take, each from his donor, and let them repair the house wherever any need of repairs is discovered." But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash, the priests had made no repairs on the house. Therefore King Jehoash summoned Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and said to them, "Why are you not repairing the house? Now therefore take no more money from your donors, but hand it over for the repair of the house." So the priests agreed that they should take no more money from the people, and that they should not repair the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joash does right for as long as Jehoiada teaches him, but his first plan for repairing the temple fails for twenty-three years, because no one is answerable for the money.

Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. The boy from the temple bedroom gets one of the longest reigns in Judah’s history, forty years, and the key to him is the last clause of verse 2. He did what was right because Jehoiada the priest instructed him: not because he sought God, or because his heart was whole, but because a particular man taught him. Jehoiada had saved his life, hidden him six years, crowned him at seven, put the book of the law in his hands and stood beside him ever since. He was the king’s uncle by marriage, husband of the aunt who carried the baby out of the massacre (11:2), and the only father the king had ever had.

The high places were not taken away. The high places (v. 3), local hilltop altars, are the standing exception in Judah, as for almost every good king. He could reform the temple; he could not change what a village did on its own hill.

Let them repair the house. The plan in verses 4–5 is sensible, and almost every institution starts with it. Three streams of income are all received by the priests, and the priests are to see the repairs done. One body collects, holds and spends, and nobody is given a specific job.

The priests had made no repairs on the house. By verse 6 Joash is about thirty, and not one repair has been made to a building a century and a half old that had been looted more than once (1 Kings 14:26; 15:18). Verse 6 does not say the priests stole the money, and neither should we; the writer is not shy about naming corruption when he sees it. What he records is that money came in for a stated purpose and the purpose was not carried out, for a generation. That is what happens when income arrives with nobody personally answerable for a specific outcome: it gets absorbed. The running costs are met, and next year’s repairs are next year’s problem. Every church treasurer knows this verse from the inside.

Why are you not repairing the house? The king asks the man who raised him directly, with no accusation, and changes the arrangements. The settlement in verse 8 is generous on both sides and slightly sad: the priests give up the collection and the responsibility with it, an honest admission, we are not going to do this, so take it off us, and far better than more years of intending to.

What came after Jehoiada. Kings does not say what happened when Jehoiada died, and its readers need Chronicles to know. “Now after the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them.” They abandoned the house of the LORD and served Asherim and idols; prophets were sent and not heard; and when Jehoiada’s own son Zechariah stood up and told them why they were failing, “they conspired against him, and by command of the king they stoned him with stones in the court of the house of the LORD” (2 Chronicles 24:17–22).

The murder Jesus remembered. The boy Jehoiada hid had Jehoiada’s son killed on the temple pavement, and the Lord Jesus was still naming it eight hundred years later, at the close of his woes against the scribes and Pharisees: “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar” (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51). Zechariah died saying, “May the LORD see and avenge!” (2 Chronicles 24:22). The next righteous man murdered in Jerusalem by the people of God prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), and his blood speaks a better word (Hebrews 12:24).

Borrowed convictions. Take verse 2 seriously as a warning. A man can be genuinely good on borrowed convictions for decades. The instruction was real, the reforms in this chapter are real, and none of it was his. The test of whether a thing has become yours is what survives the burial of the person who taught it to you.

What it does not mean. It is a warning, not a sentence on everyone who came to faith through someone else. Almost everyone does: Timothy’s faith dwelt first in his grandmother and his mother (2 Timothy 1:5). Borrowed faith becomes your own when it fastens on Christ himself rather than on his messenger, as the Samaritans told the woman at the well: “we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world” (John 4:42). Faith that rests on him does not depend on any teacher’s lifespan, because it is held by one who “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25).

Does Kings contradict Chronicles, which says he turned bad? No. The Hebrew of verse 2 can be read all his days, because Jehoiada instructed him, as the ESV takes it, or all his days in which Jehoiada instructed him, as the KJV renders it: all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him. Chronicles says the same in plain words, that he did right “all the days of Jehoiada the priest” (2 Chronicles 24:2), and then tells what came after.

Isn’t faith just an accident of birth? Joash looks like the sceptic’s textbook case: when the man who raised him died, his belief went too. Many conclude that all religion works this way: born in Riyadh you would be a Muslim, born in Chennai a Hindu, so how can anyone think the faith of their own upbringing happens to be true? The point is fair. But the philosopher Alvin Plantinga noticed that it cuts both ways: born elsewhere or in another century, the person making the argument would probably not hold the modern Western conviction that all religions are equally products of culture either. Where a belief came from does not settle whether it is true; only weighing its claims can do that. Joash never did; he inherited conclusions he had not examined, and they did not survive a funeral. The gospel does not ask anyone to believe because a parent or a priest did. It points to a public event, a tomb outside Jerusalem, and invites people to do what the Bereans did, “examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (Acts 17:11). Faith that has looked for itself can outlive its teachers.

Which Zechariah? Matthew calls the murdered Zechariah “the son of Barachiah” (Matthew 23:35), while Chronicles names his father Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:20). Some think Jesus means Zechariah the prophet, son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1), murdered in the temple at an unrecorded time; others that Barachiah was a grandfather, or that the name was miscopied. The likeliest reading is the priest of Chronicles, the last martyr in the Hebrew Bible’s order of books, as Abel was the first.

Uncertain wording. The three kinds of money in verse 4 are compressed and hard to pin down. They are probably the money from a census levy (compare Exodus 30:13–16, and “the tax levied by Moses” in 2 Chronicles 24:6), payments set by valuation for vows (Leviticus 27:2–8), and freewill gifts. The word rendered “donor” in verses 5 and 7 is also uncertain: it may mean an acquaintance, the worshipper each priest knew, or an official who assessed or sold the offerings. The point is clear either way: the priests received the money personally.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — A Chest and a Hole in the Lid
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A simple, honest arrangement does what years of good intentions had not. Jehoiada sets a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar, where every gift goes in publicly (v. 9). When it fills, the king’s secretary and the high priest count it together and pay it straight to the overseers of the work, for carpenters, builders, masons, timber and stone (vv. 10–12). The building comes before silver and gold furnishings (vv. 13–14). The foremen are trusted without audit, because they deal honestly (v. 15), and the priests keep their lawful income (v. 16). It is a reform, not a purge.
verseByVerse.theology: The fix is structural rather than moral: nobody preaches at anybody.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 keeps the reform from tipping into suspicion of everyone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest and bored a hole in the lid of it and set it beside the altar on the right side as one entered the house of the LORD. And the priests who guarded the threshold put in it all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD. And whenever they saw that there was much money in the chest, the king's secretary and the high priest came up and they bagged and counted the money that was found in the house of the LORD. Then they would give the money that was weighed out into the hands of the workmen who had the oversight of the house of the LORD. And they paid it out to the carpenters and the builders who worked on the house of the LORD, and to the masons and the stonecutters, as well as to buy timber and quarried stone for making repairs on the house of the LORD, and for any outlay for the repairs of the house. But there were not made for the house of the LORD basins of silver, snuffers, bowls, trumpets, or any vessels of gold, or of silver, from the money that was brought into the house of the LORD, for that was given to the workmen who were repairing the house of the LORD with it. And they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money to pay out to the workmen, for they dealt honestly. The money from the guilt offerings and the money from the sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A chest beside the altar, opened by two officials together and paid straight to the workmen, gets the temple mended: a wise reform that protects the honest, trusts the faithful and punishes no one.

Took a chest and bored a hole in the lid of it. The solution to years of failure is a box with a hole in the lid, standing beside the altar, on the right as you come in, the first thing a worshipper passes. The money no longer goes to a priest who receives and holds it. It goes through a slot into a locked chest, in public, where the giver can see it go. Nobody is rebuked and no sermon is preached; Jehoiada has made it structurally impossible for the problem to recur, at the cost of one chest and a drill.

The king’s secretary and the high priest. Two men from two institutions open it together, the secretary for the crown and the high priest for the temple. Neither can open the box alone or count alone, and each is a witness to what the other does. It is dual control, invented for the reason it is always invented: an honest man handling money alone can be ruined by one false accusation, and a dishonest one is handed a temptation he need never have faced. Good systems do not make men honest. They protect honest men and remove opportunities from the rest, and building them is not cynical. It is a kindness.

Basins of silver, snuffers, bowls, trumpets. Verses 13–14 set a discipline about priorities that went against the grain. Silver basins, gold bowls and trumpets are visible: the things a donor can look at and a king is remembered for. Rafters and quarried stone are not. The rule was that nothing was spent on the furnishings until the fabric of the building was sound. Any congregation that has had to choose between a new sound system and the drains will recognise the decision, and this time somebody made it the right way round.

For they dealt honestly. The reform does not turn into suspicion of everyone. Having installed dual control at the chest, they impose no audit at all on the foremen paying the wages. Those men had been tested and found reliable, and they were left alone. That is the balance, and institutions almost always get it wrong one way or the other. A system that treats everybody as a suspect is not more righteous than one that treats nobody as a suspect; both have stopped asking who has actually earned trust.

It belonged to the priests. The priests keep their living. The reform took the building fund out of their hands and left their income where the law had put it (Leviticus 7:7; Numbers 18:9). Nobody was punished or replaced. It is a reform and not a purge, and in a book this full of purges the difference stands out.

Jesus at the treasury. Centuries later, in the rebuilt temple, Jesus “sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box” (Mark 12:41). He counted a poor widow’s two coins, all she had, as more than all the rest. Honest arrangements matter, and Jehoiada’s chest is a model of them; but the One who watches the giving sees the heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — He Sent These to Hazael
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king who repaired God’s house empties it to buy off an enemy, and dies at his own servants’ hands. Hazael of Syria takes Gath and turns toward Jerusalem (v. 17). Without seeking the LORD, Joash sends him all the sacred gifts of four generations of kings and all the gold in the temple and palace treasuries, and Hazael withdraws (v. 18). Then the reign ends in a conspiracy: two of his servants strike him down, and he is buried in the city of David (vv. 19–21). Chronicles supplies the reason Kings leaves unsaid: the blood of Jehoiada’s son.
verseByVerse.theology: He spent the middle of his life restoring that building and the end of it emptying it, his own dedicated gifts among the rest.
verseByVerse.examples: The king who had done what was right all the days somebody was instructing him now consults no one, asks nothing, and pays. Chronicles supplies what Kings withholds about his end, as the note below explains.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Hazael king of Syria went up and fought against Gath and took it. But when Hazael set his face to go up against Jerusalem, Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers, the kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts, and all the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and of the king's house, and sent these to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem. Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? His servants arose and made a conspiracy and struck down Joash in the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla. It was Jozacar the son of Shimeath and Jehozabad the son of Shomer, his servants, who struck him down, so that he died. And they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Hazael threatens Jerusalem, the king who repaired God’s house empties it to buy him off, without seeking God; and his own servants kill him.

At that time Hazael king of Syria went up. Hazael, the man whose cruelty Elisha foresaw and wept over (8:11–12), is now at the gates of Judah. He has taken Gath, on the coastal plain, which puts him past Judah’s western defences with the road to Jerusalem open. And then, the writer says, he set his face to go up.

All the sacred gifts. Read the inventory the writer has laid out: four generations of things given to God, gathered up and sent to Damascus in a convoy. This is the man who spent the middle of his life organising the repair of that building. He mended the house and then emptied it.

No prophet in sight. There is no prophet anywhere in this chapter. Nobody is consulted, no word of the LORD comes, nothing is asked. Hezekiah, in the same city facing a worse army, will take a letter up to the temple and spread it out before the LORD (19:14). Joash counts what is in the treasury and pays.

Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem. It worked, in the sense that Hazael went away. Anybody with enough gold can have that sort of success, but only once, because then the gold is gone.

His servants arose and made a conspiracy. His own household kills him. Kings names the two men, their fathers and the place, and offers no motive. Chronicles supplies it, and it is the sentence this chapter has been walking towards: his servants conspired against him “because of the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest” (2 Chronicles 24:25). So the reign closes as it opened, with a priest’s family and a king. Jehoiada’s wife carried him out of a massacre, and every good thing recorded here came from Jehoiada’s teaching. When Jehoiada was dead, Joash had his son stoned in the court of the house he had repaired, and two of his own servants killed him on his bed for it.

They buried him with his fathers in the city of David. Chronicles adds one more detail: they did not bury him in the tombs of the kings (2 Chronicles 24:25).

Uncertain wording. “The house of Millo” was probably a building on the terraced fill (the Millo) of the old city of David, but “on the way that goes down to Silla” names a place mentioned nowhere else, and no one knows where it was.

12.theology:
Borrowed convictions (v. 2). After Jehoiada's funeral Joash listened to the princes and had Jehoiada's own son stoned in the temple court. The test of whether a thing has become yours is what survives the burial of the person who taught it.

What actually went wrong (v. 6). No theft is alleged. Money arrived for a stated purpose with nobody personally answerable for it, and was absorbed year after year. That is the ordinary failure of institutions, and not usually a moral one, which is exactly why preaching does not fix it.

A structural remedy, with a limit (vv. 9-16). Good systems do not make anyone honest; they protect the honest and remove opportunities from the rest. But controls went only where the failure had been: the honest foremen were trusted and the priests' livelihood was left untouched. This is a reform, not a purge.

Fabric before furnishings (vv. 13-14). The visible items are the ones donors look at and kings are remembered for; rafters and quarried stone are not. This time the choice was made the right way round.

The house mended and emptied (vv. 17-18). Hezekiah will take a threatening letter up to the temple and spread it out before God; Joash counts the treasury and pays. It worked, as it works for anybody with enough gold, once.
12.examples:
Then: Year after year, into the twenty-third of the reign, the money for the temple repairs came in and the repairs were not done, and nobody had stolen anything. Then a priest drilled a hole in the lid of a box, set it where every worshipper walked past, and had it opened by two men who did not work for the same master.

Now: First, verse 2. If you can trace your convictions to one person, a parent, a minister, a friend, ask what would be left the year after their funeral. Joash's good years were real and none of them were his. The answer is not to try harder at conviction but to look past the teacher to Christ, who does not die and holds on to those who rest on him (Heb. 7:25). Second, the chest. Money given for a purpose, with nobody personally answerable for it, gets absorbed; no amount of preaching cures that, and the fix is a box with a hole in it and two signatures. Third, the balance in verse 15. Put the controls where the failure was and nowhere else. Treating everyone as a suspect is not integrity, and it costs you the people who were never the problem.

keyVerse.quote: And Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him.
keyVerse.note: The whole reign hangs on the last clause. Joash’s goodness was real, but it was held up by his teacher, and Chronicles shows what happened once Jehoiada died (2 Chronicles 24:17–22). The verse is a warning to every child of a believing home and every new believer: faith must come to rest on God himself, who never dies.

12.reflection:
Joash did right “because Jehoiada the priest instructed him” (v. 2), and after Jehoiada died he turned away (2 Chronicles 24:17–22). How can we tell whether our faith is our own or borrowed? What makes borrowed faith become real (John 4:42)?

The repair money vanished into running costs for twenty-three years (vv. 4–8). What practical lessons does the chest beside the altar (vv. 9–15) teach churches and families about money, accountability and trust?

The foremen were not audited, “for they dealt honestly” (v. 15). How do we balance sensible checks with the trust that honest people have earned?

Faced with Hazael, Joash emptied the treasuries without asking God (vv. 17–18), whereas Hezekiah later spread out his enemy’s letter before the LORD (19:14). What do we reach for first when we are threatened?

13.title: Jehoahaz, Jehoash and the Death of Elisha
13.text: <sup>1</sup>In the twenty-third year of Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned seventeen years.<sup>2</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from them.<sup>3</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them continually into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael.<sup>4</sup>Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel, how the king of Syria oppressed them.<sup>5</sup>(Therefore the LORD gave Israel a savior, so that they escaped from the hand of the Syrians, and the people of Israel lived in their homes as formerly.<sup>6</sup>Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin, but walked in them; and the Asherah also remained in Samaria.)<sup>7</sup>For there was not left to Jehoahaz an army of more than fifty horsemen and ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing.<sup>8</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz and all that he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>9</sup>So Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria, and Joash his son reigned in his place.<sup>10</sup>In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years.<sup>11</sup>He also did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin, but he walked in them.<sup>12</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, and the might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>13</sup>So Joash slept with his fathers, and Jeroboam sat on his throne. And Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.<sup>14</sup>Now when Elisha had fallen sick with the illness of which he was to die, Joash king of Israel went down to him and wept before him, crying, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!"<sup>15</sup>And Elisha said to him, "Take a bow and arrows." So he took a bow and arrows.<sup>16</sup>Then he said to the king of Israel, "Draw the bow," and he drew it. And Elisha laid his hands on the king's hands.<sup>17</sup>And he said, "Open the window eastward," and he opened it. Then Elisha said, "Shoot," and he shot. And he said, "The LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Syria! For you shall fight the Syrians in Aphek until you have made an end of them."<sup>18</sup>And he said, "Take the arrows," and he took them. And he said to the king of Israel, "Strike the ground with them." And he struck three times and stopped.<sup>19</sup>Then the man of God was angry with him and said, "You should have struck five or six times; then you would have struck down Syria until you had made an end of it, but now you will strike down Syria only three times."<sup>20</sup>So Elisha died, and they buried him. Now bands of Moabites used to invade the land in the spring of the year.<sup>21</sup>And as a man was being buried, behold, a marauding band was seen and the man was thrown into the grave of Elisha, and as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet.<sup>22</sup>Now Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.<sup>23</sup>But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them, and he turned toward them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, nor has he cast them from his presence until now.<sup>24</sup>When Hazael king of Syria died, Ben-hadad his son became king in his place.<sup>25</sup>Then Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again from Ben-hadad the son of Hazael the cities that he had taken from Jehoahaz his father in war. Three times Joash defeated him and recovered the cities of Israel.
13.overview:
Where we are. Jehu’s dynasty rules the north, as God promised (10:30), and Hazael of Damascus, who took the whole Transjordan in Jehu’s day (10:32–33), keeps grinding Israel down. Elisha, silent since he sent a young prophet to anoint Jehu (9:1), appears one last time.

The message. God keeps a faithless people alive for the sake of his promise, not their merit. He hears a compromised king’s prayer because he sees his people suffer; he offers victory through a dying prophet, and gives as much as the king has faith to take; and even from his prophet’s grave he gives life. Israel still stands “because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (v. 23).

Why it was said. Readers in exile wondered how God could bear with Israel so long and then let it fall (see the introduction). The chapter answers that his patience was real and rooted in his covenant, but that relief without repentance could not last: “until now” (v. 23) is a warning.

How the chapter makes its case. Jehoahaz keeps the calves and is crushed; he prays and is given a deliverer, yet nothing changes, and his army dwindles to ten chariots (vv. 1–9). His son Joash also does evil (vv. 10–13), yet weeps over the dying Elisha (v. 14), who lays his hands on the king’s to shoot the LORD’s arrow of victory (vv. 15–17); but Joash strikes the ground only three times (vv. 18–19). Elisha dies, and a dead man thrown into his grave comes to life (vv. 20–21). For his covenant’s sake the LORD turns toward Israel, and Joash recovers its cities three times (vv. 22–25).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by pattern. The unnamed saviour of verse 5, like the deliverers of Judges, rescued Israel for a while, and the people went back to their calves; Jesus is the Saviour who “will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). The covenant with Abraham that held Israel up is the covenant God remembered in sending Christ (Luke 1:72–73). And the dead man who stood up at the touch of a prophet’s bones points to the One who did not stay in his grave, at whose voice “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29).

For us. God hears desperate prayers, even from compromised people; but relief is not repentance, so ask what is still standing in your life after he has helped you. Do not strike three times and stop: take God at his word and ask largely. And rest your hope not on your own faithfulness but on his covenant, kept for you in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Like the Dust at Threshing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hears even a compromised king’s cry, but relief without repentance changes nothing. Jehoahaz, Jehu’s son, keeps the golden calves, so the LORD hands Israel over again and again to Hazael and his son (vv. 1–3). Jehoahaz seeks the LORD’s favour and is heard, because God sees his people’s oppression, and he gives Israel an unnamed saviour, so that families live in their homes again (vv. 4–5). Nevertheless they keep Jeroboam’s sins, and the Asherah still stands in Samaria (v. 6). The army is left with fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers, beaten like dust at threshing (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin's cost can be counted: a nation that kept its idols watched its strength reduced to almost nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: God's compassion for a suffering people is wider than the merit of the man who prays for them.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-third year of Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned seventeen years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from them. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them continually into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and into the hand of Ben-hadad the son of Hazael. Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel, how the king of Syria oppressed them. (Therefore the LORD gave Israel a savior, so that they escaped from the hand of the Syrians, and the people of Israel lived in their homes as formerly. Nevertheless, they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, which he made Israel to sin, but walked in them; and the Asherah also remained in Samaria.) For there was not left to Jehoahaz an army of more than fifty horsemen and ten chariots and ten thousand footmen, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust at threshing. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz and all that he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? So Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria, and Joash his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoahaz keeps Jeroboam’s calves and Israel is crushed; he prays, God hears for his suffering people’s sake and sends a deliverer, yet afterwards nothing changes.

Jehoahaz the son of Jehu. The verdict on Jehu’s son is the verdict on his father. The golden calves are still at Bethel and Dan, because Jehu, who pulled down the house of Baal, would not pull them down (10:28–29). So God gives Israel continually into Hazael’s hand: not one campaign but a whole reign of them, seventeen years of being handed over.

Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD, and the LORD listened to him. Verse 4 ought to stop anybody who has decided that their own prayers are disqualified. Here is a king who keeps the golden calves, leaves an Asherah standing in the capital and, as verse 6 will tell us, changes nothing afterwards. He seeks the LORD’s favour because he is being crushed, and God listens. And the reason given is not the king’s sincerity: for he saw the oppression of Israel. The mercy is aimed at the suffering of a people, and the man asking is simply the one who happened to ask.

The LORD gave Israel a savior. The writer does not name him. He may mean Joash or Jeroboam II, who recover territory in this chapter and the next; or pressure from Assyria on Damascus that took the weight off Israel without anybody in Samaria knowing why. Assyrian inscriptions do record Adad-nirari III crushing Damascus around 800 BC and taking tribute from Joash of Samaria. The text leaves it open, and the openness is part of the point: the deliverance came, and the people delivered could not have told you how. The people of Israel lived in their homes as formerly: not a spectacle, but the ordinary life of ordinary families, given back. Most rescues look like that to those being rescued.

The pattern of Judges. It is the pattern the book of Judges taught Israel: the people cry out, and God raises up a deliverer, the same Hebrew word as savior here (Judges 3:9, 15). Every one of those saviours was temporary, and the people they rescued went back to their calves. The angel’s word to Joseph names the Saviour the pattern was waiting for: “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Not only from Syria, and not only for a while.

Nevertheless. Verse 6 gives the sad half in one word. They prayed under pressure, they were heard, they were delivered, and they went back to exactly what they had been doing. Relief is not repentance. A great many people have mistaken the one for the other in their own lives, and what gives it away is what is still standing afterwards: the Asherah also remained in Samaria.

Fifty horsemen and ten chariots. Set that against what this kingdom used to be. Assyrian records of the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC credit Ahab of Israel with two thousand chariots, the largest chariot force in the coalition they list. Some think the figure inflated or miscopied, but even a fraction of it dwarfs ten. Jehu’s son has ten.

Like the dust at threshing. The fine chaff that blows off the threshing floor and is not gathered. Elisha wept in a room in Damascus because he had been shown what Hazael would do to this country (8:11–12), and this verse sets down what he wept over as a count of the soldiers left. There is something bleak in the closing formula, and his might, applied to a man with ten chariots.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — You Should Have Struck Five or Six Times
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Through a dying prophet God offers a king victory, and the king takes only part of it. Joash, Jehoahaz’s son, also does evil, and the writer closes his reign early (vv. 10–13) before going back to one scene. Joash weeps at Elisha’s bedside with the very words Elisha once cried after Elijah (v. 14). The prophet lays his hands on the king’s hands on the bow, and the arrow shot eastward is the LORD’s arrow of victory over Syria (vv. 15–17). Told to strike the ground with the arrows, Joash strikes three times and stops, and the angry prophet tells him he will defeat Syria only three times (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: A king the writer has just called evil sees, at least for a moment, that his country's real defence is a man with the word of God.
verseByVerse.examples: What we receive from God is sometimes shaped by how much we expect of him.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years. He also did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin, but he walked in them. Now the rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, and the might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? So Joash slept with his fathers, and Jeroboam sat on his throne. And Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joash, the third king of Jehu’s line, also does evil, and the writer closes his reign at once, so that he can go back to the one scene that matters.

He also did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. The third generation of Jehu’s house, and the third identical verdict. Hold on to it, because in the next verse this man does something that does not fit it at all.

So Joash slept with his fathers. The writer gives the usual closing summary (vv. 12–13) and then goes back, because one scene from this reign remains, and he will not leave it out.

The might with which he fought against Amaziah. That war is told in the next chapter: Amaziah of Judah challenged him, and Joash broke down the wall of Jerusalem and plundered the temple (14:8–14). The “Jeroboam” who succeeds him is Jeroboam II, whose long reign comes in 14:23–29. Joash was no weakling, and the strength he had, as the next scene shows, came from the word of a dying prophet.

Do the dates add up? Jehoahaz begins in the twenty-third year of Joash of Judah and reigns seventeen years (v. 1), yet his son begins in that king’s thirty-seventh year, not his fortieth. The likeliest answer is that the son was made co-regent in his father’s last years, as kings often were in dangerous times, and his years were counted from then; counting part-years at both ends of a reign accounts for a little more. The numbers are not careless; they follow the counting customs of the time (see Regnal years).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Elisha had fallen sick with the illness of which he was to die, Joash king of Israel went down to him and wept before him, crying, "My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
An evil king weeps over the dying Elisha with the very words Elisha cried after Elijah, because he knows the prophet was Israel’s true defence.

Elisha had fallen sick with the illness of which he was to die. Elisha has not appeared in the story for more than forty years, since he sent the young man to anoint Jehu (9:1). The prophet who raised the dead dies of an ordinary illness, like anyone else; even so, his bones have one more story to tell (v. 21).

My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! These words have been heard before. The young Elisha stood by the Jordan and watched chariots and horses of fire come between him and Elijah, and shouted after him, my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! (2:12). Then he tore his clothes in two and picked up the cloak. Some fifty years later a king of Israel stands over Elisha’s own deathbed and says the same thing. The line opens the ministry and closes it, and both times it means that the real defence of this country has never been its cavalry. Israel has ten chariots left, and the king weeping in that room knows that what is dying in the bed is worth more than all of them.

Joash king of Israel went down to him and wept. Look whose mouth it comes out of. Three verses ago the writer said this man did evil and walked in the sins of Jeroboam. He is not a good king and he is not going to become one. He is also weeping over a dying prophet, calling him father, and grasping the one thing about his kingdom that his grandfather Jehu never grasped. People are not tidy. A man can see something true, feel it to the point of tears, and go home unchanged, and the Bible reports both halves without embarrassment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elisha said to him, "Take a bow and arrows." So he took a bow and arrows. Then he said to the king of Israel, "Draw the bow," and he drew it. And Elisha laid his hands on the king's hands. And he said, "Open the window eastward," and he opened it. Then Elisha said, "Shoot," and he shot. And he said, "The LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Syria! For you shall fight the Syrians in Aphek until you have made an end of them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With his hands on the king’s hands, the dying prophet has Joash shoot an arrow toward Syria and declares it the LORD’s arrow of victory.

Elisha laid his hands on the king’s hands. A dying man puts his hands over a king’s hands on a bowstring. He has not the strength to draw it himself; what he can do is lay his hands on the hands that can. The picture is exact: the power was never in the prophet’s arm, and the king’s arm will do nothing on its own either.

Open the window eastward. East lies over the Jordan toward Gilead and Damascus: the territory Hazael has taken and the direction the trouble comes from.

The LORD’s arrow of victory. The promise is not modest: until you have made an end of them. Aphek, east of the Sea of Galilee, is where Ahab had routed Ben-hadad’s army two generations before (1 Kings 20:26–30). The promise came true: Joash won back from Hazael’s son the towns his father had lost (vv. 22–25).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Take the arrows," and he took them. And he said to the king of Israel, "Strike the ground with them." And he struck three times and stopped. Then the man of God was angry with him and said, "You should have struck five or six times; then you would have struck down Syria until you had made an end of it, but now you will strike down Syria only three times."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Told to strike the ground with the arrows, Joash strikes three times and stops, and so takes three victories where he might have had complete victory.

A fair objection. This exchange troubles readers, and the trouble should be faced rather than talked around. He was never told how many times to strike. How is he at fault for stopping?

What he did know. He had just been told that the arrow in his hand meant victory over Syria until you have made an end of them. He had felt the prophet’s hands close over his own, and he was holding a fistful of arrows from a dying man whose every word in fifty years had come true. He hit the floor three times, stopped, and waited to be told what came next. It was an invitation, and he treated it as a formality, a thing to be performed correctly and got through, rather than an opening he was being handed. The measure of the answer was left to him, and he took a small one.

Not too few. The reader of this book has seen that before. A widow was told to borrow empty vessels, and not too few, and the oil flowed until she ran out of jars and then stopped, not because the supply failed but because she could receive only as much as her borrowed jars would hold (4:3–6). God has more than once let the size of what he gives be settled by the earnestness of the asking.

How feeling fades. Notice the distance travelled in four verses. He came into that room weeping; by the time he holds the arrows he is going through the motions. Feeling is not the same as faith, and it does not last as long.

What it does not mean. None of this makes God stingy. Joash was given three real victories he had done nothing to deserve, by a prophet on his deathbed, in a kingdom with ten chariots. He simply had five or six within reach and put the arrows down.

Then the man of God was angry with him. These are the prophet’s last recorded words, and they stand: Joash would win three victories and no more (see the note on vv. 20–25). It was left to his son Jeroboam to win back more of Israel’s lost ground (14:25–28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Because of His Covenant With Abraham
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s life-giving power outlasts his prophet, and his covenant outlasts Israel’s sin. Elisha dies and is buried without ceremony; when raiders surprise a funeral, the body is thrown into Elisha’s grave, and the dead man touches the prophet’s bones and stands up (vv. 20–21). Though Hazael oppressed Israel all through Jehoahaz’s reign, the LORD was gracious and turned toward them because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and had not cast them off “until now” (vv. 22–23). When Hazael dies, Joash defeats his son three times and recovers Israel’s cities, exactly as Elisha said (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing Elisha does happens after he is dead, and it is done for a stranger. God's work does not end when his servants' lives do.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel survives on a promise made to men long dead, and so does every one of us who stands before God at all.

verseByVerse.quote: So Elisha died, and they buried him. Now bands of Moabites used to invade the land in the spring of the year. And as a man was being buried, behold, a marauding band was seen and the man was thrown into the grave of Elisha, and as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet. Now Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz. But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them, and he turned toward them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, nor has he cast them from his presence until now. When Hazael king of Syria died, Ben-hadad his son became king in his place. Then Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again from Ben-hadad the son of Hazael the cities that he had taken from Jehoahaz his father in war. Three times Joash defeated him and recovered the cities of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elisha dies an ordinary death, yet a dead man thrown into his grave comes to life; and God keeps Israel standing, not for its merit, but for his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

So Elisha died, and they buried him. Seven words for the end of a fifty-year ministry. His master went up in a whirlwind with horses of fire and was never buried at all. Elisha, who asked for a double portion and got it, dies of an ordinary illness and is put in a tomb like anybody else, and the writer moves straight on to a note about seasonal raiding.

The man was thrown into the grave of Elisha. Then verse 21, almost comic and entirely undignified: a funeral party sees raiders, tips its corpse into the nearest open tomb and runs, and the dead man touches the bones of Elisha and stands up. The last miracle of Elisha’s ministry happens after his own funeral, to a man nobody has named, in front of witnesses who were running away at the time and were not looking for anything of the kind.

What should be kept. The power that worked through that man for fifty years was never his. It did not belong to his lungs or his hands or his voice, and it did not stop when his heart did. He had asked for a double portion of Elijah’s spirit and received it, and there was still enough in a grave to raise a stranger.

The resurrection foreshadowed. There is a hint here that the rest of Scripture makes explicit. A dead man touched what was left of a servant of God and stood on his feet. The Son of God did not stay in his grave at all, and “an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29). The graves of his people will not be the end of them either.

Because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Verse 23 does for the northern kingdom what the promise of a lamp did for Judah, and the two should be set side by side. Of Judah, five chapters ago: “Yet the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (8:19). Two kingdoms, neither deserving anything, are both still standing, and in each case the reason is a promise made to a man dead for centuries. Judah is carried by David. Israel, which has no David, no temple and no lamp, is carried by Abraham. That same oath to Abraham is what Zechariah sang of when Christ was coming: God had remembered “his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:72–73).

He turned toward them. Mark what God did. He was gracious, he had compassion, and he turned toward them: the language of a face, of someone choosing to look at people who had given him no reason to.

Until now. Then come the last two words, the coldest in the chapter. The writer is composing this after the end, and he knows how it finishes. God had not yet cast them out at the point his account has reached, which is not the same as saying he never would. Four chapters from now an Assyrian army will take Samaria and carry that kingdom off the map, and this verse is quietly telling us that the only thing holding it up meanwhile was an old promise, and that God’s patience does not mean sin will go unpunished.

Three times Joash defeated him. Joash got every one of his three victories, three real defeats of Syria, more than his father saw in seventeen years. And the man who told him he could have had it all lies in a grave that has already produced one more miracle than the king ever will.

What it does not mean. The passage draws no lesson from the bones. Nobody is recorded going near that tomb again, no shrine is built, and the bones are never mentioned again in Scripture. There is no warrant here for venerating relics, and it would be a poor use of the verse to find one.

Uncertain wording. “In the spring of the year” (v. 20) renders an unusual Hebrew phrase, literally something like “a year came”. Most take it, as the ESV does, to mean the spring, when raiding and campaigning began (compare 2 Samuel 11:1); some render it “year after year”. Either way, the raids were a regular hazard.

13.theology:
A bad king prays and is heard (vv. 4-6). God listened because he saw a suffering people, not because of the king's sincerity. Yet relief is not repentance, and what gives it away is what is still standing afterwards.

The bookend (v. 14). The cry Elisha raised at the Jordan returns over his own deathbed, meaning both times that the country's real defence was never its cavalry. People are not tidy: a man can see something true, feel it to the point of weeping, and go home unchanged.

The arrows (vv. 18-19). He was never told how many times to strike, and the anger looks unfair until you count what he did know. It was an invitation and he treated it as a formality; the measure was left to him and he took a small one, as the widow's oil ran only until she ran out of borrowed jars. He came in weeping and was going through the motions by the end of the visit. Feeling is not faith, and does not last as long.

After the funeral (vv. 20-21). The passage builds no shrine and never mentions the bones again, so there is no warrant here for relics. The power at work in Elisha was never his own and did not stop when his heart did.

The north's lamp (v. 23). Two undeserving kingdoms are each carried by a promise made to a man dead for centuries. But until now warns that God’s patience is not a promise never to punish, and Samaria falls in chapter 17.
13.examples:
Then: A burial party carrying a body saw raiders on the skyline, tipped the corpse into the nearest open tomb and ran, and the dead man touched what was left of Elisha and stood up on his feet.

Now: First, verse 4. If you have concluded that your prayers are disqualified by the state of your life, look at who is praying here and at the reason God gives for listening; you come with better standing than Jehoahaz, in the name of the Son who pleads for you. Second, the arrows. Joash was not disobedient; he was half-hearted, and it cost him a kingdom's worth of victory.
