The God who invited him is the one who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Eph. 3:20), so ask largely, in prayer most of all; and where you have stopped at three, the invitation is still open. Third, the four verses between his tears and his three taps on the floor. He meant the weeping. It simply did not survive the next few moments, and the Bible reports both halves of him without surprise.

keyVerse.quote: But the LORD was gracious to them and had compassion on them, and he turned toward them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, nor has he cast them from his presence until now.
keyVerse.note: This verse explains why the northern kingdom still existed: not for anything in it, but because of a promise God made to men who had been dead for centuries. It shows the heart of God, gracious and turning toward people who had given him no reason to. Its last words, “until now”, warn that patience is not indifference, and the promise to Abraham finds its full answer in Christ (Luke 1:72–73).

13.reflection:
God listened to Jehoahaz “for he saw the oppression of Israel” (v. 4), yet afterwards nothing changed (v. 6). Why is relief not the same as repentance? What is still standing in your life after God has helped you?

Joash wept over Elisha (v. 14) but struck the ground only three times (vv. 18–19). Where are you tempted to treat God’s promises as a formality rather than an invitation? What would it mean for you to strike “five or six times”?

A dead man came to life at the touch of Elisha’s bones (v. 21). What does this show about where the power in God’s servants comes from, and how does it point to the resurrection (John 5:28–29)?

Israel survived “because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (v. 23). How does it comfort you that God’s dealings with you rest on his promise in Christ rather than on your record? And what do the words “until now” warn us about?

14.title: Amaziah and Jeroboam II
14.text: <sup>1</sup>In the second year of Joash the son of Joahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>2</sup>He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddin of Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not like David his father. He did in all things as Joash his father had done.<sup>4</sup>But the high places were not removed; the people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places.<sup>5</sup>And as soon as the royal power was firmly in his hand, he struck down his servants who had struck down the king his father.<sup>6</sup>But he did not put to death the children of the murderers, according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. But each one shall die for his own sin."<sup>7</sup>He struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and took Sela by storm, and called it Joktheel, which is its name to this day.<sup>8</sup>Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face."<sup>9</sup>And Jehoash king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, "A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife,' and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle.<sup>10</sup>You have indeed struck down Edom, and your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory, and stay at home, for why should you provoke trouble so that you fall, you and Judah with you?"<sup>11</sup>But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another in battle at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah.<sup>12</sup>And Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home.<sup>13</sup>And Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Jehoash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and came to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for four hundred cubits, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.<sup>14</sup>And he seized all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's house, also hostages, and he returned to Samaria.<sup>15</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoash that he did, and his might, and how he fought with Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>16</sup>And Jehoash slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and Jeroboam his son reigned in his place.<sup>17</sup>Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.<sup>18</sup>Now the rest of the deeds of Amaziah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>19</sup>And they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there.<sup>20</sup>And they brought him on horses; and he was buried in Jerusalem with his fathers in the city of David.<sup>21</sup>And all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah.<sup>22</sup>He built Elath and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers.<sup>23</sup>In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, began to reign in Samaria, and he reigned forty-one years.<sup>24</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin.<sup>25</sup>He restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the LORD, the God of Israel, which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher.<sup>26</sup>For the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, for there was none left, bond or free, and there was none to help Israel.<sup>27</sup>But the LORD had not said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven, so he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash.<sup>28</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam and all that he did, and his might, how he fought, and how he restored Damascus and Hamath to Judah in Israel, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>29</sup>And Jeroboam slept with his fathers, the kings of Israel, and Zechariah his son reigned in his place.
14.overview:
Where we are. Jehu’s dynasty has reached its third and fourth generations, and Syria’s grip on Israel has just been broken, as the dying Elisha promised (13:14–25). Chapter 14 sets Amaziah of Judah beside Jeroboam II of Israel, whose reign is the north’s last bright years.

The message. God’s word is worth obeying when it costs something, and the most dangerous moment in a life is often a success. Amaziah obeys one sentence of the law against his own interest, then lets a single victory lift up his heart and ruins his city. Meanwhile God rescues Israel through a king who never turned from the golden calves, for no reason but pity: “there was none to help Israel” (v. 26).

Why it was said. The first readers had seen both kingdoms fall (see the introduction). It showed them that their kings’ pride had been warned against in plain words, and that Israel’s good years had been God’s undeserved patience, not proof that all was well.

How the chapter makes its case. Amaziah does right, “yet not like David” (vv. 1–4); he executes his father’s murderers but spares their children because the Law of Moses says so, and he defeats Edom (vv. 5–7). Proud of the victory, he challenges Israel, is mocked with a fable of a thistle and a cedar, refuses sound advice, and loses his freedom, part of Jerusalem’s wall and the temple’s treasures (vv. 8–16). He dies in a conspiracy (vv. 17–22). Then Jeroboam II, evil in the LORD’s sight, restores Israel’s borders as Jonah had prophesied, because the LORD saw their bitter affliction and had not yet said he would blot them out (vv. 23–29).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by the character of God it shows and the need it exposes. The LORD who saved Israel when “there was none to help” is the God who says through Isaiah, “I looked, but there was no one to help… so my own arm brought me salvation” (Isaiah 63:5); in the end that arm was his own Son. Amaziah’s half-hearted obedience and pride show the need for a King who obeys wholly and humbles himself. And the Jonah named here became, in Jesus’ own words, a sign of his death and resurrection: “something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41).

For us. Ask where your obedience stops once it becomes costly, and where a success has quietly lifted your heart. Hear the truth even when it comes wrapped in an insult. And if life is going well, do not read that as God’s approval: it may be his patience, giving you time to turn to the Saviour who came for people with nothing to offer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — According to What Is Written
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king obeys a sentence of God’s law at the very moment it costs him. Amaziah’s reign opens with a qualified verdict: right in the LORD’s eyes, yet not like David, and the high places stay (vv. 1–4). Once his throne is secure he executes the officials who murdered his father, but he spares their children, because the Law of Moses forbids putting children to death for their fathers’ sin (vv. 5–6). In a book where rival families are routinely wiped out, that restraint stands out. Then comes a real victory over Edom (v. 7), and it is this success that will undo him.
verseByVerse.theology: Consider what the surrounding chapters have accustomed us to. Seventy of Ahab's sons beheaded and sent in baskets; forty-two Judean travellers killed at a cistern; a queen destroying her own grandchildren. Wiping out a rival's family was not an atrocity in that world; it was procedure. Here a king with every political reason to finish the job stops because of a sentence in a book.
verseByVerse.examples: Obedience of this kind rarely looks dramatic. It is a sentence consulted at the moment it is inconvenient, and allowed to win against advisers, precedent and self-interest together.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year of Joash the son of Joahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, began to reign. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddin of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not like David his father. He did in all things as Joash his father had done. But the high places were not removed; the people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. And as soon as the royal power was firmly in his hand, he struck down his servants who had struck down the king his father. But he did not put to death the children of the murderers, according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded, "Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. But each one shall die for his own sin." He struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and took Sela by storm, and called it Joktheel, which is its name to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amaziah is a good king by halves, yet at one costly moment he lets a sentence of God’s law overrule what every king around him would have done.

Yet not like David his father. He was not like David; he was exactly like his father Joash (the Joash of Judah saved from Athaliah, not his namesake in Israel), which means good for a while, on borrowed convictions, and finishing badly. And the high places stayed (v. 4).

He struck down his servants who had struck down the king his father. Joash had been murdered by two of his own officials (12:20–21). Once secure, Amaziah executes them: justice, and what any king in the region would have done.

He did not put to death the children of the murderers. Jehu had seventy of Ahab’s sons beheaded (10:7); Baasha wiped out the house of Jeroboam and Zimri the house of Baasha, leaving no male alive. Killing a dead enemy’s sons was routine, and any adviser would have urged it, since such sons grow up and seek revenge.

Each one shall die for his own sin. The writer quotes Deuteronomy 24:16 in full, which he almost never does. That law had stood for centuries, yet nowhere earlier in these books does a king let it overrule a decision he had every political reason to make the other way. A written word, consulted at cost and obeyed against interest, is one of the rarest events in these kingdoms, and it takes one verse.

Ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. Then a real victory south of the Dead Sea, and an Edomite fortress taken and renamed. Keep it in view: nothing in this chapter goes wrong until something goes right.

What Chronicles adds. After this very victory Amaziah set up the gods of Edom and worshipped them (2 Chronicles 25:14). Kings gives the overall verdict, Chronicles the decline.

The one death where the innocent died for the guilty. No human court may punish the innocent for the guilty. Yet at the cross the innocent did die for the guilty, and justice was satisfied, not broken, because no court imposed it: the Son gave himself freely, and the Judge himself provided the sacrifice. “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).

Does this contradict Exodus 20:5? No. Deuteronomy 24:16 governs human courts; Exodus 20:5 speaks of God’s own dealings with families that go on hating him, and cases like Achan’s were God’s own judgments, not a court’s.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride after success ruins what obedience had begun well. Flushed with his victory over Edom, Amaziah challenges the king of Israel for no reason (v. 8) and is answered with a fable: a thistle that thought itself a cedar’s equal, trampled by a passing beast (v. 9). The advice that follows is sound and almost kind: be content with your glory and stay at home (v. 10). He will not listen. Judah is routed at Beth-shemesh, the king is captured, two hundred yards of Jerusalem’s wall are torn down, and the gold of the temple and the palace is carried off to Samaria (vv. 11–14). Jehoash of Israel dies and Jeroboam succeeds him (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The fable is contemptuous and it is accurate. Jehoash is not pretending to be a good man and the counsel he gives is better than anything in Amaziah's own court: one victory over Edom has convinced a small king that he is a large one, and the cure prescribed is to stay at home and enjoy what he has.
verseByVerse.examples: The wall is the part to feel: Jerusalem's defences demolished at leisure by a brother kingdom, because a king could not leave well alone. A generation later Uzziah was still building towers at the Corner Gate (2 Chron. 26:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face." And Jehoash king of Israel sent word to Amaziah king of Judah, "A thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son for a wife,' and a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle. You have indeed struck down Edom, and your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory, and stay at home, for why should you provoke trouble so that you fall, you and Judah with you?" But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced one another in battle at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah. And Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his home. And Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Jehoash, son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh, and came to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for four hundred cubits, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. And he seized all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's house, also hostages, and he returned to Samaria. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoash that he did, and his might, and how he fought with Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Jehoash slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and Jeroboam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Swollen by one victory, Amaziah picks a needless fight with Israel, ignores sound advice from a man he despises, and leaves Jerusalem broken open and its temple stripped.

Come, let us look one another in the face. A challenge to battle, though Judah and Israel are not at war. Having beaten Edom, Amaziah wants to see whether he can beat Israel too. Chronicles adds a grievance: Israelite mercenaries he had dismissed had raided Judah’s towns (2 Chronicles 25:6–13).

A thistle on Lebanon. The reply is a fable, and beautifully cruel. A thistle, a weed at ankle height, proposes a marriage between its family and a cedar of Lebanon, the most prized timber of the ancient world; and a passing animal treads the thistle into the ground without noticing. The insult is not only that Judah is small, but that it would be destroyed by something not even fighting it (compare Judges 9:8–15).

Be content with your glory, and stay at home. Then, having been thoroughly rude, Jehoash gives genuinely good advice. His diagnosis, a heart lifted up, is correct, and nobody in Jerusalem said anything so useful to that king. It came from a man the writer calls evil, wrapped in a joke at his expense.

But Amaziah would not listen. He had already silenced the prophet who rebuked his new gods (2 Chronicles 25:16, 20). Whoever will not hear God’s word in one place soon cannot hear good sense in another.

Four hundred cubits. The battle is fought at Beth-shemesh, “which belongs to Judah”, on the challenger’s own ground. Four hundred cubits is about two hundred yards (see cubit). Holding the king, Jehoash need not storm the city. Killing Amaziah would solve nothing; a two-hundred-yard hole in the north wall leaves Judah unable to threaten anyone for a generation.

All the vessels that were found in the house of the LORD. The temple is emptied again. Joash had stripped it to buy off Hazael (12:18); now what is left goes north to Samaria, taken by fellow Israelites, because a king of Judah wanted to see how a war would go. Ahaz will empty it again (16:8).

Jehoash slept with his fathers. Jehoash, who wept at Elisha’s deathbed (13:14), dies having beaten Syria three times and Judah once.

The idol of comparison. Amaziah had won. But “Come, let us look one another in the face” is the cry of a man who cannot enjoy a victory until he has measured it against someone else’s. C. S. Lewis argued that this is what pride essentially is: not the pleasure of having something, but of having more of it than the next man. Our screens set us beside the best moments of thousands of strangers, and there is always another cedar. Jesus showed why it also blinds us to God: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (John 5:44).

A verdict that ends the contest. The cure is not trying harder to think less of yourself. In Christ, God accepts his people for his beloved Son’s sake, not by their ranking against anyone else. And the Son is everything Amaziah was not: with every right to glory, he did not grasp at it but humbled himself to the cross (Philippians 2:6–8). Whoever is accepted in him need not march to Beth-shemesh to find out who he is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows mercy to a people who have earned none, through a king who deserves no credit. Amaziah outlives his conqueror by fifteen years, then is hunted down by conspirators at Lachish, and the people crown his sixteen-year-old son Azariah (vv. 17–22). In Israel, Jeroboam II reigns forty-one years, does evil, and yet restores the borders from Lebo-hamath to the Dead Sea, as the prophet Jonah had foretold (vv. 23–25). The reason given is not his merit but the LORD’s pity: Israel’s affliction was bitter and there was none to help, and God had not yet said he would blot out their name (vv. 26–27). Not yet.
verseByVerse.theology: That is the Jonah of the book that bears his name (Jon. 1:1). The prophet who ran to Tarshish had also been the prophet of Israel’s recovery, whose word to Israel was that the borders would come back. Set that beside a commission to preach to Nineveh so that Nineveh might be spared, and his reluctance stops being a curiosity.
verseByVerse.examples: A wicked king is used to save a people God pitied. Forty-one years of recovered territory and returning prosperity, and yet Amos and Hosea preach in this reign, which tells you what the country was like underneath. God had not said he would blot out the name of Israel; not yet.

verseByVerse.quote: Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel. Now the rest of the deeds of Amaziah, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent after him to Lachish and put him to death there. And they brought him on horses; and he was buried in Jerusalem with his fathers in the city of David. And all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king instead of his father Amaziah. He built Elath and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers. In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, began to reign in Samaria, and he reigned forty-one years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. He restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath as far as the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the LORD, the God of Israel, which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher. For the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, for there was none left, bond or free, and there was none to help Israel. But the LORD had not said that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven, so he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash. Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam and all that he did, and his might, how he fought, and how he restored Damascus and Hamath to Judah in Israel, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Jeroboam slept with his fathers, the kings of Israel, and Zechariah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amaziah dies as his father did, at the hands of his own people; and in the north God gives Israel its most prosperous reign through a wicked king, for no reason but pity, as Jonah had foretold.

And they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem. After fifteen years over a humiliated kingdom and a broken wall, his own people come for him. He flees to Lachish, some thirty miles away, and they follow. Chronicles dates the plot “from the time when he turned away from the LORD” (2 Chronicles 25:27). He had executed his father’s murderers; now he dies the same way.

Azariah, who was sixteen years old. Another boy king, crowned by “all the people of Judah” after an assassination. He is also called Uzziah (15:13; Isaiah 6:1). He rebuilds Elath, Judah’s port on the Red Sea (v. 22), and will reign fifty-two years; the next chapter tells how it ended.

He reigned forty-one years. Jeroboam II gets seven verses for the most successful reign in the northern kingdom’s history. The borders go back out to where they were under Solomon, from Lebo-hamath in the far north to the Dead Sea (the Sea of the Arabah), and Samaria grows rich. Yet the verdict is the usual one: he did evil and kept the calves of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, whose name he bore.

Jonah the son of Amittai. This is the Jonah of the book that bears his name (Jonah 1:1), and this verse even gives his home town, Gath-hepher in Galilee. He had promised Israel its lost borders, and was proved right. Then he was sent to preach to Nineveh, capital of the empire that would one day destroy his country, so that it might be spared; his reluctance stops being a puzzle. He named the trouble himself: “I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster” (Jonah 4:2). He did not want Assyria forgiven.

The affliction of Israel was very bitter. Verses 26–27 explain the success, and neither says anything good about the king. There was nobody to help Israel, so the LORD helped them, through a man who kept the calves at Bethel for forty-one years. It is the third time in a few chapters that God acts from pity alone (13:4, 23).

The LORD had not said. The careful clause is a warning: he “had not said” he would blot out Israel’s name. Not yet. It echoes the “until now” of 13:23, and this prosperity is the last Israel will have. Amos and Hosea both prophesied in this reign (Amos 1:1; Hosea 1:1), and underneath the boom they found a country that sold “the needy for a pair of sandals” (Amos 2:6).

Zechariah his son reigned in his place. The fourth generation from Jehu; he will reign six months (15:8).

Something greater than Jonah is here. Jesus took up this same man. Asked for a sign, he said none would be given “except the sign of the prophet Jonah”: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the great fish, so the Son of Man would be in the heart of the earth; and the men of Nineveh would condemn that generation, “for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:39–41). The prophet who wanted mercy kept for Israel pointed to the Saviour who carried it to the nations. And when the Pharisees said “no prophet arises from Galilee” (John 7:52), Gath-hepher, a few miles from Nazareth, had already produced one.

What it does not mean. Prosperity is not God’s approval. A nation, a church or a life can flourish under his patience while rotting underneath: “God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance” (Romans 2:4).

Uncertain wording. “Restored Damascus and Hamath to Judah in Israel” (v. 28) is obscure in the Hebrew, and translations differ. It most likely means that Jeroboam brought back under Israel’s control territory that had once belonged to David’s kingdom (2 Samuel 8:5–10). “Lebo-hamath” (v. 25), once rendered “the entrance of Hamath”, is now usually taken as a town on the northern frontier.
verseByVerse.note: Gath-hepher is usually identified with a site a few miles north-east of Nazareth.

14.theology:
A written word obeyed against interest (v. 6). Executing an assassin's sons was standard practice. Amaziah spares them because of a text, quoted in full, and this is the first king in these books recorded letting the law overrule a decision he had every reason to make the other way.

How a life comes apart (v. 10). Not by failure. By a success, honestly earned, that quietly raises a man's opinion of himself, so that he judges the next thing he attempts by that opinion instead of by the facts. Your heart has lifted you up was said by a wicked king, inside an insult, and was truer than anything Amaziah's own court told him. True things often come that way.

Jonah before Nineveh (v. 25). The man who ran to Tarshish was also the prophet of Israel's borders, whose word to his own nation was recovery and who was proved right when the borders came back. Then he was sent to preach to the capital of the empire that would destroy his country, so that it might be spared, and he told God exactly what his objection was: I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful... and relenting from disaster (Jon. 4:2).

Saved on the ground of pity (vv. 26-27). Nothing good is said about Jeroboam anywhere. God acted because the affliction of Israel was very bitter and there was none to help. That is the third time in a few chapters (13:4; 13:23). And the qualifying clause is ominous: he had not said he would blot out the name of Israel. Not yet.

What Kings does not say about those forty-one years. Amos and Hosea describe a country lying on beds of ivory while it sold the needy. The most prosperous stretch in the northern kingdom's history was the one its prophets found most rotten.
14.examples:
Then: A king with the throne newly secure, the men who murdered his father freshly executed, and every political reason to finish their families as well, opened a book instead and left the children alive.

Now: Verse 6 is what obedience looks like when it costs something: a written sentence consulted at the moment it is inconvenient, and allowed to reverse a decision already made. The God who gave that law is the one who pitied Israel when it had earned nothing (v. 26), and for us the obedience that counts was Christ's, who never once set a word of his Father aside; his Spirit now in us is what makes our own costly obedience possible, and where we have overruled the text instead, the way back is to confess it.

The thistle is the other lesson. Amaziah was ruined not by defeat but by his one genuine success, which quietly raised his opinion of himself, and the counsel he ignored came from somebody he despised. If the most accurate thing said about you lately came wrapped in an insult, that is not a reason to discount it.

keyVerse.quote: For the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, for there was none left, bond or free, and there was none to help Israel.
keyVerse.note: This verse explains the chapter’s strangest fact: the most prosperous reign in Israel’s history belonged to a king who did evil. The reason is not merit but the LORD’s pity for a helpless people. It is the same compassion that, when there was no one to help us, sent his own Son.

14.reflection:
Amaziah spared the murderers’ children because of one sentence in the Law (v. 6), against every political instinct. Where has obeying a clear word of Scripture cost you something? Where are you tempted to let “what everyone does” overrule it?

Amaziah’s ruin began not with a failure but with a victory (vv. 7–10). Why is success so often more spiritually dangerous than defeat? How does comparing ourselves with others feed it, and how does the gospel free us from it?

The best advice Amaziah received came, inside an insult, from a king he despised (v. 10). How do you respond to true criticism from people you do not respect? What would it look like to hear it humbly?

God gave Israel its best years through a wicked king, “for the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter” (v. 26), while Amos and Hosea saw rot underneath. How should we read good times in our lives, churches or nation? How does God’s pity here point to Christ?

15.title: Kings in Quick Succession

His mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.<sup>4</sup>Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away. And Jotham the king's son was over the household, governing the people of the land.<sup>6</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Azariah, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>7</sup>And Azariah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Jotham his son reigned in his place.<sup>8</sup>In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, Zechariah the son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in Samaria six months.<sup>9</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done. And so it came to pass.)<sup>13</sup>Shallum the son of Jabesh began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah, and he reigned one month in Samaria.<sup>14</sup>Then Menahem the son of Gadi came up from Tirzah and came to Samaria, and he struck down Shallum the son of Jabesh in Samaria and put him to death and reigned in his place.<sup>15</sup>Now the rest of the deeds of Shallum, and the conspiracy that he made, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.<sup>16</sup>At that time Menahem sacked Tiphsah and all who were in it and its territory from Tirzah on, because they did not open it to him. Therefore he sacked it, and he ripped open all the women in it who were pregnant.<sup>17</sup>In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah, Menahem the son of Gadi began to reign over Israel, and he reigned ten years in Samaria.<sup>18</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin.<sup>29</sup>In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and he carried the people captive to Assyria.<sup>30</sup>Then Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah and struck him down and put him to death and reigned in his place, in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah.<sup>31</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Pekah and all that he did, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.<sup>32</sup>In the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>33</sup>He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok.<sup>34</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah had done.<sup>35</sup>Nevertheless, the high places were not removed. The people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD.<sup>36</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jotham and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>37</sup>In those days the LORD began to send Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah.<sup>38</sup>Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
15.overview:
Where we are. Jeroboam II’s long, prosperous reign has ended (14:23–29), and Judah’s Azariah is in the middle of an even longer one. Chapter 15 runs the two kingdoms side by side for about forty years, and the north begins to fall apart.

The message. A kingdom that has turned from God cannot hold itself together. In Judah, a great king is struck with leprosy and ends his days shut out of the temple. In Israel, five kings rise in quick succession and four are murdered, each usurper buying a little more time, until Assyria arrives and begins to carry the people away. God’s word is kept to the letter, and the end of a nation can begin as a minor border war.

Why it was said. The first readers lived after these collapses (see the introduction). Here they could see that the fall of the north was not sudden bad luck but a long unravelling, foretold and patiently delayed, and that even in Judah’s good reigns the high places stayed and the danger grew.

How the chapter makes its case. Azariah (Uzziah) reigns fifty-two years, but all we are told of them is that “the LORD touched the king” and he lived out his life a leper (vv. 1–7). In Israel, Zechariah lasts six months, ending Jehu’s four promised generations (vv. 8–12); Shallum lasts a month (vv. 13–15); Menahem savages an Israelite town and pays Assyria a thousand talents to keep his throne (vv. 16–22); Pekahiah is murdered by his captain (vv. 23–26); and under Pekah, Assyria carries off Galilee and the north (vv. 27–31). Back in Judah, Jotham reigns well, but “the LORD began to send” Syria and Israel against him (vv. 32–38).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by the need it exposes. In the year Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the true King on his throne (Isaiah 6:1), and John says he saw the glory of Christ (John 12:41). The very lands deported in verse 29, Zebulun and Naphtali, received Isaiah’s promise that “the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2), and there Jesus began to preach (Matthew 4:13–16). And a throne passed from murderer to murderer shows the need for a King who did not grasp at power but emptied himself.

For us. Pride is most dangerous when we are strong; power seized has to be defended for ever; and decline often begins quietly. But no darkness is beyond Christ’s reach: the region emptied first was the first to see the light.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Leper to the Day of His Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king’s greatness cannot protect him from the God whose holiness he presumes upon. Azariah, also called Uzziah, comes to the throne at sixteen and reigns fifty-two years, longer than any king in either kingdom before him, doing what is right while the high places remain (vv. 1–4). Then a single sentence covers the rest of his life: the LORD struck him with leprosy, and he lived in a separate house while his son Jotham governed (v. 5). Chronicles explains why: he grew proud and tried to burn incense in the temple. He is buried with his fathers, and Jotham succeeds him (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Kings gives the fact and withholds the reason; Chronicles supplies it, and the note on v. 5 tells the story. Kings is content to record that the LORD did it, and to let the reader feel how little else a long and glittering reign leaves behind.
verseByVerse.examples: The year he died is one of the great dates in the Bible, though this chapter does not say so: it is the year the young Isaiah saw the throne that never changes hands (see the comment on vv. 1-7).

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah the son of Amaziah, king of Judah, began to reign. He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done. Nevertheless, the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. And the LORD touched the king, so that he was a leper to the day of his death, and he lived in a separate house. And Jotham the king's son was over the household, governing the people of the land. Now the rest of the acts of Azariah, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And Azariah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and Jotham his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Uzziah’s long and successful reign ends with the LORD striking him with leprosy, so that the king spends his last years shut away and shut out of the temple. Kings states the fact without the reason; Chronicles gives it.

He reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. The longest reign either kingdom had yet seen; only Manasseh will outlast it. He is called Azariah here and Uzziah in Isaiah, Amos, Hosea and Chronicles; both names belonged to him. By every earthly measure the years were magnificent. Chronicles records the army, the towers, the cisterns, the engineers and the trade: “his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong” (2 Chronicles 26:15).

The LORD touched the king. Apart from rebuilding Elath (14:22), the leprosy is the only event in those fifty-two years the writer records, and he gives no reason. A reader of Kings alone is left with a bare affliction.

What Chronicles adds. “When he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction” (2 Chronicles 26:16). He went into the temple to burn incense, which was the priests’ work, not a king’s. Azariah the priest and eighty others followed him in and told him to his face, “It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD” (2 Chronicles 26:18). He raged at them with the censer in his hand, and leprosy broke out on his forehead; they rushed him out, “and he himself hurried to go out, because the LORD had struck him” (2 Chronicles 26:20).

He lived in a separate house. The man with the longest reign and the greatest achievements finished it in isolation, excluded from the temple he had entered uninvited, while his son ran the country. The law required it: a man with leprosy “shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:46). He could no longer sit in public, judge, or enter the house of the LORD.

The true priest-king. Uzziah reached for a priesthood that was not his. Only one King was ever entitled to both crown and censer: the Son of David to whom God swore, “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7). And the King who could not be touched in his separate house points by contrast to the King who touched lepers. “Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him” (Mark 1:41), and the uncleanness did not pass to him; his cleanness passed to the leper.

The year Uzziah died. Anyone under fifty had never known another king. And in the year the throne finally emptied, the young Isaiah was shown a different one: “In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple” (Isaiah 6:1). The throne that had seemed permanent was vacant, and Isaiah was shown the one that is not. John adds that Isaiah “saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41): the King on that throne was Christ.

When he was strong. Chronicles names the danger in one clause: “when he was strong, he grew proud.” Not when he was weak or failing. The dangerous season was the one that looked like the reward for earlier faithfulness. Success is the time to be most watchful, and most thankful that all we have was given.
verseByVerse.note: Azariah is also called Uzziah (v. 13, ESV note); the two names mean much the same, “the LORD has helped” and “the LORD is my strength.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people who reject God’s king find no stable king of their own. The north comes apart in twenty-four verses. Zechariah reigns six months and is murdered, the last of Jehu’s four promised generations (vv. 8–12). Shallum lasts one month (vv. 13–15). Menahem seizes the throne, savages an Israelite town that would not open to him, and pays Assyria a thousand talents, taxed from sixty thousand men, to secure his grip (vv. 16–22). His son Pekahiah is murdered by his own captain (vv. 23–26). Under Pekah, Assyria carries off Galilee and Naphtali in the first deportation (vv. 27–29). Then Hoshea murders Pekah (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 12 is the quiet horror of the section: God's reward to Jehu is fulfilled and used up in the same sentence, four generations exactly and no more (see the comment on vv. 8-31). A promise kept to the letter is not necessarily a promise you would want.
verseByVerse.examples: What Menahem does at Tiphsah is what Elisha wept over in Damascus (8:12), now done to an Israelite town by an Israelite king. The atrocity the prophet could not speak of without crying has come home.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, Zechariah the son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in Samaria six months. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done. He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. Shallum the son of Jabesh conspired against him and struck him down at Ibleam and put him to death and reigned in his place. Now the rest of the deeds of Zechariah, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. (This was the promise of the LORD that he gave to Jehu, "Your sons shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation." And so it came to pass.) Shallum the son of Jabesh began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah, and he reigned one month in Samaria. Then Menahem the son of Gadi came up from Tirzah and came to Samaria, and he struck down Shallum the son of Jabesh in Samaria and put him to death and reigned in his place. Now the rest of the deeds of Shallum, and the conspiracy that he made, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. At that time Menahem sacked Tiphsah and all who were in it and its territory from Tirzah on, because they did not open it to him. Therefore he sacked it, and he ripped open all the women in it who were pregnant. In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah, Menahem the son of Gadi began to reign over Israel, and he reigned ten years in Samaria. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart all his days from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. Pul the king of Assyria came against the land, and Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, that he might help him to confirm his hold on the royal power. Menahem exacted the money from Israel, that is, from all the wealthy men, fifty shekels of silver from every man, to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not stay there in the land. Now the rest of the deeds of Menahem and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Menahem slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah his son reigned in his place. In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned two years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. And Pekah the son of Remaliah, his captain, conspired against him with fifty men of the people of Gilead, and struck him down in Samaria, in the citadel of the king's house with Argob and Arieh; he put him to death and reigned in his place. Now the rest of the deeds of Pekahiah and all that he did, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. In the fifty-second year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twenty years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and he carried the people captive to Assyria. Then Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy against Pekah the son of Remaliah and struck him down and put him to death and reigned in his place, in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah. Now the rest of the acts of Pekah and all that he did, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The northern kingdom falls apart as kings murder their way to the throne, one usurper buys his crown from Assyria, and the empire begins to carry Israel away. Read it as one story, not a list: five kings, four murders, and each murderer takes the crown off the body.

Zechariah the son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in Samaria six months. God had told Jehu, “your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel” (10:30). Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam, and now Zechariah: he is the fourth. The promise is kept exactly, and used up in the sentence that fulfils it. The fourth generation got six months and a public assassination.

And so it came to pass. A word from God kept to the letter is not always a word you would have wanted. Jehu got the four generations he was promised, and not one day of it was security.

He reigned one month in Samaria. The man who murdered a king to take the throne held it for a month and was murdered on it.

He ripped open all the women in it who were pregnant. Menahem does this to an Israelite town, because it would not open its gates to him. The reader has met this exact atrocity before, foretold in a room in Damascus while a prophet wept. Elisha told Hazael, “I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel… you will kill their young men with the sword and dash in pieces their little ones and rip open their pregnant women” (8:12). It was foretold of a foreign enemy. Here the king of Israel does it to Israelites, over a gate. Israel no longer needs a foreign enemy to destroy it.

Pul the king of Assyria came against the land. Here is Assyria, for the first time in this book, and everything from now on runs toward it. Pul is Tiglath-pileser III, who turned Assyria from a regional power into an empire, with a standing army and a policy of mass deportation. He is the beginning of the end for both kingdoms, and the writer brings him in almost in passing.

To confirm his hold on the royal power. What Menahem buys with a thousand talents is not his people’s safety but his own throne: a usurper with a weak claim is paying an emperor to guarantee it. Do the arithmetic the verse invites. A thousand talents is three million shekels; at fifty shekels a head, that is sixty thousand propertied Israelites. It worked, in the sense that the Assyrians went home. But Assyria now knew that Samaria would pay.

Pekah the son of Remaliah, his captain. Pekahiah is killed by his own officer, with fifty men of Gilead, inside the palace citadel.

He carried the people captive to Assyria. Verse 29 is the first deportation, about 733 to 732 BC, and Tiglath-pileser’s own inscriptions describe the campaign. Assyria’s method was not merely conquest but removal: take a population off its land, scatter it across the empire, and settle strangers in its place, so that no nation is left to rebel. The writer names the towns one after another like a casualty list: Gilead, Elijah’s country, already stripped by Hazael; and Galilee, “all the land of Naphtali”, the whole north.

Then Hoshea the son of Elah made a conspiracy. The fourth murder in the chapter puts the last king of Israel on the throne. Tiglath-pileser’s annals tell it from his side: the people overthrew Pekah their king, and he set Hoshea over them, which suggests Hoshea struck with Assyria’s blessing. His nine years will end with Samaria gone.

First emptied, first to see. Hold beside verse 29 a promise Isaiah made in Jerusalem in these very years about these very districts: “In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:1–2). Matthew quotes it at the point where Jesus leaves Nazareth, settles at Capernaum “in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali”, and begins to preach (Matthew 4:13–16). The first piece of the promised land to be emptied by an empire is the first to see the Messiah. Deported, resettled, mixed with foreigners and still looked down on from Jerusalem in Jesus’ day (John 7:52), it is where the light comes up first and stays for most of his ministry.

Why is seized power never secure? Every man who seized this throne had to spend his reign guarding it: Shallum for a month, Menahem with sixty thousand men’s silver, Pekahiah until his own captain came for him. Power taken teaches everyone watching that power can be taken. The same law runs through offices, families and churches: whatever we seize to make ourselves safe we must then spend our lives defending, until it owns us. Checks and balances help, but Scripture goes deeper, to the heart that grasps (Hosea 8:4). Its answer is a King who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7), and who told his disciples that the kings of the Gentiles lord it over their people: “But not so with you” (Luke 22:26). His is the one throne never seized, and so the one that never needs defending. Those who belong to him can hold their own small powers loosely, because the Father has already given them the kingdom (Luke 12:32).

Why do the reign lengths and dates not seem to add up? Israel and Judah counted reigns differently at different times: one counted a king’s accession year as his first year, the other did not; and sons often reigned alongside their fathers as co-regents, the overlapping years counted to both. Allowing for these practices, the dates largely fit together, as Edwin Thiele showed, and match Assyrian records at key points, such as Ahab at Qarqar in 853 BC, Jehu’s tribute in 841 BC and the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. Some knots remain, and it is honest to say so. Pekah’s twenty years (v. 27) cannot fit between Menahem’s tribute, about 738 BC, and Hoshea’s accession, about 732 BC; many think Pekah had already ruled a rival kingdom east of the Jordan from about 752 BC (note the fifty men of Gilead, v. 25) and counted his years from then. Jotham’s “twentieth year” (v. 30), when he reigned sixteen, probably counts on into Ahaz’s reign, and Azariah’s fifty-two years include years as co-regent with his father, which is why his accession is dated so late in Jeroboam’s reign (v. 1). These are questions about ancient counting, not about whether the events happened.

Textual note. Where the ESV reads that Shallum struck Zechariah down “at Ibleam” (v. 10), the Hebrew is usually taken to mean “before the people”, that is, publicly; the ESV follows some manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation. If Ibleam is right, Jehu’s dynasty ended at the place where Jehu had begun his bloodshed against the house of David (9:27).

Uncertain wording. Which town “Tiphsah” was (v. 16) is uncertain. The only other Tiphsah in Scripture lies far off on the Euphrates (1 Kings 4:24), which hardly fits a town reached “from Tirzah on”. Some ancient Greek copies read Tappuah, a town in the hills not far from Tirzah, and many think that is the place meant.
verseByVerse.note: Tiglath-pileser’s annals list Menahem of Samaria among the kings who paid him tribute, about 738 BC.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–38 — In Those Days the LORD Began to Send
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good reign can still stand at the start of a long decline that God himself is directing. Jotham reigns sixteen years and does what is right, though the high places stay, and he builds the upper gate of the LORD’s house (vv. 32–36). Then one sentence sets up all that follows: in those days the LORD began to send Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel against Judah (v. 37). It reads like an ordinary border war, but the word “began” looks ahead to Ahaz’s panic, Assyria’s arrival and, in the end, exile. Jotham dies, and Ahaz his son reigns in his place (v. 38).
verseByVerse.theology: Note who is doing the sending. The two kings marching on Jerusalem are described as sent by the LORD, and the writer says it in passing as though it needed no defence.
verseByVerse.examples: The word began is the one to feel. This is the opening of a pressure that will run through the next ten chapters and end with both capitals gone, and it starts as a border problem in the reign of a good king who built a gate.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, began to reign. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah had done. Nevertheless, the high places were not removed. The people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD. Now the rest of the acts of Jotham and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? In those days the LORD began to send Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah. Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jotham is a decent king with an unremarkable reign, but in his days the LORD begins to send enemies against Judah, the quiet start of a pressure that will run to the end of the book.

Jotham the son of Uzziah. He had already run the country for years while his father lived in a separate house, so he comes to the throne experienced, and he is a good king by this book’s measure.

He built the upper gate of the house of the LORD. There is something quietly moving about the summary of a decent reign: sixteen years, nothing scandalous, one gate, and the high places left where his father and grandfather left them. Most good lives read like that in the ledger, and the writer is not sneering.

The LORD began to send Rezin. Not “Syria and Israel attacked Judah”, which is what happened, but the LORD “began to send” them. It is the claim these books make throughout, about an arrow drawn at random, an army routed by a sound, empires arriving on schedule: the politics of the region are not outside the will of God. The word to feel is “began”. A border war of the kind the region had seen a hundred times, in the last years of a competent king: that is how the end of a kingdom looks when it begins. Not a catastrophe, but a nuisance on the frontier, filed at the bottom of a good man’s obituary.

Where it leads. The pressure runs from here to the last chapter. Rezin and Pekah will besiege Jerusalem in the next chapter, and Ahaz will write to Assyria for help. Assyria will come and never leave. Within a few years Samaria will be gone, and Judah will be a vassal, a kingdom that must obey and pay its master, on the edge of an empire it invited in.

The Lord of history. If the LORD sends even Judah’s enemies, then nothing in a believer’s life is outside his hand either. That is not a reason for fatalism, but for the trust Isaiah would soon urge on Ahaz (Isaiah 7:4, 9), and for the deeper comfort of the cross, where the worst that enemies could do was what God’s hand had planned for our salvation (Acts 4:27–28).

15.theology:
When he was strong (v. 5). The clause to carry away is from Chronicles: when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction (2 Chron. 26:16). And the year that reign ended is the year Isaiah was shown a throne that does not empty.

Fulfilled and exhausted (v. 12). The promise to Jehu was kept exactly to the generation named and stopped there. A reward for outward zeal, honoured to the letter, gave his house no security at all.

The horror comes home (v. 16). The cruelty Elisha wept to foresee in a foreign enemy is done by an Israelite king to his own people. A nation that has left God does not need an enemy to destroy it.

What the money bought (v. 19). Assyria enters the book almost in passing. Menahem's thousand talents are not spent on his people's safety but that he might help him to confirm his hold on the royal power, and sixty thousand men were taxed to pay for it.

The first to be carried off, the first to see the light (v. 29). Galilee, Naphtali and Gilead are emptied and deported. Isaiah, prophesying in these very years, said of those districts that after the contempt the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light (Isa. 9:1-2), and Matthew quotes it at the moment Jesus settles at Capernaum in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali and begins to preach (Matt. 4:13-16). The first piece of the land an empire emptied is the first piece the Messiah lived in.

The LORD began to send (v. 37). The politics of the region are not outside the will of God, and the end of a kingdom starts as a border nuisance at the bottom of a decent man's obituary.
15.examples:
Then: Five men held the throne of Israel inside one chapter (six months, one month, ten years, two years, twenty years), and four of them were murdered, each by the man who took the crown off the body.

Now: Uzziah had fifty-two years, an army, towers, cisterns, engineers and international fame, and it all went wrong in the season of strength, not the season of struggle, over a religious act that was not his to perform; and he would not be told so. The prosperity that follows years of faithfulness is the part to watch, and the guard against it is to remember where the strength came from: he was marvelously helped (2 Chron. 26:15). Humility is not achieved by effort of will; it grows as the Spirit keeps showing us that everything we have was given, and that the one perfectly faithful servant, who never reached for what was not his, is Christ, whose standing is counted as ours.

Verse 37 has a quieter lesson. If you are looking for the moment something in your life began to go wrong, it is rarely the crisis; it is the small recurring difficulty that everybody, including you, filed as normal for that stage of life.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD touched the king, so that he was a leper to the day of his death, and he lived in a separate house. And Jotham the king’s son was over the household, governing the people of the land.
keyVerse.note: In one verse the longest and most successful reign yet ends in isolation, because the king grew proud and reached for what belonged to God. It sets the tone for a chapter in which no king, great or murderous, can secure his throne. And it clears the stage for Isaiah’s vision, in the year Uzziah died, of the King whose throne is never empty.

15.reflection:
Uzziah grew proud “when he was strong” (2 Chronicles 26:16), and the LORD struck him with leprosy (v. 5). Why is strength a more dangerous season than weakness? What guards a believer’s heart when things are going well?

Five kings, four murders: every man who seized Israel’s throne had to spend his reign defending it (vv. 8–31). Where do you see the same pattern in work, family or church? How does Christ, who did not grasp at equality with God (Philippians 2:6–7), free us to hold power and position loosely?

The first lands carried off by Assyria (v. 29) were the first to see the light of Jesus’ ministry (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:13–16). What does that tell you about how God deals with places and people that seem lost?

“The LORD began to send” Syria and Israel against Judah (v. 37). How does it help to know that God rules even over the beginnings of troubles? How would you speak of this to someone facing a slow decline in health, work or family?

16.title: Ahaz and the Altar from Damascus
16.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, Ahaz the son of Jotham, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>2</sup>Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as his father David had done,<sup>3</sup>but he walked in the way of the kings of Israel. He even burned his son as an offering, according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree.<sup>5</sup>Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to wage war on Jerusalem, and they besieged Ahaz but could not conquer him.<sup>6</sup>At that time Rezin the king of Syria recovered Elath for Syria and drove the men of Judah from Elath, and the Edomites came to Elath, where they dwell to this day.<sup>7</sup>So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, "I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are attacking me."<sup>8</sup>Ahaz also took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasures of the king's house and sent a present to the king of Assyria.<sup>9</sup>And the king of Assyria listened to him. The king of Assyria marched up against Damascus and took it, carrying its people captive to Kir, and he killed Rezin.<sup>10</sup>When King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw the altar that was at Damascus. And King Ahaz sent to Uriah the priest a model of the altar, and its pattern, exact in all its details.<sup>11</sup>And Uriah the priest built the altar; in accordance with all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, so Uriah the priest made it, before King Ahaz arrived from Damascus.<sup>12</sup>And when the king came from Damascus, the king viewed the altar. Then the king drew near to the altar and went up on it<sup>13</sup>and burned his burnt offering and his grain offering and poured his drink offering and threw the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.<sup>14</sup>And the bronze altar that was before the LORD he removed from the front of the house, from the place between his altar and the house of the LORD, and put it on the north side of his altar.<sup>15</sup>And King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, saying, "On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering and the king's burnt offering and his grain offering, with the burnt offering of all the people of the land, and their grain offering and their drink offering. And throw on it all the blood of the burnt offering and all the blood of the sacrifice, but the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by."<sup>16</sup>Uriah the priest did all this, as King Ahaz commanded.<sup>17</sup>And King Ahaz cut off the frames of the stands and removed the basin from them, and he took down the sea from off the bronze oxen that were under it and put it on a stone pedestal.<sup>18</sup>And the covered way for the Sabbath that had been built inside the house and the outer entrance for the king he caused to go around the house of the LORD, because of the king of Assyria.<sup>19</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Ahaz that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>20</sup>And Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
16.overview:
Where we are. In Jotham’s last years “the LORD began to send” Syria and Israel against Judah (15:37). Now his son Ahaz takes the throne, the pressure becomes a siege, and Assyria, already carving up the north (15:29), is about to be invited into Judah.

The message. When God’s people trust anything but God in a crisis, the rescue they buy becomes a master they must serve. Ahaz, offered God’s help freely, chooses Assyria’s instead, pays for it with the temple’s treasures, and then reshapes the LORD’s house to suit his new master, while God is kept in a corner to be consulted. Yet the chapter ends with Hezekiah, the best king Judah ever had, born in that household.

Why it was said. The first readers had seen where Judah’s foreign alliances and borrowed religion ended (see the introduction). This chapter shows the moment the pattern was set: a king who would not trust the LORD and gave his kingdom away a piece at a time.

How the chapter makes its case. Ahaz is measured against David and fails without qualification: he burns his son as an offering and worships at every shrine (vv. 1–4). Besieged by Syria and Israel, he sends to Tiglath-pileser, “I am your servant and your son,” strips the temple to pay him, and Assyria crushes Damascus (vv. 5–9). Visiting his new master there, he copies a Syrian altar, has his compliant priest build it, and moves Solomon’s bronze altar aside for private divination (vv. 10–16). He cuts up the temple’s bronze and rearranges its entrances “because of the king of Assyria” (vv. 17–18). He dies, and Hezekiah reigns (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise and by contrast. Kings does not tell it, but Isaiah does: in this very crisis God offered Ahaz a sign, and when he refused it, gave him one anyway, “the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:14), which Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 1:22–23). Where Ahaz, a son of David, trusted Assyria, the true Son of David says, “I will put my trust in him” (Hebrews 2:13). Where Ahaz burned his son for his own ends, God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

For us. In a crisis, the help we grab instead of God always sends a bill. Beware a faith that keeps God on hand for guidance while something else holds the centre. And never write off a family: grace is not inherited, and it is not prevented by what a household has been.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — I Am Your Servant and Your Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faced with danger, a son of David refuses to trust God and sells himself to an empire instead. Ahaz fails the comparison with David without any qualification: he walks in the ways of Israel’s kings, burns his son as an offering like the nations driven out of the land, and worships at every shrine (vv. 1–4). When Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besiege Jerusalem, and Judah loses Elath (vv. 5–6), he writes to Assyria, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me,” and strips the temple and palace to pay (vv. 7–8). Tiglath-pileser takes Damascus and kills Rezin (v. 9). The rescue God had offered free, Ahaz buys at the price of his freedom.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the crisis of Isaiah 7, and Kings does not mention the prophet at all. Read the two side by side and the letter of verse 7 becomes a choice: Ahaz had been offered God's help in person, and wrote to Assyria instead.
verseByVerse.examples: One of the greatest promises in the prophets was handed to the worst king in David's line so far, given over the top of his refusal to a man who had burned his own son and was about to offer himself to an emperor as a servant and a son.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, Ahaz the son of Jotham, king of Judah, began to reign. Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as his father David had done, but he walked in the way of the kings of Israel. He even burned his son as an offering, according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. And he sacrificed and made offerings on the high places and on the hills and under every green tree. Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to wage war on Jerusalem, and they besieged Ahaz but could not conquer him. At that time Rezin the king of Syria recovered Elath for Syria and drove the men of Judah from Elath, and the Edomites came to Elath, where they dwell to this day. So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, "I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are attacking me." Ahaz also took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasures of the king's house and sent a present to the king of Assyria. And the king of Assyria listened to him. The king of Assyria marched up against Damascus and took it, carrying its people captive to Kir, and he killed Rezin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz is the worst king Judah has yet had: he burns his own son as an offering, and when enemies besiege him he refuses God’s offered help and buys Assyria’s instead, making himself its vassal.

He did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God. Judah’s kings are always measured against David, and Ahaz fails flatly. There is no “nevertheless” and no qualification.

He even burned his son as an offering. A son of David, on David’s throne, burned his own child as a sacrifice. We have seen it once before, from the king of Moab in despair (3:27); now it is the king of the covenant people. The law had said in advance, “You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech” (Leviticus 18:21), and the Canaanites had lost the land for such things. Judah is now doing exactly what they were driven out for.

Under every green tree. Earlier good kings left the high places standing, and the writer counted it a failure. Ahaz does not merely leave them; he uses them.

They besieged Ahaz but could not conquer him. Syria and Israel have allied against Assyria and want Judah in it. Judah will not join, so they march on Jerusalem meaning to put their own man on the throne (Isaiah 7:6). The city holds, but the king is young, surrounded and terrified (Isaiah 7:2).

What Isaiah adds. Kings does not mention it, but Isaiah records the greatest thing that ever happened to this king. God sent him to meet him “at the end of the conduit of the upper pool”, where he was inspecting the water supply as a man does before a siege (Isaiah 7:3). Isaiah told him the two kings were only “two smoldering stumps of firebrands”, all smoke and no fire (Isaiah 7:4), and then said the sentence that hangs over the whole reign: “If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all” (Isaiah 7:9).

The sign offered and refused. Then God offered the king a sign of his own choosing: “Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven” (Isaiah 7:11). Ahaz refused with an echo of Scripture (Deuteronomy 6:16): “I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test” (Isaiah 7:12). It sounds like reverence and is not: the letter to Assyria was as good as written. Isaiah answered, “Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?” (Isaiah 7:13).

The sign given anyway. Over the top of the refusal the sign came: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). The verse Matthew reaches for to explain who has been born in Bethlehem (Matthew 1:22–23) was first given to this man. God with us, announced to a man who had gone to great trouble to be without him.

Rezin the king of Syria recovered Elath. Judah’s Red Sea port, rebuilt by Uzziah (14:22), is lost, and it stays lost.

I am your servant and your son. Every word of the letter is a surrender. “Servant and son” is the formal language of a vassal submitting to a greater king. No earlier king of Judah is recorded writing like that. He calls himself the son of the king of Assyria, having put his own son in a fire, and the one thing he was offered free, a sign from God, he turned down as too presumptuous.

The silver and gold that was found in the house of the LORD. The temple is emptied for the third time in a few chapters: by Joash for Hazael (12:18), by Jehoash of Israel after Beth-shemesh (14:14), and now by Ahaz.

And the king of Assyria listened to him. It worked. Tiglath-pileser’s own tribute list names “Jehoahaz of Judah”, the full form of Ahaz’s name, and Damascus fell in about 732 BC. But the rescue Ahaz bought had already been promised him for nothing, and what he really purchased was an empire’s permanent interest in Judah, which lay on the road to Egypt.

The Son of David who trusted. In this same crisis Isaiah said, “I will wait for the LORD… and I will hope in him” (Isaiah 8:17), and Hebrews puts the words in Christ’s mouth: “I will put my trust in him” (Hebrews 2:13). Ahaz the son of David sold himself to save his throne; Jesus the Son of David trusted his Father to the cross. Ahaz burned his son for his own ends; the Father “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), to save us.

In everyday life. Ahaz’s pattern is common: a crisis, a decision already half made, and a pious reason for not asking God. The help we grab instead of him always sends a bill.

A question of ages. Ahaz was twenty when he began to reign and reigned sixteen years, yet Hezekiah was twenty-five at his accession (18:2), which would make Ahaz a father at about eleven. Ahaz most likely reigned alongside his father Jotham for some years, so his sixteen years are counted from a co-regency.

Where Christians differ: how was the sign to Ahaz fulfilled in Jesus? Some read Isaiah 7:14 as a direct prediction of Christ alone; critics see only a child of Ahaz’s day. Isaiah promised a child in whose early years the two kings would be gone (Isaiah 7:14–16), yet called him “Mighty God”, whose throne has no end (Isaiah 9:6–7). This commentary’s view: a child born in those years was the near sign, and the prophecy reached beyond him to Immanuel himself, as Matthew says (Matthew 1:22–23).

Uncertain wording. Isaiah’s word for “virgin” (Isaiah 7:14), almah, means a young woman of marriageable age and is used of unmarried girls; some modern versions translate it “young woman”. The Jewish translators of the Greek Old Testament, working long before Christ, rendered it parthenos, virgin, and Matthew quotes that rendering. The ESV, like the KJV, keeps “virgin”. In verse 3 the Hebrew says literally that he made his son pass through the fire; some have suggested a dedication rite rather than a killing, but Chronicles says plainly that he “burned his sons as an offering” (2 Chronicles 28:3; compare Jeremiah 7:31).
verseByVerse.note: The Syro-Ephraimite war: Syria and Israel tried to force Judah into an alliance against Assyria.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — A Model of the Altar, Exact in All Its Details
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship reshaped to please the powerful puts God in the corner. Paying homage to Tiglath-pileser in Damascus, Ahaz admires the altar there and sends home a detailed model (v. 10). Uriah the priest has a copy built before the king even returns (v. 11), and Ahaz offers the full round of sacrifices on it himself (vv. 12–13). Solomon’s bronze altar, which stood before the LORD, is pushed to the north side; the new altar takes all the public offerings, and the old one is kept for the king to “inquire by” (vv. 14–15). Uriah does everything he is told (v. 16). Worship made to God’s pattern now follows one from Damascus.
verseByVerse.theology: The speed is the accusation: the high priest of Israel has the thing built so that there is something to show the king when he walks in, and not one word of hesitation is recorded, then or afterwards.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice that the bronze altar is not destroyed. Solomon's altar, the one he knelt in front of with his hands spread to heaven, is simply moved out of the middle and left standing at the side. The old thing is not denied, argued with or removed; it stands at the north side, available, and not used for anything that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: When King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw the altar that was at Damascus. And King Ahaz sent to Uriah the priest a model of the altar, and its pattern, exact in all its details. And Uriah the priest built the altar; in accordance with all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus, so Uriah the priest made it, before King Ahaz arrived from Damascus.
