And when the king came from Damascus, the king viewed the altar. Then the king drew near to the altar and went up on it and burned his burnt offering and his grain offering and poured his drink offering and threw the blood of his peace offerings on the altar. And the bronze altar that was before the LORD he removed from the front of the house, from the place between his altar and the house of the LORD, and put it on the north side of his altar. And King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, saying, "On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering and the king's burnt offering and his grain offering, with the burnt offering of all the people of the land, and their grain offering and their drink offering. And throw on it all the blood of the burnt offering and all the blood of the sacrifice, but the bronze altar shall be for me to inquire by." Uriah the priest did all this, as King Ahaz commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz replaces the altar God appointed with a copy of one from Damascus, and his high priest builds it without a word of protest; the LORD’s own altar is moved aside and kept for the king’s private use.

He saw the altar that was at Damascus. Paying respects to his new master in a city just emptied of its people, Ahaz admires the local altar and has it measured, drawn and sent home.

Its pattern, exact in all its details. That word “pattern” has a history. God showed Moses “the pattern of the tabernacle” on the mountain (Exodus 25:9, 40); David gave Solomon the plan of the temple, received “in writing from the hand of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 28:19). Israel’s worship had always been made to a pattern that came down from God. This one came from Damascus.

Before King Ahaz arrived from Damascus. The high priest is the villain of this paragraph, and the writer convicts him with a timetable. The king was still travelling, and Uriah had the altar built and standing before his master got home. No threat and no deadline are recorded. He was not asked to be quick, and he was quick; that gives him away. Isaiah names “Uriah the priest” as one of his “reliable witnesses” (Isaiah 8:2), very probably this man: trusted by the prophet, yet when a Syrian pattern came through the door he built it without a syllable of protest.

Burned his burnt offering and his grain offering. The king conducts the full round of offerings himself, on an altar copied from a conquered pagan capital. His grandfather Uzziah was struck with leprosy in that temple for taking a censer (2 Chronicles 26:19). Nothing happens to Ahaz at all, and God’s silence is not his approval.

The bronze altar that was before the LORD. This is Solomon’s altar of the dedication, where fire came down and the glory filled the house. Ahaz does not smash it or denounce it. He moves it to the north side and puts his own where it stood. The writer calls the new one “his altar”, and the old one “the bronze altar that was before the LORD”. He is not confused about whose is whose.

For me to inquire by. The whole public worship of Judah moves to a copy of a Syrian altar by a king’s order, and Solomon’s altar is demoted from the place where a nation worships to a private device the king uses when he wants to know something.

Uriah the priest did all this. Verse 16 is the last word on him: he did everything on the list, exactly as instructed. His office existed to guard the worship of God, and he simply carried out the king’s orders.

The true altar and the true pattern. Israel’s worship was “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), and the reality was Christ, the one sacrifice every altar in that courtyard pointed to. Worship is not ours to redesign to suit the powers we admire; God tells us how to come to him, and the way he has given is his Son.

Using God and enjoying him. Augustine taught that some things are to be enjoyed for their own sake and others used, and that the disorder of the human heart is trying to enjoy what we should use and to use the God we were made to enjoy. Ahaz has done exactly that. The altar from Damascus, the alliance and Assyria’s favour are what he loves; the LORD is kept on as a means, a bronze device in the corner for inquiring by. That is perhaps the commonest religion of a comfortable age: God consulted for guidance, calm and the occasional answered prayer. Its sadness is that a God you only use cannot give you what you are using him for, because what he gives is himself. The psalmist had found the other way: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25). And God did not treat us as we treat him: he did not keep us in a corner for what we might be good for, but gave himself for us.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “inquire by” (v. 15) is rare, and its exact sense is uncertain. It probably means seeking omens or guidance, perhaps by examining sacrifices; at the least, the LORD’s altar is reduced to the king’s private use.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–20 — Because of the King of Assyria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A surrender made once in a crisis goes on costing long after. Ahaz cuts up the bronze stands, basins and great sea that Solomon’s craftsman had made (v. 17), probably for metal to pay tribute, and reroutes the Sabbath walkway and the king’s own entrance to the temple “because of the king of Assyria” (v. 18). The house of the LORD is being rearranged around a foreign emperor. Then the usual closing formula, and one clause that changes everything: Hezekiah his son reigns in his place (vv. 19–20). The son of the worst king will be the best.
verseByVerse.theology: Everything Solomon made is being cut up for the metal or rearranged for a foreigner's convenience, and the reason is not a conviction, a reform or a vision. It is the king of Assyria. Once you have written I am your servant and your son to somebody, the furniture starts moving on its own.
verseByVerse.examples: The last words of the chapter are the turn. This king emptied the temple, replaced its altar, cut up its furnishings and burned his own child; and his son is Hezekiah, of whom the writer will say that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, before or after. Grace did not wait for a better father.

verseByVerse.quote: And King Ahaz cut off the frames of the stands and removed the basin from them, and he took down the sea from off the bronze oxen that were under it and put it on a stone pedestal. And the covered way for the Sabbath that had been built inside the house and the outer entrance for the king he caused to go around the house of the LORD, because of the king of Assyria. Now the rest of the acts of Ahaz that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahaz goes on dismantling the temple to serve Assyria, but his reign closes with the name of his son Hezekiah, the king who will trust the LORD as no other did.

Cut off the frames of the stands. Now he cuts up the furniture. The stands, basins and great bronze sea were made for Solomon by Hiram of Tyre, and 1 Kings spent most of a chapter on them: lions, oxen and cherubim on the panels, lily-work on the rim, the sea on the backs of twelve bronze bulls (1 Kings 7:23–37). He is stripping metal, probably for tribute, a piece at a time from the least noticeable end. Not desecration in a rage, but the slow disassembly of a man who needs the bronze and no longer cares where it came from.

Because of the king of Assyria. The reason comes last, in six words. The Sabbath walkway and the king’s ceremonial entrance are rerouted to suit an emperor who is not even present. This is what the letter of verse 7 cost: written once, in an emergency, paid for once out of the treasury, and years later the building is still being rearranged around a man in Assyria. Ahaz bought a rescue from two burnt-out sticks and is still paying for it in architecture. Nobody chooses how far a surrender goes once it has been made.

Buried with his fathers in the city of David. That is more than Chronicles allows him: there, he is buried in Jerusalem but not brought “into the tombs of the kings of Israel” (2 Chronicles 28:27).

Hezekiah his son reigned in his place. The last words of the chapter change everything. The man who burned one son had another, and of that son this writer will say, “there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him” (18:5). Hezekiah will smash the high places his father used and spread an Assyrian emperor’s letter before God in the house his father had rearranged.

Unpredictable grace. Nothing in this chapter would let you predict that. A boy grew up watching an altar from Damascus take the middle of the courtyard and a brother go into the fire, and became the king who trusted the LORD as no king of Judah did before or after him. Remember it about anyone’s children, and anyone’s parents: grace is not inherited, and it is not prevented by what a household has been.

Uncertain wording. What “the covered way for the Sabbath” (v. 18) was is not known, and the Hebrew is obscure; the point is clear enough: the king’s part in temple worship was rearranged to please Assyria.

16.theology:
Immanuel was given to this man (vv. 5-7; Isa. 7). The verse Matthew quotes to explain the birth at Bethlehem was spoken to a king who refused God's offer of a sign by quoting Scripture, with his letter to Assyria already drafted. He had burned his own child and would sign himself another king's son. Piety used to avoid an obligation is not piety, and Isaiah said so to his face. God gave the sign over the top of the refusal, and the promise did not depend on the man who heard it.

He burned his son (v. 3), and signed himself a son (v. 7). The one practice named as the reason the previous inhabitants were expelled (Lev. 18:21), done by a king of Judah, and then I am your servant and your son to Tiglath-pileser. He gave away his child, his treasury and his kingdom's independence, and the one thing offered him free he declined as too presumptuous to accept.

The pattern (v. 10). Israel's worship was always made to a pattern that came down from God (Ex. 25:9, 40; 1 Chron. 28:19). This one came from Damascus, and worship shaped by what impresses us rather than by what God has given is the same mistake in any age.

Uriah's speed (v. 11). The writer convicts the high priest with a timetable: he had it built before King Ahaz arrived. Nobody threatened him and no deadline is recorded; he was not asked to hurry and he hurried, and that gives him away. The guardians of worship can fail by eagerness to please as surely as by open apostasy.

Moved, not destroyed (vv. 14-15). Solomon's altar is not smashed but relocated, left visibly present while something else takes the middle where the traffic goes, and kept for me to inquire by. That is the fate of God in a great many lives: not denied, not removed, moved to one side and kept for consultation.

Because of the king of Assyria (v. 18). One letter written in an emergency is still rearranging the house of God years later, around a man who is not even present. A compromise made to escape one pressure tends to become a master that keeps asking.
16.examples:
Then: A high priest received a drawing of a pagan altar by courier from a king who was still on the road home, and had it built and standing in the courtyard of the house of the LORD before his master arrived, without a recorded word of objection.

Now: Almost nobody throws the old altar out. It gets moved to the north side and left standing, while the thing that actually governs the week takes the middle of the courtyard. Ask what stands at the centre of your life, not what is still kept somewhere in it. Verse 15 is worse: the LORD is kept only to inquire by, consulted for information when it suits, and not worshipped. And there is Ahaz's piety in Isaiah 7: he turned down help from God with a Bible verse because accepting would have complicated a decision already made. The answer to all three is the sign Ahaz refused. God is Immanuel, with us before we have put him back in the middle, and in Christ he has given the whole-hearted worship we keep shifting to the side; his Spirit is the one who moves him back to the centre, and the first step is simply to confess where he has been standing.

keyVerse.quote: So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who are attacking me.”
keyVerse.note: This letter is the hinge of the chapter and of Judah’s later history. A son of David, offered God’s help for nothing (Isaiah 7), signs himself the servant of Assyria instead, and everything after, the emptied treasury, the Syrian altar, the rearranged temple, is the bill. It is the opposite of the trust shown by the true Son of David.

16.reflection:
Ahaz refused God’s offer of a sign with a pious-sounding reason (Isaiah 7:12), because he had already decided to send to Assyria (v. 7). When have you used religious language to avoid asking God about something you had already decided? What “Assyria” are you tempted to run to in a crisis?

Ahaz kept the LORD’s altar “for me to inquire by” (v. 15), while something else held the centre. What does it look like to use God rather than love him? How does Psalm 73:25 point the other way?

Uriah the priest built the altar before the king even got home (v. 11). Why is eager compliance with wrong sometimes worse than reluctant compliance? Where might you be under pressure to reshape worship or conviction to please the powerful?

The worst king’s son became the best king (v. 20; 18:5). How does that encourage you about your own family, or about someone else’s? How does the gift of Immanuel, given to the faithless Ahaz, show the kind of grace God gives?

17.title: The Fall of Samaria
17.text: <sup>1</sup>In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign in Samaria over Israel, and he reigned nine years.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him.<sup>3</sup>Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria. And Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute.<sup>4</sup>But the king of Assyria found treachery in Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt, and offered no tribute to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year. Therefore the king of Assyria shut him up and bound him in prison.<sup>5</sup>Then the king of Assyria invaded all the land and came to Samaria, and for three years he besieged it.<sup>6</sup>In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria, and he carried the Israelites away to Assyria and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.<sup>7</sup>And this occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and had feared other gods<sup>8</sup>and walked in the customs of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel, and in the customs that the kings of Israel had practiced.<sup>9</sup>And the people of Israel did secretly against the LORD their God things that were not right. They built for themselves high places in all their towns, from watchtower to fortified city.<sup>10</sup>They set up for themselves pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree,<sup>11</sup>and there they made offerings on all the high places, as the nations did whom the LORD carried away before them. And they did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger,<sup>12</sup>and they served idols, of which the LORD had said to them, "You shall not do this."<sup>13</sup>Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying, "Turn from your evil ways and keep my commandments and my statutes, in accordance with all the Law that I commanded your fathers, and that I sent to you by my servants the prophets."<sup>14</sup>But they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the LORD their God.<sup>15</sup>They despised his statutes and his covenant that he made with their fathers and the warnings that he gave them. They went after false idols and became false, and they followed the nations that were around them, concerning whom the LORD had commanded them that they should not do like them.<sup>16</sup>And they abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God, and made for themselves metal images of two calves; and they made an Asherah and worshiped all the host of heaven and served Baal.<sup>17</sup>And they burned their sons and their daughters as offerings and used divination and omens and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger.<sup>18</sup>Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them out of his sight. None was left but the tribe of Judah only.<sup>19</sup>Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but walked in the customs that Israel had introduced.<sup>20</sup>And the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel and afflicted them and gave them into the hand of plunderers, until he had cast them out of his sight.<sup>21</sup>When he had torn Israel from the house of David, they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king. And Jeroboam drove Israel from following the LORD and made them commit great sin.<sup>22</sup>The people of Israel walked in all the sins that Jeroboam did. They did not depart from them,<sup>23</sup>until the LORD removed Israel out of his sight, as he had spoken by all his servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day.<sup>24</sup>And the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the people of Israel. And they took possession of Samaria and lived in its cities.<sup>25</sup>And at the beginning of their dwelling there, they did not fear the LORD. Therefore the LORD sent lions among them, which killed some of them.<sup>26</sup>So the king of Assyria was told, "The nations that you have carried away and placed in the cities of Samaria do not know the law of the god of the land. Therefore he has sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the law of the god of the land."<sup>27</sup>Then the king of Assyria commanded, "Send there one of the priests whom you carried away from there, and let him go and dwell there and teach them the law of the god of the land."<sup>28</sup>So one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel and taught them how they should fear the LORD.<sup>29</sup>But every nation still made gods of its own and put them in the shrines of the high places that the Samaritans had made, every nation in the cities in which they lived.<sup>30</sup>The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth made Nergal, the men of Hamath made Ashima,<sup>31</sup>and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.<sup>32</sup>They also feared the LORD and appointed from among themselves all sorts of people as priests of the high places, who sacrificed for them in the shrines of the high places.<sup>33</sup>So they feared the LORD but also served their own gods, after the manner of the nations from among whom they had been carried away.<sup>34</sup>To this day they do according to the former manner. They do not fear the LORD, and they do not follow the statutes or the rules or the law or the commandment that the LORD commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel.<sup>35</sup>The LORD made a covenant with them and commanded them, "You shall not fear other gods or bow yourselves to them or serve them or sacrifice to them,<sup>36</sup>but you shall fear the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm. You shall bow yourselves to him, and to him you shall sacrifice.<sup>37</sup>And the statutes and the rules and the law and the commandment that he wrote for you, you shall always be careful to do. You shall not fear other gods,<sup>38</sup>and you shall not forget the covenant that I have made with you. You shall not fear other gods,<sup>39</sup>but you shall fear the LORD your God, and he will deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies."<sup>40</sup>However, they would not listen, but they did according to their former manner.<sup>41</sup>So these nations feared the LORD and also served their carved images. Their children did likewise, and their children's children—as their fathers did, so they do to this day.
17.overview:
Where we are. Five kings in quick succession, four of them murdered, have left Israel weak (chapter 15), and Assyria has already carried off Galilee (15:29). Now the last king of the north takes the throne, and the kingdom that began with Jeroboam’s golden calves about two hundred years earlier comes to its end.

The message. Israel fell because it would not trust and obey the God who had rescued it, though he warned it for two centuries by every prophet. The judgment was not sudden or unfair; it was the end of long patience. And the same danger threatens Judah, and every people who keep God as one god among others: you cannot fear the LORD “also”.

Why it was said. The first readers were Judeans who had gone the same way and lost everything too (see the introduction). By refusing to let them read Samaria’s fall as news from abroad (“Judah also”, v. 19), the writer calls them to own their sin and return to the LORD alone.

How the chapter makes its case. First the event: Hoshea, the least bad of Israel’s kings, turns from Assyria to Egypt, is imprisoned, and Samaria falls after a three-year siege; its people are scattered across the empire (vv. 1–6). Then the historian stops and preaches: Israel sinned against the God who brought them out of Egypt, copied the nations, ignored every prophet, would not believe, became as empty as the idols they followed, and so was removed from God’s sight; Judah too (vv. 7–23). Finally the land is resettled by foreigners who add the LORD to their own gods, taught by a priest of the calf cult, and their children do the same “to this day” (vv. 24–41).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. Israel was removed “out of his sight” (v. 18); on the cross the one faithful Israelite cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), bearing that turning away so that all who come to him are never cast out. And the mixed people of this chapter are the Samaritans whom Jesus sought at a well, telling one of them that the true worshippers will “worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23).

For us. God’s patience is long, but it is not endless; do not mistake it for indifference. Ask what you have added to the LORD, and what your children are learning from it. And if you fear God has turned his face from you, look to the cross, where he turned it from his Son instead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — For Three Years He Besieged It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom that would not trust God falls, and no clever alliance can save it. Hoshea, the last king of Israel, does evil, “yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him” (vv. 1–2). Made a vassal of Shalmaneser of Assyria, he stops paying tribute and looks to Egypt for help; Assyria imprisons him (vv. 3–4). The Assyrian army invades and besieges Samaria for three years, and in Hoshea’s ninth year the city falls (vv. 5–6). The people are carried hundreds of miles away and scattered across the empire, so that the northern kingdom never returns. Judgment falls on a better-than-average king, because it was never only about him.
verseByVerse.theology: The end did not come in the worst reign, not under Ahab or Jeroboam or in the chapter with five kings and four murders. It came under a man who was an improvement (see the comment on vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.examples: With one verse a kingdom disappears: ten of the twelve tribes, two centuries of history, a capital, an army and a state religion, taken off the map and resettled across an empire, and they do not come back.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign in Samaria over Israel, and he reigned nine years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him. Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria. And Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute. But the king of Assyria found treachery in Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt, and offered no tribute to the king of Assyria, as he had done year by year. Therefore the king of Assyria shut him up and bound him in prison. Then the king of Assyria invaded all the land and came to Samaria, and for three years he besieged it. In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria, and he carried the Israelites away to Assyria and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The northern kingdom ends: its last king turns from Assyria to Egypt, Samaria falls after a three-year siege, and the people are carried off to the far side of the empire.

Yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him. Not what anyone expects: the last king of Israel was the least bad of them. After nineteen kings, nine dynasties, a temple to Baal in the capital and a queen who killed prophets as policy, the reign in which the kingdom is destroyed belongs to a man the writer ranks above his predecessors. That governs how the chapter should be read. The guilt being judged had been building for two centuries, and the judgment was never a verdict only on the king on the throne when it fell. Judgment often falls later than people expect, on someone doing rather better than average, because it was never about him alone.

He had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt. Hoshea stops paying and writes to Egypt: Ahaz’s manoeuvre in the last chapter, in the other direction. Ahaz wrote to Assyria to escape Syria and Israel; Hoshea writes to Egypt to escape Assyria; and the prophets of these years said neither would work (Isaiah 30:1–3). Even an Assyrian envoy could see it: Egypt was “that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it” (18:21).

For three years he besieged it. No help comes from Egypt; the Assyrian army does. The king is apparently in prison before the siege begins, so the city held out three years with no king in it at all. Omri chose that hill well, an isolated summit with steep sides, and it took the greatest military power in the world three years to get in. The reader has seen what a siege does to that city (6:25): this was three years of what the covenant had warned about in detail (Deuteronomy 28:52–57).

In the cities of the Medes. The place names show the distance. Halah and the Habor are in upper Mesopotamia, hundreds of miles away; the cities of the Medes are further still, towards modern Iran. Assyrian policy was deliberate: scatter a people in small groups so far apart that they cannot combine, cannot go home, and within two generations cannot remember, and move strangers in behind them.

The end of a kingdom. The kingdom that began when Jeroboam set up calves and said, “Behold your gods, O Israel” (1 Kings 12:28), lasted about two hundred years (roughly 930 to 722 BC), and this is its end. Shalmaneser V besieged Samaria, and it fell in 722 BC, just as he died; his successor Sargon II claimed the victory, and one of his inscriptions says he deported 27,290 people from Samaria. They did not come back: “So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day” (v. 23).

What became of the ten tribes? Many were absorbed among the nations. Others had already fled south, and members of the northern tribes appear later in Judah (2 Chronicles 30:11; Anna, “of the tribe of Asher”, Luke 2:36). Theories that Western nations descend from the lost tribes have no basis in Scripture or history.

Uncertain wording. No Egyptian king called “So” (v. 4) is known. He may have been a minor ruler in the Nile delta, where Egypt was then divided among several rulers; some think “So” is the name of a city, Sais, rather than of a king. Either way, the point stands: Hoshea leaned on a broken reed.
verseByVerse.note: Some date the fall of Samaria to 721 BC rather than 722.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel was exiled because it sinned against the God who had rescued it, and refused every warning he sent. Here the historian stops and preaches. He begins from the exodus (v. 7): Israel copied the nations driven out before them, built shrines everywhere, and served idols (vv. 8–12). Yet the LORD warned them by every prophet and every seer, and they would not listen or believe (vv. 13–14). They went after emptiness and became empty; they made calves, worshipped the stars and Baal, and burned their children (vv. 15–17). So God removed them from his sight, and Judah too followed Israel’s customs (vv. 18–20). It all goes back to Jeroboam and his calves (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: In two long books this writer records reigns, quotes oracles, notes fulfilments, and lets the pattern do the arguing. This is the longest continuous piece of interpretation in either book, and it reads like a sermon at a graveside.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 is the sentence to carry away: they went after false idols and became false. The same word stands in both halves: they pursued emptiness and turned into it.

verseByVerse.quote: And this occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and had feared other gods and walked in the customs of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel, and in the customs that the kings of Israel had practiced. And the people of Israel did secretly against the LORD their God things that were not right. They built for themselves high places in all their towns, from watchtower to fortified city. They set up for themselves pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree, and there they made offerings on all the high places, as the nations did whom the LORD carried away before them. And they did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger, and they served idols, of which the LORD had said to them, "You shall not do this." Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying, "Turn from your evil ways and keep my commandments and my statutes, in accordance with all the Law that I commanded your fathers, and that I sent to you by my servants the prophets." But they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the LORD their God. They despised his statutes and his covenant that he made with their fathers and the warnings that he gave them. They went after false idols and became false, and they followed the nations that were around them, concerning whom the LORD had commanded them that they should not do like them. And they abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God, and made for themselves metal images of two calves; and they made an Asherah and worshiped all the host of heaven and served Baal. And they burned their sons and their daughters as offerings and used divination and omens and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger. Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them out of his sight. None was left but the tribe of Judah only. Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but walked in the customs that Israel had introduced. And the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel and afflicted them and gave them into the hand of plunderers, until he had cast them out of his sight. When he had torn Israel from the house of David, they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat king. And Jeroboam drove Israel from following the LORD and made them commit great sin. The people of Israel walked in all the sins that Jeroboam did. They did not depart from them, until the LORD removed Israel out of his sight, as he had spoken by all his servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel was carried away because it sinned against the God who had rescued it from Egypt, copied the nations, refused two centuries of warnings, and would not believe; and Judah is no better. At the moment the northern kingdom disappears, the writer stops the story and preaches.

Who had brought them up out of the land of Egypt. He begins not with the calves or Baal but with the exodus, “from under the hand of Pharaoh”. The sin is measured against the rescue. That is the shape of the whole law: the Ten Commandments open, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery”, and only then, “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:2–3). God’s claim was never simply the right to command. It was the claim of a rescuer on the rescued, and their obedience was meant to be the answer of a people already redeemed, never the price of being redeemed.

The customs of the nations. Israel took up the very practices for which the Canaanites had been evicted. The land was not given to Israel because Israel was better; it was taken from the Canaanites because of what they did in it, and Israel was told plainly that the land would “vomit you out” for the same (Leviticus 18:28).

From watchtower to fortified city. An idiom for every kind of settlement, from a lookout hut in a field to the largest walled town: no place was too small for a shrine. And “secretly” matters. The calves were royal policy, but much was ordinary people in ordinary villages building small shrines nobody wrote down. A nation’s apostasy is rarely announced from a palace; it is a slow accumulation of private arrangements.

On every high hill and under every green tree. A stock phrase of the prophets (Deuteronomy 12:2; Jeremiah 2:20) for where Canaanite fertility religion was practised: on summits, thought nearer the gods, and under evergreens, whose year-round green pictured the fertility the religion promised. The worship was in the landscape. You could avoid a temple; you could not avoid the hills, and children grew up thinking that was what a hill was for.

Provoking the LORD to anger. The standing formula of these books deserves to be taken seriously. The Bible never presents idolatry as a harmless preference or an error to be corrected with better information. It presents it as an injury done to someone, by people who owed him everything, and describes his response in the language of one who has been wronged, not of an official enforcing rules. The alternative to a God who can be provoked is not a kinder God. It is one who does not care what you do.

Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah. Then the mercy inside the indictment. The reader has met the prophets and seers of verse 13: Ahijah tearing his cloak into twelve pieces, the man of God who cried against the altar at Bethel, Jehu the son of Hanani, Micaiah in a cell, Elijah on Carmel and in the vineyard, Elisha for fifty years, Jonah, and at the end Amos and Hosea. Two hundred years of them, and the message never varied: “Turn from your evil ways.” The exile is not God losing patience. It is the end of two centuries of being told, by men mocked, hunted, imprisoned and killed for saying the same short sentence. Nobody in Samaria could say they had not heard.

But were stubborn. Then the root (v. 14). “Stubborn” is literally “they hardened their neck” (compare Deuteronomy 10:16; Acts 7:51), like a plough ox that will not bend its head to the yoke: not ignorance but refusal. Underneath it lies unbelief: they “did not believe in the LORD their God”. Behind two centuries of high places and calves is a settled failure to take God at his word, handed down “as their fathers had been” like a family trade.

They went after false idols and became false. Verse 15 carries the whole diagnosis. The same Hebrew root stands twice, hevel, vapour, the word Ecclesiastes uses for everything under the sun: they went after emptiness and turned into emptiness. That is a law of the soul: “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8). Paul says that those who would not honour God “became futile in their thinking” (Romans 1:21). Worship shapes the worshipper into the likeness of what is worshipped; give yourself to something with no substance and you will not merely be disappointed, you will become emptier yourself. That is also the hope on the other side: “beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The law does not change; only what we look at does.

Metal images of two calves. The list accumulates: two calves, meant to represent the LORD; an Asherah; the host of heaven, the sun, moon and stars, which Deuteronomy had warned against by name (Deuteronomy 4:19); then Baal. Nothing was ever discarded, so that by the end the religion of Israel was everything at once, which is to say nothing in particular.

Burned their sons and their daughters as offerings. It ends where it always ends, with children in the fire: a Moabite king on a wall (3:27), then Ahaz in Jerusalem (16:3), and now a whole people. And “sold themselves to do evil” had been said of one man before: “There was none who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD like Ahab” (1 Kings 21:25). The whole nation has grown into the shape of its worst king.

Removed them out of his sight. The writer’s phrase for the exile, three times in six verses, is not the obvious one. Not “destroyed” or “punished”, but removed “out of his sight”: he put them where he would not be looking at them. Set that against the blessing pronounced over this people since Sinai: “the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:25–26). Everything Israel had lay in the fact that God was looking at them, and the worst thing that can be said of a nation is said here. It is also what they had asked for: two centuries of preferring gods with no eyes ended with the God who sees turning his face away.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? That sentence is the background to the darkest cry of the cross. The one Israelite who never wavered between the LORD and other gods cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). He bore the turning away that his people’s sin deserved, so that whoever comes to him is never cast out (John 6:37), and the blessing of the shining face returns to them “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). If you fear that God has turned his face from you, this chapter is not your verdict. The cross is, and there he turned from his Son instead.

Judah also did not keep the commandments. Then the turn, aimed at the reader. After twelve verses of airtight case against the north, a man in Jerusalem is waiting for a sentence beginning “But Judah”. Instead he gets “Judah also”, and then “all the descendants of Israel”. This book was written for people in the south, perhaps already in Babylon, and it will not let them read the fall of Samaria as news from abroad. It lays the same charge on them in one line, without softening it.

Jeroboam drove Israel from following the LORD. The sermon ends where the kingdom started. Jeroboam, afraid that if his people kept going up to Jerusalem he would lose them, made two calves and said, “Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28). It was religion invented for a political purpose, and as politics it worked perfectly. The formula repeated reign after reign, “He did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin”, is the writer’s way of saying that nothing ever changed at the foundation, whatever changed on top. Jehu tore down the house of Baal and left the calves; so did everyone else. And it all happened “as he had spoken by all his servants the prophets”, by men nobody listened to.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “did secretly” (v. 9) occurs only here in the Old Testament, and its meaning is not certain. Most take it as acting in a covered or hidden way, as the ESV does; others suggest “spoke against” or “ascribed falsely”. Either way, the charge is a worship of the LORD corrupted at every level of the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–41 — They Feared the LORD but Also Served Their Own Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people can add the LORD to their gods and still not fear him at all. Assyria fills the emptied land with settlers from five nations (v. 24). When lions kill some, they decide they must learn the ways of “the god of the land”, and a priest of the old calf cult is sent back to teach them at Bethel (vv. 25–28). Each nation still sets up its own gods in the old shrines, and some burn their children (vv. 29–32). So “they feared the LORD but also served their own gods”, which verse 34 calls not fearing him at all (vv. 33–34). God’s covenant is restated: “You shall not fear other gods” (vv. 35–39). They would not listen, and their grandchildren did the same (vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.theology: The arrangement the new population settles into is exactly the one the old population was deported for. They add the God of the land to the gods they brought, keep both, and pass the arrangement to their children.
verseByVerse.examples: The empire asked for an expert in the local god and got one: a priest of the very cult that had emptied the country, stationed at Bethel, where the calf had stood.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the people of Israel. And they took possession of Samaria and lived in its cities. And at the beginning of their dwelling there, they did not fear the LORD. Therefore the LORD sent lions among them, which killed some of them. So the king of Assyria was told, "The nations that you have carried away and placed in the cities of Samaria do not know the law of the god of the land. Therefore he has sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the law of the god of the land." Then the king of Assyria commanded, "Send there one of the priests whom you carried away from there, and let him go and dwell there and teach them the law of the god of the land." So one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel and taught them how they should fear the LORD. But every nation still made gods of its own and put them in the shrines of the high places that the Samaritans had made, every nation in the cities in which they lived. The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth made Nergal, the men of Hamath made Ashima, and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim. They also feared the LORD and appointed from among themselves all sorts of people as priests of the high places, who sacrificed for them in the shrines of the high places. So they feared the LORD but also served their own gods, after the manner of the nations from among whom they had been carried away. To this day they do according to the former manner. They do not fear the LORD, and they do not follow the statutes or the rules or the law or the commandment that the LORD commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel. The LORD made a covenant with them and commanded them, "You shall not fear other gods or bow yourselves to them or serve them or sacrifice to them, but you shall fear the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm. You shall bow yourselves to him, and to him you shall sacrifice. And the statutes and the rules and the law and the commandment that he wrote for you, you shall always be careful to do. You shall not fear other gods, and you shall not forget the covenant that I have made with you. You shall not fear other gods, but you shall fear the LORD your God, and he will deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies." However, they would not listen, but they did according to their former manner. So these nations feared the LORD and also served their carved images. Their children did likewise, and their children's children—as their fathers did, so they do to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new settlers of Samaria add the LORD to their own gods, and the writer says that to fear the LORD in that way is not to fear him at all; their children inherit the same arrangement. This mixed people is the origin, in Jewish eyes, of the Samaritans of the Gospels.

Placed them in the cities of Samaria. Verse 24 is the other half of Assyria’s policy: take one people off its land, and move others onto it, five populations from five places, mixed together so that none can become a nation again.

The LORD sent lions among them. The lions are the one point in this section where God acts, and they are not only a threat. A population deported from five countries has been dumped in a ruined province, and nobody has told them anything. The God of that land does the one thing that will make a people of that age ask a religious question, and they ask it at once and send for a teacher. It is a rough mercy, but a real one: God did not leave the new tenants of his land ignorant of him. What they did with it is the rest of the chapter.

The law of the god of the land. The report to the emperor sums up the religion of the ancient world. Every territory has its god, each with his own procedures; move into his country and you must learn the local requirements or there will be trouble. The Syrian officers assumed the same when they decided that Israel’s gods were “gods of the hills” (1 Kings 20:23), and so did Naaman when he asked for two mule-loads of Israelite soil to take home (5:17). These settlers are not irreligious; they are very religious. What they have not grasped is that the God of that land is not a local god at all, but the God of every land.

One of the priests whom they had carried away. The irony is complete, and the writer does not point at it once. The man sent back is a priest of the northern kingdom, which means a priest of the calf cult, the very religion the last seventeen verses blamed for emptying the country. Jeroboam had “appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites” (1 Kings 12:31). Of all the towns in Samaria, this priest lives at Bethel, where the calf stood, and teaches the newcomers “how they should fear the LORD”. Nothing good could come of that arrangement.

The shrines of the high places that the Samaritans had made. Here the word Samaritans appears for the first time in the Bible, as a neutral description of the people of Samaria. The reader who knows the Gospels should mark the page. The new arrivals did not need to build anything; they put their own gods into the shrines the previous tenants had left standing.

Burned their children in the fire. Five gods named, and then a clause about the Sepharvites’ children that stops the list dead. Verse 17 gave this as one reason Israel was deported; within a few years the people brought in to replace them are doing it in the same towns. The land has changed hands and the practice has not.

So they feared the LORD but also served their own gods. They add the LORD to the collection and staff his shrines as Jeroboam did, with “all sorts of people”. The summary of verse 33 returns almost word for word in the last verse, framing the whole section. It is not a description of paganism but of what Elijah named on Carmel: “How long will you go limping between two different opinions?” (1 Kings 18:21). That was Israel’s sin, and it emptied the country. The newcomers, from five nations with no history in the place, settled into the same arrangement within a generation. The LORD and something else beside him: it is the most natural religion in the world.

They do not fear the LORD. Verse 33 says they “feared the LORD”; verse 34 says they “do not fear the LORD”. Both are true. They feared him in that they had him in the building, gave him a shrine, kept his festivals, and would have said so if asked. They did not fear him at all, because a fear of God held alongside five other gods is not a smaller version of the real thing but a different thing entirely. You cannot have the LORD “also”.

You shall not fear other gods. The command comes three times in four verses: the writer is saying again, in the same words, what has been said many times and has not gone in. And the ground is the same as in verse 7: not “because I am powerful”, but the LORD “who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm” (v. 36). The claim rests on the rescue, every time.

However, they would not listen. Verse 40 repeats the verdict of verse 14. Two different populations, one with centuries of covenant history and one with none, taught by prophets in the first case and by a single deported priest in the second, and the same verdict on both. The problem was never a shortage of information about God, and it was never peculiar to Israel.

Their children did likewise, and their children’s children. Verse 41 repeats verse 33 with three generations added. Whatever else is inherited, this is: a settled arrangement about God, reached by adults for practical reasons, becomes the ordinary assumption of a grandchild who never chose it and cannot remember anything else.

From the LORD also to the LORD alone. The Jews of Jesus’ day traced the Samaritans to this mixed people, which is why a Samaritan woman could say, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain”, and expect an argument, and why John explains that “Jews have no dealings with Samaritans” (John 4:9, 20). That makes what Jesus did very deliberate. He “had to pass through Samaria” (John 4:4), sat by a well and asked a woman of that people for a drink. Without pretending the history away (“salvation is from the Jews”), he told her that “the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth”, on neither mountain (John 4:21–23). He made a Samaritan the hero of his most famous story (Luke 10:33), and of ten lepers healed, the one who came back to thank him was a Samaritan (Luke 17:16). After the resurrection he named Samaria straight after Judea as a place for his witnesses (Acts 1:8); Philip preached there, “so there was much joy in that city” (Acts 8:8). It took more than seven hundred years, and a man sitting at a well at noon, to bring Samaritans from the LORD “also” to the LORD alone.

In a pick-and-mix faith, who is god? The settlers’ arrangement sounds modern. Few people today throw God out. They keep him, with a little Eastern calm, the therapist’s vocabulary and the right causes, and assemble a spirituality that suits them. It feels humble and generous. But ask who decides what goes on the shelf. In any pick-and-mix faith the one really in charge is the one doing the picking, so the true god of the arrangement is the self, and the LORD is one more product. That is why verse 34 can say that people who fear the LORD do not fear him. A God admitted as one option among several is not being worshipped at all, any more than a husband is loved by a wife who keeps him as one of several. (On other faiths, see the note on Isaiah 45:22–23.) The LORD’s claim is not that he is the best item on offer, but that he is the one “who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (v. 36). In Christ he has made that claim again, at the cost of his own Son, and a love bought at that price cannot be one item among many.

Where Christians differ: how far does this chapter explain the Samaritans? The Samaritans themselves traced their descent to Israelites who stayed in the land, not to foreign settlers, and many historians think their community took its distinct shape centuries later, with its own temple on Mount Gerizim. This commentary’s view: this chapter shows where the mixed people of Samaria began and what the Jews of Jesus’ day had in mind when they spoke of Samaritans; the full history of the community is more complicated, and the Bible does not require us to say more than it does.

Uncertain wording. Little is known for certain about most of the gods named in verses 30–31. Nergal was a Mesopotamian god of the underworld; Succoth-benoth, Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, Adrammelech and Anammelech are otherwise unknown or uncertain, and some of the names may have been reshaped in Hebrew, perhaps in mockery. Even the location of Sepharvaim is disputed.
verseByVerse.note: The origin of the Samaritans, despised by Jews in Jesus’ day.

17.theology:
The least bad king (v. 2). Judgment usually falls later than we expect and on somebody doing better than average, because it was never about him. God's patience is real, and so is its end.

The one sermon in Kings (vv. 7-23). The indictment begins not with the calves but with the exodus, because God's claim on Israel was always the claim of a rescuer on the rescued. Obedience answers grace; it never buys it.

Two hundred years of warning (v. 13). Every prophet and every seer brought one message that never varied. The exile is not impatience but the end of two centuries of being told, by men who were mocked, imprisoned and killed for saying it. Nobody in Samaria could say they had not heard, and the God who sent them so long and so often is the same God who still sends his word before he judges.

Became false (v. 15). We become like what we worship: those who make them become like them (Ps. 115:8), and those who exchange the glory of God for images become futile in their thinking. That is the warning of this verse and also the hope of the gospel, since by beholding the glory of the Lord we are being transformed into his image (2 Cor. 3:18). The way it works does not change; only what we look at does.

Judah also (v. 19). The writer will not let his readers in the south treat the fall of Samaria as news from abroad. The sentence a Jerusalem reader is waiting for is but Judah, and he gets Judah also. Scripture does not let any reader stand outside its indictments, and it does not leave him there without a Saviour.

The god of the land (v. 26). The settlers are not irreligious; they diagnose a problem in the terms everybody in that world used. What they have not grasped is that the God of that land is the God of every land, and that he cannot be added to a shelf of local deities and managed by procedure. And the expert sent to teach them is a priest of the calf cult, stationed at Bethel.

The LORD, and (vv. 33, 41). What Elijah called limping between two opinions is here a settled national religion with its own clergy. Verse 34 flatly denies what verse 33 asserts, on purpose: you cannot have the LORD also, and that is what these two books have been arguing throughout.
17.examples:
Then: Five deported peoples were resettled in an emptied country, found lions in it, worked out that they did not know the local god's requirements, and asked the empire for a teacher, and were sent a priest of the golden calf to live at Bethel and instruct them how to fear the LORD.

Now: Nobody is left unchanged by what he gives himself to; chase what has no substance and you end up emptier yourself. Take an honest look at what has had your attention for the last year and ask what it has been making you into, remembering that the remedy is not greater resolve but someone better to look at: the Spirit changes us as we look at Christ.

A reader settling comfortably into somebody else's indictment gets his own name in the middle of it. None of us has kept this covenant, and the only one who has is the Son who was forsaken in our place, so the right response to Judah also is not despair but confession, and coming to him who casts out no one.

Then there is also. The sin that emptied a country was not the rejection of God but the addition of other things to him, held together comfortably for generations. The question is not whether God is in your life but whether anything else is in there beside him on the same terms.

keyVerse.quote: Yet the LORD warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways and keep my commandments and my statutes, in accordance with all the Law that I commanded your fathers, and that I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” But they would not listen, but were stubborn, as their fathers had been, who did not believe in the LORD their God.
keyVerse.note: These verses are the heart of the writer’s sermon on the fall of Samaria. The exile was not God losing his temper but the end of two centuries of patient warning, and its root was not ignorance but unbelief. The same verdict falls on the newcomers too (v. 40), and it leaves every reader needing a heart that will listen, which only Christ gives.

17.reflection:
The writer begins his explanation of the exile with the exodus (v. 7) and ends his restatement of the covenant the same way (v. 36). Why does it matter that God’s commands come from a rescuer? How does the gospel shape our obedience in the same way?

“They went after false idols and became false” (v. 15). What do people around you give themselves to that has no substance? How have you seen worship shape the worshipper, for good or ill (2 Corinthians 3:18)?

“They feared the LORD but also served their own gods” (v. 33), and yet “they do not fear the LORD” (v. 34). What might the LORD “also” look like in your life or church today? Why is a God kept as one option among many not truly worshipped at all?

Israel was removed “out of his sight” (v. 18), yet Jesus later sought out the Samaritans who came from this mixed people (John 4). How does the cross, where Jesus cried “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”, answer the fear of being cast out of God’s sight?

18.title: Hezekiah and the Rabshakeh
18.text: <sup>1</sup>In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah the son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign.<sup>2</sup>He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abi the daughter of Zechariah.<sup>3</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done.<sup>4</sup>He removed the high places and broke the pillars and cut down the Asherah. And he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it (it was called Nehushtan).<sup>5</sup>He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him.<sup>6</sup>For he held fast to the LORD. 18.overview:
Where we are. Samaria has fallen (chapter 17), and Judah now stands alone. The new king is the son of Ahaz, who burned his own son and set a Syrian altar in the temple (chapter 16).

The message. The chapter turns on one question, put by an enemy: “On what do you rest this trust of yours?” (v. 19). Hezekiah is praised above every king of Judah because “he trusted in the LORD” (v. 5), and yet when the crisis comes he first trusts silver and gold, and it buys nothing. Everyone leans on something. The Rabshakeh can knock away every human support, but the LORD is not one more god in a list of gods who failed.

Why it was said. The first readers had seen Jerusalem fall to Babylon and had heard the same taunts from their conquerors (see the introduction). This chapter shows them trust in the best of their kings, how weak it could be and how cunningly it was attacked.

How the chapter makes its case. First the king: Hezekiah removes the high places, breaks the bronze serpent, holds fast to the LORD and rebels against Assyria, while Samaria falls thirty-five miles to the north (vv. 1–12). Then the lapse: Sennacherib takes the fortified cities of Judah, and Hezekiah apologises and strips the gold from the temple doors, but the payment does not stop the army (vv. 13–16). Then the assault on trust itself: the Rabshakeh attacks every ground of confidence, Egypt, the reform, Judah’s weakness, even the LORD’s own commission, then offers the men on the wall a counterfeit of God’s promise and a list of gods who could not save (vv. 17–35). The people answer not a word, and the officials carry everything to the king (vv. 36–37).

Where it leads. The chapter points to Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Even the king with none like him trusted by halves, on a ladder with a chisel. Only one man ever trusted God perfectly, and he too heard the Rabshakeh’s taunt from the foot of his cross: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43). God answered by raising him from the dead. And the bronze serpent Hezekiah broke was a picture Jesus took of his own cross (John 3:14–15).

For us. Ask what you are resting your weight on, and whether it can carry you. Watch for good gifts that have become substitutes for God, and for offers that borrow his promises and hide the price. If your first response to a threat was fear, Hezekiah’s story did not end at verse 16, and Christ trusted perfectly for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — He Broke in Pieces the Bronze Serpent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah does what no king of Judah before him had done, because he trusted the LORD. He is measured against David and found faithful (vv. 1–3). He removes the high places, which six good kings had left standing, and breaks the bronze serpent of Moses, because the people had turned it into an object of worship (v. 4). The reason given for the verdict is that he trusted and held fast to the LORD, and the LORD was with him (vv. 5–7). He throws off Assyria and pushes the Philistines back to Gaza (vv. 7–8). Meanwhile Samaria falls for refusing to listen, a warning set beside a king who did (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology: The serpent was not a pagan object. God told Moses to make it, and Israelites bitten in the wilderness looked at it and lived (Num. 21:8-9). Centuries later they were burning incense to it, and the most dangerous thing in the temple was the one piece that had genuinely come from God and had genuinely worked.
verseByVerse.examples: The name he gives it as he breaks it dismisses it as a mere piece of bronze, and that is the reform in one gesture: not contempt for what God had once done through it, but a refusal to let a relic of real grace go on being treated as a source of it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah the son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Abi the daughter of Zechariah. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done. He removed the high places and broke the pillars and cut down the Asherah. And he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it (it was called Nehushtan). He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him. For he held fast to the LORD. He did not depart from following him, but kept the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses. And the LORD was with him; wherever he went out, he prospered. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and would not serve him. He struck down the Philistines as far as Gaza and its territory, from watchtower to fortified city. In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria and besieged it, and at the end of three years he took it. In the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria was taken. The king of Assyria carried the Israelites away to Assyria and put them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD their God but transgressed his covenant, even all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded. They neither listened nor obeyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of the worst king of Judah so far becomes the king with none like him, because he trusts the LORD: he clears away false worship, even a sacred relic, and throws off Assyria, while Samaria falls next door for refusing to listen. The writer measures Hezekiah by David, by Moses and by the north’s fate, and he passes on every count.

According to all that David his father had done. Only two kings in Judah’s history receive this verdict without qualification, and Hezekiah is the first (the other is Josiah, 22:2). Remember whose son he is. He grew up in the palace of the man who burned one of his own children, copied a Syrian altar into the temple courtyard, and cut up Solomon’s bronze furniture for tribute (chapter 16). Nothing in the previous chapters would have led anyone to expect this.

He removed the high places. Every good king in this book has carried the same footnote: Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Amaziah, Azariah and Jotham all did right, and “nevertheless the high places were not taken away.” Six times the writer has recorded the same failure. Hezekiah is the first to act, and it must have been bitterly unpopular, because every village lost the shrine on its own hill.

The bronze serpent that Moses had made. Then the most interesting object in the chapter. In the wilderness, with people dying of snakebite, God told Moses, “Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live” (Numbers 21:8). Moses made it of bronze, and it worked, exactly as promised. This was no pagan idol smuggled in by a foreign queen, but a genuine object, made at God’s command, through which God really saved lives.

It was called Nehushtan. Hezekiah smashes it, and the name is a dismissal. Nehushtan plays on the Hebrew words for serpent and for bronze; the sense is roughly “a bronze thing”, a bit of metal.

The most dangerous objects. Nobody in Jerusalem had to be persuaded that an Asherah pole was a problem. The hardest thing in the city to remove was the thing that had truly come from God, had truly worked, had a real history of real grace attached to it, and had over the centuries quietly stopped being a signpost and become a destination.

Looked at, not looked through. Jesus took this very object as a picture of his cross: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). So the thing Hezekiah broke was, all along, a picture of Christ. It was never wrong to value it. The trouble was that people had begun to look at it instead of through it, and a signpost people worship in front of has stopped doing the one job it was made for.

He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. The reason for the verdict is one word: he trusted. Not competence or success, but where he rested his weight; and that is exactly what the Rabshakeh will attack again and again from the foot of the wall.

For he held fast to the LORD. The verb in verse 6 (dabaq) means to cling or be glued to. A man is to “hold fast to his wife” (Genesis 2:24), and Israel was told, “You shall serve him and hold fast to him” (Deuteronomy 10:20). It is not the language of agreement but of gripping something and not letting go.

He rebelled against the king of Assyria. Ahaz had written, “I am your servant and your son” (16:7), and made Judah a vassal. Hezekiah stops paying, a declaration of independence from the largest empire the world had yet seen, and the writer records it straight after saying that the LORD was with him.

He struck down the Philistines as far as Gaza. His father had lost towns in the lowlands to Philistine raiders (2 Chronicles 28:18); Hezekiah pushes the other way, as far as Gaza, “from watchtower to fortified city”, the same phrase used of Israel’s shrines in the last chapter (17:9): the whole range of it.

Samaria was taken. The fall of Samaria is told again to place it in Hezekiah’s reign. It did not happen in some earlier age. It happened thirty-five miles from Jerusalem, six years into his reign, in the middle of his reform. He probably knew refugees who could describe the siege, and when Sennacherib’s army arrives he knows exactly what these people do. The writer’s reason, “They neither listened nor obeyed” (v. 12), stands beside the king who did both.

None like him, and Josiah too? Almost the same is said of Josiah: “Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart” and “nor did any like him arise after him” (23:25). The two men are commended for different things, Hezekiah for trust and Josiah for turning to God with his whole heart according to the law of Moses, and Hebrew praise of this kind is not a ranking of one king against another. Both statements are true in their own terms.

Did the bronze serpent break the second commandment? No. The commandment forbids making images to bow down to and serve (Exodus 20:4–5); God himself commanded this one as a sign to look at, as he commanded the cherubim over the ark. It became a snare only when people began making offerings to it.

How old was Ahaz when Hezekiah was born? Taken at face value, 16:2 would make Ahaz about eleven. The likeliest answer is that Ahaz’s reign overlapped his father Jotham’s, so his sixteen years are counted from an earlier start. The figures are difficult, and it is honest to say so.

Why do the dates not seem to fit? Samaria fell in Hezekiah’s sixth year and Sennacherib came in his fourteenth, yet those events were twenty-one years apart (722 and 701 BC). Hezekiah most likely reigned with his father Ahaz from about 729 BC and alone from 715 BC; the dates in verses 9–10 count from the co-regency, the date in verse 13 from his sole reign.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV note on “Nehushtan” points out the same wordplay on “bronze” and “serpent.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the first great test of his reign, the king who trusted the LORD tries to buy his way out, and it does not work. Sennacherib sweeps through Judah and takes every fortified city (v. 13). Hezekiah sends word to him at Lachish, confessing that he has done wrong and offering to pay whatever is demanded (v. 14). The price is enormous: all the silver in the temple and the palace, and the gold he himself had laid on the temple doors (vv. 15–16). The writer sets this failure directly after the highest praise in the book, honestly showing that even the best of men trust by halves, and that what was paid did not buy peace (vv. 17ff.).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the part that gets left out. Chronicles, telling the story for its own purpose, passes over it (2 Chronicles 32:1–23), and Isaiah 36–39, which repeats most of these chapters almost word for word, skips these three verses; leaving something out is not contradicting it. The king of whom it was said that there was none like him surrenders, admits fault, and pays, by doing precisely what his father Ahaz did in the same building for the same reason.
verseByVerse.examples: And it does not work: the tribute is paid in full, and the next verse has an Assyrian army outside Jerusalem anyway. Faith is not a possession a man acquires and then owns (see the comment on vv. 13-16).

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And Hezekiah king of Judah sent to the king of Assyria at Lachish, saying, "I have done wrong; withdraw from me. Whatever you impose on me I will bear." And the king of Assyria required of Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. And Hezekiah gave him all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's house. At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of the temple of the LORD and from the doorposts that Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid and gave it to the king of Assyria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Sennacherib overruns Judah, the king who trusted the LORD panics, confesses to the wrong master, and empties the temple to buy him off, and it buys nothing. The writer sets this failure nine verses after the highest praise in the book, and he does it on purpose.

Sennacherib king of Assyria came up. This is one of the best-attested events in the Old Testament. Sennacherib’s own account of the campaign claims forty-six walled cities of Judah taken, two hundred thousand people counted as spoil, and Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage”. His palace at Nineveh had a whole room panelled with carved reliefs of the siege of Lachish, with ramp, siege engines, archers and prisoners, and the panels are now in the British Museum. The annals agree with Kings on thirty talents of gold but claim eight hundred of silver, perhaps on a different weight standard or simply inflated; and, tellingly, they have the tribute sent on to Nineveh afterwards without ever claiming the city was taken.

I have done wrong; withdraw from me. Judah has been reduced to one city. Sennacherib is at Lachish, Judah’s second city, some thirty miles south-west of Jerusalem, guarding the road up from the coastal plain. Then comes the sentence most accounts of Hezekiah leave out. The king with “none like him among all the kings of Judah” capitulates. He apologises to an idolatrous emperor for having stopped paying him, offers a blank cheque, and asks him to go away. Nobody should soften that.

Three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. A talent was a weight of about thirty kilograms, so this was roughly nine tonnes of silver and one tonne of gold: more than the kingdom could find without emptying the temple.

That Hezekiah king of Judah had overlaid. Verse 16 names Hezekiah twice in one sentence: the king who strips the doors is the king who gilded them. It was part of his reform; the young king who meant it had overlaid the doors of the house of the LORD with gold. Now he is on a ladder with a chisel, peeling his own gold off his own doors for the king of Assyria. His father did exactly this, in this building, for this reason (16:8); the only difference is that Hezekiah had more to undo.

Faith is not a possession. It is not a quality a man acquires at twenty-five and then owns, so that everything he does afterwards can be assumed to flow from it. The man in this paragraph and the man in the next chapter who spreads a threatening letter before God in that same temple are the same man, in the same crisis. He did the wrong thing first, and God did not drop him for it. The mercy that met him was not earned by the gold on the doors or lost by its removal. Only one king ever trusted his Father without a lapse, and his faithfulness is counted to all who trust him, Hezekiahs included.

It did not work. That is the ordinary return on buying off a threat, and Hezekiah had a family precedent he might have consulted: his father bought Assyria’s help once and spent the rest of his reign rearranging the temple to suit them. Sennacherib took the money and sent the army anyway (v. 17).
verseByVerse.note: The campaign is dated to 701 BC.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–37 — On What Do You Rest This Trust of Yours?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The real battle is not for the walls but for the people’s trust in the LORD. Assyria’s officials stand where Ahaz once refused God’s sign (vv. 17–18). The Rabshakeh asks the decisive question, “On what do you rest this trust of yours?” (v. 19), and knocks away every support: Egypt is a broken reed, the reform has offended Judah’s God, Judah has no cavalry, and the LORD himself has sent Assyria (vv. 19–25). Refusing to speak Aramaic, he offers the men on the wall a counterfeit of covenant peace with deportation hidden in it (vv. 26–32), and ends by putting the LORD among the gods who failed (vv. 33–35). The people keep silent, as ordered, and the officials take the words to the king (vv. 36–37).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the word: trust comes back again and again in his mouth, and he is asking exactly the right question. On what do you rest this trust of yours? is what any honest man should be able to answer. What he cannot conceive is that there might be an answer other than Egypt, or horses, or nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: He stands to say it at the precise spot where Isaiah met Ahaz a generation earlier (see the comment on vv. 17-37). Ahaz stood on that ground and sent for Assyria; now Assyria is standing on it, shouting at his son.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rab-saris, and the Rabshakeh with a great army from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem. When they arrived, they came and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, which is on the highway to the Washer's Field. And when they called for the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebnah the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Assyria’s payment has bought nothing: its senior officers arrive with an army and stand on the very spot where Hezekiah’s father once refused God’s offer of help.

The Tartan, the Rab-saris, and the Rabshakeh. Titles rather than names: three of the highest officers of the empire, of whom the Rabshakeh did the talking.

From Lachish. The delegation comes straight from the siege of Judah’s second city, where Hezekiah had just sent his apology and his gold (vv. 13–16). The payment has not bought peace.

By the conduit of the upper pool. They stand at the exact spot, named in exactly the same words, where God sent Isaiah to meet Hezekiah’s father a generation earlier: “Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer’s Field” (Isaiah 7:3). Ahaz was standing there, inspecting the water supply, when a prophet told him not to be afraid and offered him any sign he liked. He refused it and wrote to Assyria instead. Now Assyria stands where he stood. The writer gives the location in Isaiah’s own words and says nothing more.

Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household. Hezekiah does not come out. He sends his three most senior officials, led by Eliakim, of whom Isaiah had prophesied that God would take the office from Shebna and give it to him: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David” (Isaiah 22:22).
