The risen Christ takes that verse for himself: he is the one “who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut” (Revelation 3:7). Eliakim held the keys of a palace about to be besieged; Christ holds the keys of a kingdom no enemy can enter.

Shebnah the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder. The secretary was the royal scribe, in charge of letters and records; the recorder probably announced the king’s decisions and kept the court’s account of events.

Uncertain wording. The three titles are Assyrian. The Tartan was the commander-in-chief, and Rab-saris means “chief eunuch” or “chief official”. Rabshakeh is traditionally “chief cupbearer”, a senior court office, though some take the title to mean simply “chief officer”. Either way, he spoke for the king.
verseByVerse.note: The Rabshakeh is the official who does the talking; his name is never given.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: On what do you rest this trust of yours? Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? In whom do you now trust, that you have rebelled against me? Behold, you are trusting now in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Rabshakeh asks the question the whole chapter turns on, what Judah is trusting, and begins to knock away its props, starting with Egypt, which really is a broken reed. He is not merely abusive. He has done his homework, and every argument he makes is built out of something true.

On what do you rest this trust of yours? The word trust occurs again and again in this speech and the next one, and it is the right question. The Rabshakeh asks it as though trust were a weakness peculiar to believers, while he himself trusts nothing he cannot count: chariots, numbers, the record of an empire that had not lost.

Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? The Hebrew is something like “a word of the lips”: talk, breath, the cheapest thing there is. He is a professional soldier contemptuous of speech, standing at the bottom of a wall conducting the whole operation by speech, because the one weapon he actually has today is his mouth. He is trying to talk a city open. And what will settle it, in the next chapter, is a word: God’s word through a prophet that a rumour will send the Assyrian king home, and that his army will not shoot an arrow at that wall (19:7, 32).

That broken reed of a staff. He is right about Egypt, and the image is exact: a reed looks like a walking staff and will take your weight until the moment you actually need it, then splinters and goes through your palm. Isaiah had been telling Judah’s court the same for years: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses” (Isaiah 31:1). An enemy at the wall is telling them what their own prophet had told them about Pharaoh.

Everyone is leaning on something. Many today feel as the Rabshakeh did: faith is for those who need it; the rest of us deal with reality. But nobody lives without putting their weight on something. We lean on our health, our savings, our competence, our country, the good opinion of people we respect, and we cannot prove in advance that any of them will hold. The real question is never whether to trust, but whether what you lean on can carry you. The Rabshakeh’s own answer could not: less than a century later Nineveh itself was destroyed, in 612 BC, so thoroughly that two centuries later a Greek army passed its ruins and recorded them under another name. Judah had long sung the alternative: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). That trust met its hardest test when the Son of God put his whole weight on his Father at the cross, was mocked for doing it, and was raised on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you say to me, "We trust in the LORD our God," is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and to Jerusalem, "You shall worship before this altar in Jerusalem"? Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them. How then can you repulse a single captain among the least of my master's servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen? Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this place to destroy it? The LORD said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Rabshakeh turns Judah’s own religion against it: the reform must have angered the LORD, Judah has no army worth the name, and the LORD himself has sent Assyria. Half of it is clever, and half of it is true, and that is what makes it dangerous.

Whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed. The cleverest thing he says is aimed at the men on the wall rather than at the king: your own God must be furious with Hezekiah. He has spent his reign pulling down shrines, including the one on your hill where your family has always gone, and forcing everyone to worship at one altar in the capital. How can you expect help from a God whose places of worship your king has been demolishing? It is aimed at exactly the people who lost something in the reform, and it is the standing tactic against every genuine reform: to accuse it of being irreligious. The man who removes what God did not ask for is always open to the charge of removing religion itself.

Make a wager with my master. The wager of verse 23 is a soldier’s insult, and an accurate one. He offers to donate two thousand cavalry horses if Judah can produce two thousand men able to ride them, knowing perfectly well that it cannot.

The LORD said to me. Then he claims a commission from Judah’s own God, and he is not simply lying. Isaiah, in these very years, was saying: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him” (Isaiah 10:5–6). Assyria really was being used. The Rabshakeh has hold of a true doctrine, that the God of Israel governs the movements of empires, and is using it at the foot of a wall to break the nerve of the people on top of it. Jehu did the same with a true prophecy over two heaps of heads at Jezreel (10:8–10). Truth in the mouth of a man who does not submit to it is a weapon like any other.

Isaiah’s answer. Isaiah answers the claim in the same passage. Assyria is the axe, and “Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it?” When the Lord has finished his work on Mount Zion, “he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria” (Isaiah 10:12, 15). Being an instrument in God’s hand is no licence to make speeches about it, and the instrument is answerable for its boasting.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and Shebnah, and Joah, said to the Rabshakeh, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall." But the Rabshakeh said to them, "Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and to drink their own urine?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials ask for a private conversation in the diplomatic language, and the Rabshakeh refuses, because his real audience is the ordinary people on the wall.

Please speak to your servants in Aramaic. Aramaic was the diplomatic language of the region, and the officials speak it. They ask for the talks to be conducted between professionals, out of earshot, which shows what they have realised: he is not negotiating at all. He is fluent in Hebrew, and he has chosen it.

Doomed with you to eat their own dung. In verse 27 he describes a siege in the plainest terms available, loudly, to the men who will be living it, and the famine in Samaria (6:24–30) shows it was no exaggeration.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: "Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria! Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you out of my hand. Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, The LORD will surely deliver us, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.' Do not listen to Hezekiah, for thus says the king of Assyria: 'Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern, until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and honey, that you may live, and not die. And do not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you by saying, "The LORD will deliver us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over the heads of the officials, the Rabshakeh speaks to the people as a rival prophet of a rival “great king”, telling them not to trust the LORD and offering them a copy of God’s own promise with exile hidden inside it.

Hear the word of the great king. The phrase is a parody of “Hear the word of the LORD”, the way every prophet in this book has opened his mouth. He is offering the people an alternative revelation from an alternative great king.

Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD. Then the real objective, stated openly. He has stopped arguing about Egypt and horses; the thing he has come to destroy is the confidence of ordinary people in God, and he says so.

Each one of you will eat of his own vine. What he offers is the most skilful thing in the speech, and it is not Assyrian language. It is Israel’s own picture of covenant peace: under Solomon “Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree” (1 Kings 4:25). It is what Micah, prophesying in Jerusalem in these very years, described as the future God would give (Micah 4:4). He has taken the exact words of their hope and put them in his own offer.

Until I come and take you away. The whole thing turns on a clause buried in a sentence about vines and honey. It is deportation, exactly what happened to the ten tribes some twenty years before, described in the warmest possible terms, a land like your own, grain and wine, olive trees and honey, and slipped into the offer after the good part.

How temptation is built. That is how every serious temptation is constructed. It is not a lie about what you want; the description of the good is usually accurate, often borrowed word for word from something God has truly promised. The price is in the small print, and the whole art is that the listener will hear “eat of his own vine” and stop listening before “take you away”.

He trusts in God; let God deliver him now. The same taunt was thrown at the foot of the cross by men who also thought the evidence was on their side: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him” (Matthew 27:43). There too the answer came after the mockers had finished, on the third day, and it was greater than anything they could imagine.

verseByVerse.quote: Has any of the gods of the nations ever delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? Who among all the gods of the lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Rabshakeh ends with the evidence of history: no god has saved any land from Assyria, not even Samaria’s, so why should the LORD save Jerusalem? After a speech in which almost everything was accurate, his one mistake is to put the LORD in the list.

Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Hamath and Arpad were Syrian cities Assyria had taken in recent decades, and people from some of these places had been resettled in the empty towns of Samaria (17:24), so the list was not abstract. Isaiah records the same boast from the king’s own mouth: “Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?” (Isaiah 10:9).

Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? The cruellest name is the last, Samaria, which was not a foreign city with a foreign god. Those were Israelites, with the same God, the same law and the same father Abraham, and some twenty years earlier they had been carried off hundreds of miles, never to return.

That the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand? He has surveyed the evidence competently, since no god anywhere in the region has stopped the Assyrian army, and drawn the obvious conclusion: the God of Jerusalem is one more god of the kind he has always beaten. Everything the next chapter does is an answer to that sentence: those gods were “the work of men’s hands”, but the LORD “made the heavens and the earth” (19:15, 18).

Uncertain wording. Sepharvaim and Ivvah were probably in the same region as Hamath and Arpad, though their sites are not certainly known; some identify Sepharvaim with Sibraim near Hamath (Ezekiel 47:16). Hena is not known at all. The point of the list does not depend on it: every name was a place Assyria had taken.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him." Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and told him the words of the Rabshakeh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people obey their king and give the Rabshakeh not a word, and the officials carry the whole speech, unsoftened, to Hezekiah.

The people were silent and answered him not a word. The reader of these books has met a silent crowd before. Elijah asked a nation on Carmel how long it would go limping between two opinions, “And the people did not answer him a word” (1 Kings 18:21), and that was the silence of people with no defence. This one is the opposite. These people are silent under orders, and it is discipline. Not one man on that wall shouts back, argues, negotiates or takes the offer.

Do not answer him. Some arguments are answered by not answering them. Everything the Rabshakeh said was designed to be engaged with, and the only reply that gave him nothing to work with was silence. The real answer was not theirs to give; it would come from God.

With their clothes torn. Tearing the clothes was the standard sign of grief or horror (see mourning customs). These are the three most composed men in the government, and they arrive shaken.

And told him the words of the Rabshakeh. They do the one useful thing available to them: they tell the king all of it, not only the parts a king might bear to hear. That is why the next chapter can begin as it does.

18.theology:
Nehushtan (v. 4). The most dangerous thing in Jerusalem was the one relic with a real history of real grace attached to it. Every long-lived Christian institution collects these: a building, a translation, a hymn book, the memory of a revival, the ministry God unmistakably used forty years ago. None were idols when given; they become idols when the gift is revered in place of the God who gave it. The Lord Jesus made that very serpent a picture of himself (John 3:14-15), and it was fatal to look at it instead of through it to him.

He trusted (v. 5). The highest verdict in the book rests on where he put his weight, which is exactly what the Rabshakeh will attack. On the apparent clash with Josiah (23:25), see the comment on vv. 1-12: the two are commended for different things, and Hebrew praise of this kind is not a ranking of one against the other.

The part that gets left out (vv. 14-16). Faith is not a possession acquired once and thereafter owned; the man who spreads a letter before God in the next chapter is the man on the ladder with a chisel in this one. God did not drop him between the two. And the payment bought nothing: Sennacherib took the silver and sent the army anyway, which is the usual return on buying off a threat.

The same patch of ground (v. 17). Where Ahaz refused God's sign and sent for Assyria, Assyria now stands. The choices of one generation are often met by the next on the very same ground.

Mostly true (vv. 19-25). Egypt really is a broken reed, and Assyria really is God's rod. A true doctrine in the mouth of a man who does not submit to it is a weapon, and the instrument is answerable for its boasting (Isa. 10:12-15).

The offer (vv. 31-32). The Rabshakeh borrows Israel's own picture of covenant peace and hides the price in a few words in the middle, until I come and take you away. That is how every serious temptation is built: the description of the good is accurate, often borrowed from something God has actually promised, and the whole art is that you stop listening before the clause that carries the price.

One item too many (vv. 34-35). His survey is competent and his last example seems unanswerable. His error is in the final line, where he puts the LORD in the list, and the whole of the next chapter is the answer.
18.examples:
Then: A king climbed a ladder at the door of the temple and chiselled off the gold he had put there himself in the first years of his reform, to pay a bill to an emperor who took the money and sent the army anyway.

Now: The hardest idol to break is never the obviously pagan one; it is the object, method or memory that really did come from God and really did work, and has quietly stopped being a signpost. Ask what in your church or your own history is being venerated for what it once carried.

Verses 14-16 are in the Bible on purpose. The king with none like him in Judah did the cowardly thing first and the faithful thing second, in the same crisis, so a bad first response to a threat does not settle what kind of person you are. None of us trusts perfectly; Christ did, to the cross, where men mocked his trust in God, and his faithfulness is counted as ours. So the way back after a failure of nerve is the way Hezekiah took: confess it, and carry the trouble to God, who has not stopped being your God.

As for the Rabshakeh's offer, almost everything he said was true, and the words that mattered were tucked into the middle of the pleasant sentence. When something is offered to you in the exact words of what you have always wanted, the terms will be in the part of the sentence you are least likely to still be listening to.

keyVerse.quote: He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him.
keyVerse.note: The writer’s highest praise for any king rests on one thing: where he put his weight. The rest of the chapter tests that trust, first by Hezekiah’s own failure and then by the Rabshakeh’s question, “On what do you rest this trust of yours?” (v. 19). It points beyond Hezekiah to the one Son of David whose trust in God never failed.

18.reflection:
Hezekiah broke the bronze serpent, an object God had once used to save lives, because people had begun to worship it (v. 4). What good gifts of God, in a church or in your own life, can quietly become things we trust instead of him? How does Jesus’ use of the serpent in John 3:14–15 help us look through such things rather than at them?

The king praised above all others for trust paid off Assyria with the temple’s gold, and it did not work (vv. 14–16). Why do you think the writer included this so soon after verse 5? What comfort is there here for someone whose first response to a crisis was fear?

The Rabshakeh asked, “On what do you rest this trust of yours?” (v. 19). What do people around you lean on, and what would happen if it gave way? What are you leaning on?

The Rabshakeh offered each man his own vine and fig tree and hid deportation in the same sentence (vv. 31–32). Where have you met an offer that borrowed the language of God’s promises and hid the price? How did Jesus answer the same taunt, “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43)?

19.title: Hezekiah's Prayer and Jerusalem Delivered
19.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz.<sup>3</sup>They said to him, "Thus says Hezekiah, This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth.<sup>4</sup>It may be that the LORD your God heard all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left."<sup>5</sup>When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah,<sup>6</sup>Isaiah said to them, "Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me.<sup>7</sup>Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'"<sup>8</sup>The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he heard that the king had left Lachish.<sup>9</sup>Now the king heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "Behold, he has set out to fight against you." So he sent messengers again to Hezekiah, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.<sup>11</sup>Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered?<sup>12</sup>Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar?<sup>13</sup>Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah?'"<sup>14</sup>Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD and spread it before the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And Hezekiah prayed before the LORD and said: "O LORD, the God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth.<sup>16</sup>Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God.<sup>17</sup>Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations and their lands<sup>18</sup>and have cast their gods into the fire, for they were not gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed.<sup>19</sup>So now, O LORD our God, save us, please, from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone."<sup>20</sup>Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Your prayer to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard.<sup>21</sup>This is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: "She despises you, she scorns you— the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you— the daughter of Jerusalem.<sup>22</sup>"Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel!<sup>23</sup>By your messengers you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, 'With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon; I felled its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses; I entered its farthest lodging place, its most fruitful forest.<sup>24</sup>I dug wells and drank foreign waters, and I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt.'<sup>25</sup>"Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins,<sup>26</sup>while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown.<sup>27</sup>"But I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me.<sup>28</sup>Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come into my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came.<sup>29</sup>"And this shall be the sign for you: this year eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs of the same. Then in the third year sow and reap and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.<sup>30</sup>And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward.<sup>31</sup>For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD will do this.<sup>32</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there, or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it.<sup>33</sup>By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD.<sup>34</sup>For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David."<sup>35</sup>And that night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies.<sup>36</sup>Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and went home and lived at Nineveh.<sup>37</sup>And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword and escaped into the land of Ararat. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.
19.overview:
Where we are. The Rabshakeh has mocked the LORD from the foot of Jerusalem’s wall and put him in a list of gods who failed (18:33–35). Judah is reduced to one city, and the officials have come to the king with their clothes torn (18:37).

The message. The LORD is the living God, and he answers those who mock him and hears those who pray to him. When Hezekiah takes the threat into the temple and lays it before God, God takes the insult as his own, turns the emperor back with a word, and saves the city without a single arrow being shot. He does it not for Hezekiah’s sake but “for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David” (v. 34).

Why it was said. The first readers knew that Jerusalem later fell to Babylon (see the introduction); this chapter shows that it did not fall because the LORD could not defend it. And it shows where hope lay even in exile: in prayer, and in God’s promise to David.

How the chapter makes its case. First the turning: Hezekiah goes into the house of the LORD in sackcloth and asks Isaiah to pray, because the living God has been mocked; Isaiah predicts a rumour, a return and a sword, and the rumour arrives with a letter attacking God directly (vv. 1–13). Then the prayer: Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD, grants every fact in it, and asks to be saved so that all the kingdoms may know the LORD is God alone (vv. 14–19). Then God’s answer, in poetry to Sennacherib: his boasts were God’s plan all along, and he will be led home with a hook in his nose; Judah will take root again, and the city will be defended for David’s sake (vv. 20–34). That night the angel of the LORD strikes the camp, Sennacherib goes home, and twenty years later he is killed by his sons in his own god’s temple (vv. 35–37).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by promise. The city is saved “for the sake of my servant David” (v. 34), the promise that one day brought David’s greater Son, for whose sake sinners are forgiven (1 John 2:12). It also shows by pattern how God saves: by his own hand, while his people stand still, as at the cross and the empty tomb.

For us. Whatever threatens you, take it to God and spread it before him, unedited. Pray honestly, and ask for what will make his name known. And rest your hope not on how well you have trusted or prayed, but on the promise God has made for the sake of his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Sent to Mock the Living God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The crisis is God’s before it is Judah’s, and Hezekiah now treats it so. The king who paid tribute a few months before now tears his clothes and goes into the house of the LORD (v. 1), and sends his officials and the senior priests in sackcloth to Isaiah (v. 2). Judah is like a mother with no strength left to give birth, but the Rabshakeh was sent “to mock the living God”, so Hezekiah asks God to answer the words (vv. 3–4). Isaiah predicts a rumour, a return and a sword (vv. 5–7). The rumour arrives at once (vv. 8–9), and with it a letter that attacks God directly: “Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you” (vv. 10–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 1 is the same man in the same year as 18:14, where he sent an apology and three hundred talents of silver to Lachish. His father had stood at that same conduit and written to Assyria; Hezekiah goes into the temple. A bad first response to a threat does not settle what a man will do next, and God had not finished with him.
verseByVerse.examples: His plea rests not on Judah's deserving but on God's insulted name, and he asks Isaiah to pray for the remnant that is left, which is all Judah now is.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This time Hezekiah takes the crisis to God: in mourning dress he goes into the temple and sends his leading men to Isaiah. Nothing outside has improved; what has changed is where he goes.

And went into the house of the LORD. The whole difference between this chapter and the last lies in that final clause of verse 1. In chapter 18 this same man, in this same year, sent an apology to Lachish and paid it by stripping gold off the doors of the house of the LORD. Now he goes in through those doors. His father, at the same conduit, refused Isaiah’s offer of a sign and wrote to Assyria; Hezekiah, with a worse army outside, goes up the hill to the temple.

Covered with sackcloth. Sackcloth was the rough goat-hair cloth of mourning and repentance (see mourning customs). The two most senior men of the government, the same two who stood at the wall, go with the senior priests, all in sackcloth: a state delegation in mourning dress, walking through a besieged city to a prophet’s house.

To the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz. Isaiah has stood behind these chapters without being named. He prophesied to Ahaz and had been preaching in Jerusalem for something like forty years, and this is the first time the writer of Kings puts him on the page.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Thus says Hezekiah, This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth. It may be that the LORD your God heard all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah admits that Judah has no strength left, and rests his plea on one thing: the living God has been mocked, so let God answer.

There is no strength to bring them forth. The image is painfully exact: a woman at full term, at the moment the child should come, with no strength left to push. It is not fear of what might happen. The decisive hour has come, and there is nothing left to meet it.

To mock the living God. Then the turn on which everything depends. Hezekiah sees the crisis in a new light: it is not first a military problem. A man has been sent “to mock the living God”, and what Hezekiah asks God to deal with is the words. He does not argue that Judah deserves rescue; his own conduct in the last chapter rules that out, and he knows it. He does not even argue that Judah is God’s people and therefore entitled. He says, in effect: your name has been dragged through the dirt in public by a man who put you in a list with carved wood, and I am asking you to answer that.

The living God. The phrase runs through the rest of the chapter, set against the gods of the nations, which were burned because they were only ever carved wood and stone (v. 18).

For the remnant that is left. By Sennacherib’s own count, forty-six fortified cities are gone and two hundred thousand people taken as spoil. Judah is now one city and whoever got inside its walls, and the king’s own word for his kingdom is “the remnant”.

verseByVerse.quote: When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah, Isaiah said to them, "Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me. Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells the frightened king not to fear, takes the insult as spoken against himself, and promises three things: a rumour, a retreat and a sword.

Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard. The first thing God says is not a plan but a command not to fear, and the reason is in the next phrase: these are words “with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me.” Hezekiah asked God to take the insult as his own (v. 4), and he does. The word for “servants” here is not the usual one for royal officials but the word for lads or underlings, probably meant to cut the great men of the empire down to size. The Rabshakeh and his colleagues are errand boys, and their master is about to be sent home.

Behold, I will put a spirit in him. One verse, three predictions: a rumour, a return, a sword at home. Mark them, because the chapter records all three fulfilled, the first in two verses (v. 9), the second in verse 36, and the third twenty years later (v. 37).

He shall hear a rumor. The greatest military power on earth is to be moved by a piece of news. An entire Syrian army once abandoned its camp outside Samaria and fled, throwing its equipment away, because the Lord made it hear chariots that did not exist (7:6–7). God does not need a battle. He can do it with a noise, or with something somebody says in a corridor.

verseByVerse.quote: The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he heard that the king had left Lachish. Now the king heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "Behold, he has set out to fight against you." So he sent messengers again to Hezekiah, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first prediction comes true at once: Sennacherib has moved on from Lachish, and news of an Egyptian army forces him to try to finish Jerusalem by letter.

Found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah. Lachish, Judah’s second city, has fallen; Sennacherib was proud enough of that siege to have it carved on the walls of his palace at Nineveh. He has moved on to Libnah, probably a few miles to the north, and the Rabshakeh goes to report that Jerusalem has not opened its gates. The army is still in Judah and the danger is not over, but the first crack has appeared.

Behold, he has set out to fight against you. The rumour arrives on schedule: an Egyptian force under a Cushite commander is on the move, and Sennacherib now faces a second front. His response is to try to finish Jerusalem by letter before he has to turn round.

Tirhakah king of Cush. Cush was the land south of Egypt (roughly modern Sudan), whose kings then ruled Egypt. Tirhakah became king about 690 BC; in 701 he led the army as a prince, and the narrator calls him by the title he later held.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered? Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sennacherib’s letter goes further than the Rabshakeh’s speech: it calls the LORD a deceiver, a god who has made a promise he cannot keep.

Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you. The letter is shorter than the speech, and worse. At the wall the Rabshakeh reached God only at the end; here he starts there and stays there. The accusation is against God directly, and the charge is fraud: that he has made a promise he cannot keep, and that whoever trusts him is being deceived.

Devoting them to destruction. The phrase (v. 11) is Israel’s own vocabulary, the root behind herem, the ban: the sentence God laid on Jericho, the thing Achan died for touching, the command Saul lost his kingdom over. It means something set apart under God’s sentence and removed from every human use, and the emperor uses it to boast of cities he burned for plunder. Conquerors have always borrowed sacred words to dignify their violence.

Gozan, Haran, Rezeph. The list is longer this time, and Gozan is on it, one of the places to which the northern Israelites had been deported some twenty years before (17:6). He is naming, to the king of Judah, a town full of Judah’s relatives.

Where is the king of Hamath? The letter ends with a roll-call of kings. Hamath and Arpad were Syrian kingdoms Assyria had swallowed within living memory, already named at the wall (18:34); Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivvah are harder to place, but people from Sepharvaim and Avva had been settled in Samaria and set up their gods there (17:24, 31). The question is meant to be unanswerable: where are they now? The chapter will answer it about the king who asked it (v. 37).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–19 — He Spread It Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith takes the threat to God before it takes it anywhere else. Hezekiah reads the letter, goes up to the house of the LORD and spreads it before him (v. 14). His prayer begins with who God is, enthroned above the cherubim, God of all the kingdoms and maker of all (v. 15). He asks the living God to hear and see what Sennacherib has written (v. 16). He grants every fact in the Assyrian case, then adds the one fact it left out: those gods were “the work of men’s hands, wood and stone” (vv. 17–18). Only at the end does he ask to be saved, and he asks it so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that the LORD is God alone (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not answer the letter. He does not convene the council, draft a reply, or send for Egypt. He carries the paper up the hill and opens it out flat in front of God, the way a man lays a document on a table and says: read that. He takes it to the one it was really addressed to.
verseByVerse.examples: The shape of the prayer is a model, and it runs opposite to how most of us pray under pressure. It opens with God's identity, not the emergency. It grants the enemy's evidence in full rather than disputing it. And it puts the request last, on the ground of God's own reputation among the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD and spread it before the LORD. And Hezekiah prayed before the LORD and said: "O LORD, the God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth. Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God. Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations and their lands and have cast their gods into the fire, for they were not gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed. So now, O LORD our God, save us, please, from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah lays the letter before the LORD and prays: he begins with who God is, grants every true fact in the letter, names the one fact it left out, and asks to be saved so that the whole world may know the LORD is God alone.

Spread it before the LORD. This is the most famous thing this king ever did. He does not draft a reply, convene the council or send to Egypt. He spreads the letter out, as a man lays a document on a table in front of someone and steps back: read it. A few months earlier he answered the last Assyrian demand by stripping the doors of this building; now he goes in with a piece of paper and no plan.

Enthroned above the cherubim. The order of the prayer matters: it begins with who God is, and the emergency is not mentioned in the first sentence at all. The ark stood in that building with two golden cherubim over it, and the space above them, empty to the eye, was where God was understood to sit. Hezekiah is standing a few yards from it.

You are the God, you alone. This is a direct answer to the letter on the floor. The Assyrians had produced a list of national gods and put the LORD at the end of it. Hezekiah says: you are not the God of Judah among others, but the God of all the kingdoms, Assyria included. And he has “made the heavens and the earth”: the empire that has taken forty-six cities never made anything.

Open your eyes, O LORD, and see. He asks God to read it himself. The gods on the letter’s list had ears that did not hear and eyes that did not see, as the psalms say of idols (Psalm 115:5–6). Hezekiah asks the living God to do the two things carved gods cannot, over a document written by a man who could not tell the difference.

Truly, O LORD. What makes this prayer honest is the part most people skip. “Truly”: he concedes it. Every fact in the Assyrian argument is granted: yes, they have laid waste the nations; yes, they burned the gods; yes, none of them stopped it. He does not dispute one word of the evidence.

For they were not gods. Then he adds the one fact the Assyrian argument had left out: those gods were not gods. Of course they burned. Wood burns. The Assyrians had been throwing statues into fires and concluding that no god anywhere could resist them. That was true of every idol they had burned, and worthless when applied to the living God. There is a way of praying that has to deny the facts to keep going, and it is exhausting and does not last. This is the other kind: grant the whole case, then name the one thing that was never in it.

Save us, please, from his hand. The request comes at the very end, in half a verse, and the reason takes more room than the request. Not: because we are your people. Not: because we do not deserve this. Not even: because the city is full of children. He asks for the deliverance of a nation on the ground of what it will show the world about God.

That all the kingdoms of the earth may know. That is the highest ground anything can be asked on, and the great prayers of the Old Testament keep finding it. When God threatened to destroy Israel, Moses argued that the Egyptians would say he had brought them out to kill them in the mountains (Exodus 32:12). Elijah on Carmel asked for fire “that this people may know that you, O LORD, are God” (1 Kings 18:37). It is also the safest ground, because it is the one request God has already committed himself to answering. The prayer the Lord Jesus taught begins there, before it mentions bread: “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — I Will Put My Hook in Your Nose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the mocker, keeps his promise, and saves the city by his own hand. Isaiah’s message tells Hezekiah his prayer is heard (v. 20), then speaks to Sennacherib himself: Zion laughs behind him (v. 21), his boasts are quoted back at him (vv. 22–24), every conquest was God’s plan long before (vv. 25–26), and he will be led home like a prisoner (vv. 27–28). Judah is promised that a remnant will take root again (vv. 29–31). The city will not see one arrow, “for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David” (vv. 32–34). That night the angel of the LORD strikes down the Assyrian camp, Sennacherib goes home, and years later his sons kill him at worship (vv. 35–37).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 25 is the answer to the entire campaign. The emperor who thought he was the author of history is told he was a tool in it: I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass. And the God who planned it is the God Hezekiah had just prayed to on the floor of the temple.
verseByVerse.examples: The picture in verse 28 is taken from Assyria's own art, whose palace reliefs show captives led by cords through the nose or lip. God tells the emperor he will go home by his own road, handled the way his own sculptors depict prisoners.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Your prayer to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard. This is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: "She despises you, she scorns you— the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you— the daughter of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Hezekiah his prayer is heard, then turns and speaks to Sennacherib: the city he despised is laughing at him as he goes.

Your prayer to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria I have heard. The answer opens by acknowledging receipt. Hezekiah asked God to hear the words of Sennacherib; God tells him he has heard his.

She despises you, she scorns you. What follows is a poem, and in it God does not address Hezekiah at all. He turns and speaks to Sennacherib, and the first thing he says is that the city is laughing at him. “The virgin daughter of Zion”: untouched, unentered, which is precisely what she is about to remain. She stands on her wall watching him go, shaking her head at his back like someone watching a man storm out of an argument he has lost.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel! By your messengers you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, 'With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon; I felled its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses; I entered its farthest lodging place, its most fruitful forest. I dug wells and drank foreign waters, and I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sennacherib thought he had insulted one more local god; in fact he had raised his voice against the Holy One of Israel, and God quotes his swollen boasts back at him.

Against the Holy One of Israel! The question of verse 22 is whether he knows whom he has insulted. He thought he was addressing a local god of the sort he had burned a dozen of. He was raising his voice at the Holy One of Israel, Isaiah’s favourite name for God.

You have mocked the Lord. Where English Bibles print LORD in small capitals they are rendering the covenant name; where they print “Lord” in ordinary letters they are rendering adonai, “Master”. This book rarely uses the second of God (7:6 is another). Without building too much on it, the title chosen where the insult is named means owner and sovereign. What Sennacherib mocked was the Master of the world, whether he knew whose name it was or not.

I felled its tallest cedars. Then his own words are quoted back at him, magnificent and swollen: the tallest cedars of Lebanon, the choicest cypresses, felled by a man who went up the mountains himself with his chariots. Assyrian royal inscriptions read exactly like this; the boasting is not a caricature.

I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt. The high point is the claim to have dried up the Nile with his foot. He means that his armies march where they like and drink what they find. But God quotes him at the point where the boast becomes a claim to do what only God does, the God who dried up the sea before Israel, and leaves it standing without comment.

verseByVerse.quote: "Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins, while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every conquest Sennacherib boasted of was planned by God long before; he is a tool taking credit for another’s work, and the nations he crushed were no stronger than grass on a roof.

I determined it long ago. The answer to the whole campaign is one sentence. The forty-six cities of Judah, the fall of Hamath and Arpad, the emptying of Samaria: the whole record Sennacherib recites as proof of his own irresistibility was planned “from days of old” and given to him to carry out. He is a tool congratulating itself on work another hand has done, as Isaiah had already put it: “Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it?” (Isaiah 10:15).

Have you not heard? There is something almost pitying in the question. The man does not know what he is. He thinks he is the one doing it all.

Like grass on the housetops. Seed blows onto the thin layer of earth on a flat mud roof, comes up green after rain, has no depth of soil, and is dead within days of the sun reaching it. That is what the conquered nations were: not opponents overcome by a great general, but roof grass.

The axe that thinks it is the woodsman. Sennacherib’s boast is the quiet creed of many a successful modern life: I built this. We rarely say it as loudly as an Assyrian inscription, but our CVs and our private accounting of ourselves run on the same grammar. Moses warned Israel that prosperity would teach them to say, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17). The trouble is not hard work; Sennacherib worked very hard. It is that the self-made story has to forget everything it was given: the health, the parents, the century, the open door. And a man who believes he made himself has to keep making himself every day, with no rest, because if the success is all his, so is the failure. God’s word to the emperor sounds like a humiliation and is really a release: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The gospel says the same about our salvation, and that is the one place where the self-made man can finally sit down.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me. Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come into my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has watched every move of the raging emperor, and will lead him home like a captive or a beast on a bridle.

I know your sitting down. Verse 27 takes the language the psalms use of ordinary people, “You know when I sit down and when I rise up” (Psalm 139:2), and applies it to the emperor of the world: his movements, campaigns and temper, all watched by the God he had listed as one more local god.

I will put my hook in your nose. The hook is borrowed from Assyria’s own picture of itself. Its palace reliefs show prisoners led away by cords run through the nose or lip, Assyria’s shorthand for a defeated man: something that used to be a king, walking where it is pulled.

My bit in your mouth. The second picture is a bridle, the bit by which a rider turns a horse or mule that has no understanding (Psalm 32:9). The charge is in the same verse: his raging and his complacency, the arrogant ease of a man who has never been refused. The beast that thought it was the rider will be turned round and walked home by the road it came on.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this shall be the sign for you: this year eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs of the same. Then in the third year sow and reap and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit. And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward. For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD will do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives Judah a sign: two lean years, then a third of sowing and harvest in safety, and a remnant that will take root again because the LORD himself is zealous to do it.

This shall be the sign for you. The sign is agricultural and entirely practical. Because of the invasion nothing was sown this year, and nothing can be sown next year either: the countryside is occupied and the people are inside the walls. So for two years they will live on whatever comes up by itself in unworked fields, thin but real. And in the third year they will plough, sow, plant vines and eat what they grow: a promise that there will be a third year, that they will be on their own land in it, and that it will be safe to plant something that takes years to fruit.

Take root downward and bear fruit upward. The order matters, and it is the way anything grows: what happens underground and out of sight comes first, and fruit is the last stage, not the first.

Out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant. The survivors shut up in the city will go out again to farm the empty countryside. “Remnant” is one of Isaiah’s great words: he named his own son Shear-jashub, “a remnant shall return” (Isaiah 7:3). It has two edges. Not all will be spared, and God will not let his people be wiped out. From that remnant, and from the stump of David’s house, would come the “shoot from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1).

The zeal of the LORD will do this. The guarantee is not Judah’s resolve or Hezekiah’s reform. Zeal is a jealous, burning commitment to what one regards as one’s own, and the same words close Isaiah’s promise of the child who will sit on David’s throne: “The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this” (Isaiah 9:7).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “what springs of the same” (v. 29) is found only here and in the parallel in Isaiah 37:30, and its exact meaning is uncertain. It probably refers to grain that grows the second year from seed dropped by the self-sown crop; either way, it means food no one planted.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there, or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it. By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD. For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not one arrow will touch Jerusalem: God will defend it for his own sake and for the sake of his promise to David, not for Hezekiah’s.

He shall not come into this city. Verse 32 makes four denials, each smaller than the last, down to a single basket of earth for a siege ramp. After forty-six cities, nothing at all will be launched at these walls.

By the way that he came, by the same he shall return. A small humiliation of its own. He will not even get a different road. Everything he passed on the way down he will pass again going home, with nothing to show for it.

For my own sake and for the sake of my servant David. Verse 34 gives two reasons, and neither is Hezekiah. “For my own sake” is exactly the ground Hezekiah prayed on. “For the sake of my servant David”: a man dead nearly three hundred years. The reader has met this before. Judah was not destroyed in Jehoram’s day “for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (8:19), and Abijam kept his throne for the same reason (1 Kings 15:4). Now the king who trusted as no other did is defended on exactly the same footing as the worst were: not for what he is, but for a promise made to someone else. Hezekiah had prayed the best prayer in the book, and when God gives his reasons, Hezekiah’s name is not among them.

Spared for the sake of David’s Son. That is the gospel in Old Testament shape. A city is spared for the sake of David, and the New Testament names the Son of David for whose sake sinners are spared: “your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake” (1 John 2:12); we are blessed “in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6); and we are kept by promises that rest on him rather than on how well we have prayed. Hezekiah’s best was never the ground of his rescue, and ours is not either.

verseByVerse.quote: And that night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies. Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and went home and lived at Nineveh. And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword and escaped into the land of Ararat. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one night God strikes down the Assyrian army, Sennacherib goes home, and years later he is murdered by his own sons in his own god’s temple: all three predictions come true.

The angel of the LORD went out. No battle. Nobody on the wall did anything. The city had been told that not one arrow would be shot into it, and none was. People got up in the morning, looked over the parapet, and saw a camp where nothing moved.

Sennacherib king of Assyria departed. Verse 36 fulfils the second prediction in one flat sentence. Verse 37 gives the third, twenty years later. The man who asked whether any god had ever delivered his people from the king of Assyria was killed at prayer, in his own god’s temple, by his own sons, and the god he was bowing to did nothing at all. Everything he had said about the gods of the nations turned out to be true of his own.

Every word fulfilled. All three predictions of verse 7 came true, the last long after most people had stopped watching for it; Isaiah’s word was not finished until it had all happened. The book’s first readers knew that this city fell to Babylon a century later, and this chapter answers the question that raised: Jerusalem did not fall because the LORD could not defend it. He had defended it here against a far greater army, and when it fell it was because he had given it up (21:10–15; 24:3–4).

Is the number believable? Scripture gives it plainly, and Assyrian field armies were very large. Some scholars suggest the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a military unit, which would make the count smaller. Either way, the army that had taken forty-six cities was broken in a single night without a battle.

Is there any record outside the Bible? Sennacherib’s own annals, extremely detailed about this campaign, never claim to have taken the city, and in an Assyrian record that silence says a great deal. The Greek historian Herodotus preserved an Egyptian story of an Assyrian army disabled overnight by mice that gnawed their equipment, which may be a distant memory of the same night. Babylonian records confirm that Sennacherib was killed by a son in a revolt, in 681 BC, and that Esarhaddon succeeded him; the sons fled to Ararat, which is Armenia.

Uncertain wording. No Assyrian god called Nisroch is known from Assyrian records. The name is probably a garbled or deliberately altered form of one of their gods, perhaps Nusku or Ninurta. The point does not depend on it: the emperor died on his knees before a god who could not keep him alive in his own temple.

19.theology:
Two responses, one year (v. 1). The man who stripped gold off the temple doors in 18:16 walks in through them here. Nothing external has changed and the army is closer; what has changed is where he takes it.

God’s honour first (v. 4). He turns a military emergency into a question of God's honour. He does not claim Judah deserves rescue, since his own conduct rules that out, nor even that Judah is entitled as God's people. He asks on the strength of the offence done to God's name in public.

Moved by a rumour (v. 7). Three predictions in one verse, fulfilled at vv. 9, 36 and 37. God does not require a battle to move an empire; a piece of news will do, as an entire Syrian army once abandoned its camp because it heard chariots that did not exist (7:6).

He spread it before the LORD (v. 14). No reply drafted, no council convened, no embassy to Egypt. Faith takes the threat to God before it takes it anywhere else, and it does not need to tidy the threat up first.

The shape of the prayer (vv. 15-19). It opens with God's identity, not the emergency. It asks the living God to do the two things carved gods cannot, hear and see. It concedes every fact in the Assyrian case with the word truly and then adds the one fact the case left out: those gods were only wood, and wood burns. There is a kind of praying that must deny the facts to keep going; this is the other kind. And the request is put last, resting on God's reputation among the nations, the ground Moses took at the golden calf and Elijah on Carmel, and the first petition the Lord taught us to pray.

I determined it long ago (v. 25). The whole record Sennacherib recites as proof of his irresistibility was assigned to him before he was born. The rulers of the world are not outside God's plan, even when they rage against him, and have you not heard? has something almost pitying in it: the man does not know what he is.

Whose sake (v. 34). The first ground is exactly what Hezekiah asked on; the second is God’s promise to keep a lamp, a line of kings, for David (1 Kgs. 11:36). The king who trusted as no other did is defended on the same footing as the worst were, as Christians are kept for the sake of David's greater Son.

The third prediction (v. 37). The man who asked whether any god had ever delivered anyone from the king of Assyria was killed at worship by his own sons. God's word is not finished until it has all happened, even when the last part takes twenty years and most people have stopped watching for it.
19.examples:
Then: A king read a letter designed to destroy his nerve, walked up the hill with it, went into the temple, and opened it out flat on the floor where God could see it, and then prayed a prayer in which he agreed with every factual claim the letter made.

Now: Verse 14 is a practical instruction and not a figure of speech. Whatever the piece of paper is, the scan result, the letter from the solicitor, the message you have now read eleven times, the thing to do with it is to take it somewhere and put it down in front of God, unedited. And you do not have to find the words alone: the Spirit himself intercedes for us when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26).

Notice too the honesty of verses 17-18. Hezekiah does not pray as though the frightening facts were untrue; he grants them in full and then names the one thing the frightening argument left out. Prayer that has to keep denying reality is exhausting and does not last.

And then verse 34. He had trusted, reformed, broken the serpent and prayed as well as anyone in these books prays, and when God stated his reasons for saving the city they were his own name and a promise made to a man dead nearly three hundred years. That is not a slight. It is the only kind of security that does not depend on how you are doing this week.

keyVerse.quote: So now, O LORD our God, save us, please, from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone.
keyVerse.note: This is the request at the end of Hezekiah’s prayer, and it rests not on Judah’s worth but on God’s glory among the nations. It answers the Assyrian boast that the LORD was one more god who could not save, and God answers it that very night. It is the same ground the Lord Jesus taught us to pray on first: “Hallowed be your name.”

19.reflection:
Hezekiah “spread it before the LORD” (v. 14). What is the “letter” in your life right now: the thing you keep rereading and worrying over? What would it look like to lay it before God, unedited, and what keeps us from doing so?

Hezekiah began his prayer with who God is (v. 15) and admitted every true fact in the Assyrian case (vv. 17–18). How can our prayers be both honest about hard facts and full of confidence in God?

Sennacherib was told that every conquest he boasted of had been planned by God (v. 25). Where are you tempted to tell the story of your life as “I built this”? How does 1 Corinthians 4:7 free us from that burden?

God saved the city “for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David” (v. 34), not for Hezekiah’s. Why is it good news that our security rests on God’s promise in Christ rather than on how well we have trusted or prayed?

20.title: Hezekiah's Illness and the Envoys from Babylon
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Set your house in order, for you shall die; you shall not recover.'"<sup>2</sup>Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, saying,<sup>3</sup>"Now, O LORD, please remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And Hezekiah wept bitterly.<sup>4</sup>And before Isaiah had gone out of the middle court, the word of the LORD came to him:<sup>5</sup>"Turn back, and say to Hezekiah the leader of my people, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you. On the third day you shall go up to the house of the LORD,<sup>6</sup>and I will add fifteen years to your life. I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will defend this city for my own sake and for my servant David's sake."<sup>7</sup>And Isaiah said, "Bring a cake of figs. And let them take and lay it on the boil, that he may recover."<sup>8</sup>And Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "What shall be the sign that the LORD will heal me, and that I shall go up to the house of the LORD on the third day?"<sup>9</sup>And Isaiah said, "This shall be the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do the thing that he has promised: shall the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back ten steps?"<sup>10</sup>And Hezekiah answered, "It is an easy thing for the shadow to lengthen ten steps. Rather let the shadow go back ten steps."<sup>11</sup>And Isaiah the prophet called to the LORD, and he brought the shadow back ten steps, by which it had gone down on the steps of Ahaz.<sup>12</sup>At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that Hezekiah had been sick.<sup>13</sup>And Hezekiah welcomed them, and he showed them all his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.<sup>14</sup>Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, "What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?" And Hezekiah said, "They have come from a far country, from Babylon."<sup>15</sup>He said, "What have they seen in your house?" And Hezekiah answered, "They have seen all that is in my house; there is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."<sup>16</sup>Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD:<sup>17</sup>Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD.<sup>18</sup>And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."<sup>19</sup>Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "Why not, if there will be peace and security in my days?"<sup>20</sup>The rest of the deeds of Hezekiah and all his might and how he made the pool and the conduit and brought water into the city, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>21</sup>And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place.
20.overview:
Where we are. Jerusalem has just been saved in a single night, “for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David” (19:34). This chapter steps back to the same years (v. 6) for two more episodes, and closes the reign.

The message. God hears the prayers and sees the tears of a dying man, and gives him life, a sign and fifteen years. But the king who trusted God in the siege is not proof against flattery when the crisis has passed: he shows Babylon everything he has, and when told that his treasures and his sons will go there, he is content because there will be peace in his days. Even the best of kings cannot secure his people’s future; that needs a better Son of David.

Why it was said. The first readers were living in the very Babylon Isaiah named here, many of them perhaps descendants of Hezekiah’s line (see the introduction). This chapter tells them their exile was foretold a century before, and began in a good king’s pride and indifference to those after him.

How the chapter makes its case. First the mercy: told to set his house in order, Hezekiah weeps and prays, and God promises healing, fifteen years and the city’s deliverance, confirmed by the shadow going back ten steps (vv. 1–11). Then the lapse: envoys come from Babylon, Hezekiah shows them everything, and Isaiah announces that all of it, and some of his own sons, will be carried to Babylon; Hezekiah calls the word good, thinking of peace in his own days (vv. 12–19). Finally the close: his tunnel brings water into the city, and Manasseh, born within the added years, takes the throne (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by the need it exposes. Hezekiah was given more years, and died; he left his sons to pay the cost of his pride. Jesus is the Son of David who went into death itself to destroy it (Hebrews 2:14–15), and who bore the cost himself for children he had not yet seen: “he shall see his offspring” (Isaiah 53:10). There is also an echo, not a prophecy: a son of David, raised from death’s door, goes up to the house of the LORD on the third day; the greater Son of David rose on the third day to endless life.

For us. Bring your fears and tears to God, who sees them. Be most watchful when the crisis is over and people treat you as important. And ask what you are content to leave for the next generation to pay; then look to the Christ who paid for his children, and let his Spirit turn your heart outward to theirs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Turn Your Face to the Wall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hears a dying king’s prayer, sees his tears and gives him life, with a sign to confirm it. Isaiah tells Hezekiah to set his house in order, for he will die (v. 1). The king turns to the wall, asks God to remember his faithfulness, and weeps bitterly (vv. 2–3). Before Isaiah has left the middle court he is sent back: God has heard and seen, and will heal Hezekiah, add fifteen years, and deliver the city for his own sake and David’s (vv. 4–6). A cake of figs is laid on the boil (v. 7). Hezekiah asks for a sign, as his father had refused to, and the shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The answer comes before the prophet is out of the courtyard. Isaiah delivered a death sentence, walked out, and was turned round in the middle court, and the whole distance between the two messages is the width of one court.
verseByVerse.examples: Note who asks for a sign here: the son of Ahaz, the king who was offered any sign he liked and refused it (Isa. 7:11-12). The same prophet, the same city, and the opposite instinct.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Set your house in order, for you shall die; you shall not recover.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same years as the Assyrian crisis, Hezekiah falls mortally ill, and God sends Isaiah to tell him plainly that he will die.

In those days. The phrase is loose, and the chapter is not in strict order: verse 6 promises deliverance from Assyria, so the illness belongs to the period of the siege rather than after it. The writer has grouped his material by subject.

Set your house in order, for you shall die. The message is as flat as a message can be: no reason given, no sin named, no comfort attached, to a man in his late thirties. Anyone who has sat in a consulting room and heard a doctor say there is nothing more to be done will know the silence of that room.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, saying, "Now, O LORD, please remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And Hezekiah wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah turns to the wall, asks God to remember his faithful life, and weeps bitterly: an honest prayer, on lower ground than his prayer for the city, but heard all the same.

Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall. It is what a man does when he wants the room to go away, and wants to be alone with God.

Please remember how I have walked before you. This is not the prayer of chapter 19. When the city was at stake he asked God to act “that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone” (19:19), the highest ground there is. Now his own life is at stake, and he asks God to remember how he has walked.

In faithfulness and with a whole heart. It is not simply self-righteousness. This is covenant language: God had made promises to those who walked before him with a whole heart, and Hezekiah is holding him to a relationship rather than claiming to have earned something. Nehemiah prays like this (Nehemiah 13:14), and so do the psalms. But the shift is there, and most of us will recognise it: it is easier to appeal to God’s glory about somebody else’s crisis than about our own. When it is our own body on the bed, the argument that comes out is usually about us.

And Hezekiah wept bitterly. Three words the writer did not have to include. He is not old. Scripture names no son of his yet (Manasseh will not be born for another three years), and as far as he knows the line of David ends in that room. And he had spent his life on a reform he will not see finished.

Why weep, if death is natural? Our culture handles the sentence Hezekiah heard in two ways. One is to keep it out of sight: the word is avoided and the funeral is called a celebration of life. The other sounds wiser: death is natural, part of the cycle, to be met with calm acceptance. Neither fits the man facing the wall. The first cannot survive the consulting room, and the second asks him to call the end of everything he loves a friend. Scripture lets a godly king weep bitterly and never tells him he is wrong to, because the Bible does not think death is natural. It calls death “the last enemy” (1 Corinthians 15:26). That is harder than calm acceptance and far more hopeful, because only an enemy can be defeated. The Son of David went into death himself, “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” and “deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15). Christians still weep at gravesides. They do not have to pretend, and they do not have to despair.

verseByVerse.quote: And before Isaiah had gone out of the middle court, the word of the LORD came to him: "Turn back, and say to Hezekiah the leader of my people, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you. On the third day you shall go up to the house of the LORD, and I will add fifteen years to your life. I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will defend this city for my own sake and for my servant David's sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers at once: he has heard the prayer and seen the tears, and he will heal the king, add fifteen years, and defend the city for his own sake and David’s.

Before Isaiah had gone out of the middle court. The prophet has not even reached the gate; the answer was not delayed by the length of a courtyard.

I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. The tears are named separately from the words, as though they counted for as much. What he said was heard, and what he could not say was seen.

Hezekiah the leader of my people. God gives the sick man two titles. He is “the leader of my people”, the word used of David when God first chose him to rule (1 Samuel 13:14; 2 Samuel 7:8), and the LORD speaks as “the God of David your father”. The man on the bed is reminded whose line he belongs to before he is told that he will live. And the first thing promised after healing is worship: “On the third day you shall go up to the house of the LORD.” Isaiah preserves the psalm Hezekiah wrote when he recovered, which ends there: “we will play my music on stringed instruments all the days of our lives, at the house of the LORD” (Isaiah 38:20).

I will add fifteen years to your life. Fifteen years, given as a number, and the city thrown in, on the same two grounds as in the last chapter: God’s own sake, and David’s. That is at least the fourth time the promise to David has held Judah up: for Abijam, for Jehoram, for the city under Sennacherib, and now for a dying king. It is beginning to look like the only thing that does.

Did God change his mind about Hezekiah? “You shall die” was the true verdict on the illness, given to draw out the prayer God meant to answer, as with Nineveh (Jonah 3:4, 10). God’s purpose did not change; he ordained the prayer as the means of the healing (James 5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaiah said, "Bring a cake of figs. And let them take and lay it on the boil, that he may recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
