God has promised the healing, and Isaiah still has a poultice of figs laid on the boil: ordinary means and a sovereign promise belong together.

Bring a cake of figs. Pressed figs were an ordinary remedy of the ancient world. God has just announced a healing and named the day, and the prophet asks for the figs anyway, with nothing inconsistent in it. Ordinary means and a sovereign promise sit together all through Scripture, and the man told he will be up on the third day still gets the dressing put on the boil. Using medicine is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "What shall be the sign that the LORD will heal me, and that I shall go up to the house of the LORD on the third day?" And Isaiah said, "This shall be the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do the thing that he has promised: shall the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back ten steps?" And Hezekiah answered, "It is an easy thing for the shadow to lengthen ten steps. Rather let the shadow go back ten steps." And Isaiah the prophet called to the LORD, and he brought the shadow back ten steps, by which it had gone down on the steps of Ahaz.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah asks for a sign, as his father once refused to, and God turns the shadow back ten steps on Ahaz’s own stairway.

What shall be the sign that the LORD will heal me? One generation earlier the same prophet offered his father any sign he liked, “let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven” (Isaiah 7:11), and Ahaz refused and wrote to Assyria. His son asks: the same house, the same prophet, and the opposite instinct, the difference between a man who wants God’s help and a man who wants to be left alone to manage. What one generation refuses, God may still give to the next.

Rather let the shadow go back ten steps. Given the choice, he thinks about it properly. Shadows lengthen; that is what they do all afternoon, and a shadow that ran on ten steps ahead of time could be explained by a man who wanted to explain it. He asks for the one that cannot: make it go back.

On the steps of Ahaz. It happens on his father’s staircase, evidently built so that the shadow moving down it marked the hours: the king’s own construction, and possibly a foreign fashion he brought back from Damascus along with the altar he copied there (16:10). The one thing his father built that is remembered is the place where God gave his son the sign his father had refused.

How did the shadow go back? Scripture does not say; it may have been a sign on Ahaz’s stairway in Jerusalem rather than a reversal of the earth’s spin. It was a miracle God gave, in the place where Hezekiah could see it.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for steps, but older versions such as the KJV render it “the dial of Ahaz”. Whether this was a stairway that also told the time or an instrument made for the purpose is not known.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — There Was Nothing That Hezekiah Did Not Show Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king who trusted God under siege falls to flattery once the danger has passed, and his pride costs his descendants dearly. Envoys come from Babylon with letters and a gift, ostensibly because of his illness (v. 12), and Hezekiah shows them everything in his treasure house and armoury (v. 13). Isaiah asks where they came from and what they saw, and Hezekiah answers both without seeing the danger (vv. 14–15). The sentence follows: all his treasure will be carried to Babylon, and some of his own sons will serve as eunuchs in its palace (vv. 16–18). Hezekiah calls the word good, because there will be peace and security in his own days (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Set verse 13 beside 19:14 and the two halves of this man are in one picture. He took a letter that terrified him up the hill and spread it out before the LORD. Now a flattering delegation arrives, and he spreads out his silver before Babylon; the writer says twice over that he held nothing back.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 19 should not be softened. He is told what will happen to his own sons, and says the word is good because it will not happen while he is alive. A man may be genuinely godly and genuinely uninterested in the generation after him. And when peace is bought for one lifetime only, the price is paid by those who come after, who had no say in it.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that Hezekiah had been sick. And Hezekiah welcomed them, and he showed them all his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon sends a friendly embassy, and Hezekiah, flattered, shows it everything he has. The danger is not in any obvious sin, but in a man enjoying being taken seriously.

Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan. The stated reason for the visit is the illness, and nobody at the time will have believed it. Merodach-baladan was a Chaldean chief who seized Babylon and spent years in and out of revolt against Assyria. A delegation from him to a Judean king who had stopped paying Assyria is not a get-well card. If the illness came before the siege, as verse 6 suggests, this visit probably did too, while both men were planning revolt. It is a search for allies on Assyria’s other flank, with letters, a present and a plausible excuse.

He showed them all his treasure house. He walked a foreign embassy through his entire treasury and his armoury, and two verses later he tells Isaiah so, almost proudly. In the last chapter it was a letter spread before the LORD; now it is his wealth, spread before Babylon. It is not hard to see why. He has just been brought back from the edge of death, his reputation is high, and here are ambassadors from a distant kingdom treating him as a serious power. It is a man enjoying being taken seriously.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, "What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?" And Hezekiah said, "They have come from a far country, from Babylon." He said, "What have they seen in your house?" And Hezekiah answered, "They have seen all that is in my house; there is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah’s questions let Hezekiah say aloud what he has done, and the king answers without seeing anything wrong.

What did these men say? And from where did they come to you? Hezekiah does not answer the first question at all. To the second he answers with something that sounds like a boast: “a far country”. Look how far they came to see me.

What have they seen in your house? This one he answers in full: “They have seen all that is in my house.” He has no idea anything is wrong; there is no sin here he could name, and if you had asked him that evening how the day went he would have said it went well. The prophet does not accuse him. He asks, and lets the king say it aloud, so that the sentence which follows answers his own words. It is how Nathan dealt with David (2 Samuel 12:1–7): the man is brought to describe what he has done before he is told what it means.

What was in his heart. Chronicles gives the inside view. In the matter of the envoys “God left him to himself, in order to test him and to know all that was in his heart” (2 Chronicles 32:31), and it records that Hezekiah later humbled himself for the pride of his heart (32:26).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD: Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD. And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah announces that everything Hezekiah showed off will be carried to Babylon, and some of his own sons will serve there as eunuchs.

Shall be carried to Babylon. This is the first time Babylon appears in this book as more than a name, and Isaiah’s one sentence holds the whole of the book’s last chapters. In little more than a century an army from that city will empty the palace and the temple (24:13; 25:13–15), and the writer’s own readers may already have watched it happen.

Some of your own sons. The second half is worse, and personal: not the treasury but the children. “Your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father”: the wording insists on it, because he has no sons yet. They will be made eunuchs in that palace, sons of David’s line left childless in a foreign court. The prophecy came true in the exile, when youths “of the royal family and of the nobility” were taken to serve in Nebuchadnezzar’s palace (Daniel 1:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "Why not, if there will be peace and security in my days?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah calls God’s sentence good, because it will not fall in his own lifetime: a good man’s care has stopped at his own funeral.

The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good. On its own, the reply would be submission, and many readers have taken it that way. But the writer will not allow it, and does something he almost never does: he tells us what the man was thinking. He has just been told what will happen to his unborn sons, and his response is relief that the bill is not due in his lifetime. Set it against the man in the previous chapter who prayed for the honour of God’s name before the nations. It is the same king, in the same years, with his own crisis past.

Peace and security in my days. Two uncomfortable things should be said. First, a man can be truly godly in some things and not in others, and his care may stop at the end of his own life. Hezekiah trusted God with his city, his health and his reputation, and never quite got round to caring what happened after the funeral. Second, this is the characteristic sin of a comfortable generation, and it very rarely feels like sin. Nobody says, “Let the next lot deal with it.” They say there will be peace in my days, and go to bed. The people who paid were his descendants.

A better promise, and a better Son. Two things should be set beside Isaiah’s sentence on the sons, though neither excuses Hezekiah. The same Isaiah later carried a promise to eunuchs, men cut off from having sons: God would give them “a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5), and an early convert in Acts is an Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah (Acts 8:27–38). And where Hezekiah was content that the cost would fall on children not yet born, David’s greater Son did the reverse. He took the cost on himself for children he had not yet seen, and Isaiah says “he shall see his offspring” (Isaiah 53:10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–21 — And Manasseh His Son Reigned in His Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah’s reign closes, and the gift of extra years leaves an uneasy legacy. The writer records one achievement above all, the pool and conduit that brought water into the city, the tunnel that had prepared Jerusalem for the siege and still runs today (v. 20). Then Hezekiah dies, and Manasseh his son, born within the fifteen added years, reigns in his place (v. 21). The writer adds no comment, but the reader who turns the page will meet the worst king in Judah’s history, and see how quickly a reform can be undone when it depends on one man.
verseByVerse.theology: The tunnel is more than five hundred yards long, cut through solid rock, and the inscription his workmen left in it describes the moment two teams digging from opposite ends heard each other's picks. A besieged Jerusalem would have water and a besieging army would not.
verseByVerse.examples: The last line is a fact laid down without comment. Manasseh was twelve when he came to the throne, so he was born inside the fifteen added years, and Scripture simply puts the two sentences next to each other and moves on.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of the deeds of Hezekiah and all his might and how he made the pool and the conduit and brought water into the city, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah’s reign ends with his great water tunnel remembered, and with Manasseh, a son born within the added years, on the throne.

He made the pool and the conduit. Of everything in a twenty-nine-year reign, the writer names one piece of engineering. Jerusalem’s water came from the Gihon spring, outside the walls, the single fatal weakness of the site. Hezekiah cut a tunnel through the rock from the spring to a new pool inside the walls, and stopped up the springs outside (2 Chronicles 32:3–4, 30). It still runs, and in 1880 a boy wading through it found the workmen’s inscription describing the moment the two tunnelling teams met. The Rabshakeh stood “by the conduit of the upper pool” (18:17) and shouted at a city that had already been made ready for him.

Manasseh his son reigned in his place. The last sentence is a fact set down without comment. Manasseh was twelve when he came to the throne (21:1), and the arithmetic is left to the reader: the boy was born within the fifteen added years. Scripture does not say the fifteen years were a mistake; anyone who reads it that way has added to it. But the writer has put two things side by side. The king wept for more time and was given it, and in it he entertained Babylonian ambassadors, fathered the worst king in Judah’s history, and was glad the disaster would fall on someone else. The next chapter is that son.
verseByVerse.note: The tunnel can still be walked today; the inscription is now in Istanbul.

20.theology:
Two prayers, two grounds (v. 3). For the city he appealed to God's glory; for his own life he asks God to remember how he has walked. It is covenant language rather than a claim to have earned something, but the shift is real, and God heard him all the same.

Heard and seen (v. 5). I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. The tears are named separately from the words, as counting for as much. Whatever the answer to our own prayers for healing, and it is not always this one, the tears are seen.

Figs on the boil (v. 7). Ordinary means and a sovereign promise sit together throughout Scripture. The man told he will be up on the third day still gets the dressing, and medicine is not a lack of faith.

The sign his father refused (vv. 8-11). Ahaz declined a sign with pious-sounding words, I will not put the LORD to the test (Isa. 7:11-12); his son asks, and it is given on the steps of Ahaz. What one generation refuses, God may still give to the next.

What gets spread out (v. 13 against 19:14). Fear sent him to God; flattery sent him to the treasury. It is not wickedness in any form he could have named, which is why God left him to himself to show him what was in his heart (2 Chron. 32:31).

Peace in my days (v. 19). The writer breaks his habit to tell us what the man was thinking. A person's godliness does not automatically reach beyond his own lifetime, and the sin here almost never feels like sin: nobody says "let the next lot deal with it," they say there will be peace and security in my days, and sleep well. The people who paid were his descendants.

The arithmetic in the last verse (v. 21). Manasseh was born inside the added years. Scripture does not say the healing was a mistake, and nobody should add that.
20.examples:
Then: A prophet delivered a death sentence, walked out through the palace, and was turned round in the middle court and sent back, the answer overtaking him before he had crossed one paved yard.

Now: Notice what you appeal to in prayer when the crisis is your own body rather than somebody else's cause; Hezekiah prayed magnificently about God's honour while the danger was a city, and about his own record when it was his life; yet God heard both.

Then there is what he showed the Babylonians. No commandment was broken that he could have named, and he would have told you the day went well. The dangerous hour is not the siege; it is the month after the crisis lifts, when someone important treats you as important.

Verse 19 is the most quietly damning sentence about a good man in these books. Ask what you are content to leave unresolved because it will not fall due in your lifetime. The answer is not to try harder to care, but to look at the Son of David who did what Hezekiah would not, bearing the cost himself for children he had not yet seen (Isa. 53:10); his care for us is counted as ours where ours has failed, and his Spirit, given to us, is what turns a heart outward to the next generation.

keyVerse.quote: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you.
keyVerse.note: God’s answer to the dying king comes before the prophet has left the palace, and it names the tears as well as the words. It shows a God who hears and sees, and who gives life for his own sake and for David’s. Hezekiah’s added years ended in death, but they point to the Son of David through whom God answers his people’s tears for good.

20.reflection:
Hezekiah prayed for the city on the ground of God’s glory (19:19), but for his own life on the ground of his faithfulness (20:3). Why is it harder to pray with God’s glory in view when the crisis is our own? What does it mean to you that God said, “I have seen your tears”?

God promised healing, and Isaiah still called for a cake of figs (v. 7). How should Christians hold together trust in God and the use of medicine and ordinary means?

Hezekiah stood firm under siege but fell to flattery once the danger had passed (vv. 12–15). Why are the times after a crisis, or after success, often more dangerous spiritually than the crisis itself?

“Why not, if there will be peace and security in my days?” (v. 19). What might we be content to leave for the next generation to pay? How does Christ, who bore the cost for children he had not yet seen (Isaiah 53:10), change the way we live for those who come after us?

21.title: Manasseh and Amon
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hephzibah.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>3</sup>For he rebuilt the high places that Hezekiah his father had destroyed, and he erected altars for Baal and made an Asherah, as Ahab king of Israel had done, and worshiped all the host of heaven and served them.<sup>4</sup>And he built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, "In Jerusalem will I put my name."<sup>5</sup>And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And he burned his son as an offering and used fortune-telling and omens and dealt with mediums and with necromancers. 21.overview:
Where we are. Hezekiah has died, after the great deliverance of Jerusalem and his foolish display of his treasures to the envoys from Babylon, and Isaiah has warned that everything in his house will one day be carried there (20:17–18). This chapter shows how that warning became a sentence: two reigns, fifty-seven years, that undo everything Hezekiah did.

The message. A people can lose everything God has given them, not in one catastrophe but by a long, comfortable slide into the religion of the nations around them, and the leader who takes them there is answerable for it, and so are those who follow. God’s patience with Manasseh was long, but patience is not approval: when the sentence comes it is total, and it rests on a history of unfaithfulness reaching back to Egypt.

Why it was said. The exiles in Babylon asked how Jerusalem could fall when David’s line held God’s promise. This chapter is the writer’s chief answer (see the introduction): the promises were never a shield to hold up against God while breaking his covenant, and Manasseh’s reign filled up the measure.

How the chapter makes its case. Manasseh reigns longest and worst: he rebuilds the high places, copies Ahab, fills the temple courts with altars to the stars, burns his son, consults the dead and sets an Asherah in the house that bore God’s name, until Judah does worse than the Canaanites (vv. 1–9). Unnamed prophets pronounce the sentence: Jerusalem measured with Samaria’s line, wiped like a dish, and even the remnant of God’s heritage handed over (vv. 10–15). Innocent blood fills the city, yet the king dies in his bed (vv. 16–18). Amon copies him for two years and is murdered, and the people of the land crown the boy Josiah (vv. 19–26).

Where it leads. To Christ above all by the need it exposes. A nation stood or fell with its king, and Judah’s king led it into ruin; it needed a King who would lead his people in God’s way and carry in himself the sentence they had earned. Jesus’ genealogy runs through Manasseh and Amon (Matthew 1:10), and he is that King. The chapter also shows God’s character as Christ reveals it: the mercy that, by Chronicles’ account, heard Manasseh in a Babylonian prison (2 Chronicles 33:12–13) is the mercy that in Christ reaches the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15–16). And the city Manasseh filled with innocent blood would one day shed the most innocent blood of all, the blood that does not cry for vengeance but cleanses.

For us. Long life, stability and success prove nothing about God’s approval. Whatever we trust for our security will in the end ask for what we love most, while the true God gave his own Son for us. No one has gone too far to be received by God through Christ, though forgiveness does not always undo the damage sin has done. And ordinary faithful people, refusing what must not happen, can hold a nation’s future.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — More Evil Than the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s longest reign is its worst, and the writer measures its evil by God’s own words. Manasseh comes to the throne at twelve and reigns fifty-five years (v. 1). He rebuilds the high places his father pulled down and copies Ahab’s altars to Baal and his Asherah (vv. 2–3), fills both temple courts with altars to the sun, moon and stars (vv. 4–5), burns his son and consults mediums (v. 6), and sets a carved Asherah in the house where God promised to put his name (v. 7). Twice the writer quotes that promise, the second time with its condition (vv. 7–8). The verdict: the people did not listen, and Manasseh led them to do more evil than the nations God had destroyed (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The worst king Judah ever had held the throne longer than any other, outlived good men and reformers, and died in peace. A long reign never proved that God approved of a king, and long success does not prove that anything else is right.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, privilege does not lower the standard. Judah held the land as a trust. Its earlier peoples had been driven out for their sins, and Israel was warned that the same sins would cost them the land. Being God's people made the betrayal worse, not more excusable.

verseByVerse.quote: Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hephzibah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the despicable practices of the nations whom the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. For he rebuilt the high places that Hezekiah his father had destroyed, and he erected altars for Baal and made an Asherah, as Ahab king of Israel had done, and worshiped all the host of heaven and served them. And he built altars in the house of the LORD, of which the LORD had said, "In Jerusalem will I put my name." And he built altars for all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the LORD. And he burned his son as an offering and used fortune-telling and omens and dealt with mediums and with necromancers. He did much evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger. And the carved image of Asherah that he had made he set in the house of which the LORD said to David and to Solomon his son, "In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever. And I will not cause the feet of Israel to wander anymore out of the land that I gave to their fathers, if only they will be careful to do according to all that I have commanded them, and according to all the Law that my servant Moses commanded them." But they did not listen, and Manasseh led them astray to do more evil than the nations had done whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s longest-reigning king was its worst: Manasseh deliberately undid his father’s reform, brought the worship of Ahab’s gods and of the stars into the temple itself, burned his son, and led his people to do worse than the Canaanites God had driven out. The writer measures the evil against God’s own words about the temple, quoted twice inside the account of its desecration.

He reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. The longest reign in either kingdom belongs to the worst king in this book. He very likely outlived Isaiah, and outlasted every adult who remembered Hezekiah’s reform. Whatever was done in those years had two generations in which to become normal.

He rebuilt the high places that Hezekiah his father had destroyed. The first thing recorded of him is demolition in reverse. Hezekiah had done what no good king before him managed: the high places came down, the pillars were broken, the Asherah was cut down, the bronze serpent was smashed (18:4). Manasseh put it all back. (High places were hilltop shrines; pillars were standing stones for Baal; an Asherah was a wooden pole or carved image of the Canaanite fertility goddess, Baal’s consort.)

As Ahab king of Israel had done. The comparison tells you how bad this is. A king of Judah, in Jerusalem, on David’s throne, is measured against the man who married Jezebel and built a temple to Baal in Samaria (1 Kings 16:31–33). Before this, the comparison had been made of Judah’s kings only when Ahab’s own daughter had married into the palace (8:18, 27).

In the two courts of the house of the LORD. His grandfather Ahaz had put a copy of a Syrian altar in the temple court and moved Solomon’s aside (16:10–14); Manasseh fills both courts with altars to the sun, moon and stars. He reigned as a vassal of Assyria at the height of its power, and Assyrian inscriptions name him among the kings who sent tribute and building materials to Esarhaddon. Worship of the heavenly bodies ran all through that world, and the overlord’s fashions probably made it easier to bring in; but the writer lays the choice on Manasseh himself.

In Jerusalem will I put my name. Verse 4 sets God’s own words about the building inside the account of its desecration: the promise and the defilement share one sentence.

He burned his son as an offering. Verse 6 runs through almost the whole of a list Moses wrote out: “anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens … or one who inquires of the dead”, and he added, “because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you” (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Manasseh has worked through the list. It is the second time in the family: his grandfather Ahaz burned his son (16:3), and his father Hezekiah, raised in that house, did not.

Idols always ask for the children. Why would a king do it? Gods like Molech were believed to secure what everyone wanted most: safety, victory, rain, a future, and the price of the future was the child. That is the logic of every idol. A culture can still hand its children over to what it worships: to a career that leaves no room for them, to the pressure that turns a nine-year-old’s week into a strategy for the family’s standing, to adult freedoms the young end up paying for. Whatever we look to for security will ask, in the end, for what we love most. The true God turns this inside out. He does not demand our son to secure our future; he gives his own: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). (See the note on Genesis 22:1–2.)

If only they will be careful to do. In verses 7–8 the writer quotes the promise again, this time with its condition. “I will not cause the feet of Israel to wander anymore” is the promise; “if only they will be careful to do according to all that I have commanded them” is the condition, spoken to Solomon about this very building (1 Kings 9:2–7). A carved Asherah now stands in the room the promise was made about. God’s promises were never a charm to be held up against him while his covenant was broken.

To do more evil than the nations had done. The verdict in verse 9 could not be more severe: worse than the Canaanites. Israel held the land as a trust. The previous occupants had been evicted for what they did in it, and Israel had been told the land would not tolerate the same conduct from anyone (Leviticus 18:24–28).

But they did not listen, and Manasseh led them astray. The blame runs both ways. The man at the top is held answerable for where a nation ends up, and so are the people who followed him; no one in Judah could plead that the king made them do it.

Uncertain wording. Verse 6 reads literally he made his son pass through the fire. A few scholars take this as a rite of dedication that did not kill the child, but Scripture speaks of the same practice as plain burning (Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31), so the ESV’s “burned his son” gives the meaning.
verseByVerse.note: “Burned his son” is literally “made his son pass through the fire” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — As One Wipes a Dish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Manasseh’s long reign with a total sentence, and Manasseh himself dies in peace. Through unnamed prophets God declares that Judah has outdone the Amorites, and promises a disaster to make the ears tingle (vv. 10–12). Jerusalem will be measured with the line used on Samaria and wiped like a dish turned upside down; even the remnant of his heritage will be handed to its enemies, for a rebellion that began in Egypt (vv. 13–15). Beyond the idolatry, Manasseh filled the city with innocent blood (v. 16). Yet he dies in his bed and is buried in his own garden (vv. 17–18), and Chronicles adds that before the end he humbled himself and was forgiven.
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgment is not random. He measures Jerusalem by the same line he used on Samaria: the standard is public, it has been applied before, and Judah had watched it applied.
verseByVerse.examples: Two things are held together here: the worst king in Judah's history was forgiven, and the sentence on the nation still stood (see the note on vv. 17-18).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said by his servants the prophets, "Because Manasseh king of Judah has committed these abominations and has done things more evil than all that the Amorites did, who were before him, and has made Judah also to sin with his idols, therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Jerusalem and Judah such disaster that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through prophets whose names are not recorded, God declares that Judah under Manasseh has outdone the Canaanites, and announces a disaster so terrible that merely hearing of it will make the ears ring.

By his servants the prophets. The prophets are plural and unnamed. The book records no prophet’s name in Manasseh’s fifty-five years, not because there were none (Isaiah’s ministry may well have run into these years) but because nothing they said was heard.

More evil than all that the Amorites did. The Amorites stand for all the peoples of Canaan, whose sins the land had “vomited out” (Leviticus 18:24–28). God had told Abraham he would wait until “the iniquity of the Amorites” was complete (Genesis 15:16), and Ahab was condemned for acting “as the Amorites had done” (1 Kings 21:26). Now the king of Judah has gone further than the nations Israel was brought in to replace. The logic of the sentence that follows is simple: a people who live like the Canaanites will lose the land as the Canaanites did.

The ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle. The picture is physical: the ringing in the ears that comes with shock. Samuel heard the same expression as a boy, about the house of Eli (1 Samuel 3:11): news so bad that those who merely hear it feel it in their bodies. Jeremiah used it again of Topheth in these same years (Jeremiah 19:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria, and the plumb line of the house of Ahab, and I will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down. And I will forsake the remnant of my heritage and give them into the hand of their enemies, and they shall become a prey and a spoil to all their enemies, because they have done what is evil in my sight and have provoked me to anger, since the day their fathers came out of Egypt, even to this day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will judge Jerusalem by the standard that condemned Samaria and Ahab’s house, and empty it as completely as a dish wiped and turned over; even the remnant of his own inheritance will be handed to its enemies. The cause is not one reign but the whole history of the nation.

The measuring line of Samaria, and the plumb line of the house of Ahab. Two ordinary builders’ tools are used the wrong way round. A measuring line lays out a foundation and a plumb line (a weighted cord) gets a wall straight; here they mark a building for demolition: surveyed, measured, condemned. And the instruments are Samaria’s and Ahab’s. The standard that destroyed Samaria is the one Jerusalem will be measured against, and by now the reader knows the result.

As one wipes a dish. The second picture is domestic and completely without dignity: not a city stormed, but a plate wiped with a cloth and stood on its face on the shelf to drain. The holy city of God, emptied, dried and put away.

I will forsake the remnant of my heritage. Israel was God’s heritage, his own inheritance among the nations (Deuteronomy 32:9). Since the fall of Samaria, Judah was all that was left of it. Now even the remnant is to be handed over, and the people who once took the spoil of Canaan will themselves become “a prey and a spoil”. This is the heaviest word in the oracle: not that enemies will come, but that God will let go.

Since the day their fathers came out of Egypt. The charge is not fifty-five years long. It is the whole national story, from the first month of the rescue.

Forsaken in our place. The only one God ever forsook who did not deserve it was his own Son, who cried on the cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Because he was let go, God can say to everyone who trusts him, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Manasseh shed very much innocent blood, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another, besides the sin that he made Judah to sin so that they did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beyond all his idolatry, Manasseh was a killer on a vast scale, and the innocent blood he shed filled Jerusalem from one end to the other.

Manasseh shed very much innocent blood. After fifteen verses of idolatry comes “moreover”: he killed people, a great many of them, not in one massacre but throughout a reign of decades. When Babylon finally comes, the writer gives this as the reason the LORD “would not pardon” (24:4). False worship and contempt for human life went together, as they still do.

The unnamed victims. We are not told who they were. An old Jewish tradition says that Isaiah was among them, sawn in two, and many readers have connected Hebrews’ “they were sawn in two” (Hebrews 11:37) with this verse. The tradition is not Scripture and should not be preached as though it were; but the men most likely to stand in his way were the ones this chapter calls “his servants the prophets”.

Innocent blood and a better word. The city Manasseh filled with innocent blood would one day shed the most innocent blood of all. Abel’s blood cried out for justice; Christ’s is “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24), and it cleanses even those who shed blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh and all that he did, and the sin that he committed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And Manasseh slept with his fathers and was buried in the garden of his house, in the garden of Uzza, and Amon his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manasseh dies in peace and is buried in his own garden; Kings says no more, but Chronicles records that God humbled him in captivity and forgave him when he repented. Both are true: the worst king in Judah’s history was forgiven, and the damage he had done still stood.

Buried in the garden of his house. Chronicles fills the silence. The Assyrians “captured Manasseh with hooks” and took him to Babylon; God had threatened Assyria’s king with a hook in his nose (19:28), and now Judah’s king is led off by one. There “he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly”, and God “heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem” (2 Chronicles 33:11–13). He threw the foreign gods out of the city and restored the altar (33:15–16).

Kings and Chronicles. Both accounts are true, and they do different jobs. Chronicles tells the story of a man; Kings is building the case for why Jerusalem fell, and for that what matters is the damage, which a late repentance did not undo.

The worst king forgiven. If God forgave Manasseh, no one who turns to God need doubt that he can be forgiven, and no reader of this chapter is entitled to conclude that he has gone too far. His name stands in the family tree of Jesus (Matthew 1:10), and the mercy that found him in a Babylonian cell is the mercy Paul meant when he called himself the foremost of sinners, saved so that Christ might display his patience to those who would believe after him (1 Timothy 1:15–16).

Forgiveness and consequences. The sentence on the nation still stood. Josiah’s reform, the most thorough in either kingdom, will not lift it: “still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great wrath … because of all the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked him” (23:26). A man may be completely pardoned and still spend the rest of his life, and his children theirs, living in the country he made. Neither truth cancels the other.

Was it fair to judge Judah for Manasseh’s sin when Josiah reformed? The people followed Manasseh into idolatry and child sacrifice (vv. 9, 16), and Josiah’s reform did not change their hearts (Jeremiah 3:10). Each generation was judged for its own sins.
verseByVerse.note: The garden of Uzza, where Manasseh and Amon were buried, is not mentioned elsewhere; neither king lies in the royal tombs of the city of David.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–26 — The People of the Land Made Josiah King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The son repeats the father, and ordinary people save the throne of David. Amon reigns two years and does nothing that is his own: he walks in his father’s way, serves his father’s idols and abandons the LORD (vv. 19–22). His servants murder him in his house (v. 23), but the people of the land execute the conspirators and make his eight-year-old son Josiah king (v. 24). The chapter closes with a second grave in the garden of Uzza (vv. 25–26). The boy who will lead Judah’s greatest reform has grown up surrounded by everything his grandfather built.
verseByVerse.theology: Amon shows how quickly a bad example is copied: a father's repentance late in life did not reach the son, who went back to the images his father had made.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithfulness is not only for people with office. Twice in this book ordinary Judeans with no title at all kept David's line from being decided by a palace plot.

verseByVerse.quote: Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Meshullemeth the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as Manasseh his father had done. He walked in all the way in which his father walked and served the idols that his father served and worshiped them. He abandoned the LORD, the God of his fathers, and did not walk in the way of the LORD. And the servants of Amon conspired against him and put the king to death in his house. But the people of the land struck down all those who had conspired against King Amon, and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place. Now the rest of the acts of Amon that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And he was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and Josiah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amon copies his father for two years and is murdered by his own officials, but the ordinary people of Judah refuse to let a palace coup decide who sits on David’s throne, and they crown his eight-year-old son Josiah.

As Manasseh his father had done. There is not one original act in these verses: every clause compares him with his father. He did as Manasseh had done, walked in the way his father walked, served the idols his father served. The writer finds nothing to say about Amon that is Amon’s own. Born in about the thirty-third year of that reign, he grew up with his father’s religion all around him; whatever Manasseh’s late repentance removed, Amon went back to the images his father had made (2 Chronicles 33:22). He inherited all of the idolatry and none of the long reign.

The people of the land. The court kills the king, and “the people of the land”, ordinary Judeans, the free landowning families outside the palace, hunt down the conspirators, execute them, and put the dead king’s eight-year-old son on the throne. They had no reason to love Amon; what they would not have was a palace coup deciding who rules the house of David.

Not the first time. When Athaliah was killed it was “all the people of the land” who rejoiced, pulled down the house of Baal and stood in the temple courts as the child was crowned (11:18–20). Twice now, at the two moments when the line of David has been most exposed, what held was not the army, the court or the priesthood on its own, but ordinary people who had decided that some things were not going to happen in their country.

Made Josiah his son king in his place. Two kings lie buried in a garden, and an eight-year-old is on the throne. Josiah is the grandson of the man who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and put a carved Asherah in the temple, and the son of a man murdered in his own house before the boy was nine. Everything he has seen of the religion of Judah is what Manasseh built. The next chapter is his.

21.theology:
Fifty-five years (v. 1). The longest reign in either kingdom was given to its worst king and ended peacefully in his own garden. God's patience is not his approval.

The promise quoted inside the desecration (vv. 4, 7). Twice the writer sets God's own words about the temple in the same verse as what was put in it, including the condition attached at the dedication. God's promises were never a guarantee that could be held against him while his people broke covenant.

More evil than the nations (v. 9). Israel held the land only because the previous occupants had been driven out for what they did in it. Judah has now done worse than they did. And the blame is assigned in both directions: the people did not listen, and Manasseh led them astray.

Builders' tools used backwards (v. 13). The line and plumb that build are used to condemn, and they are Samaria's and Ahab's: the standard already applied to the north is stretched over the south.

What Kings leaves out (v. 18). Chronicles records Manasseh's humbling, prayer and restoration (2 Chron. 33:11-13); Kings, building the case for the exile, records the damage. Together they say two things at once: the worst king in Judah's history was forgiven, and the sentence on the nation stood (23:26). Being forgiven does not undo the consequences, and neither truth cancels the other.

The people of the land (v. 24). For the second time (the first was after Athaliah, 11:18-20), ordinary Judeans with no office at all keep a palace clique from deciding who sits on David's throne.
21.examples:
Then: A boy came to the throne at twelve, reigned for fifty-five years, put a carved image inside the house God had promised to put his name in, filled the city from one end to the other with innocent blood, and died peacefully and was buried in his own garden.

Now: Three things. First, if you measure whether something is right by how long it has lasted or how well it has gone, this reign settles the question: the longest and most stable stretch in Judah's history was its worst. Second, Manasseh is the strongest case in Scripture against the idea that anyone has gone too far to be received. If you fear you have, his story is written for you. He was not received for making up the damage, which he could not do, but because he humbled himself before a God who hears; the way back is the same for us, confession resting on Christ's obedience counted as ours (1 John 1:9; Romans 5:19). And being received does not undo what was built: if you are forgiven and still living in the wreckage, you are in the ordinary Christian position. Third, twice in this book the thing that saved the promise was ordinary people who decided that something was not going to happen in their country.

keyVerse.quote: But they did not listen, and Manasseh led them astray to do more evil than the nations had done whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel.
keyVerse.note: This is the writer’s verdict on Manasseh’s reign, and it explains the exile before it happens: Israel held the land only because the nations before them were driven out for these sins, and Judah has now done worse. The blame falls on both the king who led and the people who would not listen.

21.reflection:
Manasseh’s reign was the longest and most stable in Judah’s history, and the worst (vv. 1–2). Why do we so easily take long success as a sign of God’s approval, in our own lives or in churches and nations?

Molech was thought to secure the future at the price of a child (v. 6). What do people in our culture, or in our own homes, sacrifice their children to, and how does Romans 8:32 change the way we think about security?

Twice the writer quotes God’s promise about the temple beside the idols set up in it (vv. 4, 7–8). How might Christians today treat God’s promises as a guarantee while ignoring his commands?

Chronicles records that Manasseh repented and was forgiven, yet the sentence on Judah still stood (2 Chronicles 33:12–13; 2 Kings 23:26). How does his story help someone who fears they have gone too far, and someone who is forgiven but still living with the consequences of their sin?

22.title: The Book of the Law Found
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jedidah the daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath.<sup>2</sup>And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the way of David his father, and he did not turn aside to the right or to the left.<sup>3</sup>In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, the king sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, the secretary, to the house of the LORD, saying,<sup>4</sup>"Go up to Hilkiah the high priest, that he may count the money that has been brought into the house of the LORD, which the keepers of the threshold have collected from the people.<sup>5</sup>And let it be given into the hand of the workmen who have the oversight of the house of the LORD, and let them give it to the workmen who are at the house of the LORD, repairing the house<sup>6</sup>(that is, to the carpenters, and to the builders, and to the masons), and let them use it for buying timber and quarried stone to repair the house.<sup>7</sup>But no accounting shall be asked from them for the money that is delivered into their hand, for they deal honestly."<sup>8</sup>And Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD." And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.<sup>9</sup>And Shaphan the secretary came to the king, and reported to the king, "Your servants have emptied out the money that was found in the house and have delivered it into the hand of the workmen who have the oversight of the house of the LORD."<sup>10</sup>Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read it before the king.<sup>11</sup>When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes.<sup>12</sup>And the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Achbor the son of Micaiah, and Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant, saying,<sup>13</sup>"Go, inquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book, to do according to all that is written concerning us."<sup>14</sup>So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter), and they talked with her.<sup>15</sup>And she said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: 'Tell the man who sent you to me,<sup>16</sup>Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will bring disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, all the words of the book that the king of Judah has read.<sup>17</sup>Because they have forsaken me and have made offerings to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the work of their hands, therefore my wrath will be kindled against this place, and it will not be quenched.<sup>18</sup>But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Regarding the words that you have heard,<sup>19</sup>because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the LORD, when you heard how I spoke against this place and against its inhabitants, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and you have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD.<sup>20</sup>Therefore, behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place.'" And they brought back word to the king.
22.overview:
Where we are. Manasseh and Amon have filled fifty-seven years with idols and innocent blood, and the prophets have pronounced Jerusalem’s sentence (21:10–15). Now the eight-year-old crowned by the people of the land has grown up. Josiah, the best king since David, is the last real hope of Judah’s history, and this chapter tells how God’s word found him.

The message. God’s word can be lost inside a busy, well-run religion, and when it is found it must be heard as true and obeyed, whatever it costs. Josiah’s heart breaks under it, and God hears him; but the word also says that the judgment on Judah will not be turned back. God’s verdict on a nation does not move, and yet he notices one man tearing his clothes and weeping.

Why it was said. The exiles knew that Judah’s best king had come too late. This chapter told them why: not because God ignored repentance, but because the nation’s sin had run for generations and its people had not truly turned (see the introduction). It also showed them, without the temple, what to do with the book that survived it.

How the chapter makes its case. Josiah reigns rightly, turning neither right nor left, and repairs the temple through an old, honest system (vv. 1–7). In the middle of the work the high priest finds the Book of the Law; the secretary reads it to the king, who tears his clothes and sends to inquire of the LORD (vv. 8–13). Huldah the prophetess answers: the disaster written in the book will come and the wrath will not be quenched, but because the king humbled himself he will be gathered to his grave in peace before it falls (vv. 14–20).

Where it leads. First by the need it exposes. Even a penitent king who obeyed with all his heart could not quench the wrath that his people’s sin had kindled; another King had to keep every word of the book and bear that wrath himself, so that “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Then by pattern: Deuteronomy’s king who keeps the law beside him and turns neither right nor left is a portrait Josiah only partly filled, and Christ fills it. And the book that broke Josiah’s heart is the book of which the risen Christ “interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

For us. A church, or a Christian, can keep everything running while the Bible lies unopened. Read it, and let it cut you: assume it is true, apply it to yourself, and ask what to do. And if you obey God in something that will not mend what is broken, your obedience is not wasted: he sees, and he hears the humble.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good king inherits a temple in need of repair and an honest system for repairing it. Josiah comes to the throne at eight and reigns thirty-one years, walking in the way of David and turning neither right nor left, the very words the law uses of a king who keeps it (vv. 1–2). In his eighteenth year he sends his secretary Shaphan to the high priest Hilkiah about the temple fund: the money collected at the doors is to go straight to the workmen, with no accounting asked of the foremen, “for they deal honestly” (vv. 3–7). It is Jehoiada’s arrangement from two hundred years before, still working through the worst reigns in Judah’s history.
verseByVerse.theology: Honesty is the quiet virtue that keeps the house of God standing. The workmen in verse 7 are trusted because they have earned it, and the whole repair depends on people nobody will ever praise by name.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, the faithful arrangements we set up in a church or a home, for money, for prayer, for reading Scripture, can go on serving long after us. That is a reason to build them carefully.

verseByVerse.quote: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jedidah the daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath. And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the way of David his father, and he did not turn aside to the right or to the left. In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, the king sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, the secretary, to the house of the LORD, saying, "Go up to Hilkiah the high priest, that he may count the money that has been brought into the house of the LORD, which the keepers of the threshold have collected from the people. And let it be given into the hand of the workmen who have the oversight of the house of the LORD, and let them give it to the workmen who are at the house of the LORD, repairing the house (that is, to the carpenters, and to the builders, and to the masons), and let them use it for buying timber and quarried stone to repair the house. But no accounting shall be asked from them for the money that is delivered into their hand, for they deal honestly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah is the king Deuteronomy describes, turning neither right nor left, and he begins his temple repair through an honest system set up two centuries earlier and still working through the worst reigns in Judah’s history.

He did not turn aside to the right or to the left. The last clause of verse 2 is a quotation. It is what Joshua was told at the beginning of the conquest (Joshua 1:7), and what Deuteronomy requires of a king who keeps a copy of the law beside him and reads it all his days, so “that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left” (Deuteronomy 17:20). It is a striking thing to say of a man who, as this chapter will show, had very likely never seen a copy of that law.

The King who matched the portrait. Deuteronomy’s king, who keeps the law beside him and turns neither right nor left, is a portrait no king of Judah fully matched, Josiah included. The one who did is Christ, who could say, in words Hebrews puts on his lips, “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book” (Hebrews 10:7).

In the eighteenth year of King Josiah. He is now twenty-six. Chronicles fills in what Kings compresses: he began to seek God at sixteen and started purging the high places at twenty (2 Chronicles 34:3). The reform was several years old before anything in this chapter happened.

Let it be given into the hand of the workmen. Two hundred years earlier Jehoiada set a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar. The money was counted by the king’s secretary and the high priest together, paid straight to the carpenters, builders and masons, and the foremen were not audited, “for they dealt honestly” (12:9–15). Josiah’s instructions are that arrangement, in the same words down to the list of trades. Count what it survived: Ahaz, who stripped the building and put a Syrian altar in the courtyard; Hezekiah, who peeled the gold off the doors to pay Sennacherib; Manasseh’s fifty-five years with a carved Asherah inside; Amon. Through all of it the box went on being emptied by two men.

Good arrangements last. A system built properly outlives the man who built it, and a good deal of the wickedness that comes after him. Good arrangements cannot take the place of godliness, but they are not its enemy either. Jehoiada’s chest was doing its work in the reign of the king who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and God often preserves his people through faithful, unglamorous arrangements made by someone long dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — I Have Found the Book of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the building work God’s lost word is found, and a king lets it break his heart. The high priest tells the secretary he has found the Book of the Law in the temple (v. 8). Shaphan reports the accounts first and mentions the book second, then reads it to the king (vv. 9–10). Josiah tears his clothes (v. 11). He does not question the book or set it aside; he believes it, sees how far his nation has fallen from it, and sends five senior men to inquire of the LORD, because “great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us” (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's word can be lost without being rejected. Nobody missed the book, because nobody was looking for it, and a religion can run for years on habit alone.
verseByVerse.examples: God brings his word back by ordinary means. It surfaces not through a reformer searching but in the middle of building work, and his providence is no less at work for being unremarkable.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD." And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it. And Shaphan the secretary came to the king, and reported to the king, "Your servants have emptied out the money that was found in the house and have delivered it into the hand of the workmen who have the oversight of the house of the LORD." Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read it before the king. When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes. And the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Achbor the son of Micaiah, and Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant, saying, "Go, inquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book, to do according to all that is written concerning us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s law had been lost inside his own temple, and when it was found and read, the king believed it at once, saw how far Judah had fallen from it, and tore his clothes in grief and fear. Three men had the same words in the same hour; only one let them break his heart.

I have found the Book of the Law. This is one of the strangest sentences in the Old Testament, and easy to read past: the book was lost. The law of God (most probably Deuteronomy, or the books of Moses together, since the curses that terrify the king read exactly like Deuteronomy 28) had been mislaid in the building that existed to house it. Not stolen or burned: lost, and turned up by accident during building work. Priests, sacrifices, festivals and an honest repair fund all carried on; the machinery ran so smoothly without the book that nobody could say when it had gone.

How it was lost. For the better part of sixty years under Manasseh and Amon that building had an Asherah in it and altars to the stars in its courts. By the time it was safe to want the law, very likely nobody remembered where it had been kept. And the reform did not begin with the book. Josiah had been purging shrines for six years already, on conscience and whatever fragments of the truth had come down to him, doing his best in the dark with no idea what he did not have.

In the church today. Any church can end up here, and nobody announces it when it happens. Nobody rejects the Bible; one generation stops opening it, the next does not know it used to be opened, and the third would not know where to look. Ask what in your own week would carry on exactly as it does if the Bible quietly went missing.

Hilkiah the priest has given me a book. Read the order of the report. First the accounts: the money handed over, the works proceeding. Then “a book”: not “the” book. The most consequential discovery in the history of that kingdom is the second item on a routine agenda, after the financial update.

Shaphan read it before the king. Shaphan had read it already, and it seems not to have changed his day. Then he does the one thing that matters: he reads it aloud to the king. Two of the three men had the words first. What broke Josiah was hearing Scripture read aloud while he sat and listened. Familiarity with Scripture and being cut by it are not the same thing. Five men are then sent to inquire, and one name matters later: Ahikam the son of Shaphan (see the note below).

When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes. Look at what he does not do with a book nobody in living memory has read. He does not question whether it is genuine, appoint a commission to consider in what sense its harder sections might be understood, observe that the religion of Judah has been getting on perfectly well without it, or put it in the treasury as an interesting antiquity. He assumes it is true, applies it at once to himself and his people, and sends to find out what to do. What he heard in it was not information about ceremonies but a measurement of the distance between what God had said and what his nation had done.

What the wrath of the LORD is. Most of us hear “wrath” and picture a temper: a God who loses patience and lashes out. God’s wrath is his settled opposition to everything that ruins what he loves, and Judah had filled his city with idols and innocent blood. A God who felt nothing about murdered children would not be kinder; he would simply not care. The gospel does not deny the wrath; it shows where it went. God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25), so that those justified by that blood will “be saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9). When a hard verse about God’s anger meets you, neither explain it away nor cower: let it show you how much your sin matters to him, then look at the cross, where that wrath has already fallen. See Wrath of God.

Because our fathers have not obeyed. That is true, but Huldah’s reply will not let his own generation off (see the note on vv. 14–20).

Was Deuteronomy written in Josiah’s day? Many scholars hold that it was composed then and “found” to support his reform. But it was recognised at once as the law of Moses, and Josiah tore his clothes because their fathers had not kept it (v. 13), which makes best sense of an old, neglected book. Copies had probably been lost or suppressed in Manasseh’s long apostasy, and one was rediscovered in the temple. Scholars still debate how and when Deuteronomy reached its final form; the account itself presents a law of Moses recovered, not composed, and this commentary reads it so (see the introduction).
verseByVerse.note: Shaphan's son Ahikam (v. 12) later protected Jeremiah (Jer. 26:24), and Ahikam's son Gedaliah became governor after the fall (25:22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Tell the Man Who Sent You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s answer through Huldah confirms the judgment and honours the man who humbled himself. The five men go to Huldah the prophetess in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem (v. 14). Her answer has two halves. To the nation: every word of the book will come true, because the people have forsaken the LORD, and his wrath “will not be quenched” (vv. 15–17). To the king: because his heart was penitent, because he humbled himself, tore his clothes and wept, God has heard him, and he will be gathered to his grave in peace without seeing the disaster (vv. 18–20). The verdict on the nation does not change, but God answers the one who trembles at his word.
verseByVerse.theology: God's word does not depend on the rank of the one who carries it. The writer records the visit to Huldah without a word of explanation, and her answer carries thus says the LORD three times.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who has wept over sin: in the middle of a sentence about wrath that will not be quenched, God stops to say that he saw one man tear his clothes and cry. Tears of repentance are never unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter), and they talked with her. And she said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: 'Tell the man who sent you to me, Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will bring disaster upon this place and upon its inhabitants, all the words of the book that the king of Judah has read. Because they have forsaken me and have made offerings to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the work of their hands, therefore my wrath will be kindled against this place, and it will not be quenched. But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Regarding the words that you have heard, because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the LORD, when you heard how I spoke against this place and against its inhabitants, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and you have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD. Therefore, behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place.'" And they brought back word to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Huldah God confirms that every word of the book will fall on Judah and his wrath will not be quenched, but he tells the king that he has seen his penitent heart and his tears, and will spare him the sight of the disaster. The verdict on the nation does not move; the man who humbled himself under it is spoken to personally.

Went to Huldah the prophetess. The high priest and four of the most senior men in the kingdom, on the most urgent business of the reign, walk across Jerusalem to a house in the Second Quarter and ask a woman. The writer gives her name, her office, her husband’s post and her district, in the tone he uses for anybody else’s address, and moves on. There were other prophets: Jeremiah had been called five years before, and Zephaniah was preaching in this reign. Nobody in the account thinks the choice of Huldah needs comment.

Tell the man who sent you to me. Everyone else in this chapter calls him the king. She calls him “the man”, not from rudeness (the rest of her message to him is extraordinarily tender) but because she speaks for God, and before God’s word a king is a man like any other.

All the words of the book. The first thing she says is that the book is right: not a syllable of it is to be discounted. And she says “they have forsaken me”, not “your fathers”. Josiah had put the blame one generation back, where reformers usually put it; Huldah includes the people standing in the city now.

It will not be quenched. This is the hardest phrase in the chapter. The most thorough reform in the history of either kingdom is about to begin, and before it starts the prophet tells the king it will not put the fire out. Josiah goes on to do everything in the next chapter anyway: every high place, every idol, every medium, a Passover such as had not been kept since the judges. Obedience is not a bargain. He did not clean out the country to buy off the judgment; he did it because it was right, knowing the judgment would still come. If you are obeying God in something that will not fix what is broken, you are where Josiah stood, and your obedience is not wasted.

The wrath that was quenched. No reform could quench this fire. Only one King ever kept every word of the book, and he did not die “in peace”: he bore the wrath himself, so that “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

Because your heart was penitent. Now the second half of the message, and the change of tone is the point. God has just said his wrath will not be quenched, and in the next breath he mentions that he noticed a man tearing his clothes. “Your heart was penitent … you humbled yourself … torn your clothes and wept”: two of the four are physical, and God names them as things he saw and is answering, as in Hezekiah’s sickroom two chapters ago, “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears” (20:5). This is the one to whom God says he will look: “he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:2).

You shall be gathered to your grave in peace. A careful reader will stop at “in peace”, because Josiah does not die peacefully. He goes out to Megiddo, is killed by Pharaoh Neco (Chronicles adds that archers shot him), and is carried back to Jerusalem dead (23:29–30). The answer is in the clause that follows, which defines the term: “and your eyes shall not see all the disaster that I will bring upon this place.” That is what the peace consists of: dying before the catastrophe. He is buried in his own tomb, mourned by his own people, in a kingdom still standing. Twenty-three years later the city is a burnt-out shell and its last king watches his sons executed before his eyes are put out. Measured against that, being killed at thirty-nine and buried by a nation that loved you is peace. His death was still a loss, and Judah wept for it; but God spared his servant the sight of what was coming, a mercy that does not look like one.

Why go to Huldah, a woman? She was a prophetess living near the palace, known and trusted, and God spoke his word through her. Prophetesses served God in Israel (Miriam, Deborah), as women prophesied in the early church (Acts 21:9). This was God’s word given directly, not the office of elder or priest, which Scripture gives to men (1 Timothy 2:12). Christians differ in good faith on how far that verse reaches; this commentary takes it to concern the elder’s office, not the gifts God gives to women.

Uncertain wording. The “Second Quarter” (Hebrew Mishneh, “second” or “double”) was probably the newer district on Jerusalem’s western hill, brought inside the walls in Hezekiah’s day; Zephaniah, preaching in this same reign, names it too (Zephaniah 1:10). Its exact bounds are not known. Likewise “keeper of the wardrobe” (v. 14) does not say whose wardrobe: most take it to be the royal one, though it may have been the priests’ vestments.

22.theology:
A system outliving its builder (vv. 3-7). Verse 7 quotes 12:15: Jehoiada's arrangement kept working through two centuries of ungodliness, including Manasseh's fifty-five years with an Asherah in the building. God often preserves his people through faithful, unglamorous arrangements made by someone long dead.

Lost in the temple (v. 8). The book was mislaid, not repudiated, and the services went on and the accounts balanced without it. Neglect, not rebellion, is the usual way God's word is lost: one generation stops opening it, the next does not know it used to be opened, and the third would not know where to look.

Three men, the same words (vv. 8-11). Hilkiah found it, Shaphan read it and reported it after the money, Josiah heard it and tore his clothes. The difference between them was not what they knew; it was whether they let the word cut them to the heart.

What he did with it (v. 13). He assumed it was true, applied it to himself and his nation, and asked what to do. What he heard in it was not ceremonial information but a measurement of the distance between what God had said and what his country had done.

Huldah (v. 14). With Jeremiah and Zephaniah in the city, the delegation goes to a prophetess, and the writer offers no explanation or defence. She calls the king of Judah the man who sent you to me.

It will not be quenched (v. 17). Josiah is told, before he starts, that the most thorough reform either kingdom ever saw will not avert the judgment, and he carries it out anyway, completely. For the Christian there is one further word: the wrath no reform could quench was borne in full by the one King who kept every word of the book, so that there is now no condemnation for those who are in him (Romans 8:1).

Torn clothes, noticed (v. 19). The verdict on the nation does not move, but God names what he saw: a man tearing his robes and weeping (compare 20:5).

In peace (v. 20), honestly. Josiah dies violently at Megiddo, but the promise is defined by its next clause: he does not see the disaster. He is buried in his own city, mourned, in a kingdom still standing.
22.examples:
Then: A civil servant walked into the palace with a financial report and a book, gave the accounts first, mentioned the book second in the flattest possible words (Hilkiah the priest has given me a book), and then read aloud the law of God to a king who had very likely never heard it in his life.

Now: Three things. First, how it got lost. Nobody in Judah decided to abandon the Scriptures; the machinery simply ran without the book. Ask what in your own week would carry on exactly as it does if the Bible quietly went missing. Second, the three men had the same words in the same hour, and only one tore his clothes. Familiarity with Scripture and being cut by it are not the same thing. Third, verse 17 with verse 19. He was told plainly that his reform would not avert the disaster, and did all of it anyway, because the God who had made Judah his own was worth obeying. If you are obeying God in something that will not fix what is broken, you are where Josiah stood. Your obedience is not wasted, and you do not do it on your own strength: the Spirit God promised to put within his people is the one who keeps them walking in his ways (Ezekiel 36:27).

keyVerse.quote: because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the LORD, when you heard how I spoke against this place and against its inhabitants, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and you have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: Huldah’s message holds both halves of the chapter in one verse: the sentence on Jerusalem stands, and God has heard the man who trembled at it. It shows what the found book is meant to do in anyone who hears it, and how God answers a humbled heart.

22.reflection:
The Book of the Law was lost in the temple, and the religion of Judah ran without it (v. 8). What in your own week, or in your church’s life, would carry on exactly as it does if the Bible quietly went missing?

Hilkiah, Shaphan and Josiah all had the same words, but only the king tore his clothes (vv. 8–11). What makes the difference between knowing Scripture and being cut by it, and how can we put ourselves in the way of the second?

Josiah was told before he began that his reform would not avert the judgment, and he obeyed anyway (vv. 17; 23:1–25). Where are you obeying God in something that may not fix what is broken, and what keeps such obedience from being a bargain with God?

God noticed Josiah’s torn clothes and tears (v. 19). How does it help to know that God sees the humble response of a single person, even when the larger situation does not change? How does Romans 8:1 go beyond what Josiah was promised?

23.title: Josiah's Reform
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the king sent, and all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem were gathered to him.<sup>2</sup>And the king went up to the house of the LORD, and with him all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the priests and the prophets, all the people, both small and great. And he read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And the king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all his heart and all his soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. But he took Jehoahaz away, and he came to Egypt and died there.<sup>35</sup>And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh, but he taxed the land to give the money according to the command of Pharaoh. He exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, from everyone according to his assessment, to give it to Pharaoh Neco.<sup>36</sup>Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zebidah the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah.<sup>37</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done.
23.overview:
Where we are.
