The Book of the Law has been found in the temple, Josiah has torn his clothes, and Huldah has told him two things: the disaster written in the book will come, and he will die in peace before it does (22:14–20). This chapter shows what he did with that answer, and then what became of Judah when he was gone.

The message. When God’s word is heard, it must be obeyed wholeheartedly, at once and to the roots, and God honours such obedience in the strongest words he uses of anyone. Yet even the best king’s reform could not change his people’s hearts or undo generations of sin: “Still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great wrath” (v. 26). What Judah needed was more than a good king; it needed a new heart.

Why it was said. The exiles knew Josiah’s reform had happened, and that Jerusalem fell twenty-three years after his death. This chapter told them that the fault was not in God’s faithfulness or in Josiah’s obedience, but in a people who joined the covenant outwardly and never returned with their whole heart (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Josiah reads the whole book to the whole nation and leads them in a covenant to keep it (vv. 1–3). He clears the temple, the city and the land of every idol, down to Topheth and the shrines Solomon built (vv. 4–14). At Bethel he fulfils to the letter a prophecy that named him three hundred years before, and the reform reaches the towns of Samaria (vv. 15–20). He keeps a Passover unmatched since the judges, puts away the mediums, and is praised in the words of the Shema (vv. 21–25). Then the turn: God’s wrath still stands (vv. 26–27); Josiah dies at Megiddo (vv. 28–30); and Egypt deposes one son and installs another, who taxes his people and does evil (vv. 31–37).

Where it leads. First by the need it exposes. The most complete reform in Israel’s history changed the land and left the heart untouched; Jeremiah, who watched it, answered with God’s promise of a new covenant, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), which Christ has brought (Hebrews 8:6–13). Then by pattern: Josiah kept the Shema better than any king, but only Jesus loved God with all his heart, soul and strength without fail, and his obedience is counted to his people. And by promise: the Passover Josiah restored pointed to the true Lamb, for “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

For us. Begin with God’s word, and let obedience follow at once and go to the roots, even where it means pulling down something a revered person built. Do not mistake outward reform for a changed heart, in a church or in yourself; only the Spirit writes the law within. And if you are doing right in a situation it will not repair, you have not made a mistake: God saw Josiah, and he sees you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — And All the People Joined in the Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Reform begins with God’s word read aloud and a covenant sworn, and then it reaches into every corner where idols had been allowed to stand. Josiah gathers all the people, small and great, reads them the Book of the Covenant himself, and binds himself and them to keep it (vv. 1–3). Then the clearance: Baal’s vessels burned and their ashes taken to Bethel (v. 4), idolatrous priests deposed (v. 5), Manasseh’s Asherah ground to dust (v. 6), the cult prostitutes’ rooms in the temple pulled down (v. 7), the high places defiled from Geba to Beersheba while their priests are fed but kept from the altar (vv. 8–9), Topheth defiled (v. 10), the sun’s horses and chariots removed (vv. 11–12), and at last the shrines Solomon built three centuries before (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: True reform begins with God's word heard, not with a programme. Josiah does not tell the people what the book requires; he reads it to them, and everything that follows comes out of that reading.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, sin that has been tolerated long enough stops looking like sin and starts looking like part of the furniture. Josiah's thoroughness is a model for dealing with what has settled in: not trimmed, but removed so that it cannot be brought back.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent, and all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem were gathered to him. And the king went up to the house of the LORD, and with him all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the priests and the prophets, all the people, both small and great. And he read in their hearing all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. And the king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all his heart and all his soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people joined in the covenant. And the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest and the priests of the second order and the keepers of the threshold to bring out of the temple of the LORD all the vessels made for Baal, for Asherah, and for all the host of heaven. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of the Kidron and carried their ashes to Bethel. And he deposed the priests whom the kings of Judah had ordained to make offerings in the high places at the cities of Judah and around Jerusalem; those also who burned incense to Baal, to the sun and the moon and the constellations and all the host of the heavens. And he brought out the Asherah from the house of the LORD, outside Jerusalem, to the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron and beat it to dust and cast the dust of it upon the graves of the common people. And he broke down the houses of the male cult prostitutes who were in the house of the LORD, where the women wove hangings for the Asherah. And he brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places where the priests had made offerings, from Geba to Beersheba. And he broke down the high places of the gates that were at the entrance of the gate of Joshua the governor of the city, which were on one's left at the gate of the city. However, the priests of the high places did not come up to the altar of the LORD in Jerusalem, but they ate unleavened bread among their brothers. And he defiled Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, that no one might burn his son or his daughter as an offering to Molech. And he removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun, at the entrance to the house of the LORD, by the chamber of Nathan-melech the chamberlain, which was in the precincts. And he burned the chariots of the sun with fire. And the altars on the roof of the upper chamber of Ahaz, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars that Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the LORD, he pulled down and broke in pieces and cast the dust of them into the brook Kidron. And the king defiled the high places that were east of Jerusalem, to the south of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. And he broke in pieces the pillars and cut down the Asherim and filled their places with the bones of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah begins with God’s word, reading the whole book to the whole nation and binding himself and the people to it by covenant; then he removes every idol in the land with a thoroughness no king had shown, down to the shrines Solomon built three centuries before.

He read in their hearing. The reform does not start with a policy or a demolition order. The king stands up before “all the people, both small and great” and works through, out loud, a document most of them have never heard.

The king stood by the pillar. This is the spot where a seven-year-old stood with a crown on his head while Athaliah shouted treason (11:14). Kings of Judah were made there, and here one of them binds himself by covenant, a solemn sworn commitment to the LORD and his law. Then comes the thing a reformer cannot manufacture: “all the people joined in the covenant.” Whatever happens later (see v. 26), on that day they were with him.

Carried their ashes to Bethel. He burns the vessels made for Baal and Asherah in the Kidron valley and has the ashes carried a dozen miles north to Bethel, a calculated insult and a promise of what is coming: Jeroboam’s shrine will be the rubbish tip for Judah’s idols before Josiah has finished with it. The idolatrous priests, a whole clergy appointed by earlier kings of Judah, are put out of office in a day (v. 5).

He brought out the Asherah. This was Manasseh’s carved image, still standing in the building after all this time, and the thoroughness is the point. It is carried out, burned and beaten to powder, and the powder is scattered over a public graveyard, so that it is unclean and can never be gathered up or venerated. It is what Moses did to the golden calf (Exodus 32:20). There is a way of removing a thing that leaves people able to go back to it, and this is not it.

Who were in the house of the LORD. Read the location in verse 7 again. There were living quarters for cult prostitutes inside the temple precincts, with a workroom where women wove for the Asherah. It was staffed, it had premises, and it had a supply chain: that is what fifty-five years of Manasseh and two of Amon left behind, long enough to become an institution.

From Geba to Beersheba. The entire kingdom, north border to south. Six good kings before him had been given the same footnote, “nevertheless, the high places were not taken away”; Hezekiah had cleared them and Manasseh had rebuilt them.

But they ate unleavened bread among their brothers. Verse 9 is easy to skim, and it shows the shape of a good reform. The priests who had served at the shrines may never again serve at the altar in Jerusalem: they are out of office, permanently. But they are not put out on the road; the priestly provision that belonged to their family still reaches them. Ezekiel later states the same principle for the Levites who went astray: they may not come near to serve as priests, yet God will “appoint them to keep charge of the temple” (Ezekiel 44:10–14). Putting a man out of an office he has disqualified himself from is one thing and punishing him is another, and the difference between reform and revenge is usually visible in exactly this detail.

He defiled Topheth. Ahaz and Manasseh had each burned a son there, and the practice was not confined to palaces: the stated purpose is “that no one might burn his son or his daughter as an offering to Molech”, which means people still were.

The name Gehenna. The name of that valley outlived the fires. Where the ESV prints “hell” on the lips of the Lord Jesus, its footnote gives the Greek, Gehenna: the name of this valley, which he uses again and again (Matthew 5:22, 29–30; 10:28; 18:9; 23:33; Mark 9:43–48). He did not invent an image. When he wanted a word for the place of final loss, he took the name of a real valley on the edge of Jerusalem, where the people of God had burned their own children.

The chariots of the sun. The kings of Judah had installed a sun cult at the entrance of the house of the LORD, with horses and chariots dedicated to the sun and an official housed beside them, whose name and chamber the writer knows. It was a department with a budget. The roof altars on Ahaz’s upper chamber were for the host of heaven, put where the sky seemed closest; Jeremiah says the whole city was burning offerings on its housetops to all the host of heaven (Jeremiah 19:13).

Which Solomon the king of Israel had built. Verse 13 has been waiting three hundred years. Solomon built these shrines for his foreign wives (1 Kings 11:5–7). Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah and Jotham were all commended, and all left them; so did Hezekiah, who cleared the high places and broke the serpent. Nobody wanted to be the man who took a hammer to something Solomon built, and the writer will not let the name go: he names the wisest man who ever ruled the nation, three centuries after his death, as the builder of the last idols in Judah. What a great man puts up at the end of his life can stand for generations, very often because nobody can bear to be the one to pull it down. Ask what stands in your church or your family for no better reason than that.

Filled their places with the bones of men. Human bones made the ground unclean under the law. He is not merely closing the sites but making them unusable by anyone who might reopen them after he is dead. His grandfather had rebuilt everything his great-grandfather pulled down, so that was a lesson he had learned at home.

Isn’t hell a barbaric idea? Few Christian beliefs embarrass modern people more. Hell sounds like the leftover of a crueller age, a threat to keep people in line. But notice where Jesus found the word: not in a torture chamber of the imagination, but in the valley where children had been burned for the gods of power and plenty. Gehenna is, first of all, God’s final no to Topheth. A world in which that valley never answers for what was done there would not be a kinder world; it would be a world in which those children did not matter. Our objection, that cruelty must not have the last word, comes from the same place as the doctrine. C. S. Lewis added in The Problem of Pain that the lost are, in a sense, rebels to the end, and that the doors of hell are “locked on the inside”. Yet Jesus did more than warn of Gehenna. He was led out of this same city to suffer “outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), and bore the judgment himself, so that no one who flees to him need ever go there.

Uncertain wording. Several words in these verses are rare. “Constellations” (v. 5) translates a word found only here, probably the signs of the zodiac or the planets. The “male cult prostitutes” (v. 7) are literally “holy ones”, men attached to the shrine, whose exact role is debated; and the women wove what the Hebrew calls “houses” for the Asherah, probably hangings or coverings for the image. “The high places of the gates” (v. 8) is unclear; some scholars suggest that a slightly different reading gives shrines of “goat idols”. And “the mount of corruption” (v. 13) is probably a bitter play on words: in Hebrew it sounds like “the mount of anointing oil”, a name for the Mount of Olives. None of these touches the meaning of the passage.
verseByVerse.note: Topheth, in the Valley of Hinnom, was where children were sacrificed to Molech.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — According to the Word That the Man of God Proclaimed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word proves true to the letter, and the reform reaches its height. At Bethel Josiah destroys Jeroboam’s altar and burns bones on it, exactly as a man of God foretold by name three hundred years before (vv. 15–16). He spares that prophet’s tomb, and with it the bones of the old prophet who once deceived him (vv. 17–18), and does the same through the towns of Samaria (vv. 19–20). Then he keeps the Passover as the book prescribes, such as had not been kept since the days of the judges (vv. 21–23), puts away the mediums and household gods (v. 24), and receives the highest verdict in Kings, in the words of the Shema (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: God's word does not lapse with time. A sentence spoken at Bethel three centuries earlier waited, unfulfilled, through thirteen generations, and was kept to the letter by a man who did not set out to fulfil it.
verseByVerse.examples: The Passover of verses 21-23 is the right ending to all the demolition. Reform only clears the ground. What fills it is the Passover, the rescue from Egypt remembered and kept as it is written.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, the altar at Bethel, the high place erected by Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, that altar with the high place he pulled down and burned, reducing it to dust. He also burned the Asherah. And as Josiah turned, he saw the tombs there on the mount. And he sent and took the bones out of the tombs and burned them on the altar and defiled it, according to the word of the LORD that the man of God proclaimed, who had predicted these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Bethel, where the northern kingdom’s false worship began, Josiah destroys Jeroboam’s altar and burns human bones on it, fulfilling to the letter a prophecy that named him three hundred years before he was born.

The altar at Bethel. Bethel is not in his kingdom. It lies in what had been Israel and is now an Assyrian province, and a king of Judah can act there because Assyria is collapsing: Nineveh will fall within a decade, and nobody is left to object.

Erected by Jeroboam the son of Nebat. The object he goes for is the altar where the northern kingdom’s whole history began: two calves, at Bethel and Dan, set up by a capable man afraid of losing his people to Jerusalem. Jeroboam’s sin is named in the verdict on king after king who followed him.

Josiah by name. Go back to the day that altar was built. Jeroboam stood at it, about to burn incense at the festival he had invented, when a man from Judah, whose name we are never told, cried against it: “O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: ‘Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you’” (1 Kings 13:2). That was about three hundred years before this day. Not a description or a title, but a name, three centuries before the child was conceived, spoken to a king who tried to have the man arrested and got a withered hand for it.

As Josiah turned, he saw the tombs. He is not consciously fulfilling a prophecy when he starts; he turns, sees tombs on the hillside, and gives an order. The writer supplies the connection afterwards, “according to the word of the LORD that the man of God proclaimed”, as a footnote to an otherwise ordinary piece of demolition. God’s word does not need the people who fulfil it to be aware of it.

Was the name written in afterwards? Many critical scholars think the name was added to 1 Kings 13 after the event. That is a judgment about whether God foretells, not something the text itself suggests. Scripture presents it as a word spoken at Bethel and kept for three centuries, and a reader who believes God declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10) has no reason to doubt it. The God who named Josiah ahead of time is the God who named the town where the Christ would be born (Micah 5:2). It is fair to say plainly that this is where the two readings part.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said, "What is that monument that I see?" And the men of the city told him, "It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and predicted these things that you have done against the altar at Bethel." And he said, "Let him be; let no man move his bones." So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah spares the tomb of the prophet who foretold all this, and with it the bones of the old prophet who had lied to him, because the old man had asked to be buried beside the one whose word he believed.

What is that monument that I see? He asks about one of the graves, and the local people know exactly. Three hundred years on, in a resettled foreign province, the men of Bethel could still tell you whose tomb that was and what he had said.

The two prophets’ graves. This is one of the quietest and best-arranged things in Scripture. The man of God from Judah had been told to eat nothing and go home by another road. An old prophet at Bethel came after him and lied to him (“an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD”), brought him back and gave him dinner, and on the road home a lion killed him. The old man collected the body, buried it in his own grave and mourned over him. Then he said to his sons: “When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones”, because the word the man of God had cried against the altar would surely come to pass (1 Kings 13:31–32).

Let him be; let no man move his bones. He knew what was coming to that hillside. Three hundred years later a king burning the bones of Bethel says “let him be”, and the writer adds, almost under his breath, “with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria.” The old liar’s remains are spared because they lie next to the honest man’s. He arranged it long beforehand, on the strength of a word he had believed and had not obeyed, and it worked.

Found beside another. The writer does not draw the lesson, but the shape is the gospel’s. The old prophet was spared not for his own record but for whose bones lay beside his. Paul’s hope was the same: to “be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own” (Philippians 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And Josiah removed all the shrines also of the high places that were in the cities of Samaria, which kings of Israel had made, provoking the LORD to anger. He did to them according to all that he had done at Bethel. And he sacrificed all the priests of the high places who were there, on the altars, and burned human bones on them. Then he returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reform reaches the old northern kingdom, and the second half of the Bethel prophecy is fulfilled as Josiah executes the priests of the northern shrines on their own altars.

All the shrines also of the high places that were in the cities of Samaria. The shrines of the northern kingdom had outlived it: the peoples Assyria settled in Samaria had put their own gods in them alongside the LORD (17:29–33). Josiah did to all of them what he had done at Bethel, carrying on what Hezekiah had begun there (2 Chronicles 31:1).

He sacrificed all the priests of the high places. Verse 20 fulfils the rest of the old sentence: “he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you” (1 Kings 13:2). It is a grim verse and exactly what was said. He does this in Samaria and not in Judah, where the deposed priests were left alive and fed (v. 9).

Was it just for Josiah to kill the priests of the high places? These were priests of idolatrous shrines in the north, and the law commanded death for those who led Israel into false worship (Deuteronomy 13:5); 1 Kings 13:2 foretold this very act. The priests in Judah, who had served the LORD at irregular places, were removed from the altar but spared (v. 9). It belonged to the time when Israel was a nation governed by God’s law, and is no model for today.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king commanded all the people, "Keep the Passover to the LORD your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant." For no such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges who judged Israel, or during all the days of the kings of Israel or of the kings of Judah. But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah this Passover was kept to the LORD in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all the burning, the reform ends with a meal: the Passover, kept as the book prescribes and on a scale not seen since the judges, puts the nation back in front of the rescue that made it a nation.

Keep the Passover to the LORD your God. Of everything he could have restored, it is this: the supper that remembers the night Israel came out of Egypt, with the blood on the doorposts and the LORD passing over the houses (see Passover). And it is kept “as it is written in this Book of the Covenant”. Everything in this chapter is measured against a document that had been lost until a few months ago.

Since the days of the judges. Some four hundred years, and this is the last Passover recorded before the exile. Hezekiah had kept a great Passover too (2 Chronicles 30), and each was unmatched in its own terms: Hezekiah’s had no equal since Solomon (2 Chronicles 30:26), Josiah’s none since Samuel and the judges (2 Chronicles 35:18).

In the eighteenth year of King Josiah. This is the year the book was found (22:3). The repairs, the discovery, the reading, Huldah’s word, the covenant, the clearing of the temple and of Bethel, and now the Passover all happened within a single year. The finding of God’s word was followed by obedience at once.

Christ our Passover. Christians read that meal with the end of the story in view. The Lord Jesus kept the Passover in the same city on the night he was betrayed and gave it its meaning: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Josiah’s Passover put Judah back in front of its first rescue; Christ’s death was the rescue every Passover had been pointing to.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Josiah put away the mediums and the necromancers and the household gods and the idols and all the abominations that were seen in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, that he might establish the words of the law that were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the LORD. Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might, according to all the Law of Moses, nor did any like him arise after him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah carries God’s law into private houses, and the writer gives him the highest verdict in Kings, in the very words of the Shema: no king turned to the LORD so wholly.

The mediums and the necromancers. The list in verse 24 is Manasseh’s list from chapter 21, worked back through in reverse. The “household gods” are the teraphim, small figures kept in the home; Rachel stole her father’s (Genesis 31:19), and Michal put one in David’s bed (1 Samuel 19:13). They were used to seek guidance (Ezekiel 21:21; Zechariah 10:2). The reform reached past the temple and the hill shrines into private houses, because the law Josiah had found forbids consulting the dead and the diviners (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and he meant “that he might establish the words of the law” everywhere.

Before him there was no king like him. Verse 25 is the highest verdict pronounced on anybody in these two books, and it is given in borrowed words. “With all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might” is from the Shema, Israel’s daily confession: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). It is very likely a sentence Josiah first heard only months earlier, sitting in a room while his secretary read to him. The commendation is written in the vocabulary of the book he found.

Hezekiah and Josiah compared. Hezekiah was praised in almost the same terms: “there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him” (18:5). He is commended for trust, Josiah for turning with his whole heart according to the law of Moses. Hebrew praise of this kind does not rank the two men; each sentence is true of the thing it praises.

The one who kept it perfectly. Jesus called this sentence “the great and first commandment” (Matthew 22:38). Josiah kept it better than any king before or after him, and still the next verse begins with “Still”. Only one Son of David loved the LORD with all his heart, soul and might without a single failure, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–37 — Still the LORD Did Not Turn
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the best reform cannot turn back a judgment earned over generations. Straight after the highest praise comes “still”: because of Manasseh, the LORD will remove Judah as he removed Israel, and cast off the city and the house that bore his name (vv. 26–27). Josiah goes out against Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo and is killed, and the people crown his son Jehoahaz (vv. 28–30). After three months Neco deposes him and takes him to die in Egypt, installs his brother under a new name, Jehoiakim, and lays a tribute on the land, which Jehoiakim taxes from the people (vv. 31–35). He reigns eleven years and does evil (vv. 36–37).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 26 is harder to accept than anything else in these two books, and it should not be softened: the most thorough reform in either kingdom, by the man verse 25 commends most highly, did not lift the judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: A nation that will not be ruled by God ends up ruled by whoever is strongest. From Josiah's death on, Judah's kings are installed, renamed and deported by foreigners.

verseByVerse.quote: Still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great wrath, by which his anger was kindled against Judah, because of all the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked him. And the LORD said, "I will remove Judah also out of my sight, as I have removed Israel, and I will cast off this city that I have chosen, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, My name shall be there." Now the rest of the acts of Josiah and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after the highest praise, God declares that his sentence on Judah still stands: the reform never reached the people’s hearts, and one good king could not undo what generations of sin had made. Neither verse cancels the other: Josiah was right, and the judgment still came.

Still the LORD did not turn. After everything in this chapter, the reading, the covenant, the clearance, Bethel and the Passover, the sentence stands. Do not soften it or explain it away, and do not let it turn into the idea that the reform was wasted. Verse 25 is in the Bible as well as verse 26, and God said what he thought of Josiah in the strongest words he uses of anybody in these books.

Reform only at the top. The first explanation comes from a man who stood in that city while it happened. Jeremiah, called in Josiah’s thirteenth year, preached right through this reform, and this is his verdict on it: “her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 3:10). The shrines came down because the king sent men to pull them down; the Passover was kept because the king commanded it. The people joined in the covenant, and among them it was outward show. A generation later, when Jerusalem falls, nothing in the population has changed.

Sin’s long consequences. The second is that the results of sin keep running after the sin has stopped. Fifty-five years of Manasseh filled a city with innocent blood and raised two generations who had seen nothing else, and one good king does not undo that, and God does not pretend otherwise. Hold this beside what Chronicles told us of Manasseh himself: taken to Babylon, humbled, forgiven, brought home. The man was pardoned; the country he made was not unmade. Anybody living in the wreckage of something they have truly repented of knows what this is like, and the Bible offers no shortcut. Forgiveness is complete and immediate; consequences run on their own timetable, and sometimes outlive everyone involved.

What no king could do. Jeremiah’s answer to a reform that never reached the heart was not a better reform but a promise from God: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Hebrews says Christ is the mediator of that new covenant (Hebrews 8:6–13). What Josiah could command from a pillar, Christ by his Spirit works within.

I will remove Judah also out of my sight. This is the phrase of chapter 17, used there of the northern kingdom. The writer warned then that “Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God” (17:19), and here the sentence he was building towards is pronounced. And God quotes his own promise about the house, “My name shall be there”, as he casts it off.

verseByVerse.quote: In his days Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt went up to the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates. King Josiah went to meet him, and Pharaoh Neco killed him at Megiddo, as soon as he saw him. And his servants carried him dead in a chariot from Megiddo and brought him to Jerusalem and buried him in his own tomb. And the people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and anointed him, and made him king in his father's place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah goes out against Pharaoh Neco and is killed at Megiddo, yet Huldah’s promise holds: he is buried in his own tomb, mourned in a kingdom still standing, and the people crown his son.

King Josiah went to meet him. Assyria is dying. Pharaoh Neco of Egypt is marching north to prop it up against Babylon, and the road runs through the plain of Megiddo. Josiah goes out to stop him.

Pharaoh Neco killed him at Megiddo. Kings gives it in one flat sentence, with no explanation and no judgment. Chronicles supplies more, and it is uncomfortable: Neco sent envoys telling him that God had not sent him against Judah, and Josiah “did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God”, but disguised himself, and was shot by archers (2 Chronicles 35:20–24). The disguise is a detail we have met before, on another plain, worn by another king who had been told not to go (1 Kings 22:30–34): Ahab put on a common soldier’s armour and an arrow drawn at random found the join in it. The king who turned to the LORD as no king before him died the way the worst king of Israel had.

Megiddo and Armageddon. Armies had fought at Megiddo since before Israel existed; Ahaziah had already died there (9:27); and many readers hear its name in the place John says “in Hebrew is called Armageddon”, the gathering for the last battle (Revelation 16:16).

Buried him in his own tomb. Huldah’s word is kept, in the sense explained at 22:20. He is shot at thirty-nine, but he is carried home by his own servants and buried in his own tomb, and his own people put his son on the throne, in a kingdom still standing. Twenty-three years later the last king of Judah will watch his sons killed before his eyes are put out. “Your eyes shall not see all the disaster”, and they did not.

The mourning in the plain of Megiddo. All Judah mourned for Josiah, and Jeremiah wrote a lament for him (2 Chronicles 35:24–25). Many readers think Zechariah remembers that grief when he describes a day when the house of David will look “on him whom they have pierced” and mourn “as great as the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo” (Zechariah 12:10–11). John saw that day at the cross (John 19:37). The best king, pierced, was mourned by a nation that could not be saved by him; the greater Son of David was pierced for his people, and the mourning over him leads to cleansing.

The people of the land took Jehoahaz. They act for the third time in this book: they crowned Joash after Athaliah, Josiah after Amon’s murder, and now Josiah’s son. It is the last time they are able to choose anything.

Uncertain wording. Older translations such as the KJV say Neco went up “against” the king of Assyria. The Hebrew preposition can carry either sense, and the Babylonian records show Egypt marching to Assyria’s aid, which is why modern versions read “to”.
verseByVerse.note: Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 BC, trying to stop Pharaoh Neco.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done. And Pharaoh Neco put him in bonds at Riblah in the land of Hamath, that he might not reign in Jerusalem, and laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. And Pharaoh Neco made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. But he took Jehoahaz away, and he came to Egypt and died there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt now makes and unmakes Judah’s kings: Jehoahaz is deposed after three months and taken to die in Egypt, and his brother is installed under a name Pharaoh gives him. From here to the end of the book, foreigners choose who sits on David’s throne.

Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old. He was not the eldest son: Eliakim, who replaces him, was two years older (v. 36). The people of the land probably chose the younger brother to keep his father’s policy against Egypt, which would explain why Neco removed him so quickly. Jeremiah calls him Shallum and tells the city to weep not for the dead king but for this one, “for he shall return no more to see his native land” (Jeremiah 22:10–12).

According to all that his fathers had done. He reigns three months, and the verdict is the old formula. Josiah’s own son, raised in the household of the most thorough reformer in the nation’s history, gets the same sentence as Manasseh.

Pharaoh Neco put him in bonds at Riblah. Riblah, on the Orontes in Syria, was Neco’s headquarters for the campaign; Nebuchadnezzar will use it the same way, and there the last king of Judah will be judged and blinded (25:6–7). The king of Judah is summoned to a foreign camp and does not come home. The tribute, a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold, is far less than Hezekiah once paid Assyria (18:14), but it is the price of a vassal, and it has to be found somewhere (v. 35).

Changed his name to Jehoiakim. Renaming a man is what an owner does (Nebuchadnezzar’s officials will do it to Daniel and his friends in a few years), and a king of Judah given his throne name by a Pharaoh is not a king in any sense David would have recognised.

He came to Egypt and died there. The whole existence of the nation began with God bringing them out of Egypt, and every commandment was framed by it: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). The story is now running backwards, and a son of David dies in the country his people were rescued from.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh, but he taxed the land to give the money according to the command of Pharaoh. He exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, from everyone according to his assessment, to give it to Pharaoh Neco.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoiakim pays Pharaoh by taxing his own people head by head, as Menahem did in Samaria twenty years before Samaria fell.

From everyone according to his assessment. He does not pay the tribute out of the treasury; he assesses the population and collects it from them individually. The last king in this book to raise money that way was Menahem in Samaria, taxing sixty thousand men fifty shekels each to buy an Assyrian guarantee of his own throne (15:20). Judah has reached the stage the north reached twenty years before it fell.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zebidah the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his fathers had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah’s son Jehoiakim reigns eleven years in evil, oppressing the poor to build his palace, and is remembered as the king who burned God’s word where his father had trembled at it.

He reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. This is the king who will have a scroll of Jeremiah’s prophecies read to him, cut it off “with a knife” three or four columns at a time, and throw it “into the fire in the fire pot” until the whole scroll is gone (Jeremiah 36:22–23).

He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. Jeremiah gives the content of the formula. While the country was being taxed for Pharaoh, Jehoiakim was building himself a palace panelled in cedar with forced labour: “Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness … who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing” (Jeremiah 22:13). And he sets him beside his father: “Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? … He judged the cause of the poor and needy … Is not this to know me? declares the LORD” (22:15–16).

Father and son. Josiah heard a book read aloud and tore his clothes. His son heard a book read aloud and cut it to pieces. Godliness is not inherited; each generation must hear the word for itself.

23.theology:
It starts with reading (vv. 1-3). Not a policy or a demolition order, but the whole population summoned and the book read aloud by the king.

Three hundred years of nobody's business (v. 13). Seven commended kings left Solomon's shrines standing, and the writer names their builder three centuries after his death. What a great man puts up at the end of his life can stand for generations, and it usually stands because nobody can bear to be the one who pulls it down.

Removed from office, not from bread (v. 9). The priests of the high places never serve at the altar again, and they eat unleavened bread among their brothers. Putting a man out of office is one thing and punishing him is another, and Josiah knows the difference.

Gehenna (v. 10). When the Lord Jesus speaks of hell, the word is Gehenna (Matt. 5:22), the Valley of Hinnom where Topheth stood. Hell is named after a place where God's own people burned their children: the word carries the weight of what sin did there.

Named three centuries early (vv. 15-18). The word spoken against Jeroboam's altar named Josiah by name (1 Kgs. 13:2), and it was kept to the letter; even the old liar's bones are spared because they lie beside the honest man's.

The commendation in borrowed words (v. 25). Josiah is praised in the words of the Shema (Deut. 6:5), very likely a sentence he first heard only months earlier.

Still (v. 26). The reform was total at the top and never reached the hearts of the people (Jer. 3:10), and Jeremiah's answer was a promise no king could keep for Judah: a new covenant, with the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34), which Hebrews says Christ has brought (Hebrews 8:6–13). And the results of sin outlast the sin: the man Manasseh was pardoned and the country he made was not un-made.

Peace, as promised (v. 30). A violent death at thirty-nine, and still the promise held: he was spared the sight of the end.
23.examples:
Then: A king clearing tombs on a hillside in a foreign province stopped, asked what one monument was, and was told by the local men that it belonged to a prophet who had stood on that spot three hundred years earlier and said his name.

Now: Three things. First, Solomon's shrines lasted three centuries because pulling down what a revered man built is the job nobody wants. Ask what is standing in your church or your family for no better reason than that it was put there by somebody nobody will contradict. Second, verse 9. Josiah put men permanently out of office and left their bread alone, and the difference between reform and revenge is usually visible in exactly that detail. Third, verses 25 and 26 together. The most complete obedience in the book did not avert the consequence, and it was still right, and God said so in the strongest words he uses about anybody. If you are doing what is right in a situation it will not repair, you have not made a mistake. Nor does your standing rest on how well you do it: the reform that never reached the heart is answered by the new covenant, in which Christ's obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19) and the Spirit writes the law within (Ezekiel 36:27).

keyVerse.quote: Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might, according to all the Law of Moses, nor did any like him arise after him. Still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great wrath, by which his anger was kindled against Judah, because of all the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked him.
keyVerse.note: The highest praise in Kings and its hardest word stand side by side, and neither cancels the other. Josiah’s obedience was real and God honoured it, but no king’s reform could change his people’s hearts or turn back a judgment earned over generations; that needed the new covenant Christ would bring.

23.reflection:
Josiah’s reform began with the whole nation hearing God’s word read aloud (vv. 1–3). What place does hearing Scripture together have in your church and home, and what changes when it comes first rather than last?

Solomon’s shrines stood for three hundred years because no one wanted to pull down what he had built (v. 13). What stands in your life, family or church mainly because someone you respect put it there? How do you tell loyalty from idolatry?

Josiah removed the priests of the high places from office but made sure they still had bread (v. 9). What does that teach about the difference between reform and revenge, in church discipline or in our own relationships?

The best reform in Israel’s history did not reach the people’s hearts (v. 26; Jeremiah 3:10). How do Jeremiah 31:33 and the work of Christ answer that problem, and how can we tell outward conformity from real change in ourselves?

24.title: Jerusalem Taken; The First Exile
24.text: <sup>1</sup>In his days, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant for three years. Then he turned and rebelled against him.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD sent against him bands of the Chaldeans and bands of the Syrians and bands of the Moabites and bands of the Ammonites, and sent them against Judah to destroy it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servants the prophets.<sup>3</sup>Surely this came upon Judah at the command of the LORD, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh, according to all that he had done,<sup>4</sup>and also for the innocent blood that he had shed. For he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD would not pardon.<sup>5</sup>Now the rest of the deeds of Jehoiakim and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>6</sup>So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place.<sup>7</sup>And the king of Egypt did not come again out of his land, for the king of Babylon had taken all that belonged to the king of Egypt from the Brook of Egypt to the river Euphrates.<sup>8</sup>Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Nehushta the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father had done.<sup>10</sup>At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up to Jerusalem, and the city was besieged.<sup>11</sup>And Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city while his servants were besieging it,<sup>12</sup>and Jehoiachin the king of Judah gave himself up to the king of Babylon, himself and his mother and his servants and his officials and his palace officials. The king of Babylon took him prisoner in the eighth year of his reign<sup>13</sup>and carried off all the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house, and cut in pieces all the vessels of gold in the temple of the LORD, which Solomon king of Israel had made, as the LORD had foretold.<sup>14</sup>He carried away all Jerusalem and all the officials and all the mighty men of valor, 10,000 captives, and all the craftsmen and the smiths. None remained, except the poorest people of the land.<sup>15</sup>And he carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon. The king's mother, the king's wives, his officials, and the chief men of the land he took into captivity from Jerusalem to Babylon.<sup>16</sup>And the king of Babylon brought captive to Babylon all the men of valor, 7,000, and the craftsmen and the metal workers, 1,000, all of them strong and fit for war.<sup>17</sup>And the king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah.<sup>18</sup>Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.<sup>19</sup>And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.<sup>20</sup>For because of the anger of the LORD it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.
24.overview:
Where we are. Josiah has died at Megiddo, and Egypt has deposed one of his sons and installed another, Jehoiakim, who taxes his people to pay Pharaoh and does evil (23:29–37). Now Babylon replaces Egypt as Judah’s master, and the sentence announced in 21:10–15 and 23:26–27 begins to fall.

The message. God’s word of judgment, long delayed, is carried out exactly, and he is the one who carries it out: raiders, siege and exile come “at the command of the LORD”. Innocent blood left a debt the nation could not pay, and the LORD would not pardon it. Yet even in the first exile God keeps hold of his purposes: David’s heir goes to Babylon alive, and the free choices of kings and emperors serve his plan.

Why it was said. The exiles of 597 BC, among them Jehoiachin and the young priest Ezekiel, needed to know that their deportation was neither chance nor Babylon’s victory over the LORD, but his own word kept, and that a God who keeps his threats will also keep his promises (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Jehoiakim serves Nebuchadnezzar three years and rebels, and God sends raiding bands; the writer names the cause, Manasseh’s sins and the innocent blood he shed, which the LORD would not pardon; and Egypt, Judah’s false hope, is finished (vv. 1–7). Jehoiachin reigns three months, surrenders, and is taken to Babylon with the temple treasures, Solomon’s gold cut up as Isaiah foretold, and ten thousand leaders and craftsmen, leaving the poorest (vv. 8–17). Zedekiah, installed and renamed by Babylon, does evil and rebels, and God casts Judah out of his presence (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. First by the need it exposes. The law said that “no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it” (Numbers 35:33), and Judah had no way to pay; only the blood of the innocent Christ, which “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24), can settle such a debt for the guilty. Then by promise. The line of David goes into exile but not out of existence: Matthew traces Jesus through Jechoniah “after the deportation to Babylon” (Matthew 1:12). And as Babylon gave a puppet the name Zedekiah, “the LORD is righteous”, Jeremiah promised a true Branch of David whose name would be “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6), the name Christ has made good for his people.

For us. God’s patience is long but not endless, and his word does not fail. If you are forgiven and still living with sin’s consequences, those consequences describe your situation, not your standing with God, which rests on Christ’s blood. Do not lean on the Egypts of this world, which always break. And never excuse your choices by God’s sovereignty: Zedekiah’s rebellion fulfilled God’s purpose and was still his own sin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The LORD Would Not Pardon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment arrives as God said it would, and the writer names its deepest cause. Jehoiakim submits to Nebuchadnezzar for three years and then rebels (v. 1), and the LORD himself sends raiding bands of Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah, as his prophets had warned (v. 2). The cause is stated plainly: the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the LORD would not pardon (vv. 3–4). Jehoiakim dies and his son succeeds him (vv. 5–6), and Egypt, the reed Judah kept leaning on, never comes out of its land again (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: God's warnings are not empty. What he said about Samaria in chapter 17 he meant for Judah too, and the time between the warning and the act was mercy, not forgetfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice that the innocent blood is given a clause of its own, separate from the idolatry. God does not forget the people a society treats as disposable.

verseByVerse.quote: In his days, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant for three years. Then he turned and rebelled against him. And the LORD sent against him bands of the Chaldeans and bands of the Syrians and bands of the Moabites and bands of the Ammonites, and sent them against Judah to destroy it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servants the prophets. Surely this came upon Judah at the command of the LORD, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh, according to all that he had done, and also for the innocent blood that he had shed. For he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD would not pardon. Now the rest of the deeds of Jehoiakim and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place. And the king of Egypt did not come again out of his land, for the king of Babylon had taken all that belonged to the king of Egypt from the Brook of Egypt to the river Euphrates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s downfall begins at the LORD’s own command: he sends raiders against a rebellious king, and the writer names the deepest cause, the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the LORD would not pardon. Egypt, the power Judah leaned on, is finished.

Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up. The world has changed hands. Jehoiakim was put on the throne by Pharaoh Neco, but Babylon has destroyed Egypt’s army at Carchemish on the Euphrates (605 BC), and every small state between the two simply changed masters. Judah’s overlord is now Nebuchadnezzar.

Then he turned and rebelled against him. Jehoiakim pays tribute for three years and then rebels, as Hezekiah did against Assyria and Hoshea in Samaria. The Babylonian Chronicle explains the timing: in 601 BC Nebuchadnezzar fought Egypt near its border, both sides suffered heavy losses, and he spent the next year at home rebuilding his chariot forces. To a king in Jerusalem it probably looked as if Egypt was back, and the rebellion was a bet on that.

Bands of the Chaldeans. What comes is not an army but bands: raiding parties from four peoples, crossing the borders year after year, a slower and more grinding thing than a siege. Moab and Ammon had old grudges and needed no prompting, yet the writer says twice in one verse that the LORD sent them, “according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servants the prophets”.

To remove them out of his sight. The reader has met the phrase in chapter 17, about the northern kingdom: “the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them out of his sight” (17:18). In the middle of that chapter one sentence was aimed at Jerusalem: “Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God” (17:19). At the end of Josiah’s reign came the announcement (23:27). Here it begins to happen.

And the LORD would not pardon. This is the hardest sentence in these two books, and it does not mean what a frightened reader will take it to mean. The man whose sins are named here was pardoned. Chronicles records that Manasseh, taken to Babylon in chains, “humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers” and prayed, and “God was moved by his entreaty” and brought him home (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). What was not cancelled was the consequence for the nation, as this book has now said three times in three chapters. If you are pardoned and still living in the wreckage, this verse describes your situation, not your standing with God.

And also for the innocent blood. The blood gets a clause to itself, and the refusal to pardon is attached to it. Moses had written down why. Bloodshed does something to a land that other sins do not: “you shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it” (Numbers 35:33). It is the principle that goes back to the first murder: “The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). Manasseh filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and then died peacefully in his own garden. The blood that polluted the land was never answered by the man who shed it, and Moses said there is no other way to settle that account.

Blood that speaks a better word. Exactly here the New Testament says something staggering, and it needs saying carefully rather than quickly. There is one place in Scripture where innocent blood cries from the ground and is answered by better blood: we have come, Hebrews says, “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for justice and got it. The blood of Jesus, shed by the innocent for the guilty, pleads for mercy and obtains it. Your standing with God rests on that blood, not on how well you repair the damage.

Jehoiakim slept with his fathers. Kings closes his reign with the usual words, and that needs a note, because Jeremiah, whose scroll this king burned, had said something very different: “With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 22:19). The writer uses the phrase he uses for every king; it means he died, not that he was honoured, and it leaves the manner of his death and burial to Jeremiah. The two do not contradict each other. Kings simply says no more.

The king of Egypt did not come again out of his land. Verse 7 marks the end of Egypt as a power. Think of everything in this book that leaned on that country. Hoshea sent to Egypt and lost Samaria for it. The Rabshakeh called Egypt “that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it” (18:21), and he was telling the truth. Now everything Egypt held, from the Brook of Egypt on the Sinai border to the Euphrates, belongs to Babylon. There is no one left for Judah to lean on but God, which had been the real position all along.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — None Remained, Except the Poorest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first exile strips Jerusalem of its king, its treasures and its leaders, just as God had foretold. Jehoiachin, eighteen, reigns three months and does evil (vv. 8–9). When Nebuchadnezzar besieges the city, he gives himself up with his mother and his court (vv. 10–12). The temple and palace treasures are carried off and Solomon’s gold vessels cut in pieces, as the LORD had told Hezekiah a century before (v. 13). Ten thousand officials, soldiers and craftsmen go to Babylon, Ezekiel among them, leaving only the poorest of the land (vv. 14–16). Nebuchadnezzar puts Jehoiachin’s uncle Mattaniah on the throne and renames him Zedekiah (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: What one generation shrugs off, another pays for. Hezekiah was content that the loss would not fall in his days; it fell on his descendants, who had no say in it.
verseByVerse.examples: God's purposes can run through defeat. The young king who gave himself up is the one through whom the line of David survives.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Nehushta the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father had done. At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up to Jerusalem, and the city was besieged. And Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city while his servants were besieging it, and Jehoiachin the king of Judah gave himself up to the king of Babylon, himself and his mother and his servants and his officials and his palace officials. The king of Babylon took him prisoner in the eighth year of his reign and carried off all the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house, and cut in pieces all the vessels of gold in the temple of the LORD, which Solomon king of Israel had made, as the LORD had foretold. He carried away all Jerusalem and all the officials and all the mighty men of valor, 10,000 captives, and all the craftsmen and the smiths. None remained, except the poorest people of the land. And he carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon. The king's mother, the king's wives, his officials, and the chief men of the land he took into captivity from Jerusalem to Babylon. And the king of Babylon brought captive to Babylon all the men of valor, 7,000, and the craftsmen and the metal workers, 1,000, all of them strong and fit for war. And the king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoiachin surrenders after three months, and Nebuchadnezzar carries him, the temple treasures and Jerusalem’s leaders and craftsmen to Babylon, exactly as God had warned Hezekiah; only the poorest are left, under a king Babylon has chosen and renamed.

He reigned three months in Jerusalem. Jehoiachin is eighteen, reigns three months, and receives the usual verdict. Remember his name: the last four verses of this book belong to him. His mother is named, as the mothers of Judah’s kings always are, and Jeremiah addressed the two of them together, most likely in those three months: “Say to the king and the queen mother: ‘Take a lowly seat, for your beautiful crown has come down from your head’” (Jeremiah 13:18).

Jehoiachin the king of Judah gave himself up. With the greatest army in the world outside the walls, he walks out of the gate with his mother and his household and surrenders. It costs him his throne, his country and thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison, and it is the reason he is alive at the end of this book, whose last scene is his. His uncle Zedekiah will choose resistance eleven years later and watch his own sons killed before they put out his eyes.

Which Solomon king of Israel had made. Two clauses in verse 13 do a great deal of work. The reader of these books watched these vessels being made, the golden altar, the table, the lampstands, the cups and snuffers and basins, itemised over most of a chapter (1 Kings 7:48–50). Solomon’s gold is being cut up for transport.

As the LORD had foretold. The second clause points to the day Hezekiah showed the Babylonian envoys everything, and Isaiah told him: “Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left” (20:17). Hezekiah called the word good, “for he thought, ‘Why not, if there will be peace and security in my days?’” (20:19). There was peace in his days. The king now led away is his great-great-great-grandson. The cost of a comfortable peace is often paid by those who come after, who had no say in it.

Except the poorest people of the land. The deportation is selective, and the selection is deliberate. They take the administration, the army and everybody who knows how to make a weapon. What is left is “the poorest people of the land”, who cannot organise a rebellion and have every reason to keep farming.

Ezekiel among the captives. It is competent imperial policy, and it is also the beginning of something nobody in that column could have seen. Among the ten thousand walking east is a priest of about twenty-five named Ezekiel, who will date his whole book from this deportation (“the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin”, Ezekiel 1:2) and who will see the glory of God leave that temple and come back again. Daniel had gone in an earlier group. The exile emptied Jerusalem of everybody who could do anything; it also produced one of the greatest books in the Old Testament, written by a man who was in these verses.

Changed his name to Zedekiah. Another king of Judah is renamed by a foreigner, the second in two chapters (Neco renamed Eliakim, 23:34). Renaming a man is what an owner does, as had already been done to four young Judeans in Babylon, given the names Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego (Daniel 1:7). Nebuchadnezzar chose Zedekiah, “the LORD is righteous”, a perfectly good Hebrew name, picked by a Babylonian, for a puppet. Jeremiah looked at the wreck of the monarchy and gave the coming king a name of God’s own choosing: “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6). It is the name of the righteous Branch from David’s line, and the New Testament says Christ has become exactly that for us, “righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

The exiled line. Jeremiah said of this king, whom he calls Coniah, “Write this man down as childless … for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David” (Jeremiah 22:30). Yet Matthew’s genealogy of Jesus runs through him, “after the deportation to Babylon” (Matthew 1:12). Some readers see here why Jesus was Joseph’s legal heir but not his physical son; others note that God later spoke of Jehoiachin’s grandson Zerubbabel as his chosen “signet ring” (Haggai 2:23; compare Jeremiah 22:24), reversing the sentence in mercy. Either way the line went into exile, not out of existence, and the promise to David passed through the prison in Babylon to Christ.

The numbers compared. Jehoiachin was eighteen; most Hebrew copies of 2 Chronicles 36:9 read eight, most likely a copying slip, which the ESV corrects to eighteen in line with this verse. The numbers of captives (vv. 14, 16; Jeremiah 52:28) differ because they count different groups: all captives, the fighting men and craftsmen, and those from Judah itself.
verseByVerse.note: This first great deportation is dated to 597 BC.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–20 — He Cast Them Out From His Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last king of Judah makes his own choice, and through it God carries out his judgment. Zedekiah, a son of Josiah, is twenty-one and reigns eleven years, doing evil like his brother Jehoiakim (vv. 18–19). The final verse sets the two causes side by side without smoothing them: because of the anger of the LORD, Judah was cast out from his presence; and Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon (v. 20). God’s purpose and the king’s free, guilty decision meet in one sentence, and the next chapter shows where they lead.
verseByVerse.theology: God's sovereignty never makes a man a puppet. Zedekiah chose freely, against clear warnings, and remained answerable for what he chose.
verseByVerse.examples: Godly parents cannot give their children faith; only God can. That is a sorrow to bring to him in prayer, not a verdict on the parent.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done. For because of the anger of the LORD it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah, another son of Josiah, repeats his brother’s evil and rebels against Babylon by his own free choice, and through that choice God carries out his anger and casts Judah out of his presence. The writer holds both truths in one verse and does not soften either.

Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. The mother’s name has appeared before: she is the mother of Jehoahaz, who reigned three months and died in Egypt (23:31). So the last kings of Judah are Josiah’s sons and grandson: Jehoahaz and Zedekiah by one mother, Jehoiakim by another, and Jehoiachin the grandson. Every one of the four came out of the household of the man who turned to the LORD with all his heart and soul and might, and every one gets the same verdict.

For Christian parents. That is not an argument against the reform or against Josiah. It is the plain report of a household, and any Christian parent who has watched it happen in miniature will recognise it. Such a parent may also remember that the last word on Josiah’s line was not written by these sons: the promise went on through them to Jehoiachin and, in the end, to Christ (Matthew 1:11–16).

Because of the anger of the LORD. Verse 20 puts the cause first: because of the anger of the LORD he cast them out from his presence. Then the act: Zedekiah rebelled. The rebellion is Zedekiah’s own. He decided it against the explicit and repeated advice of Jeremiah, who told him to submit to Babylon and live; he broke an oath sworn in God’s name to do it; and Ezekiel says God held him to that oath (Ezekiel 17:15–19). Nobody made him. And the writer makes that free act the means by which a nation was put out of God’s presence.

God’s purpose through choices. These books have shown from the beginning that God carries out his purpose through acts that look like chance or free choice. An arrow drawn at random found the one gap in Ahab’s armour. A Syrian army heard chariots that did not exist and ran. A free, explicable political decision by a young king is the door through which the exile comes. Neither truth, God’s purpose or Zedekiah’s responsibility, is softened to make room for the other, and the writer evidently did not think they needed reconciling.

Brought near. To be cast out from God’s presence is what the exile meant, and it is the Bible’s picture of what sin finally deserves. The gospel answers it at the cost of Christ: “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

If God is in charge, am I a puppet? Many people picture sovereignty and freedom as a seesaw: the more God decides, the less we do. Either he runs the world and we are puppets, or we are truly free and he watches from the side. Zedekiah fits neither picture. His rebellion was entirely his own, chosen against advice and sealed by breaking his oath; and it was the means by which God carried out his purpose. Scripture never solves this by shrinking one side. Think of the difference between a character in a novel and its author. The author is not one more character competing for room on the page; he works on another level altogether, and it is his writing that makes the characters real enough to choose. The plainest case is the worst act in history. Peter told the crowd in Jerusalem that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and in the same breath, “you crucified and killed” him “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). Both were wholly true, and the free wickedness of men became the salvation of the world.

24.theology:
Out of his sight (v. 3). Warned in chapter 17, announced at 23:27, and executed here.

The LORD would not pardon (v. 4). It does not mean Manasseh could not be forgiven; he was (2 Chron. 33:12-13). It means the consequence for the nation was not cancelled. Forgiveness is immediate and complete; consequences run on their own timetable and often outlive everybody involved. The innocent blood Manasseh never answered for (Num. 35:33) points to the only blood that can settle such an account, shed by the innocent for the guilty.

The reed finally breaks (v. 7). Isaiah had warned for years against leaning on Egypt. Now there is nobody for Judah to lean on but God, which had been the real position all along.

As the LORD had foretold (v. 13). Isaiah's word to Hezekiah (20:17) is kept a century later, to the letter.

Who was taken (vv. 14-16). Competent imperial policy emptied Jerusalem of everybody who could do anything, and God used it to send Ezekiel among the exiles.

Both halves, unreconciled (v. 20). God's anger is the cause and Zedekiah's free rebellion is the door through which the exile came. These books have said the same about a random arrow and a rumour in a camp, and never tried to smooth it out.
24.examples:
Then: An eighteen-year-old three months into his reign walked out of the gate of Jerusalem with his mother and his household and handed himself to the man besieging him, and spent the next thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison.

Now: Three things. First, verse 4, which frightens people who read it about themselves. The man whose sin is named in it was personally forgiven; what was not cancelled was the wreckage. If you are pardoned and still living in the consequences, this verse describes your situation, not your standing with God, which rests on the blood that speaks a better word and not on how well you repair things. Second, Hezekiah's peace and security in my days, paid for five generations later. The cost of a comfortable peace is paid by those who come after, who had no say in it. Third, the surrender. Jehoiachin yielded and got thirty-seven years in a cell, and his uncle chose to fight and watched his sons die before he was blinded. The last four verses of this book are about the man who yielded.

keyVerse.quote: Surely this came upon Judah at the command of the LORD, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh, according to all that he had done, and also for the innocent blood that he had shed. For he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD would not pardon.
keyVerse.note: Here the writer names the cause of the exile: not Babylon’s power but the LORD’s command, and not one bad decision but generations of sin and innocent blood that the nation never answered for. It shows the debt that only the blood of Christ, shed by the innocent for the guilty, could settle.

24.reflection:
The writer says the LORD sent the raiders and that the exile came “at the command of the LORD” (vv. 2–3). Why might that have been a comfort as well as a warning to the exiles in Babylon? How does it help us to see God’s hand in hard events?

Manasseh was personally forgiven, yet the nation was not spared the consequences of his sin (vv. 3–4; 2 Chronicles 33:12–13). How would you help a Christian who confuses the lasting consequences of past sin with God’s refusal to forgive them?

Hezekiah was content with “peace and security in my days”, and his descendants paid the price (v. 13; 20:17–19). What comfortable choices might we make now whose cost will fall on our children or on the next generation in the church?

Zedekiah’s rebellion was his own free and guilty choice, and also the means by which God carried out his purpose (v. 20). How does Acts 2:23 help us hold God’s sovereignty and human responsibility together, and why does it matter that we do not drop either?

25.title: The Fall of Jerusalem
25.text: <sup>1</sup>And in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem and laid siege to it. And they built siegeworks all around it.<sup>2</sup>So the city was besieged till the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.<sup>3</sup>On the ninth day of the fourth month the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land.<sup>4</sup>Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, by the king's garden, and the Chaldeans were around the city. And they went in the direction of the Arabah.<sup>5</sup>But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook him in the plains of Jericho, and all his army was scattered from him.<sup>6</sup>Then they captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and they passed sentence on him.<sup>7</sup>They slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains and took him to Babylon.<sup>8</sup>In the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month—that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan, the captain of the bodyguard, a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>And he burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down.<sup>10</sup>And all the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down the walls around Jerusalem.<sup>11</sup>And the rest of the people who were left in the city and the deserters who had deserted to the king of Babylon, together with the rest of the multitude, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile.<sup>12</sup>But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen.<sup>13</sup>And the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD, and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the house of the LORD, the Chaldeans broke in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon.<sup>14</sup>And they took away the pots and the shovels and the snuffers and the dishes for incense and all the vessels of bronze used in the temple service,<sup>15</sup>the fire pans also and the bowls. What was of gold the captain of the guard took away as gold, and what was of silver, as silver.<sup>16</sup>As for the two pillars, the one sea, and the stands that Solomon had made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these vessels was beyond weight.<sup>17</sup>The height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits, and on it was a capital of bronze. The height of the capital was three cubits. A latticework and pomegranates, all of bronze, were all around the capital. And the second pillar had the same, with the latticework.<sup>18</sup>And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold;<sup>19</sup>and from the city he took an officer who had been in command of the men of war, and five men of the king's council who were found in the city; and the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the city.<sup>20</sup>And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.<sup>21</sup>And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was taken into exile out of its land.<sup>22</sup>And over the people who remained in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, he appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, governor.<sup>23</sup>Now when all the captains and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah governor, they came with their men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, namely, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of the Maacathite.<sup>24</sup>And Gedaliah swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid because of the Chaldean officials.
