Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you."<sup>25</sup>But in the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, came with ten men and struck down Gedaliah and put him to death along with the Jews and the Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah.<sup>26</sup>Then all the people, both small and great, and the captains of the forces arose and went to Egypt, for they were afraid of the Chaldeans.<sup>27</sup>And in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison.<sup>28</sup>And he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon.<sup>29</sup>So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table,<sup>30</sup>and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, according to his daily needs, as long as he lived.
25.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of Kings. Zedekiah, Babylon’s puppet, has rebelled (24:20), and Nebuchadnezzar returns to carry out the judgment announced since Manasseh’s day (21:10–15; 23:26–27).

The message. Every word God spoke comes true, his threats as surely as his promises. Judah goes into exile exactly as the prophets warned. Yet the book does not end in the ashes: God had promised David a lamp, and in the last scene David’s heir is alive, freed and fed at a king’s table. The judgment is complete; the promise is not cancelled.

Why it was said. The book was finished in exile, for people who had lost land, temple and king (see the introduction). They needed to know why it had happened, that it was the LORD’s doing and not Babylon’s triumph over him, and whether God had anything left to say to them. The last paragraph answers that final question.

How the chapter makes its case. After siege, famine and breach, the king runs, is caught in the plains of Jericho, and is blinded at Riblah after watching his sons killed (vv. 1–7). Temple and city are burned, Solomon’s bronze carried off and the leaders executed: “So Judah was taken into exile out of its land” (vv. 8–21). Gedaliah tries to keep the survivors alive in the land, is murdered by a man of the royal family, and the people flee back to Egypt (vv. 22–26). Then, thirty-seven years on, Jehoiachin is released and given a daily allowance at the king’s table for life (vv. 27–30).

Where it leads. Chiefly by promise. The lamp promised to David (8:19) is still burning in Babylon, and Matthew runs the line of Christ through this very man, Jechoniah, “after the deportation to Babylon” (Matthew 1:12). By the need it exposes, too: David’s last heirs save themselves and kill the one shepherd left, and Israel needed a King who would give himself for his people rather than run. And by pattern: the glory that left the temple returned in the Word made flesh (John 1:14), and a son of David fed by grace at a table he had no claim on pictures every sinner Christ brings to his own table.

For us. God’s warnings are as true as his promises. When the visible signs of his favour are gone, his word is not, and grace often comes as Jehoiachin received it, enough for today, every day. The lamp that would not go out in Babylon became the light of the world, and those who belong to him will eat at his table for ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — They Overtook Him in the Plains of Jericho
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The end comes as the prophets said it would, and the king who should have shepherded his people saves himself and loses everything. Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem on a day later kept as a fast (vv. 1–2), and the famine leaves no food for the people (v. 3). When the wall is breached, the soldiers and the king slip out by night and run for the Jordan, leaving the city behind them (v. 4). He is overtaken in the plains of Jericho, where Israel first entered the land, deserted by his own army (v. 5). At Riblah his sons are killed before his eyes, and he is blinded and taken in chains to Babylon (vv. 6–7), fulfilling two prophecies no one could have fitted together beforehand.
verseByVerse.theology: The writer does not look away from suffering, and neither should we. God's judgment is real, and so is the cruelty of the men who carried it out, for which God held Babylon to account.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone in a long siege of their own: the lines about mercies new every morning (Lam. 3:22-23) were written in the ruins of this city, while the grief was still fresh.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem and laid siege to it. And they built siegeworks all around it. So the city was besieged till the eleventh year of King Zedekiah. On the ninth day of the fourth month the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land. Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, by the king's garden, and the Chaldeans were around the city. And they went in the direction of the Arabah. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook him in the plains of Jericho, and all his army was scattered from him. Then they captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and they passed sentence on him. They slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains and took him to Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The siege ends as the prophets had warned: famine, a breach in the wall, and a king who runs from his people, is caught where Israel first entered the land, and is blinded after watching his sons die. Two prophecies about him that seemed to contradict each other both come true.

On the tenth day of the month. This writer seldom dates anything to the day; he gives reigns in years and events in seasons. Here he puts down the day Nebuchadnezzar arrived, the way a man does when he was there or writes for people who were, and that day was still being kept as a fast decades later (Zechariah 8:19).

So the city was besieged. From the tenth month of the ninth year to the fourth month of the eleventh, with siegeworks all round it: about eighteen months, or nearer thirty, depending on how the regnal years are counted.

The famine was so severe in the city. The reader has already seen what such a famine contains, at Samaria: a donkey’s head sold for eighty shekels, and two mothers who had agreed to eat their sons (6:25–29). Lamentations, written by someone who watched these months, says what this verse leaves unsaid: infants’ tongues sticking to the roofs of their mouths for thirst, children begging for bread with no one to give it, and “the hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children” (Lamentations 4:4, 10).

A breach was made in the city. When the wall goes, the army goes with it. They break out by night through a gate by the king’s garden, at the southern end of the city, and head east down towards the Jordan valley. The king goes with them, and the city they leave is full of people who cannot run.

In the plains of Jericho. This is where the nation entered the land. The Jordan’s waters stood up in a heap to let them cross, twelve stones were set up at Gilgal so that children would ask what they meant, and Jericho was the first city God gave them (Joshua 3–6). Centuries later the last king of David’s line is run down on the same flat ground, going the other way, and all his army was scattered from him: in the end nobody stands with him at all.

To the king of Babylon at Riblah. Riblah, far to the north in Syria, has been in this book before: there Pharaoh Neco put Jehoahaz in chains twenty-three years earlier (23:33). The same town, the same procedure, a different empire, and this is the last of Judah’s kings to be sentenced there.

They slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes. Do not look away from verse 7, because the writer does not. They killed his sons in front of him, and then they blinded him. The order is the cruelty: the last thing he ever saw, the sight he would carry for the rest of his life in the dark, was chosen for him deliberately. He was thirty-two years old.

Put out the eyes of Zedekiah. Two prophecies had been given about this man, and they looked like a flat contradiction. Jeremiah told him to his face, “You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face” (Jeremiah 34:3). Ezekiel, in Babylon, said, “I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans, yet he shall not see it, and he shall die there” (Ezekiel 12:13). Before the event anyone would have said one prophet was wrong. He met Nebuchadnezzar face to face at Riblah, was blinded on the spot, and was led to a city he lived and died in and never saw. Only the event showed how both were exactly true, which is worth remembering whenever two things in Scripture seem not to fit.

A king who ran, and a King who stayed. The last king of David’s house fled by night to save himself, and could save neither his people nor his own sons. Israel needed another kind of king. When they came for the Son of David by night, he did not run: he stepped forward and said, “let these men go” (John 18:8), and was bound and led away to be sentenced in his people’s place. “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

New every morning. Lamentations, written in the same ashes, also holds the lines the grieving have leaned on ever since: “his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23). They were not written after the suffering was over, but in the middle of it.

Did God approve of Babylon’s cruelty? No. Babylon was the instrument of his judgment, but the cruelty was Babylon’s own, and God said through Jeremiah that he would repay Babylon “for all the evil that they have done in Zion” (Jeremiah 51:24).

Uncertain wording. “The gate between the two walls” cannot now be located with certainty. It was evidently at the south-eastern corner of the city, near the king’s garden and the pools, where Isaiah also mentions “a reservoir between the two walls” (Isaiah 22:11); the walls may be those of the old City of David and the western hill, or an inner and an outer wall. The route is clear even if the gate is not.

Textual note. In the Hebrew of verse 3 the month is not named (it reads “on the ninth day of the month”); translations supply “the fourth month” from Jeremiah 39:2 and 52:6, where the date is given in full.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem fell in 586 BC (some date it 587). The date in v. 1 was later kept as a fast (Zech. 8:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–21 — Every Great House He Burned Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is not spared when his people have despised its God, and the account of the kingdom is closed. A month after the breach Nebuzaradan burns the house of the LORD, the palace and every great house, and the walls come down (vv. 8–10). The rest of the people are deported, and only the poorest are left to tend the vines and fields (vv. 11–12). The bronze cast for Solomon’s temple is broken up and carried off, itemised as carefully as 1 Kings 7 recorded its making (vv. 13–17). The priests, officers and leading citizens are executed at Riblah, and the writer closes Judah’s story with the sentence he used for Israel’s: “So Judah was taken into exile out of its land” (vv. 18–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing made for God is safe from judgment once his people have turned it into a lucky charm. The temple's treasures could not protect a nation that trusted them instead of him.
verseByVerse.examples: The loss of the building teaches what Jesus later said plainly: God seeks worshippers in spirit and truth, and his presence was never confined to a building.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month—that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan, the captain of the bodyguard, a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem. And he burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down. And all the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down the walls around Jerusalem. And the rest of the people who were left in the city and the deserters who had deserted to the king of Babylon, together with the rest of the multitude, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile. But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen. And the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD, and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the house of the LORD, the Chaldeans broke in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon. And they took away the pots and the shovels and the snuffers and the dishes for incense and all the vessels of bronze used in the temple service, the fire pans also and the bowls. What was of gold the captain of the guard took away as gold, and what was of silver, as silver. As for the two pillars, the one sea, and the stands that Solomon had made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these vessels was beyond weight. The height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits, and on it was a capital of bronze. The height of the capital was three cubits. A latticework and pomegranates, all of bronze, were all around the capital. And the second pillar had the same, with the latticework. And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold; and from the city he took an officer who had been in command of the men of war, and five men of the king's council who were found in the city; and the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the city. And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was taken into exile out of its land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A month after the breach the house of the LORD is burned, the city destroyed, Solomon’s bronze broken up for scrap and the leaders executed, and Judah goes into exile as Israel did. The writer closes the account of the kingdom with the same sentence he used for the north.

He burned the house of the LORD. Nearly four centuries earlier Solomon had stood before this house on the day it was finished, spread out his hands to heaven, and asked God to keep his eyes open toward “the place of which you have said, ‘My name shall be there’” (1 Kings 8:29); and the glory of the LORD filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister. Now a Babylonian officer puts a torch to it, and the writer gives it half a verse. He is not being cold: he has spent forty-seven chapters explaining why it would happen, and has nothing left to add.

Broke down the walls around Jerusalem. The walls go too, and they stay down. About a hundred and forty years later a cupbearer in a Persian palace was told, “The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire”, and he sat down and wept (Nehemiah 1:3–4). This is the day it happened.

Some of the poorest of the land. The poorest are left to work, because a province that produces nothing is no use to an empire. It is not meant as mercy, but it is the reason there is anybody left in the land for the next paragraph.

The pillars of bronze. Now the inventory, one of the most deliberate passages in these books. In 1 Kings 7 Hiram of Tyre cast two bronze pillars eighteen cubits high, with capitals, latticework and four hundred pomegranates; a sea of cast metal standing on twelve bronze oxen, its brim like the flower of a lily; ten stands with panels and wheels, carved with lions, oxen and cherubim; and the pots, the shovels and the basins. Every one of those objects is in these verses, being broken up. The writer is closing an account: what was itemised going up is itemised coming down, with the same care, and the gold and silver leave as gold and as silver (v. 15), no longer vessels of the house of the LORD but only metal.

The height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits. He measures the pillars one last time: some twenty-seven feet high, with a capital of four and a half feet and pomegranates all round it. They had names. Solomon called the south pillar Jachin and the north pillar Boaz (1 Kings 7:21), names usually understood to mean he establishes and in him is strength. They stood at the door of that house for nearly four centuries and went to Babylon as scrap metal. The strength had never been in the bronze.

Seraiah the chief priest. The list is the leadership of a nation, from the high priest to the officer of the muster, and they are walked some two hundred miles north to Riblah and executed. Seraiah’s son Jehozadak went into exile (1 Chronicles 6:14–15), and his grandson Joshua would be high priest when the exiles came home (Haggai 1:1).

Sixty men of the people of the land. The people of the land are not anonymous in this book. Three times, when the line of David was most exposed, it was they who acted: after Athaliah (11:18–20), after Amon’s murder (21:24) and after Megiddo (23:30). They seem to have been the landholding citizens of Judah, and three times the promise to David came through them. Now the last of them on this list are put to death.

So Judah was taken into exile out of its land. This is the sentence the whole book has been moving towards since the kingdom split. The account of Samaria’s fall ended, “So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day” (17:23), and in the middle of that chapter the writer had put one line aimed at the south: “Judah also did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God” (17:19). Here he closes the second account exactly as he closed the first.

The glory came back in a person. The rest of the Bible says more than Kings does. Ezekiel, in exile, saw the glory of the LORD leave that house before it burned (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). The next time God’s glory dwelt among his people it came in a person: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14), and he spoke of the temple of his body, which would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21).

When the story of progress breaks. The modern West has lived for two centuries on a story: history is going somewhere, and on the whole it is going up. But the historian Christopher Lasch argued, in The True and Only Heaven, that belief in progress is not the same thing as hope: optimism counts on the trend, while hope can look straight at the wreckage and still trust. If our confidence rests on the line going up, a chapter like this, or a century like the last one, leaves us nothing. The Bible’s confidence rested on a promise, and the promise did not need the building to survive. Christian hope is not optimism about the trend. It is trust in someone who has already been through the fire and come out alive.

Seventh day or tenth? Here the temple is burned in the fifth month on the seventh day, in Jeremiah 52:12 on the tenth. Perhaps the seventh is the day Nebuzaradan arrived and the tenth the day of the burning, or the fire began on the seventh and was finished on the tenth.

Three cubits or five? 1 Kings 7:16 and Jeremiah 52:22 give the capital as five cubits, not three. The figures may measure different parts of it, or a copyist may have slipped; nothing in the meaning turns on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–26 — And They Went to Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even after the judgment there was a way to live, and fear threw it away. Babylon appoints Gedaliah, grandson of the Shaphan who read the Book of the Law to Josiah, as governor of those left in the land (v. 22). The surviving captains come to him at Mizpah (v. 23), and he gives them Jeremiah’s counsel: do not be afraid; live in the land, serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you (v. 24). Within months Ishmael, “of the royal family”, murders him (v. 25), and the whole remnant, small and great, flees to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans (v. 26), undoing the exodus with which their story began.
verseByVerse.theology: Faithfulness often runs quietly in families that never hold power. God noticed this one, and the writer kept its name in the record.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, fear can pass itself off as good sense. The few left in the land had a workable path and a godly governor, and fear still carried them away from it.

verseByVerse.quote: And over the people who remained in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, he appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, governor. Now when all the captains and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah governor, they came with their men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, namely, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of the Maacathite. And Gedaliah swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid because of the Chaldean officials. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you." But in the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, came with ten men and struck down Gedaliah and put him to death along with the Jews and the Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah. Then all the people, both small and great, and the captains of the forces arose and went to Egypt, for they were afraid of the Chaldeans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s governor, from a family faithful through every crisis, offers the survivors a way to live in the land, but a man of David’s own house murders him, and the remnant runs back to Egypt. Fear undoes the exodus with which the nation began.

Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan. The reader of this book has met all three names. Shaphan was the secretary who was handed the rediscovered book, brought Josiah the accounts first and the book second, and read it aloud to the king (22:8–10). Ahikam went to Huldah for Josiah (22:12), and years later, when the priests and prophets said of Jeremiah, “This man deserves the sentence of death” (Jeremiah 26:11), “the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death” (Jeremiah 26:24). Gedaliah is the last man to govern anything in Judah. Three generations of one family stood on the right side of every crisis: the man who read the book, the man who saved the prophet, and the man who tried to hold the remnant together. None of them sat on a throne, and the writer has quietly kept their name in the record.

All the captains and their men. The surviving officers come in from the hills to Mizpah, a few miles north of the ruined city, armed men deciding whether to accept the new arrangement.

Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon. His policy is Jeremiah’s, almost word for word. Through the whole crisis Jeremiah had urged submission: “Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people and live” (Jeremiah 27:12); and he had told the exiles to build houses and seek the welfare of their city (Jeremiah 29:5–7). Gedaliah offers the survivors the same: stay, farm, serve, and it will be well with you. It was the only sane course and the godly one, and it seems to have lasted about two months.

Of the royal family. The writer inserts the words on purpose: the man who murders the last governor of Judah is a descendant of David. Whatever his motives (Jeremiah records that the king of the Ammonites had sent him, Jeremiah 40:14), David’s line, which was meant to shepherd this people, does its last act in this book by killing the one man left who was trying to keep them alive on their own land.

Arose and went to Egypt. The last movement of the people of God in this book is back to Egypt. Nobody deported them. They were the ones left behind, on their own land, under a policy that would have worked, and they were afraid. Every commandment God gave this people was framed by the rescue from that country: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). The whole story ran forward from that door, and here they walk back through it, taking Jeremiah with them against his will (Jeremiah 43:6–7).

The Son who came out of Egypt. Here the nation undoes its exodus, and its royal house strikes down its shepherd. Matthew saw the story begin again in Jesus, taken down to Egypt as a child and brought back, so that the word was fulfilled, “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15). Where Israel went back in fear, the true Son came out and walked the road of obedience; and where a son of David killed the shepherd, the Son of David let himself be struck down for the sheep (Matthew 26:31).

Where the book could end. The book could have stopped here. Everything the writer set out to explain has been explained: why Israel fell, why Judah fell, and how a people that came out of Egypt ended up going back into it. It is a complete and coherent ending, and it is unbearable. But there are four more verses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–30 — He Dined Regularly at the King's Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promise to David outlives the end of the kingdom. The book could have closed with the flight to Egypt, but the writer adds a last scene. In the thirty-seventh year of his exile Jehoiachin, still called “king of Judah”, is freed by the new king of Babylon (v. 27), spoken to kindly and given a seat above the other captive kings (v. 28). He changes out of his prison clothes and eats at the king’s table (v. 29), with an allowance for each day’s needs as long as he lived (v. 30). It is not a restoration, but it is a lamp still burning: David’s line is alive, and the promise is not cancelled.
verseByVerse.theology: God's promises outlast the worst that can be done to his people. Grace in these verses comes unearned, through a pagan king's kindness, and it is enough for each day.
verseByVerse.examples: If your own hope has shrunk to almost nothing, notice how small the light is at the end of Kings, and that it is still alight. God keeps small lamps burning.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison. And he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table, and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, according to his daily needs, as long as he lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirty-seven years into exile, David’s heir is released from prison, spoken to kindly and fed at the king’s table for the rest of his life: not a restoration, but proof that God’s lamp for David has not gone out. The book ends with the promise neither visibly fulfilled nor cancelled.

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile. Jehoiachin was eighteen when he handed himself over; he is fifty-five now. Nebuchadnezzar has died, and in the first year of the new king, Evil-merodach (in Babylonian, Amel-Marduk, “man of Marduk”; the English spelling has nothing to do with “evil”), the prison door opens.

Graciously freed. The Hebrew says he “lifted up the head” of Jehoiachin, the idiom Joseph used when he told Pharaoh’s cupbearer that Pharaoh would bring him out of prison and restore him (Genesis 40:13, 20). Kings ends, as the Joseph story did, with an exile raised from prison to a foreign king’s favour.

Jehoiachin king of Judah. Look at what the writer calls him, twice in one verse, after everything has been lost. There has been no Judah for a generation: no throne, no city wall, no temple. He has been a prisoner for thirty-seven years and is about to be a pensioner. And he is still king of Judah, because that title was never Babylon’s to take away.

He spoke kindly to him. The Hebrew is, he spoke good things to him: the first kind word recorded to this man since he was eighteen. There were other deposed kings kept at the palace in Babylon, as trophies and as insurance, and Jehoiachin is given a seat above them all.

So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. After thirty-seven years he is given something else to wear, and he sits down to dinner. This is not a metaphor but a plain report, the last event narrated in Kings. Babylonian tablets dug up in that city list rations of oil for named foreigners, among them “Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud”, and his sons; they come from earlier in his captivity, but show the arrangement was real.

According to his daily needs, as long as he lived. The last phrase decides how the whole ending reads. It is not a settlement, a restoration or a throne, but an allowance, issued according to what he needed that day, for the rest of his life. The reader has seen that arrangement before. A widow at Zarephath with a handful of flour was not given a granary; she was promised, “The jar of flour shall not be spent, and the jug of oil shall not be empty” (1 Kings 17:14), and day after day found a day’s worth in it. So it was with the manna in the wilderness, and so the Lord Jesus taught us to pray: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).

At the king’s table. There is an older echo too. David once sent for Mephibosheth, the lame grandson of King Saul who had hunted him, and told him, “you shall eat at my table always” (2 Samuel 9:7), for no reason but kindness. The last thing recorded in the history of the kings of Israel and Judah is David’s own heir being fed, daily, at a table he has no claim on, by the generosity of somebody else.

A lamp for David. Why do these four verses end the book? Because God had promised David a lamp. The word turns up three times in these books, and the promise behind it once more, always when it looks least secure. He kept one tribe for Solomon’s son “that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem” (1 Kings 11:36). He kept Abijam on the throne, though “his heart was not wholly true” to the LORD, for David’s sake (1 Kings 15:3–4). He would not destroy Judah under Jehoram, who married Ahab’s daughter and murdered his brothers, “since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (8:19). He defended Jerusalem against Sennacherib “for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David” (19:34).

What a lamp is. A lamp is a small thing: the clay dish with a wick in it that an ordinary household kept burning all night so that the house was never wholly dark. It does not light a room. It refuses to go out. And here it is at the end of the book: no throne, no temple, no city, no country, but one descendant of David, alive, out of prison, in clean clothes, eating.

Not a happy ending. The temple is ash; the people are in Babylon and Egypt; the man at the centre is a pensioner in a foreign palace who will never go home, and the book records his allowance until death, not his restoration. It ends like an unfinished sentence. The writer has spent forty-seven chapters showing that the word of the LORD never once failed: Elijah’s word about the rain and the dogs, Micaiah’s about Ahab’s death, the man of God at Bethel who named Josiah, Isaiah’s about the treasury. God had also said there would always be a lamp, and there the history of the kings stops: the promise not visibly fulfilled and not cancelled, and a light that is very small and has not gone out.

After the deportation to Babylon. Some six hundred years later Matthew wrote the family tree of Jesus Christ in three sets of fourteen generations, and he put its turning point exactly here: “Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel” (Matthew 1:11–12). Jechoniah is Jehoiachin. The man in these four verses stands in the genealogy of Christ, at the lowest point the line ever reached, and the lamp kept burning in Babylon is the line through which the light of the world would come.

A seat at the King’s table. Jehoiachin’s release is also a picture of the gospel. A condemned man with no claim on anyone is brought out of prison, given new clothes and fed at a king’s table. Christ does that for sinners: he brings us out, clothes us in his own righteousness, and calls us to a feast: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). The difference is the King. Jehoiachin was fed by a foreign ruler’s favour for as long as he lived; we are fed by a King who died for us, and his table has no end.

What about Jeremiah 22:30? Jeremiah had pronounced a fearful word over this same king: “Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah” (Jeremiah 22:30). No son of Jehoiachin ever did reign. Yet the legal line of David’s kingship runs through him to Joseph, the husband of Mary and the legal father of Jesus without being his physical father. Many think this is one reason Matthew’s genealogy and Luke’s run by different routes; on that reading a curse on a bloodline cannot touch the one who inherits the title and not the blood. Nor was the curse God’s last word on that family. Jeremiah had said that even if Jehoiachin were the signet ring on God’s hand he would be torn off (Jeremiah 22:24); after the exile God told his grandson Zerubbabel that he would “make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you” (Haggai 2:23). That is how the promise worked all the way through: it was carried by people who had forfeited every right to it, and kept by a God who had bound himself and would not go back on his word.

Where Christians differ. Some, notably the scholar Martin Noth, read these four verses as a bare closing notice: the history ends in judgment, with no hope signalled. Others, following Gerhard von Rad, see a deliberate pointer to the promise to David. Others again think the writer meant mainly that the exiles could live at peace under Babylon, as Jeremiah had urged.

This commentary’s view. The ending is placed on purpose and points to hope. A book that has traced the lamp for David through every crisis, and calls this prisoner “king of Judah” twice, is not closing the file on David’s line; and Matthew confirms the reading by carrying that line through Jehoiachin to Christ (Matthew 1:12).
verseByVerse.note: Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk) succeeded Nebuchadnezzar in 562 BC; the release is usually dated 561 BC.

25.theology:
The plains of Jericho (v. 5). The story of the land ends where it began, run backwards.

Two prophecies that could not both be true (v. 7). Jeremiah's eye to eye and Ezekiel's he shall not see it were both fulfilled, in a way nobody could have worked out beforehand.

The inventory (vv. 13-17). What 1 Kings 7 listed going up is listed coming down: the account is closed.

The same last line (v. 21). So Judah was taken into exile out of its land closes this account exactly as so Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria closed the other (17:23). Two kingdoms, two sets of prophets sent for two hundred years, and one identical last line.

Three generations (v. 22). Shaphan, Ahikam and Gedaliah never sat on a throne and stood on the right side of every crisis; the last of them is murdered by a son of David's house.

Back to Egypt (v. 26). The rescue that began the nation is undone, not by an army but by fear.

Still king of Judah (v. 27). The writer gives him the title twice, after everything else has been lost.

According to his daily needs (v. 30). Like the widow's jar and the manna, grace is given day by day.

The lamp, and the genealogy (vv. 27-30). God promised David a lamp (1 Kgs. 11:36) and kept it for Abijam (1 Kgs. 15:4), for Jehoram (8:19) and over Jerusalem against Sennacherib (19:34). A lamp does not light a room; it refuses to go out. Matthew put the turning point of Christ’s genealogy exactly here (Matt. 1:11-12), and the curse of Jeremiah 22:30 was not God's last word on the line (see the note on vv. 27-30).
25.examples:
Then: A man of fifty-five who had gone into a Babylonian cell at eighteen was brought out, spoken to kindly, given a seat above the other captive kings, handed something else to wear, and sat down to dinner; and the last sentence in the history of Israel's kings is a note about his daily food allowance.

Now: Three things. First, verse 7 and the two prophecies. Two statements that nobody could fit together in advance both turned out to be exactly true. When two things in Scripture will not fit together, the difficulty is real, and so is the possibility that the event which will explain them has not yet come. Second, verse 26. They had their own land, a workable arrangement and a godly governor, and fear took them back to Egypt, the place the whole story began by leaving. Fear will return you to the very thing you were rescued from, and it will feel like prudence; its answer is not braver resolve but remembering who brought you out, and leaning on the Spirit he gives his people, who is not a spirit of fear (2 Timothy 1:7). Third, the last four verses. If you are looking for the promise of God in your own life and finding no throne and no visible fulfilment, this is the note the history of the kings ends on: a man with no kingdom, in clothes somebody gave him, being handed what he needs for today, and the lamp still lit.

keyVerse.quote: So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king’s table, and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, according to his daily needs, as long as he lived.
keyVerse.note: The book could have ended with the temple in ashes and the people fleeing to Egypt; instead its last words are about one man’s daily bread. David’s heir is alive, clothed and fed by grace, the lamp God promised David still burning, and the line that will lead through this man to Christ is not cancelled.

25.reflection:
Jerusalem fell exactly as the prophets had warned for generations (vv. 1–21; 17:13–14). Why do people, then and now, find it so easy to assume God’s warnings will never be carried out? How does the cross show both how serious God’s judgment is and the way of escape from it?

Zedekiah ran from his people by night, and Ishmael, “of the royal family”, murdered the one man trying to keep them alive (vv. 4–5, 25). How does Jesus, the Son of David who “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11), differ from these kings, and what difference does that make to how we trust him?

The survivors had their land and a godly governor, yet fear took them back to Egypt (v. 26). Where might fear be leading you back towards something God once rescued you from, while it feels like good sense?

The book ends with a daily allowance, not a restored throne (vv. 27–30). How does it help to know that God often keeps his promises through grace given one day at a time? Where do you need that grace today?
